en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Moggallāna Pañcaka,
titled *Sāratthavilāsinī*.
The Discourse on the Homage and Other Preliminaries from the Pañcikā-Ṭīkā:
Even for one who merely recollects the wealth of knowledge, [it is beneficial].
Having placed in my heart— filled with joy and reverence—
that King of Dhamma, whose fame is a pure and radiant garland,
and who is the sole cause for bringing forth the jewel of the purification of wisdom.
The *Laddhammahodaya*, the Great Compassionate One (*Mahādaya*) [who is] full of serene confidence (*Sampasāda*), the Reciter (*Japasa*) [as found in the manuscript];
the Three Jewels (*Ratana-dvaya*) whose virtues are honored by Sakka and others (*Sakkādisakkataguṇa*) [as found in the manuscript];
the *Yāpañcikā* [which is] the profound realization born of the Supreme Teacher (*Guruvarappabhavātyagāhā*) [as found in the manuscript].
Therefore, O disciples, let us enter into this with a humble mind.
Victorious here is the sage Moggallāyana of great wisdom,
whose fame, arising from his excellent virtues, is spread everywhere.

Thus, out of fear for the remainder of one's life, and through the application of power that prevents calamities, misfortunes, and injuries, desiring the specific accomplishment of all internal and external obstacles and the attainment of the intended goal,
[one should pay homage] to the Triple Gem— which is the object of that [homage], which is the cause of its realization,
which is endowed with the distinguished qualities of extraordinary radiance, and which is most greatly venerable even among the great.
Having performed that recollection as an object of veneration in accordance with one's own faith, in order to fulfill the instructions of the teacher:
"But those who have no longing for the feet of the teachers here, even though they are covered with the dust from their feet, are indeed the virtuous ones who possess discernment."

Based on his own statement—having made the promise at the beginning of the *Pañcikā-vivaraṇa* with the words "I shall explain the *Pañcikā* on the path," and so forth—and because he has now begun the praise of the work starting with "Mahādayo" and so forth as a description of the virtuous people [who composed it], we shall begin the praise of this text. [Objection: Is it not the case that this teacher has already applied himself to the commentary on the *Vutti* text?

How then can he proceed here with the unmentioned [topics] such as "Mahādayo"? [Response: [We shall explain this by means of the following: the homage to the Three Jewels, the author of the text, the basis of the text, the commencement of the text, and the fruit and subject matter [of the text].
*Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a traditional Pali commentary (Ṭīkā) discussing the structure and purpose of a grammatical treatise.*
[This is] for the purpose of demonstrating the encouragement of those who have the need [for the work] and those who possess the capacity.

Therein, the performance of the homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing, without obstacles, the composition of this treatise—which was intended to be composed—by generating a specific merit that destroys the demerit which causes obstacles.
Furthermore, the verbal homage herein is also productive of the aforementioned purpose for the listeners; thus it was performed by the Master as well.

The meaning has already been shown by the passage beginning with “In this context, the demonstration of the homage to the Triple Gem,” and so forth. Furthermore, since the subject matter here concerns verbal instruction, there is verbal homage;
[by implication] there is also bodily homage and mental homage. The indication of the author of the work is for the purpose of clarifying the extent and nature of the composition.
The indication of the basis of the composition is for the purpose of demonstrating its purity by way of indicating that it does not belong to oneself (i.e., is not one's own property).
The demonstration of the fruit of undertaking a treatise is for the purpose of preventing those who would oppose it;
the demonstration of the connection consisting of the subject matter is for the purpose of encouraging the audience of listeners— since the activity of a teacher proceeds preceded by an inquiry—
to apply themselves with diligence to the treatise, as it has been said:
For indeed, regarding any treatise or any action whatsoever, by whom can it be grasped as long as its purpose has not been stated? [One might object:
"Should not the connection between the treatise and its purpose also be stated, such that one knows, 'This is its purpose'? To this:
One who desires to hear the established purpose and the established connection must first state the listener and so forth,
[showing] that the connection possesses a purpose. To this,
the following reply is given:

The subject matter (*satta*), the purpose (*payojana*), and both the connection (*sambandha*) and the support (*nissaya*)—these are not stated separately from the narrative because they are already included therein.

As for the purpose of the purpose (*payojanappayojana*), it is to be understood by the teacher himself through his own capacity, according to the method stated [in the commentary] beginning with: "But what is the fault in not knowing the characteristics of words? and so forth.
Therein, by the two verses beginning with “mahādayo,” the homage to the Triple Gem is shown;
by “yo iddhimantesu,” etc., the author of the work is indicated; by “saddasatthaṃ,” etc., the source of the composition is shown;
and by the phrases “by way of summary” and “the essence, vast in meaning, and unconfused,” both the fruit of undertaking the composition and the encouragement of the audience are presented.
As for the purpose, which is designated as the "subject matter," it is indicated by the term ‘commentary’ (saṃvaṇṇanā) through an etymological designation:
it is called a “commentary” because the meaning is “commented upon”—that is, explained and expounded in detail—by means of it.

Furthermore, this act of explaining in detail is called the “subject matter” because it depends upon the treatise of grammatical instruction; thus, it is the subject matter by virtue of the entire treatise taken together.
The meaning of "that which is to be spoken" (*vacanīyattha*) refers precisely to the purpose consisting of the instruction of the words as they are stated in the manuscript;
this is the collective meaning here.
Furthermore, the individual meaning here is as follows: the term *dhammarāja* is an indefinite expression, and its masculine gender is established here by its reference to the word *yo*.

Herein, the specific qualities being described serve as an illustration of the excellence of the person who possesses them. He "protects" (dayati) by removing suffering and bestowing happiness upon others;
or he is "protected" (dayīyati) by noble persons, meaning he proceeds within his own continuum;

or he "protects" (dayati) in the sense of harming the suffering of others; or he "protects" (dayati) in the sense of taking up the suffering of others, thereby experiencing mental distress himself on their account.
“Dayā” means she gives; from the root *day*—meaning “to give, to go, to harm, or to take”—the suffix *-a* is applied according to the rule “*itthiyam-aṇattikayak-āca*” (5-49).
Because her object is vast, or because her compassion is great or praiseworthy, she is “mahādayo.

In this descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*), the statement regarding the experience of suffering while accumulating the perfections (*pāramitā*)—which will be explained under the rule “*saddhāditva*” (4-84)—is the statement of the cause (*hetuvacana*).

"Beings" (*janā*) refers to the world of sentient beings produced by kamma and defilements; by this term, even those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) are included, because they too bestow benefit in the form of a pleasant dwelling in the present life.

"For the welfare of beings" (*janatāya hitāya*) means for their increase and for making them partakers of the bliss of Nibbāna, which is free from all the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);
this is what is meant. And the word "beings" is connected with both the words "fulfill" (*sampūraya*) and "experience no suffering" (*adukkhamanubhavi*). "Enlightenment" (*sambodhi*)...

Here, the prefix *sam-* indicates the sense of "together" (*sāma*); therefore, it is *sambodhi* because by means of this [wisdom], one awakens to and penetrates the four truths as nothing other than doubt (*saṃsayam eva*).
From the verbal root *budh-* preceded by *sam-*, the suffix *i* is added according to the rule for the *ṇvādi* group (Pāṇini 3.1.134).

Furthermore, the Blessed One’s knowledge of the path to Arhatship, which abandons all defilements along with their latent tendencies, is also called "the knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
They say: it brings one to attainment, thus it is "that which brings to attainment" (*sampāpaka*). "That which brings to enlightenment" (*sambodhisampāpaka*) is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*).
What kind of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) are intended here by the word "phenomena"? The perfections (*pāramī*), the five great renunciations (*pañcamahāpariccāga*), and so forth.

For these also are called "phenomena" (*dhamma*) because they support themselves—that is, they sustain their own nature—and because, through their capacity to bring about enlightenment, they support others as well.
They are called [Dhammas]. From the root *dhṛ* in the sense of "holding" (*dhara = dhāraṇe*), by means of the rule beginning with *vi-ādi*, the suffix *ṇvu* is applied;

thus, it is the "birth of Dhammas" (*dhammānaṃ jātaṃ*) or "that which is born as Dhamma" (*dhammā eva jātaṃ*). It is a descriptive compound (*visesanasa-māso*) meaning "that which brings about perfect enlightenment and is the birth of Dhamma.

The word "fulfilling" (*sampūrayanti*) is the object (*kamma*) for this [verb]; they fulfill it through the application of perfected practice, even though it was already within reach of their hands at the feet of Dīpaṅkara.
Having abandoned even Nibbāna, because his heart has become cooled through union with the quality of compassion as previously described, he—

properly fulfilling and increasing [the perfection] by being the sole cause for the escape from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa), thinking, "How shall I liberate these beings who have fallen into the suffering of the round,
which is so utterly difficult to endure?"— is said to be reaching growth, increase, and fullness; this too is indeed for the sake of the cause.

Great compassion (*mahādayatā*), moreover, is the successive cause for the experience of suffering. [The word] *dukkha* means "it digs badly" (*duṭṭhu khanati*) bodily [pain]; it is called *dukkha* because one experiences bodily pleasure as "bad" (*duṭṭhu*).

Regarding the term *khanismā*, [the commentary says]: "'Kvī' is *kvi*; 'suffering' (*dukkha*) refers to bodily painful feeling. As for what kind [of suffering it is], he says: "of infinite form" (*anantarūpa*).

Here, the word *rūpa* expresses the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), as in "a lovely form" (*piyarūpa*) and so forth; and those [feelings] have suffering as their intrinsic nature (*dukkhasabhāva*). They are "infinite" (*ananta*).

By way of infinite causes; therefore, because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is infinite form, it is "infinite-form" (*anantarūpa*). He experienced and found that suffering. To the question "Like what?", he said: "Or like pleasure" (*sukhaṃ vā*).
It is called "pleasure" (*sukha*) because it thoroughly (*suṭṭhu*) digs into [the body] and afflicts the physical frame.

The word *iva* indicates a simile characterized by commonality of attributes (*sadhammatta*); for a simile consists in the commonality of attributes between the object of comparison and the thing compared. For it has been said: "Between the object of comparison and the thing compared..."

"Could there be similarity [with suffering]? What is meant is this: "Even though painful feeling has the nature of experiencing what is undesirable, because it shares the commonality of being an experience, the Great Compassionate One attains a state of similarity with happiness due to his possession of the excellence of noble aspiration;
thus, although it is suffering, he experiences it as if it were happiness. Otherwise, how could he [protect] the entire world from the suffering of saṃsāra?

"Samuddharaṇaṃ siyā" means "there may be an uprooting. Alternatively, the meaning is that he experiences such suffering—which, though not something to be experienced by others—as if it were pleasure, as if he were actually finding pleasure, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world. Therefore, he says "akhinnarūpo"; the analysis of the compound is:
"one whose nature (rūpa) or essential character (sabhāva) is unexhausted (akhinna), that is, one who has not reached exhaustion or weariness."
The term *dhammarāja* (Dharma King) is an exclusive designation for that person who is the substratum of the specific qualities mentioned, though not previously specified by the word "he";
or it means he rules by Dhamma and not by non-Dhamma; or he is the king—the master—of the Dhamma through his mastery over what has been personally realized;
or he rules and shines forth therein while himself penetrating the Dhamma as it is being penetrated by him.
Alternatively, he is a *dhammarāja* because he rules over others by means of the Dhamma, having practiced for that very purpose;
or, he is a *dhammarāja* because he proclaims the Dhamma to others. The connection is: "having bowed to that *dhammarāja*," which means "having paid homage.
To the question "of what kind?", he says: "the hero who has conquered Māra, shining like well-polished gold. In this context, he is both Māra and a hero, thus "Māravīra."

The heroic Māra was conquered, his power destroyed; it is not that the heroic Māra alone was conquered. For although the Māras consisting of the sons of the gods (*devaputta*), the defilements (*kilesa*), the formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the aggregate of death (*maccu*) were indeed already conquered, nevertheless, because the sons of the gods as Māras are included by virtue of the presence of the word "hero" (*vīra*), it should be understood that by his victory, the others too are indeed said to have been conquered.
It is well-polished, well-blown, and well-extracted—thus it is "well-polished" (*sudhanta*).
*Suvaṇṇameva sovaṇṇaṃ*: it is gold itself; *sudhantañca taṃ sovaṇṇañca*: it is both well-polished and gold; "the radiance (*nibhā*) or splendor (*sobhā*) of that" is the compound.

Alternatively, in the compound *sudhantañca taṃ suvaṇṇañca* ("it is both well-polished and gold"), by applying the suffix *ṇa* according to Pāṇini 4.3.4 (*tassidam*), and by applying the medial *vṛddhi* according to Pāṇini 4.1.26 (*majjhe*), one obtains *sudhantasovaṇṇaṃ*, meaning a statue-form of well-polished gold.
That which is similar to or like that is *tena nibho*. That [is the meaning].
And to this extent:

"The cause, the fruit, and the welfare of others— this entire collection of praise [covers] everything prior to full enlightenment as the cause, and whatever is other than that [is] subsequent to it."
Having first shown the salutation preceded by praise for the Jewel of the Buddha by way of the stated causes, fruits, and benefits to sentient beings, he now says,

“And the Dhamma that destroys the blinding darkness of delusion,” in order to show the act of prostration toward the Jewel of the Dhamma, which is itself worthy of worship even by that King of the Dhamma.
And therein, the word “ca” (and) [is used] in the sense of having paid homage, as in the phrase “having bowed to the Dhamma” (*namitvā*)— that is, after the act of paying homage (*namassanakriyāya*).
He compiles the Dhamma; as to what kind [of Dhamma], he says: "It destroys the blindness and darkness of delusion. That which causes one to be deluded is *moha*—that is, ignorance (*aññāṇa*).
It makes one blind by depriving one of the visual consciousness of the capable eye, thus it is *andha*. That which is both blind and dark is *andhatama*, meaning thick gloom.
Because it is similar to that [darkness], delusion itself is called *andhatama*. He destroys—that is, he utterly eliminates—that *andhatama*.

Regarding "by virtue" (*sīlena*): it is for the purpose of clarifying the state of one who has destroyed the blindness of delusion. Since the sense of "kind" (*pakāra*) is already included within the sense of "together with" (*sa-*)—as in the phrase "together with the scriptures"—the supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhammā*) are ninefold:
the four paths beginning with stream-entry, their four fruits, and Nibbāna.
It should be understood that the supramundane path has been taken up; otherwise, only the path of Arahatship would have been taken up.
But why is only the abandoning of delusion mentioned here, and not the others? Because all defilements are rooted in that [delusion];
for when its abandoning is stated, the abandoning of the others is also effectively stated by way of that.
Having thus shown the homage to the Jewel of the Dhamma, one now pays homage to the Jewel of the Saṅgha, which serves as its support, with the words:
“The Saṅgha, so well-knit by virtues. In this context, the word *tathā* (so) means either “also” or “in accordance with.

In the latter sense, the particle *ca* (and) must be supplied to connect it, [the meaning being]: “It is called *saṅgha* because it binds (*saṃhanati*) and destroys (*hiṃsati*) the defilements and so forth.”

Regarding *saṅgha*: from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *kvim*, [it forms *saṅgha*] according to the rule "in *kvim*, it is like *ghopa* and *paripacca*" (5.100). Here, the *han* becomes *gha*;

and "affliction by the defilements" (*kilesahiṃsana*) is included here by way of the "abandoning of that factor" (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and so forth. By the general designation "by means of qualities" (*guṇehi*), this includes both the conventional Saṅgha (*sammutisaṅgha*) and the four who are practicing (*cattāro paṭipannā*) and the four who are established in the fruits (*cattāro phale ṭhitā*).
“This Saṅgha is upright, composed in wisdom and virtue.
By this, the eight noble persons (ariyapuggala) are understood; “by qualities” means by mundane and supramundane qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth; “united” means well-knit.
Thus, for the purpose of completing the composition without obstacle, [homage is paid] to him who is like a crest-jewel at the peak of the three worlds, distinguished by infinite qualities.

Having shown homage to the Triple Gem, the author now, desiring to undertake the composition of this work preceded by a demonstration of the meaning as it has been stated regarding the author and others, says:
"He who among those possessed of psychic power... and so forth. In this context, the word "who" (*yo*) is connected with the phrase "by that name.
By means of this [power], beings succeed (*ijjhanti*), become successful (*iddhā*), prosperous (*vuddhā*), and reach the pinnacle of excellence.

“Exist” (*honti*) means that they possess psychic power (*iddhi*), such as the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*) and so forth, both mundane and supramundane; thus they are “possessors of psychic power” (*iddhimanta*).
Among those possessors of psychic power—meaning, in the midst of the great disciples who possess psychic power—the sense is:
“one who has attained greatness,” that is, one who has reached the state of greatness (*mahantabhāva*). “By that name” (*tannāmadheyyena*) means: he whose very name is that, by him.
What was said by the sage rich in asceticism? [It was: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who possess psychic power, namely Moggallāna.

Thus, the teacher—by way of modesty—refers to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the second chief disciple, who was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessing psychic power, [using] that very same name.

Without mentioning his name and so forth in the regular order, by means of his own crooked conduct he reveals his name as Moggallāna, his attainment of the position of Great Master (Mahāsāmi), his timely wisdom and proficiency, and his service to the Buddha’s dispensation. The connection is with the words "that which was composed" (*yaṃ racitaṃ*);

"composed" means "made. To the question "What? he says: "The science of grammar" (*saddasatthaṃ*). "Science of grammar" refers to the *Sutta*, which has other names such as *Saddalakkhaṇa* and *Byākaraṇa*.

For it is called *saddalakkhaṇa* because "sounds (*saddā*) are characterized (*lakkhīyanti*), instructed (*sāsīyanti*), and taught (*anusāsīyanti*) by means of this" through the formulation of the divisions of bases, suffixes, and so forth;
and it is called *byākaraṇa* because "words are explained (*byākarīyanti*) and expounded (*kathīyanti*) by means of this" through the process of producing words.
Furthermore, the *vutti* and other such works are termed *saddasattha* or *saddalakkhaṇa* by virtue of being its auxiliary instruments.
It should be understood that it is called "explanation" (*byākaraṇa*); "anunā" is its qualification;

the meaning is "complete" (*sampuṇṇa*) because there is no other thing to be stated, owing to its inclusive nature as the characteristic of all [words]; "atha" is a particle used in the sense of immediate succession, meaning "immediately after the composition of the treatise on grammar" (*saddasattha*);
the connection is "of that [treatise], the exposition (*vutti*) and the compounds (*samāsa*) have been made"; thus the Sutta is being commented upon.
"Etāya" means "by this"; it is called a *samāsa* because it is composed (*samassate*) and condensed (*saṅkhipīyati*).
"Tassāpi" means "of that [composition] as well. A *saṅkhepa* is a casting together (*saṅkhipana*), having gathered [the elements] and, by way of the words, made them as if contracted;

the method (*naya*) or sequence of that is the *saṅkhepanaya*. By that [method], he who is the author of the composition of the science of grammar (*saddasattha*)—[addressing him as] "O, sir! (*bhovā*)—[is meant].

Thus, now, at this time when the opportunity has arrived immediately following the composition of the Sutta-exposition, one should "undertake," that is, make a proper commencement, and attend to the initial moment of action among the many moments of activity; for what purpose?
For the sake of the "commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanā*)—so called because the meaning is "well-decorated" (*saṃvaṇṇīyati*) by it, and because it is "compounded," "expanded," and "made clear."
Or, it is called *pañcikā* because "functioning (*vutti*) occurs by means of it," or because "it explains that [meaning]";
thus, having personally undertaken the task to be done, immediately thereafter, based on the statement: "Bhikkhus, there are two conditions for the arising of right view (which two?):
the voice of another and wise attention within oneself."

Since all success in the Dispensation is dependent upon right hearing, and because that hearing is the fundamental cause for the exposition of the practice of the Dispensation, [the author], urging virtuous people toward such hearing, says:
"That which is the essence," and so forth. In this context, although the word *yaṃ* (which) is absent, it refers to the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanaṃ*) because it is the subject under discussion;

thus the connection is: "Let them hear that. Regarding the word *sādhu*: *Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the explanation of the term "sādhu". The translation reflects the available portion.*
The meaning is: "Having observed that the phrasing conforms to the meaning and the meaning conforms to the phrasing, listen attentively with undistracted minds.

This is done by fixing [the teaching] in the heart so that it does not perish, like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel; for attentive listening alone brings benefit to listeners. Thus, he says "being present" (*santo*).
[The author] shows that those who perform the act of hearing [the Dhamma] are likewise [worthy], as well as the preeminent nature of the exposition itself;

for it is only such noble persons (sappurisa) who desire to hear with great care. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says "Consisting of essence" (sārabhūta), and so forth. Here, the word *bhūta* has the sense of "existing," as in expressions such as "an offense of expiation (pācittiya) regarding a living being" (*bhūtasmiṃ*).
Because it lacks the state of being mere sapwood (pheggu), it is not to be discarded; thus, "essence" (*sāra*) means firmness.

Because it possesses both meaning and phrasing, it is "substantial" (*sāra*) and "real" (*bhūta*); or else, because it serves as the singular means for accomplishing the preeminent mundane and supramundane qualities, it is "substantial" in the sense of being excellent and "real," thus it is "substantial and real" (*sārabhūtā*). It is this [text] alone that is summarized here;

however, the meaning is also shown in every respect through the grasping of the underlying method (*nayaggāhitā*). Thus, one who grasps the vast meaning is called "one who grasps the vast meaning" (*vipulatthagāhī*).
Because it rejects a disordered order of commentary due to the specific sequence of the commentary being prescribed, it is "unconfused" (*anākula*), meaning that there is nothing confused therein.
Furthermore, this demonstrates that such a state does not exist in the commentaries on the *Kaccāyana-vutti*.
Thus, because he has exceeded [the standard] in this way, this teacher, having first proceeded with the opening verse beginning with "He who is great-hearted," now...
Having introduced the very words of the treatise worthy of praise—presenting them precisely through the manner of avoiding redundancy—he says “*idha*,” etc., in order to explain it.
Therein, “*idha*” means in this section concerning the composition of the grammatical characteristics (*saddalakkhaṇa*) of the Māgadhī language;
that which belongs to the Māgadhīs is “Māgadhika”; “Māgadhika-saddalakkhaṇa” is a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*).

"Desirous of composing" means desirous of making. "Produces delight" (*ratiṃ janeti*) is *ratana*; or, it is *ratana* because it causes one to rejoice (*ramayati*) or delights (*ra-tayati*), by means of the suffix *-ana*.

Alternatively, that which in the world is called a "jewel" (*ratana*) due to its being honored and so forth, this [work] is also called a "jewel" because of its similarity to that. And thus they have said:
"Adorned, of great value, incomparable, and rare to behold;
the enjoyment of extraordinary beings—therefore it is called a 'jewel' (ratana).
This is a designation for the Buddha and others. That which has three parts (avayava) is "threefold" (tayaṃ); it is a collective term for the triad of jewels (ratana-tayaṃ).
The Three Jewels (*ratanattaya*); however, because a whole cannot exist apart from its parts, they are called precisely "the three jewels.

*Paṇāma* means bowing; it is the inclination toward the qualities of the Three Jewels. Alternatively, *paṇāma* is that by which they bow; thus it is the wholesome volition (*kusalacetanā*) that brings about the act of bowing.
"Bowing to the Three Jewels" (*ratanattayassa paṇāmo*) is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*). *Abhidheyyo* means that which is expressed or communicated.
The meaning is to be expressed by the entire grammatical science (*sattha*), and that by which something is conveyed becomes its meaning.

This [conveying] consists in the arrangement of words through the application of the divisions of primary suffixes (*pakatipaccaya*), secondary suffixes (*paccaya*), and so forth; for it is precisely the arrangement of words that is conveyed by the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
Thus, [the phrase] "the homage to the Triple Gem and the subject matter" means "the homage to the Triple Gem and the subject matter."

This is a *catutthī-samāsa* (genitive compound); its meaning is "that whose purpose is the demonstration of that. What is this sentence? [The words] "tā vā" are used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*). [Objection:
One might object, "Even if this is an addition, only the mere subject matter (*abhidheyya-matta*) should be shown; what is the use of such a verbal elaboration?
For the accomplishment of the desired goal occurs through one's own attainment even by means of merit consisting of body and mind. Keep this objection in mind.
Having set aside the salutation of speech, he said "In that regard," and so forth, in order to show the dependence upon the welfare of others and the purpose through its analysis.
Here, the word *guṇa* (quality) has the sense of "benefit" (*ānisansa*), as in such passages as "A gift possessing a hundred qualities is to be expected.
"Anuguṇa" means favorable to or conforming with those qualities, that is, the benefits; this is a qualifying term implying a cause, and it is brought to the state of being the primary factor.
"Exquisite" (*paṇīta*) means "most excellent. "More exquisite" (*paṇītatara*) means "exceedingly exquisite.
"Continuity of consciousness" (*cittasantāna*) is the stream of the mind. "That which is both more exquisite and a continuity of consciousness" is a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*).
[Alternatively,] it is a possessive compound (*aññapadattha*) meaning "those whose continuity is favorable through the production of that name," and so on. Of them... [the rest follows].

The intention is that as those listeners, by means of their prostration to the Triple Gem, obtain an excellence of merit and possess a mental continuum conducive to obtaining an excellence of manifold benefits, so too does their mental continuum become pre-eminent;

this also stands as the cause for these [benefits]—namely, that they have attained... [and so on]... an uninterrupted continuity—and "attained" (*adhigatā*) means they have reached many (*aneke*) or numerous (*bahū*) specific benefits.
The analysis is: "those who possess life, beauty, happiness, strength, eloquence, and so forth";
and "for such listeners as those whose internal or external obstacles, fears, and so on, have been withered away and dried up.
These [qualities] are the causes for [the attainment of] the goal. The fruit is precisely the comprehension of the composition that has been aimed at, undertaken, and brought to completion.
For the sake of its successful completion, what is the purpose of demonstrating the homage to the Triple Gem?
It is said, raising one's arms: "It is true, it is indeed true!
There is no self-interest whatsoever for one who does not act for the benefit of others."

Considering that only the welfare of others is to be performed by the virtuous (sappurisa), and that when the welfare of others is accomplished, one’s own welfare is indeed perfected, he said, “This very same,” and so forth.

It should be understood from this very statement that what is accomplished through the conduct of body and mind is likewise accomplished through the conduct of speech; thus it is to be understood by one’s intelligence.

In this context, "preceded by intelligence" (*buddhipubba*) means that the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is prior is the intelligence; those who act with such [intelligence] are "those whose actions are preceded by intelligence" (*buddhipubbakārino*).

That which has the prior attainment or knowledge of the subject matter is "that which is preceded by the attainment of the subject matter" (*abhidheyyādhigamapubbako*). "Entry" (*avatāro*) refers to the process of occurrence.
Because even when referring to a single part, the designation for the whole is seen—as in the expression "the ocean has been seen"—it is stated [in the commentary] as "by the final foot."
The meaning is: "by means of the constant [application] of the characteristic of words (*saddalakkhaṇa*), which constitutes a portion of the latter part [of the compound].

*Sādhiya* refers to the arrangement of words; *sādhana* is grammar (*byākaraṇa*). That which has this as its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*)—that is, its inherent nature (*sabhāva*)—is "characterized by the basis of what is to be established" (*sādhiyasādhanalakkhaṇo*).

This is the means of establishing (*sādhana*) for that which is to be established (*sādhiya*), and this is the object to be established for the means of establishing; thus, the relationship is the inherent nature of the cause for the state of "this being for that."

It has been stated that the purpose (*payojana*) is the arrangement of words as indicated by the word denoting the subject matter (*abhidheyya*). In this context, the connection (*sambandha*) is included therein...
because the means (*sādhana*) is also shown by way of indicating the goal (*sādhīya*), through the indication of the basis (*nissaya*); [the term] *ussukka* means right effort (*sammāvāyāma*);
*buddhatta* is omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); and "having fulfilled" (*pūretvā*)—
Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender, the cause [of merit], meeting with a Teacher,
going forth, perfection of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
The meaning is: having become endowed with the aspiration (abhinīhāra) characterized by the eight qualities as described, and having fulfilled the perfections (pāramitā) and other such qualities;
"arrived" (āgatā) means arrived through the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma);
"here" (idha) means in this world; "arrived" (āgatā) means attained or arisen; and "Tathāgata" refers to those Blessed Ones who have just now been born.
The meaning is that he likewise went facing north with a stride of seven steps;
"just born" means immediately upon birth—this is what is intended—and "he strode" means he went.
Having gone seven steps, he surveyed the directions; this refers to the fact that, monks, it is the natural law for Bodhisattas immediately upon birth...
Because it is stated in the canonical text beginning with “Having stood firm on his feet,” that the surveying of all directions occurred after the seven strides, it was said:
“He surveyed the directions all around. This, moreover, should be understood as occurring immediately after [the verse] “He touched the earth with level feet”;
for he surveyed the ten directions immediately after touching the earth with his feet. These are called the eight factors—
“Distinct, beautiful, intelligible, worth hearing,
not dispersed, clear, deep-sounding”— thus is the voice eightfold. Having thus stated the eight factors,
he said “Alternatively,” and so forth, in order to show a separate explanation of the meaning of the term “Tathāgata.”
"By the noble bridge" means by the supreme path known as serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*).

By the phrase "and so forth," it includes such terms as "Tathāgata"—wherein the meaning of *tathā* is "come" (*āgata*) or "attained" (*adhigata*) according to reality (*tathaṃ*), that is, according to how things truly are (*yathāvato*)—and where the meaning of *gata* is "understood" (*buddha*) or where the meaning of *buddha* is "gone" (*gata*).

Thus, it encompasses [definitions] such as "Tathāgata. Regarding the word "there, there": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends with "tatthatatthāti". The full commentary would typically explain the repetition as referring to each respective instance of the term "Tathāgata" in the various suttas.)*
In various long discourses (*dīghāgama*) and others, the term *tathāgata* means "the state of a Tathāgata," that is, his existence or accomplishment.

Regarding the phrase "having paid homage" (*namassitvā*), because it is connected with the act of homage, this [term] clarifies that the Tathāgatas and so forth function as the object (*kamma*) of that act.

Furthermore, because it serves as a qualifier for the act of homage, the expression "having paid homage" (*namassitvā*) may be understood as "having performed the act of homage"; thus, it refers to the act of homage already mentioned.
Because it is a qualifier, [the word] "of the Bodhi" (*bodhiyā*) refers to the knowledge in the four paths; the Blessed One has attained that here, thus [it is called] *bodhi*.
[The phrase] "of the Bodhi-tree" (*bodhirukkhassa*) means of that tree. "At the root" (*mūle*) means in the vicinity of the root, as in such passages as:

"As far as the shadow spreads at midday and leaves fall in a windless place—to that extent is the 'root of the tree' (*rukkhamūla*)," and so forth. But are there not others who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*)?

Having considered the inquiry—namely, that [the defilements] are indeed eliminated according to the method to be explained starting with “by the highest path” (aggamaggena)—it was stated, “together with the residual impressions” (saha vāsanāya).
For no one other than the Blessed One is able to abandon the defilements along with their residual impressions;
by this, he shows that the Arahantship of the Blessed One is unique and not shared with others. For this very reason, regarding the word *iddha*...
Showing the meaning, he will say "for even these," and so forth. What is this so-called "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*)?

It is a specific capacity residing in the defilements, which serves as the cause for an application similar to the application of one who has abandoned the defilements, even though the defilements themselves have not been abandoned—just as in the case of the Venerable Pilindavaccha’s conduct toward the outcaste. By the "highest path" means by the path of Arhatship; [it abandons] all defilements...
Regarding passion and the rest, Arahantship is the supreme fruit. As for the term "conventional," it refers to the state of being a deva through rebirth;

however, because this is surpassed by the state of being a deva of purity, which is fully accomplished, he says, "by the state of being a deva of purity. The meaning is: by the state of being a deva of purity, characterized by the qualities of omniscience attained through the removal of all the turbidity of the defilements.
‘*Idha-saṃsiddhiyaṃ*’: those who possess success (*iddhi*) are called *iddhavanto* by means of the suffix *-atta*. ‘*Guṇa-āmantaṇe*’: this is a remainder from the *bhūvādi* class;
they are called *guṇā* by means of the suffix *-ka*, because they are multiplied (*guṇīyanti*) or accumulated by those who seek excellence.

‘*Tepi*’: even those disciples and paccekabuddhas. The word ‘*hi*’ indicates a reason; the meaning is: “because [they possess] the foremost... [and so on]... qualities that are not deficient, therefore. ‘*Sabbaññutādīnaṃ*’ and so forth refers to their [qualities].
This is a statement of reason based on the fact that [the Tathāgata] lacks the qualities possessed by the omniscient Buddhas.

Some, imagining a corrupted meaning—thinking "it would be one who has accomplished the quality of torpor (middha), thus 'one whose quality of torpor is accomplished' (siddhamiddhaguṇa)'—vitiate this sentence.

However, they [ignore] both the fact that "there is no such thing as a quality called torpor" and that "the Tathāgata does not possess the quality of torpor. If he were such [a person], there would be no worship offered to him based upon his knowledge.

And not knowing that [the word] *pakata* (prepared) is useful here, you say: "After you have spoken, they should be sent away. In this context, the inclusion of the word *siddha* (established/accomplished) is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*);
for auspicious words and the like possess unimpeded flow and are desired by the Venerable Expositor and those who wish to hear.

By the phrase "of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha," since the meaning of the compound (*samāsa*) resides in the whole even when there is an analysis (*viggahe*) of its parts, this is a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound whose meaning lies in something other than its constituent members).
He explains that [the compound] signifies the recognition of those qualities; therefore he says, “in the sense of another word,” and so forth.

Even though they have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*)—that is, even though they are non-primary or function as qualifiers—the connection with the action is understood because the other word’s meaning is primary.

For even though the constituent factors (*dhamma-saṅghā*) have become subordinate, their connection with the act of homage is understood through their inseparability from it. He demonstrates this very point with the words, “Thus he said,” and so forth.

"Existing together with the son" (*puttena saha vattamāno*) is understood as "the son has also come," because it is a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound whose referent is other than its members) characterized by the recognition of that quality;
thus, the arrival of both is equal. In the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), the locative case (*sattamī*) is used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). By "himself" (*attan*), he indicates the Dhamma.
"Bearing" (*dhārento*) means placing within oneself, causing to proceed, or causing to arise. The four states of misery are referred to collectively as "misery" (*apāye*) by way of their commonality.
The three rounds have been mentioned by way of the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), the round of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*), and the round of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). Among these, there is suffering.
"It bears that" means, in terms of its meaning, the destruction of the defilements that produce the states of misery and so forth;
and since that occurs through the state of being an object for the total eradication and the pacification of those very defilements, he said: "He... by way of... and so on.
Since even the nine [factors] are called "Dhamma" because they are the causes for its attainment, it is said, "the ten," and so forth.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "because they are rooted in that," and so on. "Because they are rooted in that" means because they have that as their cause.
"By way of the commonality of virtue and view" means by way of the shared state of noble virtue and noble view; for the virtue and views of the Noble Ones have come about through the Path.
Since they are entirely identical, they are "conjoined" (saṃhata) even when situated anywhere;
thus, in this sense, the word *saṅgha* should be understood as established in its meaning. However, this is stated according to what is intended:
it should be understood that even a conventional *saṅgha* (sammuti-saṅgha) is indeed worthy of homage because of its commonality in terms of mundane virtue and view.

Now, as to what those sounds are whose characteristics they will explain by means of the term "designated" (paṭiññāta), he says: "Sounds such as 'pot,' 'cloth,' and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), trees and the like are included.
One might ask: "Are there not also the sounds of clouds, the ocean, and so on? [The answer is:

No, because here it is not for the sake of mentioning things that are useless; rather, this characteristic applies only to those useful sounds which, in accordance with worldly convention, make an object known. Furthermore:

It should be understood that by stating "sounds are [words such as] 'jar,' 'cloth,' etc.," [the author] indicates that there is no possibility for a fixed sequential order—as there is for things like pillars or railings—and furthermore, it demonstrates that even though sounds are produced according to that sequence, they do not deviate from their worldly nature.
Now, in that context, does the meaning of the sound as a communicator occur through the aggregate (*samudāya*) or through each individual phoneme (*pacceka-vanna*)? In this regard:

If individual phonemes were to manifest the meaning, then in the word "ghaṭa," the letter *gha* alone would manifest the meaning of "pot," and likewise, other letters such as *a* and so forth would have no purpose.
Alternatively, if they were to manifest it when combined, then because phonemes perish immediately after being uttered, there could be no combination at all;
this being the case, how could sound manifest the meaning? [The answer is: by means of the syllables (*akkhara*) grasped sequentially by the ear, the mind, and so forth.

And whatever word is to be understood from the Pāli as being meaningful and within the range of the mind—even for such a word within the range of the mind, the grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) is performed through a mere conceptual construction (*kappanāmatta*) by way of the analysis of roots (*pakati*) and so forth, and not by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Therefore he said: "The root and so forth.

For surely, when there is a restriction to correct words such as *go* and so on, it is understood that *gotā* and the like are incorrect words, just as when there is a restriction to the path to be traveled, [other paths are excluded].
Just as there is a path to be traveled, or just as in the restriction of incorrect words such as *gotā* and so on, words like *go* and so on are correct;

and just as in the restriction of the path to be traveled, there is a path not to be traveled—having raised this doubt, "What is the use of the grammatical exposition (*anvākhyāna*) of words?", he states the purpose with the words "And if there is a statement of the characteristics" (*lakkhaṇābhidhānaṃ ce*) and so on.
He says "In another way" (*aññathā*) and so on in order to show that the recitation of the rules (*paṭipadapāṭha*) is not the means for the acquisition of words. "In another way" (*aññathā*) means...

In the absence of a specific designation, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase *sakkatādi* includes *pākata* and others. Its manifold nature is due to its being *sakkata*, *pākata*, *pesācika*, and *apabbhaṃsa*.

Regarding the derivation of the words *māgadha* and *māgadhi*—from the sense "known in Magadha" by means of the suffix *ñ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.70 (*aññasmiṃ*), and from the sense "this belongs to the Magadhans" by means of the suffix *ṇa* according to Pāṇini 4.3.121 (*ṇo*)—the forms are established.
In order to show that [the language] is to be known, he says: “In Magadha,” and so forth. In order to explain the intended meaning of the phrase “known in Magadha,” and so forth, he says:
“This is what is meant,” and so forth. Therein, “this” refers to the Magadhan language which will be spoken of presently...

“is meant” means that this is what has been stated; the sense is that by one who declares the characteristic of Magadha to be [the language] found in Magadha, it has been made clear. The word “hi” (for/indeed) [connects] with the phrase “in Magadha,” and so forth.
It is said that [the word] "vutti" qualifies the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), meaning it specifies the characteristic of the term *saddalakkhaṇa*.
Because the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound is predominant, the author of the commentary (*vuttikāra*) specifies and delimits the characteristic by means of the word "Māgadha.
The phrase "by way of meaning" (*atthato*) refers to by way of implication (*sāmatthiyato*). And since the term is thus specified, the term *saddalakkhaṇa* is delimited to the Māgadha language alone.
This is the intended meaning here: having taken the word *māgadha* in the sense of "known among the Magadhans," [the text says] "this belongs to them as *māgadha*.

Since the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is specified by the word *māgadha* in the phrase "the sound characterized by phonetic rules" (*saddalakkhaṇasadda*), it follows by implication that the sound itself is also specified:
if the sound were not Māgadhan, how could the characteristic be Māgadhan? Therefore, by the force of the context, the sound is also specified.

If it is asked, "Does it not follow that [the term] *saddalakkhaṇa* (phonology) would be redundant here, since the word *māgadha* already indicates that the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is connected to the Māgadha language?"—it does not follow so, because there is freedom to employ a word even when its meaning is already understood, or because the compound term *saddalakkhaṇa* is established in the sense of the whole phrase. Thus: "In this regard, this..."
In passages such as "the measure of the Sugata’s robe," the word *kopana* (irascible) and so forth functions as a definition (*lakkhaṇa*).

Since this demonstrates the purpose (*payojana*) consisting of the subject matter (*abhidheyya*), the objection is directed toward inquiring about that purpose. The response begins with "It is said, etc.":
"One who desires the welfare of oneself and others in every way [should be] beloved, respected, and venerable, a speaker and one who endures being spoken to."
One who delivers profound discourse and does not direct one toward improper matters—
such a teacher is endowed with these and other superior qualities praised by those mentioned previously and others.
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should strive for proficiency in the syllables.
"By properly attending to the teacher with the five [duties] beginning with rising.
According to this statement, by one who attends properly through rising, waiting upon, service, obedience, and the thorough reception of the craft,
the characteristic of the word (*saddalakkhaṇa*)— which is to be understood by means of hearing, grasping, retaining, questioning, and cultivation— is to be known after having resolved all doubts.
Likewise, a person who has not understood the characteristics of the words is one whose characteristics of the words are uncomprehended (*aviññātasaddalakkhaṇo*).
Here, the word *hi* is used for emphasis; it should be understood in the sense that "he is not skilled in the Dhamma and Vinaya.
He is not skilled—that is, he is not proficient—in those [teachings], namely, in both the Dhamma and the Vinaya, which consist of the Suttantas and what is reckoned as the Abhidhamma. Why?
"One who does not train in language, even while training in the Three Piṭakas, will be in doubt at every word, like a blind elephant in the forest.
From this statement, the intended meaning here is as follows:
"Due to confusion regarding the words produced according to the method already described, one is also confused regarding the meaning of those words..."

"Because of the possibility of delusion, and because of the failure to unravel views as presented in the Suttantas, there might be incompetence regarding the discernment of name-and-form contained in the Abhidhamma, and regarding the restraint and non-restraint specified in the Vinaya. Thus, "in accordance with the Dhamma" means:
the meaning of the term *dhammavinaya* is that which is comprised of the Vinaya-suttas and the Abhidhamma; [the phrase means] not transgressing that meaning, being unable to practice accordingly.
One who is unskilled is unable to proceed in those very trainings in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom that have been taught in each respective instance;
however, one who is skilled is able [to do so] because of the attainment of the light of distinguished wisdom. For it is said:
"As long as the Suttantas endure, and as long as the Vinaya shines..."
“They shall see the light, just as when the sun has risen.

Regarding “the practice” (*paṭipatti*): it is called “practice” because one practices it; thus, it refers to the threefold practice as previously described. “Having violated” means having destroyed it; for practice is lost among those very people because they have entered upon a wrong path.
And so it has been said: “When the Suttantas no longer exist, and the Vinaya has been forgotten...”
"It will be darkness in the world, as when the sun has set.

He becomes a partaker of the suffering of *saṃsāra* alone... because the domain of attainment is to be acquired through practice corresponding [to the goal] by not abandoning the aforementioned sequence;
because it is the state of being free from the pathless (*visatha*), which is the security of *nibbāna*. For its being rooted in practice conformable to that [security] has indeed been stated:
"When the Suttanta is protected and remains intact, practice is protected;
the wise person established in practice does not fall away from the security from bondage.
Having thus far shown the loss of its own meaning for one who has not understood the characteristics of words, [the author] now shows that which is rooted in the attainment of its own meaning.

Regarding "the attainment of the welfare of others": because that [attainment] is absent, it is shown by the words beginning with “and not” (*na cā*) that such a person is unable to become a condition for others as well. "Establishment" (*patiṭṭhā*) means supporting;

here, this refers both to the instruction in the Dhamma and Vinaya of various sons of noble family, and to their deliverance from their respective tasks and so forth. Both of these together constitute the "connection with the sun" (*anhasaṅgika*).
The foundation is, moreover, the establishment [of the listener] in the perfectly pure virtue that is the root of that [wisdom]; the purpose of the training and so forth is to serve as its equipment.
Here, however, the person who is the means of accomplishment (sādhana) should be understood figuratively as the "foundation.

The word *hi* is a particle used in the sense of "capability" as previously stated; furthermore, the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is expressed by the phrase "only those who know the characteristics of words."
This was stated by way of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*) in order to show that only one who possesses those [qualities] is capable;
for, due to the lack of a well-guarded aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), no one at all is able to become a foundation for the aforementioned qualities.

Since the stability of the True Dharma (*saddhamma*) and the state of being a foundation for oneself and others are rooted in that very [virtue], it was for this reason that the Blessed One, while demonstrating the benefits (*ānisaṃsa*) for one who holds the Vinaya, made that [virtue] his primary focus.
Making that the foremost, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, there are these five benefits for a person who upholds the Vinaya.
What are the five? His own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected; he is a refuge for those overcome by remorse;
he dwells with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha; he effectively refutes adversaries with reasoned argument."
It is said, “and he is one who practices for the endurance of the true Dhamma. *Atthānurūpaṃ* means suitable as the expression of the meaning intended to be stated;
*byañjanānurūpaṃ* means suitable as the meaning to be expressed by the expression. In the phrase “in probation and so forth,” the word “and so forth” includes rehabilitation and other such acts.
*Tantam-kammaṃ* refers to each respective formal act, such as probation and the like. *Añño* refers to one who knows the characteristics of words.
It was said, beginning with the words “But not knowing,” to show that it was not only his own welfare and the welfare of others that were destroyed, but indeed the true Dhamma as well.
“Practicing otherwise” means not practicing in the manner in which one who knows the characteristics of language should practice—
namely, applying the expression in accordance with the meaning and the meaning in accordance with the expression.
And thus he will say: "For he, not knowing the characteristics of words," and so forth.

"The threefold True Dhamma" refers to the True Dhamma itself, which is threefold by way of the scripture (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*adhigama*). Among these, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas is called the True Dhamma of scripture;
it consists of the thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), the fourteen rules of conduct for the Khandhakas, and the eighty-two great rules (*mahāvatta*).
This is called the True Dhamma of Practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*); the four paths and the four fruits are called the True Dhamma of Realization (*adhigama-saddhamma*).
He supports the meaning stated by "tathā hi" and so forth, and in order to stabilize that [meaning] through the Canon (*pāḷi*), he says "for it has been said" (*vuttaṃ hetaṃ*) and so on.
In this context, "dhammā" means causes (*hetu*); "of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammassa*) refers to the threefold True Dhamma as previously described; and "word and phrasing" (*pada-byañjanaṃ*)...

Regarding "both the word and the phoneme" (*padañca byañjanañca*): therein, a "word" (*pada*) refers to that which ends in a case-ending (*syādyanta*) or a verbal suffix (*tyādyanta*). A "phoneme" (*byañjana*) is so called because meaning is manifested (*byañjīyati*) by it; thus it is a sentence (*vākya*).

Alternatively, a "word" (*pada*) is so called because meaning is reached or understood (*pajjate gamyate*) by it—referring to forms ending in case-endings and the like—and a sentence is indeed a phoneme.
Or, according to the method already stated, even a single word consisting of soft or hard consonants is a "phoneme"; thus, [the compound] is "word-phoneme" (*padabyañjana*).
That [instruction] was poorly placed, badly set down, established in a way that violates [the rules], and spoken [so as to be] misunderstood;
and since the meaning was also wrongly interpreted, it is "due to being poorly placed" because the very words and syllables were poorly understood.

It is so called because of its state of being the opposite of what was stated by the phrase "one who has not understood the characteristics of words," etc., due to its being the contrary of having understood the characteristics of words and so forth.
For this exposition is primarily concerned with the state (*bhāva*), or there is an elision of the suffix *-tta*; for it is not logical that "the self should be known by the self.
Having concluded what was stated previously with the words "That very [self]," etc., he shows the purpose for the formulation of the technical term (*saññā*).

The word *taṃ* is a particle used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*); the meaning is: "because the knowledge of the characteristics of words is the purpose (*saṃsaṃ*) [of this work], therefore. The word *evaṃ* is used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*).
The connection is that [the particle] "nipāto" means "thus it is purposeful," or else the collection of particles beginning with "tadevaṃ" occurs in the sense of "in the manner already stated.

Now, one might think: "But surely, when the technical terms (*saññī*) and the definitions (*saññā*) are to be stated, since sentences such as 'a, ā, etc., are the forty-three phonemes' are each quite extensive, how can there be brevity in the Teacher's work? Anticipating this, he says "For thus... and so forth.

It establishes the existence of brevity within the system of grammatical designation (*saññāvidhāna*); by the restrictive particle *eva* ("indeed"), it shows that [brevity] does not fail to exist in some cases, as it might in other treatises.
Furthermore, brevity of practice (*paṭipattilāghava*) also exists here;

for instance, in the rule "a vowel (*savaṇṇa*) is also [treated as] following a consonant" (1-24), those who have extracted the technical terms (*saññā*) such as "vowel" (*vaṇṇa*) and so on are unable to understand their own meaning [without this brevity]. Others [hold this view].

It should be known by asking; therefore, it would be subject to perception (*saññā*); thus, from that [perception], there is the discernment of perception and the percipient, and subsequently its non-arising.
Because of the absence of reverence for the practice, there must be a dependence on a succession [of causes]. Now, in order to show the sequence of the Teacher’s method in brief, he says:
"Thus, first," and so forth. "First" means initially. "Because of being employed" means because of being made to function.

The *visaya* (domain) is that sphere where these suffixes (*sy-ādayo*) are prescribed; together with that domain, they are called *savisayā*. That which is performed first is the *pakati* (base), from which the suffixes are prescribed;
together with that base, they are called *sappakatikā*. Regarding the term *liṅgādikaṃ*, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), singularity (*ekattādi*) in examples such as *salabhacchāyaṃ* is included.
Those derived from gender (*liṅga*) are the feminine suffixes (*itthividhayo*). *Ekattībhāva* is compound (*samāsa*); by means of that, because of their commonality in general.

Because of the application [of the suffix] *tuṇ* and so forth when there is equality, [the word *paccādo*] occurs in the sense of "a descendant" (*apaccādi*) for both types of distinguished persons— such as kings and the like, as well as those distinguished by their lineage,
such as the Vasiṣṭhas and the like. Thus ends the section on the Homage to the Triple Gem and so forth in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*,
a commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*.
1. Commentary on the First Section:
The Chapter on Perception (Saññādhikāra) 1. The Vowels beginning with *a* (A-ādayo)
Because all utterances—whether meaningful, meaningless, or ambiguous—give rise to doubt when expressed through examples such as "this," etc., it was stated: "Not yet...
because of being meaningful," in order to demonstrate its meaningfulness by means of an illustration. The phrase "the speech of a madman, etc.
refers to such expressions as "ten pomegranates, six cakes, a goat-skin, a bundle of straw," and so forth; [it refers to] the mutual connection of the constituent parts.
Because there is no meaning derived from a collective whole, [the words] would be meaningless; the "initial statement" refers to the passage beginning with "mind is foremost, mind-made.
However, it possesses meaning because the mutual connection between the word-meanings is understood.
Now, since other alternatives such as "this statement is for the purpose of explaining the correctness of words like *ādi* and so forth" are possible, how [is this to be understood]?

Fearing that the purposefulness of what has been stated in the *Vutti* might be doubted, he says "this very meaning will be explained," and so forth, in order to demonstrate their utility here in due sequence.

That which has its meaning to be explained in the *Vutti* by means of the passage beginning "the vowels, etc., ending in the *niggahīta*," is described as such; it is the instruction (*anusāsana*) regarding the word *sādhu* and other similar terms.
The analysis of the compound is: that whose *ākhyāna* (narration), *attha* (meaning), and *payojana* (purpose) [is this work].

Here, the term "instruction for correctness" (*sādhusaddānusāsana*) is used because we observe the instruction regarding the correctness of words such as *kattha*, etc., in [the rule] beginning with “*katthettha kutrātrakvehidhā*” (4.100);
and because their state of correctness is explained by another grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*), starting from the prefix *ā-* and the root *diś*.
Regarding the expression *dādhātvī* (5-45): when the suffix *ippi* is applied and the vowel *ā* is elided, the form *ādī* arises.

In a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound of different referents), when the suffix *yu* is added, by the rule *yosu jhissa pume* (2-93), the *ṭe* [of *ādī*] becomes *ā*. Thus, in the compound *catu-catvāriṃśat*, by the rule *tadaminādīni*, the *ca* is elided and the word is shortened to *catvāriṃśat*.
From the root *vaṇ* in the sense of describing color, the suffix *ghaṇ* is applied according to the rule *bhāvakārakesu ghaṇa ghakā*.
(5-44) Because [the rule] is established by both "appaccaye yo mhi" and "ṭādese vaṇṇā," the purpose is to restrict the usage;
that is, the word beginning with *a* is employed only when followed by words consisting of forty-three phonemes (*vaṇṇa*).

This is for the sake of restricting usage, as this alternative possibility is observed in the application of the rule "abhūtatadbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārā co" (4-119), which restricts usage even for one who is meditating (*jhāyamāna*).

"Regarding the phrase *ṭhānyādesatthaṃ* (for the purpose of the substitute for the original): in place of the word *a-ādi* (beginning with *a*), there are forty-three phonetic words as substitutes, or that [term] belongs to them;
*tadanurūpāya* means by the genitive case ending corresponding to the original and the substitute;

*ato yeva* means precisely because of the absence of a genitive case ending corresponding to the original and the substitute; and *agamāgami-bhāvatthaṃ* means that the forty-three phonetic words belong to the word *a-ādi*."

There may be an *āgama* (augment) for them, or it may belong to them; there is doubt even regarding these, because of the observation of augments and substitutes such as in "yavāsare" (1-30) and "suññasassa" (2-53).
Because there is an absence of the characteristics of an *āgama*—namely, the absence of the sounds *u*, *k*, and *m*—the purpose is to distinguish between the qualifier and the qualified:
among the forty-three phonemes, the word beginning with *a* is the qualifier. Or else, [it refers to] "those" or "that"; here too, there is doubt.

Because the relationship between qualifier (*visesana*) and qualified (*visesya*) is seen in other instances such as "blue lotus" (*nīluppala*), it was stated [by some] that this is not according to the rules of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*), since the formation of words is the primary function of grammar. He states the reason for this:

"because there is an absence of a distinguishing mark (*upalakkhaṇa*) for a specific form. The meaning is that there is an absence of a cause (*nimitta*) which serves as a distinguishing mark for a specific form; for a qualifier... [is not present].
Once a specific state has been established, the formation of a specific form for words such as *a-ādi* (beginning with) might be performed;

however, if this alone were understood as "phonetic formation" (*saddasaṅkharaṇa*), then it would follow that even compounds like *nīluppala* (blue lotus) and so forth would have to be called by that name.
Therefore, this [formation] is not considered to have that meaning [of phonetic formation], because in the world, the qualities of a lion are seen even in a young boy.
By way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), even the attribution of those qualities [to something else]—such as "this young man is a lion"—is observed;
however, this [term under discussion] does not have that purpose. To demonstrate this, it is stated: "It does not have the purpose of attributing those qualities.

The quality (*guṇa*) of that sound beginning with *a* (the *ādi-sadda*), or of those forty-three phonemes (*vaṇṇa-sadda*), is its being the first (*āditta*) and so forth. The attribution (*ajjhāropana*) of that [quality] occurs among the forty-three phonemes.
Or, the application [of the rule] is only to the words beginning with *vā* (or); the meaning is that this sutta does not apply for the sake of that [meaning].

He states the reason for this: “Precisely for this reason,” and so forth. Precisely for this reason—because it is by way of the nature (*bhāva*) characterized by a specific form (*rūpavisesūpalakkhaṇā*)—the formation of the word (*saddasaṅkharaṇa*) is established.
In the absence of the aforementioned alternative options, this would apply to both meanings; therein, it does not serve the purpose of a general maxim (*paribhāsa*).

Because of the absence of a specific characteristic (*tallakkhaṇatta*) and because of what will be stated later, one resorts to the method of elimination (*pārisesa*) and says "perception and the perceiver," etc.
It is said: "The word 'etcetera' (*ādi*) is seen to have four kinds of usage:
as a limit, as a manner, as proximity, and as a constituent part."

The word “beginning” (*ādi*) here has the sense of a limit (*mariyāda*); thus he says, “arisen as a beginning-limit. Because it is a characteristic mark (*upalakkhaṇa*), it is subordinate (*appadhāna*) by virtue of being the cause for grasping the forms (*ākāra*, etc.
that are being characterized; therefore he says, “of the characteristic mark which has become subordinate.
By the “effect” (*kāriya*), such as the arising of phoneme-designations (*vaṇṇasaññā*) and so forth, there is no bringing even of cows; [for] the cows are subordinate.

Because the actual state (*bhūtattā*) of the external referent (*aññapadatthassa*) itself is predominant, and because there is an absence of the phonetic designation (*saññā*) for the vowel *a*, [the term] "rūpanti" refers to the forty-three phonemes (*tālīsārūpa*).
The word division (*padacchedo*) is either "titālīsā vaṇṇā" or "titālīsa vaṇṇā. Since even a constituent part of a sutta is connected to the sutta as a whole, it is stated:
"In the case of a consonant, long and short [vowels are used]" (1.33). However, the status of being "short" is established by the rule "long and short [vowels]."

By means of a grammatical split (yogavibhāga); otherwise, if only the shortening of the vowel following a consonant were shown, the word *titālīsa* would not be formed when there is no following consonant—this is what is understood.
Furthermore, since there ought to be a plural number for the fourth case in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*), he says:
“The singular number as well,” and so forth. *Vippaṭipatti* is a state of being otherwise; [it refers to] the forty-three syllables through the short *e* and *o* vowels.

Regarding the connection: in the word *okāre*, the third case (*tatiyā*) is used in the sense of concomitance (*sahatthe*). Regarding the phrase *sakkatānusārenāti*, it means according to the authority of the venerable [teacher], following what was stated [by him]:
"There are no short vowels among the *yak* consonants. The word *koci* indicates that [authoritative] teacher, namely the Venerable Cūḷābhaya, the pupil of Buddhapiya;

this is the intention of the author when he says "not [the one who says] *hi* and so forth. In the expression *rassāiva*, the particle *iva* indicates a comparison based on similarity (*sādhammopamā*).

Or it may be an illustration by way of similarity of nature (*sādharmya-upamā*). If it is first an illustration by way of similarity of nature, then because the short vowel occurs among the *okāra*s of the short-dharmas, and because those [long vowels] persist for a long duration, they would be long;

but if it is an illustration by way of similarity of nature, then because the short-dharma occurs among them and persists for a short duration, they would indeed be short—[this is the case] in such instances as "here" (*ettha*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the shortness [of the *e* and *o* vowels] occurs precisely at the time of their pronunciation," the word "precisely" (*eva*) indicates that the short duration of the *e* and *o* vowels is established by valid means (*pamāṇa-siddha*) and is ultimately real (*pāramatthika*), because there is no such thing as "time" apart from phonemes (*vaṇṇa-vinimmutta-kāla*) and because phonemes are established through direct perception (*paccakkha-siddhattā*). Regarding the passage beginning with “*ettha*”: if the *e*-vowels and others were long by nature, yet became short due to being preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), then it would follow that even in the word *atthā*, the long vowel *ā* would be pronounced as if it were short because it is preceded by a conjunct.
Therefore, the status of being short or long must be understood as being determined solely by the duration of pronunciation.
This is the explanation of the Kaccāyana-vutti; in the phrase *taññāpane*, it refers to other phonemes external to those [already mentioned].
Regarding the statement "because there is no purpose in making known," he expresses the absence of anything desirable that ought to be accomplished by it.
He asks: "Is the completion of the sentence here in the aggregate, or in the individual parts? He replies: "In each [part].

Otherwise, if the completion of the sentence were in the aggregate—as in the case of "trees, a forest" and so forth—then rules such as "the vowels *i* and *u*, when followed by *jhal*, [become long] before *nam*" (1.9) would not apply.

Regarding the word *sijjhati*: by means of such statements as “each individual letter is not a name” and “the letter *a* is indeed a name, the letter *ā* is indeed a name,” and so forth, [the author] provides an example as the reason even though the word “each” (*pacceka*) was not explicitly stated in the commentary on the section beginning with *avayavecca*.

The meaning is that when an example is brought forward, it is possible to understand easily; for here, even though “each” was not stated, [it is understood] from expressions such as “Let Devadatta be fed.”
The act of eating is completed individually; therefore he says, "And it is not said," and so forth.
Alternatively, since a sentence is completed even within a collective whole, words that function for the whole may also apply to its parts.

Thus, there is no fault, just as when one sees a portion of the ocean, it is still called "the ocean," or as in the case of "the aggregate of wisdom" (*paññā-khandha*) when wisdom is only a single part of the aggregate.
For that very reason, it was not stated as "individual" (*pacceka*) in the *Vutti*.

Even though the word *vaṇṇa* has multiple meanings such as "quality" (*guṇa*) and so forth, because of the context (*pakaraṇa*), only the vowels beginning with *a* are intended here; thus he says, "it is colored" (*vaṇṇīyati*), and so on. For meaning is also distinguished by context, as it is said:
"Meaning is determined by context, by gender-mark (*liṅga*), by fitness (*ocitya*), and by place and time."
It is the meanings of words that are analyzed, not the words themselves alone.

Having kept in mind the objection—“Why was the designation *guru* (heavy) applied instead of applying the designation *lahu* (light), as is done with designations such as *jhal* and so forth?”—it is explained that among the two types of designations, namely those based on conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) and those based on literal meaning (*anvattha*), the designation *jhāl* belongs to the category of conventional usage; because it lacks a literal meaning, its purpose is merely for the sake of ease in linguistic convention.
To show that the designation *anvatthasaññā* (designation according to meaning) serves both that specific purpose and other purposes as well, he says:

“*Evaṃ*,” etc. The meaning is expressed (*vaṇṇīyati*) by these [words]; thus, the designation of phonemes (*vaṇṇasaññā*) that follows the expressed meaning is the *anugatatthā* (following-meaning) designation. “Of that which is to be understood through sound” means of that which is to be cognized by means of sound.
“That which has phonemes as its root” is *vaṇṇamūlaka*; the state of being such is *vaṇṇamūlakatā*. This refers to the meaning.

He establishes that the meaning [of the word *vaṇṇa*] is based on its appearance (*vaṇṇa*) by means of the words beginning with “that too” (*sāpi*). Those things which have appearance, form, or intrinsic nature are "appearance-forms" (*vaṇṇarūpāni*).

A sentence is a "collective form" (*samudāyarūpa*) because it has the form of a collection of words. A word is a term ending in a case-suffix that expresses a meaning; a sentence is a collection of words.
All of this, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), comes to be expressed by the word "appearance" (*vaṇṇa*) as being "consisting of appearance" (*vaṇṇamaya*).
Every meaning, whether distinguished as conventional (*sammuti*) or ultimate (*paramattha*), is indeed to be understood through sentences and is known by means of phonemes (*vaṇṇa*) alone;

therefore, the intention is that because it is not possible to show the specific distinctions of the aforementioned meanings by means of a "light" designation (*lahusaññā*), the "heavy" designation of phonemes (*vaṇṇasaññā*) beginning with *a* and so forth has been established for that purpose.
Conventional (*sammuti*) refers to linguistic usage (*vohāra*) proceeding by way of convention (*saṅketa*); the ultimate (*paramattha*)...
The five aggregates are associated with nibbāna. Yet, there is no third category distinct from these two; thus it has been said:
"The Fully Enlightened One, the best among speakers, proclaimed two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—a third is not found."

But is it not said by those who know its characteristics: "A Sutta is that which has few syllables, is non-contradictory, possesses a progressive sequence, has a hidden meaning, and has a clear purpose"?
Regarding the statement “the forty-three initial vowels” or “the forty-three [vowels] beginning with *ā*,” if it were so stated, the Sutta would become ambiguous.
Is it not the case that a word must begin with a consonant (*satthādo*) for it to be a benedictory expression (*maṅgalavacana*), since the letter *a* also has the sense of negation?

No, because the word *siddha* is placed at the beginning. Furthermore, even if there were a designation such as “preceding vowel” (*pubbā jhālādi*), it is because its purpose is merely to establish the phonetic form of the word (*saddasādhanamattappayojanattā*).

"But since the designation of all [grammatical] types has its boundary in the technical designations (*saññā*) of the ancient masters, what further purpose is served by the formulation of designations for vowels and so forth, which merely results in an increase in the bulk of the text?
This is true; however, some designations are also restated here in order to demonstrate respect for the ancient masters and to follow their tradition.
If this were the case, then even the elision of conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), the elision of all nouns (*sabbanāma*), and so forth, would also be designations established by the ancient masters.
"Are they not called 'to be spoken' (vattabbā), Master? Have we not already stated that 'certain phonemes (saññā) are being explained'?

But how can you understand even those [phonemes] by means of that explanation? Even for some, there is purposefulness because they are taught here as imitations of phonemes—such as the unperceived letters *a* and so forth—which have no visible meaning; thus, they possess meaning through the meaning of what they imitate."

The case ending (*vibhatti*) exists indeed from the beginning [of the alphabet] as *a* and so forth; however, because it is indicated through elision (*lopa*), it is not heard. Its non-mention is due to the absence of a desire for a word-form with a suffix (*sannikasa-vacana*).

In the *saṃhitā* (continuous text), there is an indication [of the vowels] according to their sequence: the vowels (*sara*) are stated first based on their places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), such as the "anterior" (*ādi*) and so forth; the consonants (*byañjana*) are those dependent upon them.

Even among the vowels, the single-place [consonants] beginning with *a* are stated first according to the sequence of places, due to their multiplicity; thereafter, the two-place [consonants] are stated according to the sequence of places.

Among those [vowels] as well, the short ones were stated first because of their lightness, followed by the long ones. Among the consonants too, the groups (*vaggas*) were stated first according to the order of their positions because of their multiplicity, followed by the *y*-series and so on.
