Within the groups, the unvoiced (*aghosa*) sounds were stated first, followed by the voiced (*ghosa*) sounds;
among those, the unaspirated (*sithila*) were stated first, followed by the aspirated (*dhanita*). Even there, because they are few in number, the sibilants (*dvija*) were stated fifth.
Then come *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* according to the sequence of their places of articulation; then follow the aspirates *sa* and *ha*.
Among these, the letter *ha* is also the source (*oras*) for some [consonants], and thus it is mentioned later because it possesses two origins.

Although some maintain that there is no distinction between *la* and *ḷa*, the letter *ḷa* is nevertheless taken as a separate syllable because it differs from *la* both in its phonetic form and in its place of articulation.
That [the *niggahīta*] is also mentioned after the letter *ha* according to its phonetic order and the sequence of positions;
however, because it is entirely devoid of vowels (*sara*) and so forth, it is mentioned last of all. This, then, is the sequence beginning with the vowel *a*.

Because this very sequence is present in the mind during the process of insight (*vipassanā*), and because the numerical limit of forty-three is thereby demonstrated, it is stated in the commentary as "beginning with the *niggahīta*"; thus it is established.
The grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of correct words (*sādhu-sadda*) is not described here because it lacks a primary purpose, being merely the arrangement of sounds.
Nevertheless, although it is not described [as such], it has indeed been described under the guise of explaining the meaning of the word "sequence" (*anukrama*),
for the purpose of severing the doubts of students as to how this particular sequence of the letters beginning with *ka* arose.
*Karaṇa* (the instrument) is that by which [sounds] are produced and articulated. In this context, the middle of the tongue is the instrument for the palatal sounds;

the tip of the tongue is the instrument for the cerebrals (*muddhaja*); the edge of the tongue is the instrument for the dentals; and for the remaining [consonants], their own respective locations are the instruments.

*Payatana* (the effort) is the exertion; it is both internal and external, arising from the articulation of phonemes. Among these, the internal effort consists in the closing of the mouth for the sound *a*.

The opening of the vocal organs (*vivatta*) pertains to the vowels and the letters *s* and *h*; the contact (*phuṭṭhatta*) pertains to the consonant groups (*vaggā*); and the slight contact (*īsaṃphuṭṭhatta*) pertains to *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v*.

As for the external effort (*bāhirapayatta*), it consists of the closure of the throat and so forth. He says, “the place as well,” etc., because there is a possibility of purpose through the occurrence of the resulting action (*kāriya*) prescribed by proximity to the place (*ṭhāna*).
It is called “place” (*ṭhāna*) because phonemes abide (*tiṭṭhanti*) therein by way of their arising.
In the sutta “e o na ma vaṇṇe” (1-37), the purpose of designating [the vowels] as *vaṇṇa* is precisely for the sake of making them known as such;

it indicates that the aforementioned meaning applies elsewhere, by means of expressions such as “*evaṃ*,” etc. Therefore, in cases such as “*dasādo sarā*” and “*tenā*,” the meaning is shown by such statements as “*tena saraiccantenā*”—that is, what is the point?
What is the purpose in which sutta? It shows: “*sarolopo sare*,” etc. Thus is the meaning.
It should be observed: it makes known [the rule] regarding the elision of a phoneme (*vaṇṇalopa*), thus it is a "rule of indication" (*ñāpaka*).
But why is it said that this [elision] is established by this very rule of indication? Is it not the case that the sutta “*tadaminādīni*” (1-47) is seen? (True;

however, even so, it should be understood that another method of indicating the elision of a phoneme is also shown. As for the word *eva*, [it implies]: "If the elision of a phoneme were to occur by means of a rule of indication, it would be by this [present rule] alone."
One determines that [the rule] is established by the *ñāpaka* (indicative example) and not by anything else. 2. Regarding the ten [rules]:

since the word "beginning with *a*" (*a-ādayo*) occurs in the nominative case, how is it that here [in the present rule] there is the locative indication "in that" (*tattha*)? To this he says, "And that," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *atthavasāvibhattivipariṇāmena*: the meaning is that by means of a change of case ending (*vibhattivipariṇāma*) due to the force of the sense (*atthavasā*).

This refers to the transformation into the seventh (locative) case ending by way of its function as a locus (*ādhārattha*), because when [the word] *ādi*—which ends in the nominative singular—is connected with the word *dasā* via the expression *ādo dasā*, it must necessarily be connected in the sense of a locus.

Thus, the sense is "by means of the transformation into the seventh case ending due to the force of the sense. It is precisely because such a transformation into the seventh case is possible through the force of the sense that the commentary (*vutti*) uses the term *tattha*, even though it does not appear in the sutta itself.

It has been stated that because the occurrence of [the letters] *a* and so forth as anything other than themselves is possible for those ten, it is also possible to conceive of *a* and the others as being their objects;

thus it was said, "when they have become objects. Furthermore, the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is indeed appropriate, because from among the collection of phonemes (*vaṇṇasamudāya*), the phonemes beginning with *a*—which constitute a single part of that collection—are selected by way of the quality of the number ten; thus, there are ten at the beginning.

When "colors" (*vaṇṇā*) is stated, it is said that there is an ellipsis (*ajjhāhāra*) for the purpose of completing the deficiency of those [factors] which, though unstated, must necessarily be mentioned:
"whether fixed or specified. Because the numbers from one up to eighteen apply to the objects to be numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*), he says:
"because they are delimited by the number ten. Just as in Kaccāyana’s grammar, even when short vowels (*ovaṇṇa*) are included among those subject to selection (*gayhupaga*).

Because they are not abandoned and are not deficient, and because there is no addition of any other vowels that are not included therein, and because the word *dasa* expresses a number, and because even among the ten there is no difference in the vowel that is added, it is said:

‘even of the ten,’ and so forth. [The form] *sayaṃ* [is derived] from *pubbā-rājā-cittiyaṃ* by means of the suffix *kvim*, with the elision of the middle portion (*antalopa*), and through compounding (*samāsa*), according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) since it begins with *ta* and *mi*.
Regarding the statement "the word *sarasaddo* is produced": it is said—"it arises by means of the suffix *a* from [the root] *sar*, meaning 'to go' or 'to think'"—in order to demonstrate this;
thus he says, "'It shines by itself,' etc.
3. Two by two.
Regarding *teti ādo*: because it ends in the locative case (*sattamyanta*), it refers to the other two [syllables] following it.

The phrase "as below" (*heṭṭhā viya*) employs a change of grammatical case (*vibhattivipariṇāma*) for the sake of the sense, as was stated previously. Thus, by virtue of the meaning being understood, it is said "in them" (*tesu*).

Furthermore, since that [locative usage] is possible when expressing a selection (*niddhāraṇa*), the phrase "two each among those syllables" (*tesaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ majjhe dvedve*) is used with the number two.
It should also be understood in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). That which has its occurrence in distributive repetition (*vicchā*) is "distributive-occurring" (*vicchāvutti*);

this word *dvi* is thus "distributive-occurring" because it is pleasing to two [sounds] by virtue of the quality of having similar sounds (*savaṇṇatta*). By the phrase "fixed according to order," he expresses that the sequence of the series of phonemes beginning with *a* is established as a sequence from time immemorial.
Now, is it not the case that the word *savaṇṇa*—meaning "having similar sounds"—is used in the sense of "phonemes that are identical"?
If [the rule] were applied, there would be a common designation (*savaṇṇasaññā*) for short and long vowels; however, this is not so because they are not identical.

Nor is it correct to say that [the designation occurs] even for those that are not identical, on the grounds that the sequence of the series of phonemes (*vaṇṇappabandha*) is established by the power of the grammatical statement itself.

Furthermore, one cannot argue that such a capacity exists in the sutta “two of the same kind are *savaṇṇā*,” because in its presence there is no specific reason [to restrict it]. Therefore, he says: “But their identity... and so forth.
The *ṭhāna* (place) refers to the throat and other locations, because the phonemes (*vaṇṇā*) remain there by way of manifestation even when they are not clearly articulated;

thus, the compound *kaṇṭhādi-ṭhāna-kata* means "produced by the place of the throat and so forth. In the word *kaṇṭhatātu*, the neuter gender is used because it is a part of the body (*pāṇyaṅga*). By the "fifth" letters, meaning the fifth letters of each group (*vagga*).

The term *antaṭṭhāki* refers to those that stand at the end of the groups (*vaggā*); thus, they are called *antaṭṭhā*. [The suffix *-ika*] is applied to that which is joined with them, as in the examples *brahmacariyā* and *guyha*.
"Of one who is joined. The word "some" is used without specific restriction; however, they say:
"The letter *ha*, when joined with the fifth [consonants] and with the dentals (*antaṭṭha*), is to be understood as *orasa*; when not so joined, it is produced from the throat (*kaṇṭhaja*)."

4. Regarding the phrase "pubbo vattate": it occurs through a change of grammatical case (*vibhattivipariṇāma*) for the sake of the sense. As for the objection beginning with "nanu ca" (but surely), the resolution begins with "nesadoso" (this is not a fault).

He states the reason for the absence of fault: "yoyo... pe... patīyate" (whichever... is understood). It was stated [in the previous section] that it is complete, by means of the passage beginning with "na hi" (for it is not).

But surely, since the word *pubba* denotes a single preceding [factor] rather than the whole, how is it understood that when "the preceding" (*pubbo*) is stated, it refers to "whichever one," and when "whichever is the preceding" (*yoyo pubbo*) is stated, it refers to "among those two"?
Furthermore, how is it easily understood here that "in each of the two" (*dvīsu dvīsu*) means "in each pair"?
Fearing that this might be an attempt to prove the unestablished by means of the unestablished, he demonstrates the absence of such a flaw.

He says "If this... and so forth in order to make it understood that the word *pubba* functions as a distributive repetition (*vicchā*). He says "due to its connection with that" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), meaning "by virtue of having that [suffix]";
this is because the suffix *a* is applied in the sense of existence (*atthi*). The same applies to what follows.
5. *Para*.

By the rule beginning with *sesamiccādi*, the phrase “in those two” is understood to mean “in the two that have the designation of being homogeneous,” and so forth. The designation *lahu* (light) applies to a short vowel;

however, the designation *guru* (heavy) need not be stated for a long vowel preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*). It is understood that this designation is applied according to the mode of pronunciation itself, as in the case of the designations *anvatta* and *saññā*, or else it is like the remaining designations not explicitly mentioned here, following the authority of the ancient teachers (*pubbācariya*).

6. Because the consonants beginning with *ka* lack the capacity to manifest meaning on their own, they are "consonants" (*byañjana*) insofar as they are extremely helpful in the manifestation of the meaning of vowels;

thus it is stated [in the rule] by means of the instrumental case as "by these. Therefore, he says "of the vowels," and so forth. This is derived from the root *añj*, preceded by the prefix *vi*, in the sense of "manifestation" (*byatti*).
Regarding the suffix *karaṇe* with the *anap* augment, the form is neuter; it is stated as "the auxiliaries" (*upakārakāni*) in order to make its neuter gender understood.

Its status as a "condiment" (*byañjana*) is clarified by the example beginning with "just as," etc.; the intention is that just as soups and so forth are condiments that assist rice, so too are they auxiliaries that assist vowels.
Furthermore, a condiment consists of half a measure of clay (or half a portion), for it is said: [text follows].
A single mora (*matta*) is short (*rassa*); joined with two moras it is long (*dīgha*);
a protracted (*pluta*) vowel is to be understood as having three moras; however, a consonant (*byañjana*) consists of half a mora.
“Anvatthā” means “according to the meaning” (*anvatthato*); the connection is: “the phonemes (*byañjanā*) are according to the meaning.”

7. Even when the word *samudāya* (collection/group) expresses a class based on commonality of origin (*sajātyapekkhā*), the letters beginning with *ka* and so forth are understood by the term *vagga* because they follow [the same pattern].
That which has five as its measure is a "five-group" (*pañcakovaggo*). [This is according to the rule: "The suffix *ṇika* is used for that which is its measure" (Pāṇini 5.1.57).

In the Sutta, the word *pañca* (five), occurring at the beginning, establishes the limit of the number five; because it leads to the multiplicity of the groups (*vaggā*) ending in *m*, it is called "the fives" (*pañcakā*).
From the plural form "groups," it is understood that they are distinct. They are called "groups" (*vaggā*) because the letters beginning with *y* are excluded;
however, the conventional designations such as "ka-group" (*kavagga*) and so forth are based on their initial syllables.
8. *Bindu*:
Because roots have multiple meanings (*anekatthattā*), it takes here the sense of "releasing" (*muccāraṇa*).

Thus, from the prefix *ni-* and the root [meaning] "to act," with the suffix *-tta*, the suffix *-ññi*, the *pādi-samāsa*, and the long vowel, he states "short" (*rassā*) and so forth to show the form; from the sense of "pressing," it means "confinement" (*niggahana*).

Regarding *niggaha*: from the rule “*ita*-adjectives [are used] for the agent (*kattari*) and the object (*kammani*)” (Pāṇini 3.4.72), it should be stated that the suffix *-ta* is added in the sense of “that which has been uttered.

Thus, the meaning is “it has been uttered. By showing the form of the month beginning with *amā* as “*niggahena itaṃ*,” he says “or by means of *niggaha* as the instrument (*karaṇaṃ niggahena vā*)” and so forth.
To establish the latter alternative, he says: “For it has been said.”
9. "Iyu catthasamāso" means a *itaretarayoga* compound (dvanda). "Atte" refers to the object expressed by words such as "sound" (*sadda*), etc.; "namati" is the object of this [verb].
That which is all genders, all numbers, and possesses all case-endings—[that is the object].
Because it bends (*namati*) toward everything, those who know it call it "name" (*nāma*).

Although there is no formal designation of "name" here, the designation "name" is established by the very force of its etymological meaning; thus he says, "by way of a designation according to its meaning.

That which is the fundamental form (*pakatirūpa*) consisting of the suffixes ending in *-si* and so forth is called "base" (*pakati*), because the suffixes are applied first [to it]; that itself is the "form," hence "fundamental form" (*pakatirūpa*).

The base form (*pakati-rūpa*) of that which ends in a *syādi* suffix—such as the word *muni* and others—is the base form ending in a *syādi* suffix. That which possesses meaning, is not a verbal root (*adhātu*), and is not a suffix (*appaccaya*) is a nominal stem (*nāmapada*).
[The term] *pāṭipadika* means "pertaining to each step" (*padaṃ padaṃ pati paṭipade*); it is that which is connected to each step (*paṭipadaṃ niyuttaṃ*).

"By way of specification" (*visesanena*) means by way of the specification of the vowels *i* and *u*, as stated in the Sutta in the phrase "paying homage" (*namassante*). "Of the verb" (*ākhyātassa*) refers to [verbs] such as *pacati*. "Occurring in the beginning or middle" refers to *inda*.

"In the specific locations" (*padesesu*) refers to the specific locations within the grammatical rules (*sutta-padesesu*), such as "the *jh* sounds [are substituted] for the final *s* of a word ending in *jh*" (*jhalā sassa no*, 2.83).
The connection is that this [rule] prevents the occurrence of an undesired consequence (*aniṭṭha-pasaṅga*).

An "undesired consequence" refers here to the undesirable application of suffixes (*anta*) or vowels occurring at the beginning or middle of words such as *nāma*, *pacati*, *inda*, *udaka*, and *pakhuma*.

Having established the designation *jhal*, if one were then to apply the substitution of *no* for the initial [of] the case-endings beginning with *sādi* by means of rules such as "for *sassa*, *no*" (2-81), there would arise the undesirable forms *pacatino*, *indano*, *udakano*, *pakhumano*, and so forth.

Is this not a valid objection? It must be stated that this is what must be addressed in the rule (*sutte vattabbaṃ*). "By way of an analytical exposition" (*byāsaniddesena*) means by way of an exposition that is not a compound (*asamāsaniddesena*). "That is inappropriate," and so forth.

The rebuttal (*parihāra*) addresses that objection by establishing its invalidity through the passage beginning with "because of *sati*," etc. Regarding the phrase "in the two subsequent rules" (*dvīsuttareṣu yogesu*), this refers to the two subsequent rules:
"in *pitthiyaṃ*" and "in *ghā*. Regarding the word "itthiyanti" (*itthiyanti idam*), in the rule "in *pitthiyaṃ*," the word "itthiyanti" is present.
There might be a specification of the vowel (*vaṇṇavisesanaṃ siyā*), because of the recurrence (*anuvattanato*) of the term "vowels *i* and *u*" (*iyuvaṇṇā*) from the rule "in *pitthiyaṃ*."
In the rule *gho*, the phrase *itthiyaṃ ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā*—meaning "in the feminine, [ending] in *i*-vowels or *u*-vowels"—would serve as a qualifier for both *ivaṇṇu* and *avaṇṇa*.

He states the contradiction regarding the qualification of the vowel in the passage beginning with *evaṃ ce*; he states the lack of contradiction in the definition of the non-compound (*asamāsa*) in the passage beginning with *nāmassante* and *byāse*.
One may provide a qualification for the name *sakka* by means of the words *itthiyaṃ* and so forth in the two rules.

In the order that will be explained hereafter: because a compound (*samāsa*) is dominated by the meaning of its final member (*uttarapadattha*), the word *nāma*—which has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) within the compound in the expression *nām’antō*—cannot be qualified by the term *itthiyam*. This is the intended meaning.

"Without a specific statement" means without a rule such as the Pāṇinian sūtra *yathāsaṅkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām* (1.3.10), which [otherwise] would apply according to the sequence of enumeration (*samāṅkhyā*).
"These are equal in number"—the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*);
by this [it is meant]: "O Lord of Sages, through your playful conversation and smiles, the cuckoos and the night-lotuses attend upon you in the forest and the water. (260)
This includes [the rules] beginning with "icca. 10. Regarding the back [of the rule]:

when it is stated that "in a feminine noun" (*itthiyam nāmssa*) and at the end "when *i* and *u* vowels [occur]," there is a relationship between the substratum (*ādhāra*) and the superstratum (*ādheyya*), wherein the superstratum depends upon the substratum.
Because it cannot occur without a process (*pavatti*), the word “occurring” (*vattamānā*) is used in the *Vutti* by way of an ellipsis (*ajjhāhāra*).

Regarding the forms ending in *ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa*, the plural form “are being distinguished” (*visesīyanti*) is used; however, since a relationship depends upon a masculine noun, when there is a connection with a feminine noun, it changes into the singular form “is being distinguished” (*visesīyati*).

11. Regarding the phrase "if there were no percipient being" (*itthiyam nāma santeti*): since a percipient being was indicated in all the preceding cases by way of perception (*saññā*), [the opponent] seizes upon the slightest flaw—the idea that because it was not separately mentioned at the outset, as if it did not exist—and thus objects.

[The author explains] by means of the passage beginning with "nanu ce" and so forth. Therein, "seto" (the white one) refers to one who exists and possesses perception (*saññī*). "By way of grammatical operation" (*kāriyena*) means by way of the grammatical operation of perception (*saññā-kāriyena*).

He resolves [the objection] by saying "this is not a fault," and so forth. "By the mere fact of being stated after" (*pacchāvuttamattena*) means by the mere fact that [the rule] is stated after the vowel *ā* in the sutta "ghā.
In the word "na ca," the particle *ca* is used to conjoin another thing to be said; it indicates that there is something else yet to be stated, which is of an unrestricted form.
The meaning [of the term *ālapanam*] is as follows. To establish that the form is not restricted [to a specific gender], he says, “in both ways,” and so forth.

The word *āsa-* [in *gosyāsa*] denotes facing toward; thus, *ālapanam* means speaking or talking by making that which was not facing toward oneself face toward oneself. The meaning is: it is that which is prescribed (*vihita*) for that speaking, for the purpose of speaking.
Thus ends the section on Nominal Derivatives (Saññādhikāra) in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*,
a commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*. Now begins the section on Conventional Rules (Paribhāsādhikāra).
13. He states the purpose for commencing the rule (*vidhi-vacana*): "That which [is intended] as a qualifier," and so forth.

In rules such as *ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe* (Pāṇini 7.3.43), the word *ataḥ* and so on, which is intended to be expressed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-bhāvena*), refers to that [word] by means of its status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatvena*) when it is being employed.
By means of that which has been indicated by sound—namely, "atoti" and so forth—which functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and which exists in some way or another at the beginning, middle, or end;
by whatever mode through the metaphorical designation of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) for names and the like that possess specific vowels such as *a* and so on;

"tadantattha" means that those qualifiers such as "atoti" and so forth are at the end, not at the beginning or the middle; that is "tadanta," and that is the meaning (*attha*) or purpose (*payojana*).
*Yassa* is a possessive compound (*aññapadattha*); *vattāyattā* means dependent upon the speaker... because the speaker’s own statement is primary, *tassa* refers to the speaker;
*sā* refers to the desire to speak; *payogānusārena* means according to the sequence of the Victor’s word (*jinavacana*);

*iti* is a particle used in the sense of cause, meaning "for this reason"; [the phrase] "there is no over-extension to all cases" refers to the rule concerning euphonic combination (*saṃhitā*) and so forth, which applies everywhere.
There is no possibility of an application [of the rule] to that which ends in it (*tadanta-vidhi*), for instance:
in the case of the rule *saro lopo sare* (1-26), since the word *sara-* exists as a qualifying term (*visesana*) in its intended meaning, *sara-* would qualify *tatra-* and so forth;

thus, there might arise an undesired application of the rule *vidhibbisesanantassa* (1-13) to those beginning with *tatra-* and ending in a vowel (*saranta*), such as *tatra-* and others that end in a vowel. But this is not the case.

Regarding the phrase “chaṭṭhiyantassā” (1-13), because there is no mention of the genitive case (*chaṭṭhī*) in the rule for *anta*, if that were so, it would follow that in passages such as “tatrime,” one would have to use forms like “ime.
Since these applications are not encountered, there is no over-extension (*ppasaṅga*) of the rule for suffixing *ta* to everything;
likewise, in the case of sutta 2-4, “gatibodhā,” there would otherwise be an over-extension to forms such as “gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ. Etc.

And this should be understood according to the appropriate application; in the *Vutti*, the rule "ato yoṇaṃ ṭāṭe" is given as an example of a sutta, while "narā nare" is given as an example of a *lakkhaṇa* (grammatical characteristic).
14. Sattadhī.

He demonstrates the fruit of the statement with the words beginning "yatthe" and so forth. "Yattha" means in which; "in the sutta" such as "saro lopo sare" and so on. "Sattamiyā" means by the locative case, as in "sare" and so on.
"Yassa" refers to that which is specified [by the locative], such as "saro" and so on. "Kāriyaṃ" refers to the grammatical operation, such as elision (lopa) and the like.
"Sambandhā visesā" means that in "sare" and so on, there is a locative of proximity (opasilesika-adhikaraṇa); and that is a locative of proximity existing within the vicinity.

"Either the prior of the posterior, or the posterior of the prior"—because there is no distinction in the suffix (*lesassa*), there is no difference in the relationship between the prior and the posterior.

"Of the posterior as well" means not only of the prior; when the sense of "being present" (*satī*) is to be indicated, the locative case is used as a substitute for the word *santa*, and thus the statement beginning with "and being existent" (*sattañca*) is consistent in this way.

The word *santi* occurs in the sense of the term *santa*. He states the reason for using the expression "in the *niddesa*" even when it is not explicitly mentioned in the *sutta*, saying "and because of existence" (*sattañca*), and so forth.

The connection is that existence (*satta*) is not possible without a *niddesa*. Only when there is a *niddesa* in the locative case is there the possibility of that existence for the purpose of such a connection;
otherwise, what else would the suffix *-anta* be established upon? This is the intended meaning. [This applies] to the preceding word (*pubba*).

Because it possesses the nature of a relative term (*sambandhi-sadda*), he asks, "Based on what is its priority [established]? and says, "The locative," and so forth. The *tan* refers to the rule (*sutta*) "A vowel is elided before a vowel" (*saro lopo sare*).

"Of the letter *u*" means of the *u* in the word "veḷu. Regarding "of the preceding" (*pubbassa*)... having performed [the elision], he says, "That which was thus attended to," and so forth, in order to show the exhortation.
Thus, in this context, the connection should be understood as involving the inclusion of the particle *sa*. "Of the preceding" (*pubbassa*)...

The seventh [case ending] refers to what precedes that which is indicated (*nirdiṣṭa*). "Immediately preceding" (*anantara*) means not separated by anything; the connection is that "nothing has been stated.

This is the intended meaning: in the Pāṇinian rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (1.1.66), the root *diś* denotes the act of utterance, and the prefix *ni-* here indicates immediate succession (*nerantariya*). In that context, "immediately following" (*nirantara*)...
When the compound *diṭṭho* is formed, the meaning "that which has been uttered immediately before" is clearly understood;
thus, grammarians such as Bhassakāra and others explain that "a grammatical operation applies even when the preceding word is separated [from the following word] if usage is observed.

However, since there is no such statement here, it might occur even when there is an intervention by vowels and so forth—this is the intended sense of the statement regarding the exclusion of vowels and the like.

He clarifies this with the words "even if" (*yadipi*) and so forth. He provides the example of Mathurā and Pāṭaliputta—despite the intervention of villages and other places in the interval between them—to show that the word *pubba-* (eastern) still functions [to denote the former]. He states "Mathurā" and so on;

because the word ending in the locative case, "in a vowel" (*sare*), refers to a proximate substratum (*opasilesika-adhāra*), there is no elision of the vowel even when there is an intervention. Thus is the brief explanation.

The meaning should be understood from the usage (*vutti*), for it is not only by means of the verbal root (*sara*) that [the meaning] is established; thus he says, "in the case of the derivative form" (*kāriye*) and so forth. The remainder [of the sentence] is:

"it exists only in the locative case as a support (*adhāra*). He states the reason: "because of the formulation of the speaker's desire regarding the word" (*vatticchānhavidhānato saddassa*). The meaning is:

because of the formulation—that is, the expression of the meaning—in accordance with the speaker’s desire (*vattivacanicchā*). For by whatever means the speaker desires to convey a particular meaning through the verbal root...
The intention is that although there is a capacity for denotation, a word does not denote a meaning other than that [already expressed].

He states the reason for this as "also by the speaker's intention" (*vatticchā*), and so forth; "speaker's intention" (*vatticchā*) means the desire of the speaker (*vattu*), that is, the author of the sutta.

Anticipating the question, "How is the speaker's intention understood from the explicit teaching (*upadesa*), and how is it understood through functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*)," he says "from this [context] also," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that.
The connection is as follows: "Therefore, it should be understood through the instruction [given] by the reason that will be stated.
He asks, "What is that reason? and says, "Because," and so forth. Here, by the word *anvaya*, the instruction of the lineage of teachers (*gurupāramparī*) is intended.

Because—on account of which reason—the *anvaya*, the lineage of teachers, is sought and investigated by approaching the teacher's family (*gurukula*) through means such as posing questions; for that reason, it is the lineage of teachers.

The meaning is that it is "mastered" (vasīyati) because the instruction has been traversed. Regarding the phrase beginning with “sāmatthiyampi” (also by implication), he says this to establish mastery.

“Implication” (sāmatthiya) is also called a specific distinction; since the application [of a rule] occurs through a concise means for the characterization of words, the composition of another statement to exclude what is remote is unnecessary.
However, the composition of another statement is appropriate, and its basis is proximity (opasilesika).
The capacity (*sāmatthiya*) here is that the specific substrate (*ādhāravisesa*) is understood through the necessity of the meaning not being otherwise possible (*aññathānupapatti*);
this capacity, as previously stated, is clarified by the phrase "in another substrate" (*ādhārantareccādi*). The reading "even in another substrate" (*ādhārantarepi*) is found everywhere;

because there is no possibility of such a contingency (*pasaṅga*), even with a different meaning, there could be the contingency of another statement regarding both "another substrate" and the "proximate substrate" (*opasilesikādhāra*), since a connection is possible.

Since no benefit is seen even in the case of proximity (*upasilesika*), dependence (*ādhāra*), and relation (*nissaya*), there is no purpose [for the term] even in the sense of a collective (*samuccaya*);
thus, the word *saddo* should be excluded. Is it not so that this description—“is it not just the preceding [word]?”—indicates the proximate substratum (*upasilesikam adhikaraṇam*) itself?
For one who thinks that the relationship of preceding and following is possible only there, this assumption is not consistent.
To demonstrate this, he said: “‘Of what precedes,’ etc. He states the reason for its inappropriateness: “Because that [relationship] is possible even in the sense of a locus (sāmīpika).

When it is said, “There is a roar on the Ganges,” since it is understood that the roar is either before or after the Ganges, the meaning is that the relationship of being before or after is possible even in a locus-sense;
thus, it is stated only to this extent—that it applies only to what precedes, not to what follows.
It is said; and thus he will say: "What then? and so forth. The connection is that more than this—such as indirect negation (*byavahita-nivutti*) and so on—is not stated.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the genitive case-construction (*chaṭṭhī-pakappanā*) is included here. The connection is that even this genitive case-construction is made according to the *sāmattiya* [rule].

"Construction" (*pakappanā*) means the formulation of construction. Thus he thinks: "From the Pāṇinian rule 'The sixth case [is used] when there is a connection with a substitute' (*chaṭṭhī-ṭṭhāne-yogā*)."
In the two *paribhāṣā* rules, “*tasmiṃ niddiṭṭhe pubbassa*” (1-1-66) and “*tasmā tyuttarassa*” (1-1-67), the mention of the genitive case (*chaṭṭhī*) is carried over; thus, [the meaning is]:
“When that which is indicated by the locative case (*tasmiṃ niddiṭṭhe*) is present, the operation applies to what precedes (*pubbassa*)”;

and “When that which is indicated by the ablative case (*tasmā*) is present, the operation applies to what follows (*tyuttarassa*)”. Therefore, because it is stated that “the genitive case indicates what precedes,” it is suitable for establishing that the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) pertains to what precedes.
The meaning is that the sixth case occurs in a word that makes [the relationship] known; thus it is said in the *Ujjotatīkā*:
"They establish the application of the sixth case [with the words] 'In whatever sutta there is no mention of the sixth case, there the application of the sixth case should be made as appropriate.
However, here, even though there is no other explicit statement, wherever there is no mention of the sixth case, it follows by implication alone.
The phrase "the sixth case-nominative is established" indicates functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*) by means of the expression "in the description of the seventh case," and so forth;
the connection is that even what is indicated by another case-ending may function [as a nominative]. The term *kāriyayo* refers to the connection between grammatical operations (*kāriya*).

For example, in the rule "in a group of consonants, the final of the group," the word "final" (*anta*), which is understood as being in the sixth case, is perceived as recurring [from a previous rule]; how then is it that in the word *vaggesu*, this [word] is not in the seventh case?
Regarding the term "niggahīta" (1-38), because its meaning was already established in the preceding sutta, the nominative case is converted into the genitive;
this should be understood as applying likewise to the seventh [case], according to the rule "pubbasse. When it is said "this much is called," it is not understood what "this" refers to;

therefore, he says "what is it? and so forth, thereby showing the sequence of the transition to synonyms by means of the words beginning with "yadāhi. What is this that is called a transition to synonyms?

Is it not the case that the statement is for the sake of restriction? [Objection: Since there is no simultaneous arising of preceding and succeeding [moments], the statement is for the purpose of piercing [the doubt] regarding non-practice based on the authority of the Teacher’s word;
why then do you not say this? [Response: He says, “because of the simultaneous contact,” and so forth. The connection is that simultaneous contact is impossible. From what [is this said]?
He says, “because of the absence of another thing to be contacted,” meaning because of the impossibility of both [contacting] simultaneously.
By way of non-existence, there is the rule: "The word *sara* is elided before *lopasara*, etc.

(Sutta 1-26). 15. By way of being a limit (*avadhi*): by means of limitation through [terms] such as *ato*; [the word] *yassa* refers to that which begins with *yo*; [the grammatical operations] are performed, such as *ṭāṭe*, etc.

Because there is no distinction in terms of being dependent on what precedes and what follows: just as when it is said, "Devadatta from the village," it is understood that he is either before or after it—thus, in the case of the state of being a limit (*avadhibhāva*), there is no distinction in terms of its dependence on what precedes and what follows;

so too here, when it is stated, "from this [base], for *ya* and *na*, *ṭā* and *ṭe*" (Pāṇini 7.1.41), whether the *ya* and *na* are before or after this [base], there is no distinction in the state of being a limit due to their dependence on what precedes and what follows.
The phrase "it is considered as if it were prior" (*maññate, pure viyātyanena*) refers back to the reason stated in the *niddesa* (explanatory rule) regarding the locative case.

In the *vutti* (commentary), we shall explain in the section on "from the beginning" (*ādissā*) how the substitutions of *ṭā*, *ṭe*, and *ā* occur due to their subsequent application when there is an exclusion of an exception, as in the case of "of men" (*narānamere*).
Now, what is the purpose of this statement? Is it not because wherever there is a description in the ablative case (*pañcamī*)...

In that regard, since it is possible to carry forward the word "following" (*para*) from the rule "In all cases, the vowel *m* is followed by a consonant" (1-21), and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the specification of its source, the meaning "of the following [consonants]" is understood;

thus, there is no possibility of applying it to those preceding [the vowel]. This is not the case, for the word "following" (*para*), as it is being carried forward, is connected with the ablative ending "from that" (*ato*).

Since there is no one who can prevent what is being applied, and because the rule stating that the substitutes *ta* and *ṭa* apply to *yoṇam* even before the suffix *kārato*, it must necessarily be *enim*.
To demonstrate this, he says: “In the statement,” and so forth. If it is asked, “If that is the case, then that very [form] should have been cited as the example;
why was ‘narānare’ cited?”—there is no fault in this, for that which is employed for another purpose here also possesses the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "it occurs": the "prior exemption" (*pubbako parihāro*) refers to the exemption stated in the preceding sutta for the purpose of excluding what is separated [by other rules], namely, "the suffix *dhak* after *sarasa* and *upasileśa*.
It does not occur here because of the absence of the locative case; it is like the mention of the word *nirdiṣṭa* among the Pāṇinīyas, which serves to exclude what is separated by another sutta.
For they [the Pāṇinīyas] apply the rule "after that, of the following" (*tasmād uttarasya*) in this context.
(1-1-67) Carrying forward the mention of *niddiṭṭha* (the specified), they establish the exclusion of what is separated by an interval, just as before.

From the word *anantare* (in the immediate), support (*nissaya*) is understood through proximity; from the word *katatthatāya* (by way of having its purpose fulfilled), it refers to the genus (*jāti*). Thus he says:
“By way of proximity, relying upon the genus. Relying upon the genus, he states the exclusion by means of proximity acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

By this [statement on] "relation" (*sambandho*), it is shown that among proximity (*paccāsatti*), pervasion (*vyāpana*), cognition (*ñāya*), genus (*jāti*), and the meaning of the word (*padatthabyatti*), the principle of proximity (*paccāsattiñāyo*) is established as the basis for the meaning of the genus (*jātipadattho*);
for it is not possible to state an exclusion based on mediation (*byavahita*) relying solely on the genus.
Thus, when the principle of proximity is not relied upon here, then by the principle of pervasion (*vyāpanañāyena*), in that which is mediated...
And since it adheres even to what is not proximate, even though there is dependence upon the genus (*jāti*), who could prevent the genus from pervading even that which is distant?
Nor can one claim that its exclusion of the distant is based solely on proximity;
for if the genus were absent, the individual (*vyakti*) would not be depended upon, and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) operates by reflecting upon the individual within the meaning of the word.
Regarding proximity (*paccāsatti*), even though it is not separated [from its object], that characteristic which is distinct [from others] operates with respect to what is not separated;

however, as for the characteristic which is distinct with respect to what is separated, let it not occur through the authority of the word that "its separation [is not intended]," for it operates even with respect to what is separated.

Therefore, it is led out by relying on both. In the context of showing the object (*visaya*), the demonstration of the possessor of the object (*visayin*) is the cause for the clarification of the meaning.

Having first shown the meaning of words whose sense is hidden within the sentence, the passage beginning with "from what" (*kato*) is commenced in order to subsequently show the compounds and so forth.
"The characteristic of the genus" (*jātilakkhaṇa*) means the unobstructed intrinsic nature of the genus.

Regarding the word "herbs" (*osadhyo*), it is stated as "of *ya* and so forth," because even among the remaining [consonants], there is the presence of *ya* and others that are separated from the following *dha* by the letter *a* in place of the *s*. "Genus" (*jāti*) means commonality (*sāmañña*).

"In as many objects as there are," such as cows and so forth—by this he states an illustration regarding the completion of the objects through the exercise of one's will, using the phrase "just as that.
In the expression "bhojayeyya," the word division is *bhojaye* + *iti*.
The meaning of the term *kasiṇa* is "entire" (*kata*), because the entire matter consisting of the brahmin caste is complete; this is the sense. This is what is meant:

When it is said, "one should feed as many as there are pillars," because of the power of the application of the word *brāhmaṇa*—which denotes a general state of being (*santāya sāmaññavutti*)—the act of eating is understood to be performed individually for each one;
thus, even the generic meaning (*jātyattha*) is considered complete.

This is according to the rule in the sutta "In the case of a consonant, long and short" (1-33), where "in the case of a consonant" (*byañjane*) is in the locative case, governing the prescription of long vowels and so forth for what precedes it.
Because of its application [in the rule] “*saramhā dve*” (1-34), the word *saramhā* here is in the ablative case; thus, the designation of the ablative is more powerful.

Consequently, regarding the two rules “*sattamiyaṃ pubbassa*” and “*pañcamiyaṃ parassā*,” which trigger the substitution of the subsequent [element], the locative case in the word “*byañjane*” is—by virtue of its connection with the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) of the subsequent element—transformed in meaning from the seventh case into the sixth case through a change of case-ending (*vibhattivipariṇāma*).
It transforms... Because of the existence of such a capacity—namely, that when there is a conflict between two rules (*sutta*), the latter is stronger—it is said:
"The application of the genitive case is also [governed] by capacity, as in the previous case. 16.
Of the beginning.
"Kiñci antassa sampattaṃ" means that whatever [substitution] does not have "ṭ" as its suffix and is multiliteral is obtained by the final letter of the word;
this refers to "chaṭṭhiyantasse" (1-17). "Kiñci sabbasse" means that whatever grammatical operation has "ṭ" as its suffix and is multiliteral is obtained by the whole word;
this refers to "ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse" (1-19). By the statement beginning with "Yadantabhāvīkāriyaṃ," etc., he demonstrates the result of the rule.

The phrase "of that which ends in the sixth case" (*chaṭṭhiyantassa*) indicates an exception (*apavāda*) to this rule; he shows that there is an exception to it by stating, "when there is a suffix with *ṭ* as its indicatory letter" (*ṭānubandhe*), and so forth.

"By way of contradiction" (*vippaṭisedhā*) means by way of contradicting the exceptions. For "of that which ends in the sixth case" is the general rule (*ussagga*), while "of the first [case]" (*ādissa*) and "of that which has *ṭ* as its indicatory letter, being polysyllabic, of the whole" (*ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassa*) are its exceptions. This provides the scope for the rule "of the first [case]."

Regarding the term *terasā*: by the rule *“ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā”* (all [suffixes] having *ṭ* as an adjunct and consisting of more than one syllable [replace the whole]), there is scope for this [rule].
Then, by the rule *“‘esu’, ‘anenā’”* (2-40), both [forms] occur here: *“ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe”* (2-41) [yathā] *“narānare”* and *“atena”* (2-108) [yathā] *“janenā”* (in that context).

There, because the rule *“ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā”* also applies, the substitution of the whole (*sabbādeso*) occurs due to the negation of those exceptions. [This applies to] the genitive singular ending. “*Chaṭṭhiyantassā*” (of the genitive singular).

Since the *patta* [suffix] of the word *dasada* is also subject to that exception, it applies to the letter *da* which has become the beginning of words such as *ādissa*; thus he says, "the vowel of the letter *da*.

17. Regarding the sixth [section], he says after the word *kotthanta*: "ending in *vasāna*" and so forth; in the rule *vaṇṇassantassa* (1-1-52), the mention of *vaṇṇa* (phoneme) is taught for the purpose of qualifying the end (*anta*).

Pāṇini [intended] that there should not be [the elision of the final vowel] of a word or a sentence; however, here, the mention of the phoneme *a* is purposeless because there is no [other] thing to be excluded.

To demonstrate this, he says "so ce" and so forth. Now, since the word *mahābrahma*, which is intended to be used as an adjective for the meaning of the qualifier *brahma*, is indicated by the genitive case, the substitution *u* [for *a*] according to [Pāṇini 6.1.194]—"or for *brahma*"—would apply to the word *brahma* at the end [of a compound] according to [Pāṇini 6.1.195]—"of that which ends in the sixth case."
If that were so, one might ask: "Since it is said that 'the end of what is designated by the genitive case—whether a word or a sentence—is not possible,' why was this stated?
It is replied: The word *mahābrahma* is not called "designated by the genitive" merely by way of its elliptical mention (*akkhepamatta*) for the purpose of qualification;
thus, there is no undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) of substituting [the suffix] *-a* for the entire word *brahma*. Or, within the compound *mahābrahmasaddo*, the word *brahma*...
The suffix *utta* is prescribed for that which ends in *atthi*.

Regarding the rule "Vānu": one might raise the objection, "Since the substitution for the final element is already established by the general rule 'Chaṭṭhiyantasse' even when an operation involving an *anu*-bindu is to be applied, what is the purpose of this new beginning? Anticipating this doubt:
Demonstrating the purpose of the statement beginning with "ṭānubandhā," etc., he says: "This undertaking is for the purpose of subverting a subverter.

For instance, the rule "ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse" (a [suffix] with ṭ as its *anubandha* replaces the whole of that which has more than one syllable) is a subverter of the rule "chaṭṭhiyantasse" (the sixth case ending of the word *anta*);

and the rule "vānubandho" (or when there is an *anubandha* *v*) is a subverter of that [first rule]. Thus, it results in being for the purpose of subverting a subverter. The prefix *apa-* is used here.

It is called an *apavāda* (exception) because it excludes, wards off, or removes; that is to say, by means of it, the characteristics of the general rule (*ussagga*) are set aside, warded off, or removed.
Since a portion of the Sutta characterizes the Sutta itself, the exception to the Sutta "ending in the sixth case" (*chaṭṭhiyantassa*) is an "exception regarding the ending" (*antāpavāda*).
That which is set forth or suspended by means of the exception is the "general rule" (*ussagga*). This is the sequence of general rules and exceptions.
In this context, it should be understood as follows:
"chaṭṭhiyantasse" is the general rule (ussagga), while its exceptions are "ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassa," "ukānubandhādyantā," and "mānubandho sarā namantā paro.
Furthermore, "ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbasse" is the general rule, while its exceptions are "vānubandho" and "mānubandho sarānamantā paro."

19. By stating the purpose for beginning the rule with "Ṭānu chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhassa iccādi" and so forth, he declares that this is a rule (*yoga*) which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ant* [at the end of a word].

He states that there is a separate connection (*paccekamabhisambandho*) by means of [the rule] beginning with "so ṭakārānubandho cādeso" and so forth, [specifying] "of what? of all [that is marked with the sixth case]."

And it says: “The sixth [case ending] is for that which has been specified,” and so forth. Now, since the substitute *ṭ* is also a multi-syllabic entity because it consists of a collection of two phonemes (*dvivaṇṇa*), one might suspect [it is not a marker];

therefore he says: “It is characterized (*upalakkhiye*)” and so forth. A "consonantal marker" (*anubandha*) is that which is attached; even when its usage is not heard, it is followed by virtue of its purpose.

By the phrase “it is characterized and then ceases during the very instruction (*upadesa*),” he shows this: “markers perish once they have been pronounced. “Instruction” refers to the first pronunciation.

20. When it is said, "The [words] beginning with *ñakā* and ending with *ati*," one asks: "How is this meaning of 'exclusion of a part' obtained? To this he says: "Of words beginning with *ādi* and ending with *anta*," and so forth.
Because words such as *ādi* and *anta* denote specific parts, and because a part cannot exist without a whole (*avayavin*), the whole is implied by the force of the context (*sāmatthiya*).
It is indicated [by the genitive]; because of the recurrence of the word "genitive" (*chaṭṭhiyā*), this genitive expresses a relationship between a part and the whole.

The meaning is understood as follows: "of that which is specified by that [genitive]," thus it is stated in the *Vutti* as ‘chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhassa’. For this very reason, in the rules for suffixes (*paccaya-vidhi*), there are no faults regarding the suffix *kū* and others.
"Precisely because of this" means precisely because of its being a non-sentient part (*tadavayavācittato*). "By the mention of that" means by the mention of the part.

"Regarding the application of *vu* whether [the suffix] *otta* has been applied or not": because there is the possibility (*pasaṅga*) of the substitution of *vu* both when *otta* has been applied and when it has not, for since *otta* is more numerous, when *bhū* is employed, even if *otta* has been applied, there must be the substitution of *vu*;

and even if it has not been applied, for that very reason—on account of the rule "The procedure concerning the application of *vu* whether [the suffix] has been applied or not is eternal"—because it is eternal, the substitution of *vu* occurs by setting aside *otta*. Then, after the substitution of *vu*, by that...
He said, "It should not be so," beginning with the words "in a part that is an end" (*antāvayave*), and so forth.
21. Regarding the suffix *m*:

if it is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*), then because the genitive case is unspecified (*avisesitattā*) as being "at the end," the suffix *m* is added without distinction from whichever [word] ends in an *anta*.

It might be argued that there is no second mention of "vowels" (*sara*) by which the end could be specified; therefore, he says, "selection" (*niddhāraṇa*), and so forth. He states the reason: "because it is heard" (*sutattā*).

The meaning is "of vowels" (*sarānaṃ*) because it is heard. By this, he demonstrates that, according to the principle—"the connection with what is heard is stronger than what is inferred"—there is no *num* augment for the letter *dh*, which is here inferred, as it is obstructed [by the heard vowel].
For in the world, [a rule applies] only to that which is of the same class (*samānajātīya*).
He says "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth to indicate that this is a case of specific selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
Just as when it is said, "The black cow among cows is the one with the most excellent milk," even though no distinction is explicitly stated, one understands that it is specifically the black cow;

so too here, when [the vowel] is selected from among vowels by virtue of being final or ultra-final, one understands that it is specifically a vowel of the same class. Therefore, it will be the final [vowel] of the vowels themselves.
The term *bhāvo* means "the purpose of specification. In the rule *ñilatasse* (5-163), since it is stated simply *assa*, there is no restriction that it must refer to this [specific] one;

therefore, the substitution of *ñi* would apply to any and every *a*. Consequently, because an undesired result would follow, the *yaṃ* which is the purpose of the specification—that is, the purpose (*attho*) or motive (*payojana*)—of the letter *la* in the rule *kattarilo* (5-18) is [indicated] by the suffix *lānusaṅgissa eva assa*. This is the meaning of the specification.
The letter *la* [indicates] "in this very [rule]," namely in this very sutta beginning with "a consonant suffix (*mānubandho*). 22. *Vippaṭi* and *para* are recurring terms;

although they have many meanings such as "other," "superiority," and "desired," here they should be understood as signifying "desired" (*iṭṭha*). [The suffix] *ghaṇ* occurs in the sense of the reciprocal action (*kammabyatihāra*).

The exchange of functions (*kammabyatihāra*) is the reversal of action, a particular state of being (*bhāvaviseso*). Regarding that, because it is prescribed generally by the rule “*ghaṇ* and *ghakā* [are used] for the agent of the state” (*bhāvakārake*), there is a negation;
thus, in the sense of a negation, there is *ghaṇ*. Therefore he says: “generally,” and so forth. He states the meaning of the word *vippaṭisedha* as “mutual negation.
Although *sidhi* occurs in the sense of accomplishment (*saṃsiddhiyaṃ*), [it is used here in the sense of negation].
"In connection with a prefix, [the term] occurs even when there is no difference in meaning"—this means "mutual contradiction.
He states that the word *vippaṭisedha* (contradiction) is well-known in the world as denoting opposition by saying "for thus," and so forth.

Having raised the doubt, "How indeed can mutual contradiction be possible in the words of the Teacher, who is himself the authority? he replies that it is possible provided both [terms] have scope (*sāvakāsatta*).
"Not otherwise" means that the textual passage beginning with "of two," etc., is what is being discussed. He says "sorrowing," etc., in order to state [the meaning].
"Not mutually dependent" means not occupied by or not embraced by one another; this is what is meant.

"Not partaking of both" refers to a portion of the object that does not belong to both; in that portion of the object which does not partake of both, there is the common object of the two affirmative rules.
The connection is that when there is the possibility of occurrence (*pavatti*) regarding a common object (*sādhāraṇo visayo*), a negation (*vippaṭisedho*) arises;

by this, he indicates that the object of the negation is the possibility of occurrence, and that in the Sutta the term "negation" (*vippaṭisedho*) is stated through the non-difference of the object and the subject of the negation.
He explains that the textual composition beginning with "of two" (*dvinnam*) was composed because the other [alternative] is shown to be threefold. If...
It shows that one should say "the subsequent [rule] prevails" (*parovā hoti*) when there is a conflict with a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

For according to the followers of Pāṇini, a grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*) applies only once to a single word-meaning (*padattha*) within a given class; thus, because its function is already fulfilled, neither of the two rules would apply to another object-domain.

This statement is for the purpose of prescribing that the subsequent (later) operation takes effect. However, in the case of a *byatti* (an individual instance), it is like the substitution of *la* and so forth in a word-meaning.
In the context of a figurative treatment (*pariyāyappasaṅge*), they have undertaken [the practice] with the sense of a restriction (*niyamattha*);

however, here, since neither of the two suttas applies to both birth (*jāti*) and proficiency (*byatti*), this statement is intended to establish the sense of an injunction (*vidhyattha*), and not the sense of a restriction. To demonstrate this, he says: "For thus," and so forth;
the connection is that it is completed according to one's own inclination (*kāmacārato*). If there is completion according to one's desire, then in all cases of one's own...

Because of the existence of its occurrence through uninterrupted pervasion within its own domain (*gocara*). Anticipating the objection, "How could there not be an occurrence even for that which is manifold?
he states the reason, beginning with "Both of these," etc. The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmā*);

because both of these are the words of the Teacher (*ācariya*), for that very reason they are authoritative (*pamāṇa*), since they are accepted by those who know grammar (*saddika*) as having the nature of a prescriptive mark (*liṅga-bhāva*) in the formulation of desired injunctions (*vidhāna*).
And because it is prescriptive, that is the meaning. He states the reason for the non-application of both [rules] due to their being authoritative measures:
“In the case of what pertains to neither,” and so forth. Since they have found their scope, they are therefore of equal strength; the word *iti* here denotes a reason.

By supplying the word *iti* after “and from the contradictory,” [the sense is: “Because these two statements—‘in the case of what pertains to neither,’ etc., and ‘from the contradictory’—are authoritative measures, there is the non-operation of both.”

The connection should be understood. Since in the world it is observed that when two things of equal strength oppose one another, there is a cessation of activity for both at the very same moment, he provides the illustration beginning with "In the world indeed" (*loke ce*).
And here, just as there is a cessation of activity for a servant who desires non-opposition, so too there is a cessation of activity for the operations of both statements of equal strength.
"Non-occurrence" (appavatti) is to be understood as a comfortable connection with the analogy.

Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of two [factors] by means of a single expression within the same class of birth (*jātipakkhe*), the possibility of alternation (*pariyāya*) was described—as in the case of "latva" and so on.
Demonstrating its inappropriateness, he said "nor even... and so forth; "because the objects are distinct" refers to the two prescriptions (*vidhi*).

Because their objects are distinct. For the application of synonyms is logical only when the objects are not distinct; therefore, in order to demonstrate that *la*-sounds and the rest have non-distinct objects, he says:

"For *la*-sounds and the rest," etc. By the phrase "without distinction" (*anavayavena*), it means by way of including all roots, since there is no possibility of excluding any part due to the rule being prescribed for the root as a whole.
Thus, while they occur in common within a certain portion of the meaning of a root...
The connection is that even by the omission or the abandonment of a portion of it, they would not be established;

and because [suffixes] such as *la* and so forth are impossible at one and the same moment, and because there would follow the consequence of the other verbal forms becoming redundant if one were already produced, they occur by way of alternation (*pariyāyena*)—this is the logical conclusion. "Here" (*iha*) means in this case of simultaneous production.
Here, he states the cause for such being the case: “The disciples... [and] the word. In that context, “therein” refers to simultaneous occurrence.

Regarding the meaning of the word *jāti*, he says “*parasmiṃ ce*,” etc., providing the application of both maxims (*paribhāsanā*)—namely, “the understanding of recurrence is established” and “in a prohibition, that which is sublated remains sublated”—by saying “*parasminti iṭṭhe*,” and as for the maxim itself...

This meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase “the understanding of the recurrence [of a rule]” (*punappasaṅgavijānanā*), when there is a conflict—known as the recurrence of two rules for a single purpose—the first [rule] is intended to apply.

If, while that [first rule] is applying, it does not cause an obstruction to the cause (*nimitta*) of the other, then the recurrence of that [other rule] and the understanding thereof are established; provided that such a conflict exists as described, the first [rule applies].
"If there is no cause for the recurrence of a rule that has been set aside by another, then that [rule] remains set aside.

To show that even in the case of *byatti* (the specific instance), this statement has the purpose of prescribing (*vidhi*) rather than restricting (*niyama*), he says: "In the case of *byatti*," and so forth.
He thinks thus: "In the case of *byatti*, which is the occurrence of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) that serves as a counter-indication (*paṭilakkhiya*), with respect to a position common to both..."

"Since those statements which appear contradictory are equal in strength due to their lack of scope for alternative application, there must be a dual practice for both, and not the possibility of them being merely figurative (pariyāya).
Showing that even regarding these contradictions, the occurrence of the aforementioned criticisms follows the stated method, he says: "Of the criticisms... and so forth.
Regarding the category of the present tense (*vattamāna*): although the grammatical markers (*lakkhaṇa*) such as *ti*, *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*,

and *mhe* are prescribed for each individual meaning within the present tense, they are designated as the first person (*paṭhama*) throughout their entire respective scope whenever there is even a single instance of occurrence—
such as in the partial phrases *gacchati* and so forth, or *gaccha* and *si* and so forth— within the context of the present tense.

The section on the singular number of the second person is completed. Because its purpose has been fulfilled, in the case of "you two go" (*tumhe gacchatha*), when two men act simultaneously, there is no [distinction] for either one; even in the case of proficiency, the characteristics do not differ from one another.
Thus, in a common situation where two act at the same time, their characteristics are distinguished by what is shared.

This statement—“there is no [simultaneous occurrence] for anyone”—is spoken with reference to the absolute non-occurrence of the three types of persons at a single moment, precisely according to the method already described.

With the intention that “the other becomes” means it becomes middling or superior, he spoke the words beginning with “kvapanā” after having brought forward the *Vutti* text starting with “yathā” etc. by way of a question; this is not our own example.
It does not cause confusion (*manaṃ bhoseti*), because this [rule] does not even fall within the scope of prohibition;

how much less so since it is established by specific portions of sentences such as "in the present tense" (*vattamāne*) and "anti," etc., which prescribe the particular person-endings for the preceding and following sets of six, namely:
"For the preceding and following sets of six, when they are singular or plural, *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* remain; the two [endings] are the second and first persons respectively. (6-14)
When the verbal form *tīmi* is employed with the second person plural (*tumhāmhase*), whether it is actually used or not, two forms each—
corresponding respectively to the first six cases and the subsequent six cases, and specifically to the middle and supreme persons—
arise in their respective order; thus, in the expression "gacchatha gacchāmā," there is no simultaneous occurrence at a single moment.

For the prohibition applies only to the simultaneous occurrence of two disciples; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was cited so that one might also be able to formulate the prohibition according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, the unconfused operation of this grammatical rule should be understood by the method stated for the word "ādissa," which concerns what has been done and what has not been done.
That which is a rule (*vidhi*) is permanent (*nicca*), whereas this [rule] is impermanent (*anicca*).

Because of the inequality of strength between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*) rules thus described as permanent and impermanent, this conjunction (*yoga*) has no operation. For among the permanent and impermanent, the permanent alone is stronger;

this inequality of strength between the permanent and impermanent will be explained later in the sutta beginning with "there is elision" (*lopo*, 1.39). We shall clarify the manner in which they function as internal and external there.
23. Regarding the statement "The convention (saṅketa)," he explains the fruit of the commencement of the discourse with the words "as for what was called 'the connection' (anubandha)," and so forth.

Although it is stated generally in the commentary that "convention is not a constituent part [of the treatise]," because of the phrase "I shall speak the Māgadhī grammar" (*saddalakkhaṇa*), it is [understood as] the grammar of words.
To show that it is understood from the *Abhidhānappakaraṇa* that [the letter] is not a constituent part of the sound, he says: "Of what," etc.
The letter *l* in the suffix *tu* is the example; this is stated in order to explain the appropriate meaning of the sentence beginning with "of the aggregate such as the base (*pakati*), etc.
The phrase "so some say" refers to certain authors of grammatical treatises, intending Pāṇini; the term "statement" refers to the rule *tassa lopo* (Pāṇini 1.3.9).
The word *payogāsamavāyitā* means non-association with the application [of a suffix], that is, the state of not being employed when used in constructions such as "the agent" (*kattā*) and so forth;

this is the intended meaning, and thus its elision (*lopa*) should be understood in this way. They say that the prefix *anu-* has the sense of binding and destruction, based on this etymological derivation (*saddabyuppatti*):
because it causes the uttered [word] to perish, it is bound and destroyed, and thus it is called *anubandho*.
24. *Vaṇṇa* (‘By this’):
Here, *ata* may be a designation for individual short vowels, or a designation for the class of short vowels, or a designation for the entire category of meanings pervading all their bases.
In that case, if it is a designation for individual short vowels, [it applies] to *buddha*, *siddha*, and so forth, wherever they may occur.

If the letter *a* were taken [in the rule], the desired result would not be established because it would fail to apply to certain cases; however, in the description of the short vowel class (*rassajātiniddesa*), the letter *a* is taken to include all endings beginning with *a*, such as those ending in *buddhasiddha* and others, as well as those like *gava* which end in *a* according to grammatical rules.

Thus, the desired result is established in every respect. There is no occurrence of an undesired result, because there is no long *ā* other than that which is distinct [from the short *a*], and because the long *ā* is absent from the short vowel class.
Therefore, in the description of the short vowel class, [the term] "from *at*" is used.
Since all this that is desired is accomplished by depending [on the rules], the short vowel (*jāti*) is not what is depended upon, nor is the shortness or distinctness (*byatti*).

However, in rules such as "yuvaṇṇānam e o luttā" (1-29), where there is a reference to shortness or the distinctness of the short vowel, the desired *eo* and so forth might occur in some instances, but not everywhere; or it might occur everywhere, as in "vāteritam."

In the cases of *samona*, etc., [the distinction] is dependent on the short vowel; therefore, for the sake of establishing the desired result in every respect, the genus (*jāti*) of the short vowel and so forth is excluded.

Alternatively, since one observes the arising of specific vowels through the combination of high, low, and both [registers] among certain places of vowel production even with respect to the utterance of a vowel, it is [distinguished] by way of those [places].
Thus, in the description of the short vowel (*rassa*), or in the description of the genus of the short vowel (*rassajāti*).

By the method already stated, when there is the attainment of the desirable and the undesirable, in order to establish the desirable in every way and in all respects, this statement—"itajjātyādi nissīyate"—is commenced so as to restrict the inclusion of "homogeneous" (*savaṇṇa*) by means of the word "color" (*vaṇṇa*). He states the purpose for commencing this statement with the words "sabbatthevā" and so forth;
"sabbatthevā" means in every single instance of the sutta's application. [An objection is raised: "But would it not have been sufficient even if one had simply said 'sayañca' (and itself)?"

The connection is as follows: since it is established that there is no form other than itself, nor that form belongs to something else, even so, the author of the *Vutti* stated "both consciousness and form" (*sañca rūpañca*) in order to make known that there is some further distinction here.

Because form is that which is to be qualified, and because it is being pointed out in the *Vutti* by the phrase "both consciousness and form," it is understood as "form. Thus: "both consciousness and..."
It is stated, "it is grasped. Regarding one who utters the word *api* for the purpose of grasping a similar form (*saṃrūpa*), he says "otherwise," etc., to state the intended meaning.

"Otherwise" means in another manner, that is, in the absence of the word *api* for the purpose of grasping a similar form; this is the intended meaning. "In the case of another referent" (*aññapadatthe*) means in the domain of compounds where there is another referent.
"Of that which has become subordinate" (*guṇībhūtassa*) refers to [the vowel] *ā*, *i*, and so forth, which have become non-primary within the compound. By means of the compound...

Because it has been stated that even when [the suffix] *padhānatū* is applied, there is a grammatical quality (*guṇa*) for the external referent (*aññapadattha*), such as the vowels *kā*, *ī*, and so on;

and since that which is being prescribed is itself the primary element (*padhāna*)—as it is said, "this exists for the sake of its occurrence"—is it not the case that, when explaining the meaning of the word *api* in the commentary, one ought to have said "and itself" (*sayañca*)?
For according to the *Nighaṇḍu*, the meaning is that both "itself" (*sayam*) and the vowels *ttā*, *kā*, *ī*, and so on, are taken.

Regarding the objection that [the word] "is possible," it is stated—"if he himself," and so forth—in order to show that when one says "and form" while placing the challenge in the mind, one speaks thus to reveal a specific meaning based on a particular intention.

According to the Nighaṇḍu statement, "The word *saṃ* is used for wealth and kinsmen, as well as for the self and one's own," the word "he" (*sa*) also includes the self. What is that? It is the nature of the sound.
It is common; there is also that which belongs to oneself (*attaniya*). However, what is uncommon to sounds is the specific form of sound (*saddarūpa*).
That being so, the form belonging to oneself is related to the sound designated as "self"; thus he says: "The specific form of sound is the uncommon form of sounds.
And this [phrase] is to be connected with "this" (*idam*); "uncommon" means the uncommon form of sound.

Since a qualifier is meaningful only when there is the possibility of its application and the possibility of deviation, it was stated that "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) form is a qualification even though the possibility of it being common (*sādhāraṇa*) also exists; thus he says, “For it is twofold,” and so on.

To indicate "form" (*rūpa*) in general—namely, what that is, whether common or uncommon—he says, “Therein,” and so on. Here, “therein” (*tattha*) is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*), [referring] to “sounds” (*saddānaṃ*).
Regarding words—whether meaningful or meaningless—of whatever kind, such as the words *buddha*, *ai*, and so forth, there is their respective "word-ness" (*saddatta*) and so on;
in both cases, the word *ādi* (and so forth) includes the "meaning.

By this, he shows that the nature of the word (*saddarūpa*) and the nature of the meaning (*attharūpa*) are each fourfold: namely, the common [nature], and likewise the uncommon. This applies to all four.
In order to show the basis for sound-form (*saddarūpa*) alone, which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*) among mental phenomena, he says “therein,” and so forth. The connection is as follows:
by the exclusion of common form—that is, by the abandonment of common form—he shows that one apprehends only the form of sound itself, and not [anything else], such as "it does not exist.
Furthermore, the word “and” (*ca*) here collects what was stated previously, namely, “this shows. This occurs when there is the apprehension of that which is indeed unique.
He states the reason: “*taṃ taṃ*,” etc. “*Itaraṃ*” means that which is common to all sounds, such as their being sound (*saddattādi*). “*Parassāpi*” means even for any other sound whatsoever.
Thus, this is established (*patitaṃ*) and well-known (*pasiddhaṃ*). Here, however, the word *iti* indicates a reason (*hetu*);
because this aforementioned [quality] is well-known, therefore it has come down from the lineage of former teachers by way of partial tradition (*padesato*).

"Upādiyanti" means "they grasp. By the power of the specific qualification of the word *saṃsa* (sound), even when grasping the non-common form (*rūpa*) of what is grasped, it is specifically the non-common *sadda-rūpa* (the form of sound) that is grasped, and not the non-common *attha-rūpa* (the form of meaning).

Because of this reason which will be stated later, he says "of the sound," etc., by way of that [text]. It is "proximate" because, due to the nature of sound, there is no difference from sound; thus, it is "by way of reversal."

The meaning is "by way of reversal" or "in the sense of not being proximate. For how could even the object of the eye (visible form) not be considered proximate to the sound that is the object of the ear?
To state another reason, he says: "And because it is not to be abandoned," and so forth. "Not to be abandoned" means not to be relinquished;
this too is a statement of the reason for their constant association. That which is the nature of sound is "constantly associated."

It is that which possesses uninterrupted conjunction; it is to be abandoned because it is the opposite [of the noble path]. Thus, by means of the word *tathāhi* (for instance), it makes known the state of being abandonable (*heyyattā*) of the object.

He states another reason with the words: "And because its form is uncommon," and so forth. Synonyms for words are common, whereas this [form] is to be understood (*paccetabbattā*) as that which is to be cognized.
Now, having combined these three reasons, by these causes the very form is the designation (*saṃnāma*) of the sound.
The phrase beginning with "tadeva" was commenced in order to demonstrate, having restricted [the meaning] by saying "it does not exist. The meaning of "tadeva" is: because it is thus, therefore that;
[this refers to] "in a word where the same form is predominant," such as in "gossā vaṅa" (1.32), etc., [meaning] in a word like "gossā" where the same form is predominant.
25. Ntu.
In order to prevent the unintended application [of suffixes] such as *jantu* and others to the word *anta*— given the rule "the *anta* which is in the first [case], etc. (2-215)—
this [section] beginning with "vantu- and vaṇṇa- [suffixes]" (4-79), "that which has the sense of 'being there' is called *mantu*" (4-78),

and "the *ktavantu* and *ktāvī* [suffixes] denote the agent in the past tense" is commenced, so that the suffixes *vantu* and others may be applied specifically to individuals (*byatti*) rather than to the genus (*jāti*).
Thus are the [grammatical operations] such as *vanti* and so forth prescribed.
Thus ends the section on *Paribhāsā* (Technical Rules) in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*,
a commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*.
Commentary on *Saralopādi*:

26. "Support" (*saro*) means "relying upon a specific supporting surface"; that is, relying upon a specific contiguous supporting surface (*opasilesikādhāra*). It refers to the contiguous supporting surface.

The connection is as follows: when another substratum (*ādhāra*) is apprehended, it is not possible to effect an exclusion of what is separated (*vyavahita-nivatti*) without another statement or another sutta.
The phrase "some" indicates the teachers Buddhapiya and others;

for they [hold that] if a euphonic combination (*sandhi*) were to occur even when there is an intervention by a consonant (*vaṇṇa*) or time (*kāla*), then the mention of the condition "in a vowel" (*sare*) would be purposeless.

Regarding the word *bhaveyya*, they recall that because of the capacity for the appropriation of the sign (*nimitta*), there is no euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*) when there is an intervention by [the words] *vaṇṇa* and so forth;
thus, thinking this, they state the sentence beginning with *animitta*. That is incorrect. The meaning is that what was stated by them through the phrase *animitta* and so forth is incorrect.
As for the reason for its being incorrect, it is precisely the absence of such capacity due to the presence of deviation (*byabhicāra*). Having thus demonstrated the deviation:
