In order to demonstrate the absence of functional capacity, he said: "At the end, etc. Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of a grammatical operation," it means that the nasal dot (*bindu*), which is the sign known as *anta-bindu*, occurs not only when there is an intervention by a vowel at the time of pronunciation—as in "This alone is the truth; may they be well-disposed" (*idaṃ eva saccaṃ, sumanā bhavantu*)—but also at the very end, as in "These are not [true];
may there be well-being" (*ete na saccena suvatthi hotū*), and in cases such as "Heedlessness is the path of Death" (*pamādo maccuno padaṃ*).
The meaning of the word *api* is that even in the absence of a function (*kāriya*), there is a purposefulness (*sātthakatā*) for the grasping of the sign;

it is stated as "purposeful" (*sātthakato*) either by the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvappaccaya*) or by emphasizing the state (*bhāvappadhāna*), whereby it is effectively said to be "because of its purposefulness.

Otherwise, if only the grasping of the sign itself were called "purposeful," the expression "because of the purposefulness of the grasping of the sign" would not be logical; this is the intended meaning here at the conclusion.

Alternatively, because there is the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of an effect, there is no functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*) characterized by "otherwise-unaccountability" (*aññathānupapatti*) in the case of a cause (*nimitta*);
however, such a cause exists even when there is an intervention, as in the expression "approaching the forest for the sake of wood.

Therefore, even when there is an intervention by the time of coloring (*vaṇṇakāla*), if the cause exists, one attains the operation of elision (*lopakāriya*) according to the rule: "or [it occurs] when the cause is present. It is elided by the rule beginning with "tatrime" and so forth.

The meaning is that it is not seen at the time of speaking; for elision (*lopa*) is merely non-appearance. Otherwise, due to the absence of the forms of words such as *tattha*, there would be no comprehension of the meaning, and thus the causative function (*kāritta*) of these [suffixes] would not occur.
Because it is stated [as] "nominated in the nominative" (*paṭhamāya niddiṭṭho*), one might say [the rule applies to] the object (*kamma*);

however, because the suffix *khādi* expresses the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object is not explicitly stated. By the word *iha*, [it is shown that] in another treatise it functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).

It clarifies the inclusion [of the term *sara*]. Regarding "the elision of a vowel" (*saralopa*): because it cannot be said that "it attains elision" or "it undergoes elision," and because the word *sara* is specified in the nominative case, there might be the suspicion that "the elision of a vowel" (*saro lopo*) refers to the vowel itself. Therefore, he says "if not" (*na ce*), etc.

Here, "here" (*iha*) means in this rule (*sutta*). Furthermore, fearing that "being" (*honti*), etc., might also be subject to the elision of the preceding vowel—as in "he kills" (*hanti*), etc.—he says "and if," etc.

The term *ossaggika* means "derived from a general rule (*ussagga*) or produced from it," or "this belongs to that"; thus, it is a compound with the elision of the initial syllable (*pubbalopa*). The state of being such is *ossaggikatta*.

This *ossaggikatta*, due to the elision of the initial syllable, is indeed overridden by exceptional rules (*apavādavidhi*) such as the elision of the following syllable (*paralopa*) through other grammatical operations; yet, that elision of the initial syllable still occurs—this is the connection [of the sentence].

By the inclusion of the word "sometimes" (*kvaci*) in the rule "the following [syllable] is sometimes elided" (*paro kvacī*, 91-27), both the elision of the preceding and the elision of the following syllables are permitted.

Due to the absence of equal strength, just as there is the nature of denial regarding the destruction of the next world (*paralopa*) because it has not been reached by one's own experience, so too, when [the mind] has entered into what is clung to, it does not exist...

because it is obstructed by the denial of the destruction of the next world. "By those" means by the denial of the next world and so forth. The faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) has an object that is entirely free from such things;
or rather, its object is free from conceptual construction (*vikappa*).
27. The connection is as follows: the statement "The word *iti* in the sense of ‘this’ is sometimes subject to elision" indicates this [rule]. To the question "In what way?", he says:
"according to usage. To the question "Of what?", he says: "of the grammatical operation consisting of the elision of the subsequent [element]. To the question "By what cause?", he says: [as follows].
Regarding the phrase "by the inclusion of *kvaci*": as to where [this occurs], he says, "here, in this sutta.

By that—that is, by the indication of the conformity to usage—and according to usage, meaning without transgressing the application of the grammatical tradition (*āgama*), there would always be elision of the following vowel (*paralopa*) after the insertion (*pakkheva*).

Thus, in cases such as *honti* and so forth, there is always [elision]; and in cases such as *latāvā*, there might be elision of the following vowel after the insertion. He thinks thus: "In what sense is it *kvā*? [The answer is: in the sense of "where" (*kasmin*).

Because it functions with an indefinite meaning through a word that expresses an indefinite sense by way of a derivative formation (*nipphanna*), and because it functions with an indefinite meaning in all instances when used in speech, the word *kvaci*—according to the traditional grammatical sources (*āgama*)—illuminates three types of rules: permanent, non-permanent, and non-existent.

Among these, the "permanent" category, such as *honti* and so forth, is the domain of the elision of the *parā* (the following vowel); the "non-permanent" category, such as *latā* and so forth, is common to both [the permanent and non-permanent].

"By the statement ‘the elision of the preceding [syllable] (*pubbalopa*) is also its domain,’ it follows that in the case of the *nicca* (eternal) alternative, there is elision of the subsequent (*paralopa*);

however, in the case of the *asanta* (non-existent) alternative, such as ‘the faculty of faith’ (*saddhindriya*), etc., the elision of the preceding alone is the domain, because this [latter] has been entirely excluded by the former.

Furthermore, among these three alternatives, it is only in the *nicca* and *anicca* alternatives that there is the nature of negation (*apavāda-rūpatā*) regarding the elision of the preceding, because of its function as a preventer of the elision of the subsequent and so forth occurring in every respect.
Or [it may be] by way of being an injunction for the elision of the subsequent [syllable], but not on the side of non-existence...

since the "daytime" (vasaratta) has been given in every respect by this very [rule] through the elision of the preceding [syllable]. As for the phrase "the foremost of the world" (lokagga), etc., because it serves as an indicator following the usage of the word *kvaci*, it is produced either by the elision of the subsequent [syllable] even when the injunction is indicated as being eternally non-existent;
thus, there is no contradiction with the *Nettippakaraṇa*. Such, then, is the case regarding the inclusion of the term *kvaci*.

The attainment of the desired [result] occurs through the avoidance of everything undesirable; how could it be otherwise in its absence? To state the contradiction in the case of its absence, he says, “In another way” (*aññathā*), and so forth.
If there were no mention of "in some cases" (*kvaci*) regarding those that occur by way of alternative application (*pariyāyena*), then the rule “the subsequent” (*paro*) would apply.

If that were so, the two rules would share the same domain and possess equal force. In that situation, since there would be no mutual exclusion (*vippaṭisedha*), the words of the authoritative teachers would be rendered purposeless.
The meaning of *mā bhavī* is "let there not be"; *iti* refers to this reason for occurrence by way of alternation (*pariyāya*).

[In the example] *pakkheva siyā*, because the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbalopa*) occurs when there is occurrence by way of alternation, the elision of the following vowel (*paralopa*) does not occur;
thus, [the form] would be *latāvāti* with the elision of the following vowel only in the case of *pakkheva*. The connection is that [the form] would not always be *honti* and so forth. And *tañca*...
The phrase *pariyāyabhavanaṃ* is used as a stylistic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāre*). The word *paṭipadaṃ* is synonymous with *padaṃ padaṃ*;
it does not exclude even a single instance. Therefore, he said "nowhere" (*na katthaci*). By this, he illustrates:

"In every case, due to attachment to alternative forms, undesirable forms such as *hanti*, *saddhindriyaṃ*, and so forth, also occur even in the Sutta beginning with 'not twice' (*na dvevā*) [Dhp 1-28] where one finds *hanti* and so on. If it were not desired in this way...
The meaning is that this aforementioned method of grammatical analysis is not even accepted by those who know the characteristics of words (*saddalakkhaṇaññū*);
he establishes that very point with the words "for there would be loss of the subsequent," and so forth.

Alternatively, if the loss of the subsequent were made in the case of the view that [the suffixes] are eternal, then in the place abandoned by it, two forms—*latā* and *latevā*—would result due to the application of the general rule (*ussagga*). Therefore, by means of what indicates conformity with usage...

Although there is the possibility of usage such as "the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is like a creeper" or "it is just like a creeper" by means of the word *kvaci* itself, nevertheless, since the third form [of the suffix] is established in the sense of impermanence (*anicca*) as "like a creeper," one should consider that it must occur by way of a figurative application (*pariyāya*), as indicated by the phrase "Is it not so? and so forth.

Now, one might reflect: "If the word *kvaci* is used in the sense of 'elsewhere' (*paro kvaci*), then because it is an exception (*apavāda-rūpa*), how can there be a figurative application? Thus he takes it to mind.

Having placed [the matter] on the side of impermanence, for the purpose of illustrating its occurrence by way of synonymy (*pariyāya*), he states that there is no fault even in the threefold form regarding the occurrence by way of synonymy—even in the exception (*apavāda*) where the Sutta says "not in two ways"—with the words "this is not a fault," and so forth.

Furthermore, with the words "for it is thus," and so forth, he establishes that the very Sutta stating "not in two ways" itself illustrates synonymy; and that occurrence in a single sense does not exist without synonymy.
"It is not possible... because they do not exist simultaneously at one moment"—this is the intended meaning.
But surely, since the aforementioned fault would apply even to a figurative usage (*pariyāya*) where something is absent in some respect, let there be no such figurative usage.

However, when the elision of the preceding and following [members] occurs with respect to distinct objects in a prohibition such as "not two," the three forms *lateva*, *latāva*, and *latāiva* are produced. Keep this objection in mind.
Having set this down, he says "nace" and so forth; therein he states the fault with the words "tathā ca sati" and so forth:
in some cases, such as *dem*, there is always elision of the preceding (*pubbalopa*); in some cases, such as *honti*, there is always elision of the following (*paralopa*);
or optionally, in some cases, such as *yathodakaṃ* or *yathāudakaṃ*, there is elision of the preceding; and in some cases, such as *itipi* or *iccapic*, there is elision of the following.
The connection is as follows: in some instances, just as in the case of *latā iva latā iva*, because both [the particle *iva*] are elided through a sequence of synonyms, both are seen to be dropped.

In this context, by the phrase "even here" (*ettha ca*), which illustrates that the rule is a fixed option (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*), when the elision of the subsequent [particle] is applied by the word "in some cases" (*kvaci*), the elision of the preceding [particle] is reached elsewhere;

thus, in the case of "not twice" (*na dvevā*), where the constant prohibition is maintained by the force of the particle *kvaci* being carried over (*anuvattamāna*), there is indeed *iccapi* (or *iccapi*).

It exists. It is connected to various suttas. Regarding "delimitation" (*pariccheda*), he says "it is delimited" (*paricchijjati*) and so forth, by way of the object of action (*kamma-attha*) or by way of the locus (*ādhāra*).
28. Not two.

The word *ca* (and) must be supplied here; for if that were so, then [the phrase] "he consumed that as one consumes water" (*aññoññam ajjhāsi taṃ yathodakaṃ yathāudakan*) and so forth would also be included under the category of *icca*, *picca*, and *ādica*.

Thus, since both alternatives—elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbalopa*) and elision of the following vowel (*paralopa*)—would apply by way of option, how can this be justified? He raises this objection with the words "If indeed... (*yajjeva*), etc. "If indeed" (*yajjeva*) means...

For this collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) occurs in the sense of initiating an undesirable state; thus, the meaning is "if it is understood in this way," and from the context, "then" (*tadā*) is understood.
He states the reason for the constant absence of *sandhi*-operations: "because of the presence of proximity" (*upaseleṣā-bhāvato*).

He supports that very point with the words "for in such cases," etc., by means of the phrase "because of the desire to speak," [indicating] that the conjunction of phonemes is separated by only a half-mora (*maddha-matta-kāla*).
This indicates that the rule for *sandhi* (euphonic combination) applies only when there is a desire for the expression of proximity (*paccāsatti*) and contiguity (*saṇṇikaṃsa*).
The phrase "or the absence of contiguity" means that there is indeed an absence of contiguity, and not otherwise; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "and in the absence of that," he states the reason for the absence of the *sandhi* operation: "because of being separated by an interval of time."
"By another time" means by a time situated between [the two], distinct from the time of pronunciation of the vowels standing in both places;
thus, a *sandhi* (euphonic junction) indeed occurs because of the state of proximity resulting from the desire for words that are closely joined (*sannikasa-vacanicchā*).

For example, in "Buddha vīra atthurājaputtaṃ ajarāmara," there is a word-division (*chedo*), even though all of this has been stated [elsewhere] by such phrases as "if it were thus," etc., in some cases solely through the power of the sound (*saddappabhāvena*).
Even so, it is stated [in the commentary] to show that the particle *api* should also be joined with *satthe*.
29. [Objection:

Is it not the case that in the Sutta, because of the ablative designation "after elision" (*luttā*), there must be the word "of others" (* paresam*); however, since the expression "according to order" (*yathākkamam*) is absent, [how can the rule apply]?
To explain how this was stated according to the sequence, he said: “In equal [numbers]” (*sameccā*). Those in which the number—that is, the count—is the same are "equal in number" (*samasaṅkhyā*).

These are the "enumerators" (*uddesino*) and the "sub-enumerators" (*anudesino*). Enumerating first and subsequently explaining is "enumeration" (*uddeso*); subsequent speaking is "sub-enumeration" (*anudeso*).
Because they possess enumeration and sub-enumeration, they are called "the enumerators and sub-enumerators. Of those enumerators and sub-enumerators who are equal in number:

There are two *uddesina* (indicative) vowels, *i* and *u*, and two *anudesina* (corresponding) vowels, *e* and *o*; thus, there is an equality in number between the *uddesina* and *anudesina* bases and their substitutes.

Furthermore, when that [equality] exists, the *māda-sā* (the rules for replacement) are applied according to their respective order. He demonstrates that this is established by common usage with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
"Ava...pe... e o" is the opinion of others; "vippaṭipatti" means a contrary or conflicting application.

Regarding the admission [of the opponent]: others say, "Even though there is the mention of *heṭṭhā* (below), because the word *kvaci* is employed in the rule ‘kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte’ (*[the substitution occurs] sometimes when a vowel is elided*), the operation of *asavaṇṇa* applies only when a vowel is elided; therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *diṭṭhupādāna*.
They argue that the governing term *kvaci* does not apply here in cases such as *mahussavo* or *mātūpaṭṭhāna*. The prefix *pati-* has the sense of a locus (*ādhārattha*); by means of that—

Regarding the term *urasaddopi* (also the word *ura*), because it is always a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*), when the analysis (*viggaha*) is made with the word *urasi*, he says— “a numeral compound (*asaṅkhyasamāsa*)”—
in order to show that it is a numeral compound by the rule "an uncountable [word] takes the case endings" (3-2).

Here, however, in the context of the connection between the base and the substitute in the sense of proximity, collection, modification, part, and so forth, [the rule] "of vowels ending in *u* and *va*" (*yuvaṇṇānaṃ*) applies.
The sixth [case ending]; therefore, the meaning is that *e* and *o* are the substitutes (*ādesā*) in the place (*ṭhāne*) of the vowels *i* and *u*.
Now, "place" (*ṭhāna*) is threefold: displacement (*apakamso*), exclusion (*nivatti*), and occasion (*pasaṅgo*). Among these, the meaning of the word "place" in the sense of displacement is:
"Let horses belonging to cows be yoked [to the chariot]" (*jinindabuddhi*). In the sense of exclusion, it is: "A bitter medicine should be given in the place of phlegm."
There is the contingency [of the rule] that "in place of *dabbhānam*, [the substitution] of *sarehi* should be applied. Among those [three alternatives], here the first and second do not apply;
because the relationship between word and meaning is permanent, removal and destruction are not applicable. However, the third [alternative] applies:

when there is the contingency of the occurrence of *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels for the purpose of expressing the meaning in a sutta, the substitutes *e* and *o* occur for the very purpose of expressing that meaning.

30. Just as in the rule "In the seventh [case], when [a word] precedes" (1-14), because the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) is prescribed for what precedes, the state of being subsequent (*paratā*) is understood from that which is indicated by the locative case;
thus it is stated in the *Vutti* as "in the subsequent" (*pare*). Likewise in the following cases: "by subsequent [sounds], this [word] becomes unbound."
In order to establish [the forms] *sabboca* and *ajjhodhī*, which are taught in the Sutta, he says "this," etc., for the purpose of showing that these [forms] are to be rejected here.
Since the sense of *abbhakkhāna* (false accusation) is already established by this very [rule], it need not be stated as "*abbho abhī*";

thus, when *iti* + *assa* stands [as the basis], he says "there is elision of the subsequent [element] of *iti*" (*iti assa paralopo*) for the purpose of demonstrating the elision of the subsequent [element]. [The suffix] *-mā* is constant in cases such as *anvagamā*.
31. “Eo puttā me atthi, asanto ettha” is the word-division. 32.
Of the cow...

The purpose of the substitution of the final letter (*antādesattha*) is as follows: the rule *vānubandho* (1-18), which is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the rule *ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā* (1-19)—itself a sublater of the rule *chaṭṭhiyantassā* (1-17)—serves the purpose of substituting the final letter. For this very reason it is said: ‘This undertaking is for the purpose of subverting what has been subverted.

[In the case of] *gavāssaṃ* and *gavacchanti*, where there is the substitution of *ava* (*avavādese*), the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralope*), and the lengthening (*dīghe*), how is this established?
Regarding the connection [of the question], "What is accomplished without 'idam' and so forth?", he says:

‘evādisse’ti, etc. The word ‘evādi’ means that which begins with ‘eva’; the connection is: "without the substitution of ‘ri’ for that [‘eva’]". The word ‘ca’ (and) is used out of its usual position; it should be construed as ‘and the prescription of the short vowel’.
Even when that [substitution] has been made—that is, even when that rule has been applied—it is not accomplished; thus, the substitution of ‘ri’ for ‘evādi’ [is required].

It is not stated [in the rule] that it is "katvā," for it is said [as such] when [the word] stands as *bhusam eva*. However, by means of the great grammatical rule (*mahāvutti*), the formal derivation (*rūpasiddhi*) of the form indeed occurs through the substitution of *i* for *eva*.
But here, in order to establish [the meaning] in a different manner as "bhusāmiva," he says "tampi" and so forth. 33.
Consonant (*byañjana*).
Regarding the phrase "of short and long [vowels]," one might ask: since this is not explicitly stated in the Sutta, how is it understood that [the rule applies] to short and long vowels?

To answer this, he says: "Of a long vowel," and so forth. The genitive case in "of a long vowel" (*dīghassa*) and "of a short vowel" (*rassassa*) is used in the sense of a relationship of position (*ṭhāna*).

The term "according to their respective positions" (*paccāsatthā*) means according to their respective places. This is stated by way of dependence (*nissaya*); for the application of dependence is one method of the Teacher’s tradition. Here, [the vowel] is always applied.
It is a *thullaccaya* offense; it does not apply here—[as in the case of] "people in the evening.

34. Regarding "connection with the place" (*ṭhānasambandha*): "place" (*ṭhāna*) means a state of being situated or a context; "connection" (*sambandha*) means the act of connecting, characterized by the substitution of one thing for another.

The connection (*sambandha*) that serves as the basis for the application of the term "place" (*ṭhāna*) is the "connection with place" (*ṭhānasambandha*); in that context, the phrase "there are two forms" indicates by implication that it is not a case of "having the same form as the principal" (*sarūpappadhāna*). He states the reason:

"because of the use of the plural number. This statement—"there are two forms," etc.—shows this point: even when there is a word for "two" (*dvi*) where the same form is the principal, [the rule applies] by virtue of the commonality of the word "two."

"Because it is not taught by the word *dvi* (two) in the context of number, and because that [word] lacks the number belonging to the thing numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*), there is only the singular number (in the text).
By this, he shows that this demonstration has the meaning as its primary focus, not the literal form; thus, while "adhipatipaccayo, adhipatipaccayo" is variable, it does not occur here.
Regarding "he rejoices here," they dig there; this is a counter-example lacking one factor. We remember that because of the absence of a subsequent [vowel], there is no doubling. 35.
In the fourth group, why is it stated as "the third and first"? Because [it applies] only to the consonants of the groups by means of the fourth (second) sounds.

Such a description is appropriate when [the letters] are being grasped; for one might suspect that "the fourth," which completes four, or "the second," which completes two, are merely words [referring to positions], and thus he says "even without" (*vināpi*) and so forth.

The connection is as follows: even without the mention of the *vaggas* (consonant groups), the designation "fourth" and so on, when applied to the letters—that is, in the domain of letters—is conventionally established and well-known (*ruḷha*) precisely with respect to the letters of the *vaggas*.
The word *iti* has the sense of a reason; the intention is that because it is so, for that reason it is said, “In the third and first [sections] of those groups.
Regarding the term *tabbagge*, the meaning is: in whichever group there are the fourth and second [sections], in that very group.

To show that the word *paccāsatti* is derived from the root *sad* preceded by *pati*—meaning "to settle," "to go," or "to weary"—in the feminine gender with the suffix *ttim*, he says: “*paccāsīdana*,” and so forth.

Regarding "as appropriate" (*yathāyoggaṃ*): having transcended the application [of the rule] such that the third consonant of the fourth class [is substituted] for the fourth, and the first for the second, by the very statement "for *dh*, the state of *dha*" (*dhassa dabhāvo*), one indicates the substitution of *da* for the preceding *dh*;

thus, [we have] "the Elder Yasa" (*yasatthero*). Here, in the word "Elder" (*thero*), the vowel *e* is not a class-consonant (*vaggakkhara*); therefore, for that [consonant], there is the second consonant of the *ta*-class...

Therefore, *to* is not its first [consonant]. Regarding the word *pantho*: although there is the letter *na*, which belongs to the *ta*-group, preceded by the letter *tha*, the second letter of the *ta*-group, even when present, that *na* is not the second letter of the *ta*-group;

thus, *to* is not its first [consonant]. In this context, [the rule] "a sound (*nigghosa*) is a nasal (*nighosa*)" and so forth is optional (*anicca*), whereas [the rule] "that which is burnt is the conclusion (*niṭṭhāna*)" is obligatory (*nicca*).

36. *Vitissa*: The word *iti* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). An imitation of a particle is by its very nature an imitation; and imitation is twofold: the form of an incorrect word (*asādhu-sadda-rūpa*) and the form of a correct word (*sādhu-sadda-rūpa*).
Among these, when someone carrying a burden, being oppressed by it, should say "Ah, what a burden! but due to a deficiency in their faculties (*satti-vekalla*), [utters it incorrectly].
One says, “Oh, what a fool! (aho bāla). When someone standing near him is asked, “What did he say? he replies, “He said, ‘Oh, what a fool!

Here, *aho bāla* is an incorrect form of word (*asādhu-sadda-rūpa*), whereas *iti* is a correct form of word (*sādhu-sadda-rūpa*). Therefore, because it possesses meaning by way of imitating that [incorrect form], the sixth case is used in connection with the location (*ṭhāna-sambandhe*) due to its meaningfulness through imitation.
37. One might object: "Is it not possible to understand that, by carrying over the expression *vā* from [rule] 1-36 (*vitisseve vā*), the rule *avaṇṇe eonaṃ vo hoti* also applies?
That being so, since it should have been stated as ‘*avaṇṇe kvaci vo hoti*’, why was it said as ‘*ahoti vā*’? Anticipating this objection, he says: ‘*okārassapi*’ and so forth.

"Because it is indicated as the substitute" means that since the substitution of *va* in "enaṃ" (1-31) exists, one might think that when the substitution of *va* occurs, the letter *o* should not again be indicated as the substitute; with this intention he says [it is so].

"Not the cause" means that the vowel *avaṇṇa* is not the cause for the purpose of the substitution of *va* in "enaṃ"; "otherwise" means if *avaṇṇa* were the cause, [the rule would apply to] the letter *o*.
The connection is "one should not recite. Regarding the addition of the letter *m*:

according to the rule "when *ya* and *ka* follow, it is called the highest," in the case of the *tanap* suffix occurring after [the base] *sve* through the application of a *taddhita* function, there is the elision of the case-ending by the rule "in the state of having the same referent" (2-119), followed by the substitution of *a*, lengthening, and the addition of the *syādi* suffixes, resulting in *svātanaṃ*.
After reduplication, it becomes *hiyyattanaṃ*. In examples such as *svātanaṃ*, the [suffix] is always present; however, here it is not.
"And others do not understand.

38. Regarding the statement, "How does there come to be an augment (āgama)?"—if there were an augment consisting of a *niggahīta* (anusvāra), then there ought to have been the mention of "augment" (*āgama*) in the Sutta.

Or, suspecting that [the suffix] might be *tya* due to the specific nature of the *anubandha* *ña* and *ma*, he says: “Even in its absence,” and so forth. He states the reason for determining it as an *āgama* (augment) with the words:

“Because of the impossibility of being a substitute (*ādeśa*). He asks how this connection with being a substitute is understood, and replies: “Because there is no mention of a locus (*sthānin*). To this, he raises an objection:
“If that were so, since there would be no mention of a source (*āgamin*), it could not even be an *āgama*,” and so forth. Having rejected that objection with the word “no,” he [proceeds] to...
He states "tassā" and so forth in order to establish precisely what has been handed down [in the tradition]: "tassā" means of the *niggahīta*;
because it occurs following a short vowel, it follows only a short vowel sound. He says "etadeva" and so forth to state that this very meaning is also shown in the *Vutti*.

Regarding the phrase "the preceding class," when the short vowel is compounded with the qualifier, there is the addition of the *bindu* (anusvāra), because the subsequent cause [of the change] has not been specified.
In the word *bahusadda*, when the augment *bindu* (anusvāra) is added, it becomes *bahuṃ*.

Furthermore, although the word *kvaci*—which indicates [the rule] according to its application—is also of the nature of a fixed option (*vavatthitavibhāsa*), the commentary states, "Because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is of the nature of a fixed option," in order to demonstrate that the particle *vā* also functions as an indicator of that very same nature. This refers to the fixed optionality of the characterized (*lakkhiya*).

An analytical exposition (*vibhāsā*) that proceeds according to specific characteristics is a "defined analytical exposition" (*vavatthitavibhāsā*). However, when there is no distinction, it is governed by the general rule;

its state is "the state of being a defined analytical exposition" (*vavatthitavibhāsattaṃ*). Therefore, [in the case of] "here it does not exist, here he rejoices," because of the absence of a specific instruction regarding the substitute (*ṭhāniniddesa*) for that which is to be replaced (*ṭhāni*), the specific cause consisting of the application of the status of a substitute (*ādesattāyoga-saṅkhāta*) is capable [of establishing the meaning].

Its state (*bhāva*) is its capacity (*sāmatthiya*), characterized by the impossibility of [the meaning] occurring otherwise (*aññathānupapatti-lakkhaṇa*); and *sa* means that traditional authority (*āgama*).

39. Regarding *lopa*: he says ‘tene’ and so forth in order to establish that the word *lopa* functions solely as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). If *lopa* were a noun denoting the object (*karmasādhana*), [it would refer to the thing being deleted].
If it were possible, one might have begun the sutta "parasaro" above after making that [term] a coreferential compound;
therefore, he states the contrast with "na parasaro," for here there is no agreement.
40. Para-
The conceptualization "you are you" does not exist here for me.

41. In the section [on sandhi], when only so much is stated—"Is it not at the end of a consonant cluster?"—then, when any vowel of a consonant cluster follows the *bindu* (anusvāra), [the following rule applies].
If the final consonant of a *vagga* were to occur without restriction, then an undesirable result might also follow;

therefore, anticipating this objection, he says "in a *vagga*, the final [consonant] of the *vagga*" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the exclusion of the undesirable by relying on proximity. "Sovā" means "only the final [consonant] of the *vagga*";
"tasmin" refers to the *vagga*-vowel.

42. "Surely, since it is a sound (*sadda*) and possesses variability, let it be called 'sound' for now. Since terms such as *saṃyata* and *saṃhita* can also occur as parts of a sound, should they not also be included?
Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'among sounds' (*yesu hi saddesu*), how can there be the designation 'sound' even for that which lacks [the suffix] *-ya*?"
To the question "What [is it]?", he says "evā" and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning: "The deviant is restricted by the non-deviant. 43.

Since the substitution of *saṃssa* for *yesaṃ* would have been established by the previous rule alone when preceded by the word *ya*, this rule was commenced so that *saṃssa* should occur specifically when followed by the letter *ya* (as in *yathā*).

44. Regarding the phrase *vanaṭṭhānīnam āsilissa gacchati pavattatīti āgamo nāma*: [the questioner] asks, "What is this *ṭhānī* (substitute) here? and replies, "It is *sarassa*. Then, [the opponent] objects:
"Since it does not exist in the sutta that follows, how can *sarassa* be obtained? He raises this objection with the words beginning "But surely... (*nanu ce*).

Even in the absence of an explicit statement regarding the substitution [of *van* etc.], there may be either the addition (*āgama*) of a consonant or of a vowel by virtue of implication (*sāmatthiya*).
If it were the addition of a consonant, [the rule] "after words beginning with *pada*, [the augment *kvaci* occurs]" (5.92) would have been stated by the Teacher;
therefore, he makes this known: "In this case, only a vowel can be the substitute (*ṭhānī*). He states the resolution with the words beginning "It is said" (*vuccateccādinā*).

Following the prefix *ni-* from the word *padi* when no suffix follows, the final portion ending in *y*—according to the rule "for *pada* and so forth, *kvaci*"—is replaced by *j* according to "of the *tavagga* and *varagga*, etc. (1-48).
Then, according to "in place of *y*, *j*" (1-49), there is the act of lying down (*nipajjana*). Regarding the phrase "in *mānantatya* and so forth," this is a governing heading;

thus, [the rule] "the suffix *kyo* is used for the sense of state or object when not in the third person, in *mānantatya* and so forth" (5-17) applies here because of the heading "in *mānantatya* and so forth."
Regarding "in another condition" (*paccayantare*): this refers to a condition other than *mānantu* and so forth.

In the *Kaccāyana*, for the purpose of establishing the form "atippagokhotāvā," the insertion of the vowel *o* and the consonant *g*—via the rule "kvaci o byañjane"—is prescribed through a different sutta.
To establish that same form by means of a different method, the commentary states "atippago kho tāvā"; it is said "atippā" and so forth in order to demonstrate that which was stated there.

46. [The opponent] objects that since the numbers six, twelve, and eighteen are plural endings, the singular form ‘chā’ is inappropriate when one ought to say ‘chakī’ (of the six); this is raised by the words “Is it not so? and so forth.
[The author] refutes this with the words “By means of *naccā*,” etc., saying: “No; this designation ‘chaḷo’ is not incorrect.”

The meaning is "it occurs"; because of the imitation of the word *cha*—that is, because of the imitation of the word *cha*—it analyzes the imitation of the form of the word *sādhu*, whose forms were stated above, by means of the passage beginning with “imitation is of two kinds.

That which has abandoned—that is, relinquished—the meaning consisting of affirmation and negation is "that which has abandoned its meaning" (*pariccattattha*). Here, however, by the word *cha*, the specific number six [is indicated].
By the phrase "it becomes [the object] from being designated," he states that the word *cha* possesses meaning through its sense as an imitation;
this is expressed in the singular number because the word *cha*—which is what is to be expressed by the word *cha*—is a unity. Regarding the term "of the imitation":

it refers to the phonetic form of the word *eka* or others, or something else, which is the imitation of that [word *cha*]. Specifically, it refers to that phonetic form of the word *eka* or others, or something else, which is the imitation.

"Specific numbers such as unity," etc., refers either to specific numbers like oneness and so forth, or something else. In the sutta, "I who am two for the two, two" (2-219), the word *dvi* is a form of the word *dvi* used as an imitation (*anukāriya*), which refers to the specific number two that is its denotation;

therefore, the plural form *dvinnam* is used as its designator. Now, why was it not stated as *ḷañi*? For if that were the case, because of the bond of knowledge (*ñānabandha*), the letter *ḷ* [would be affected].
Keeping in mind the objection that [the letter *ḷ*] ought to be an initial constituent (*ādyavayava*), he says, beginning with "by the word *cha*," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: the letter *ḷ*, being prescribed by way of an exception to the final [constituent], becomes an augment (*āgama*) for a following *sadda*... [etc.

...by the phrase "by way of an exception to the final," he indicates through the genitive designation "of *sarassa*" that this [rule] falls within the scope of the rule "chaḷīyantassa," [which applies] to a following [word]. Regarding the term "following" (*parassa*):
By the mention of the ablative case in *iminā ‘chā* ("by this *cha*"), it shows that the scope of the rule *pañcamiyaṃ parassā* (1-15) [is established];

and by *ādissā*, because *ḷa* is a single phoneme (*ekavaṇṇa*), it demonstrates the attainment of the substitute *ādisa* for the *sara* "ādi" by means of the term "end" (*anta*)—according to the sutta *ādissā*—showing that even though there is a distinction between the beginning and the end, they are both *sara*.
This is the intended meaning here: because of the mention of the ablative case as *‘chā’*, [the rule] *pañcamiyaṃ parassā* applies.

Because they share the same phonetic color (*ekavaṇṇattā*), the *kāriya* (grammatical operation) that has arrived at the other reaches the final letter (*anta*)—as in the rule "of that which ends in the sixth" (1-17)—and reaches the initial letter (*ādi*)—as in the rule "of that which begins with the first" (1-16).

The phrase "it becomes as if it were the initial itself" means that even though the letter *ñ* is not present, by virtue of following the inclusion of the augment (*āgama*), it does not destroy the vowel of the augment but rather becomes a constituent part of its beginning.
Thus, they apply the letter *l*, according to the rule: "the augments *y*, *v*, *m*, *t*, *r*, *l*, and *ā*."

By means of the sutta, the employment of the letter *l* and the statement that it applies without distinction to both demonstrate the inappropriateness [of the objection] through the phrase "tesampi" and so forth.
"Tesampi" means "even for the Kaccāyanas. "In the designation of phonemes (*akkharasaññā*)" refers to the designation of phonemes being prescribed in the rule: "The phonemes and words are forty-one.

"In the absence of distinction" means in the absence of any difference between *l* and *ḷ*. By the phrase "is evident," he demonstrates that the difference between the *su* and *li* scripts is established by direct perception.
For in that context, "hearing" (*suti*) refers to the distinct apprehension of individual syllables by the process of auditory consciousness;

it is like the script (*lipi*) of the inhabitants of various regions for their respective garments. Their distinction is established through direct perception, as they fall within the domain of auditory and visual consciousness.
In the alternative where there is the insertion of the letter *ḷ*, the form is *chaḷabhiññā*.

47. Then, because of the insertion of the vowel *a* [into *issa*], and because of the rule "the letter *da* [is inserted] after vowels" (1-44), as well as by this other word beginning with "padantarena," they become correct;
thus, in order to state the meaning of the reading in the Vutti, it says: "they become correct."

He says, “By way of nipātana (irregular derivation). Regarding this, he states the reason: “*Yaṃ*, etc. Nipātana consists of bringing about what has not been reached and the negation of what has been reached;
here, the reading of those [terms] refers to the reading of those very terms as intended by them in this context—namely, in this sutta beginning with *tadaminaṃ*.
As for *uddha*, it is derived from *udū*; thus, in the sense of “above the vault,” in a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound of another referent), it becomes *uddhaṃkha*.

This being established, there is the substitution of *udu* for the word *uddhaṃ*. Regarding the word *asasa*, it is derived from the root *asa* in the sense of "eating" with the suffix *aṇ* by means of the rule *kvacaṇa* (Pāṇini 5.4.15);
thus he says, "from eating meat (*pisita-masanā*). Regarding the word *mayūra*, it is derived from the root *ru* in the sense of "crying out" (*ravati*) preceded by *mahi*;
when the compound is formed by this very same list of exceptions (*gaṇa-nipātana*) under the rule *kvacaṇa*, the word *mayūra* is produced; thus he says, "of the word *mahi*," and so forth.

Because this group, beginning with *assa*, belongs to the class of *āgatigaṇa* (groups formed by the addition of suffixes), it is connected with the phrase "and so too others. The word "stated" (*vutta*) is an elliptical supplement to the text.

Regarding the "five Nikāyas, such as the Dīghanikāya," it is said: "The Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara, and Khuddaka—these five Nikāyas are profound in terms of both the Dhamma and its meaning."

Regarding the five Nikāyas, such as the Dīgha Āgama and others that have been spoken: "should be known" means they are to be understood by way of their phonemes (*vaṇṇa*), syllables (*gama*), and so forth;

the connection is that "the fivefold, five-aspected etymology (*nirutta*) is pronounced. Etymology (*nirutta*) is a verbal derivation (*nibbacana*); the suffix *-tta* is used here in the neuter sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

The meaning is that it is the pronunciation preceded by an explanatory statement of the sense (*atthakathā*). Furthermore, the treatise (*sattha*) that expresses that [etymology] is also included under the term "expression," because the designator (*abhidhāna*) is [figuratively] treated as the designated (*abhidheyya*).

Or it is called *nirutta* because it conforms to that meaning; by the phrase "it should be understood according to the characteristics of the stated *nirutti*," etc., this indicates that among the words in the treatise on *nirutti* which produce a derivation step-by-step, this is the general method of derivation.

In the case of *dovārika* ("doorkeeper"), derived from *dvāre niyutto*, there is the insertion of the vowel *o* between the letters *da* and *va* in the suffix *ṇika*. [The form] *hiṃsimsu*... [etc. (Note: The ellipsis indicates that the text continues with further examples of grammatical derivation.)

From the root *hiṃsa* with the suffix *-hiṃsāya*, by means of the zero-suffix (*appaccaya*)—according to the rule "In the presence of suffixes beginning with *gha* or *ṅ*, [the preceding vowel] becomes long" (5-44)—there is the zero-suffix;

thus, in *nijaka*, the letter *ja* becomes *ya*, resulting in *niyaka*. Now, since it was stated that there is a modification of phonemes (*vaṇṇavikāra*), let the forms such as *niyaka* be established through the substitution of the sound *ja* for *ya*.
But how are forms such as *susāna* established? Since they involve modifications of the word *chava* and so on, he says: "such as *susāna*."

‘Even a modification of the word,’ and so forth. The point is that if the replacement of a collection of phonemes (*vaṇṇasamudāyādesa*) were not separately mentioned, then the restriction of the number—namely, that “etymology is fivefold” (*pañcavidhaṃ niruttaṃ*)—would not be tenable in the case of *chabbhitopatti*.
“Yoga” means connection. By the phrase “tathāhi,” etc., he makes manifest the connection of the verbal root with its specific meaning.
“The action of sounding” (*ravanakiriyā*) refers to the connection with the actions of making sounds other than the *kekā* (the cry of a peacock).
Regarding the word *mayūra* here, it refers specifically to the cry of a peacock, not to the mere act of crying in a general sense;
this is the intended meaning. (48) *Tava vaṇṇamattasseva* means "of the mere commonality of color"; here the word *matta* expresses "commonality. And [the same applies to] the letter *ya*.

The connection is with the word *cādeso* (“substitution”). By this [rule], for those [sounds] ending in *j*, which have *j* as their final letter—referring to that which has *j* as its final letter according to the rule *“vaggalasehi te”* (1-49)—there is an *asaṅkhyasamāsa* (compound of non-numbered items) in the sense that they function with reference to themselves (*attānam adhikicca*).
49. *Vagga*.

Even though there is a constant relationship between the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ*, because their referents have already passed away (*pakkantavisayattā*), the word *taṃ* does not depend upon the word *yaṃ*.

Thus he says: “*Taṃ* [means] ‘the immediately preceding,’ and so forth. For the word *taṃ*—being one whose referent has passed away, whose referent is well-established, and whose referent has been experienced—does not depend on the word *yaṃ*.
And just as this [word *taṃ*] does not depend on the word *yaṃ*, all of that has been explained by the Great Master (Mahāsāmi).
In the *Subodhālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*:
"The moon arisen from the Lord of Sages has been anointed with the sandalwood-paste of laughter;
its sprouts are white as new shoots, yet there is no sprout of a lower lip. (122)
This verse should be understood by us according to the method explained in detail, so that it may be applied appropriately to both transitive and intransitive verbal roots.
50. *Kiñcāpi*:
although this [particle] *kiñcāpi* (as it appears in the manuscript) is used for the purpose of expressing an alternative (*vikappana*), it does not differ from the preceding [particle *api*].
Although it is understood [in that way], nevertheless, by this formulation it is merely a grammatical alternative (*vikappa*);

however, according to the previous rule, in certain instances following a root ending in *ha*, when the suffix *dhyana* is applied, there should indeed be forms such as *mehyaṃ*, *dohyaṃ*, *sinehyaṃ*, and *lehyam*.

Regarding the statement "the words *vattu*, *utta*, *ppadhāna*, *tta*, and *matta*": although the word *ādi* has multiple meanings, it is stated here as a term denoting a specific constituent part (*niyatāvayava*).

The word *ādi* is used here in the sense of an object (*kamma*), meaning "that which is taken" (*ādīyati*); thus, it refers to the phonemes (*byañjana*) that are joined together (*saṃyujjati*) and remain situated in one place.

This meaning should be understood according to the method explained by us in the commentary on the *Khuddasikkhā*, titled *Sumaṅgalappasādani*, specifically in the passage: "those who were ordained from the beginning (*ādito upasampannā*). 1.2.3. *Sannipāta*: "That which is joined" (*saṃyujjati*) is a *saṃyoga*—phonemes situated together in one place.
54. Having set aside the statement "yaṃvattata" (as far as it goes) from the *Vicchā* [section], he begins to explain its meaning with the words "sambhavāpekkhāya" (in view of possibility), etc.
Furthermore, even though the word "yaṃvattata" does not actually exist in the sutta, there is freedom of usage regarding a word whose meaning is understood through implication.
It is stated in the *Vutti*: although the word *yasadda* (the relative pronoun) functions in the sense of indefiniteness (*aniyatattha*), it cannot exist as anything other than a word or a sentence;

and since it occurs in both the distributive (*vicchā*) and the frequentative (*ābhikkhañña*), he says: “A word or a sentence is [defined] with regard to possibility. The connection is as follows: that which is possible is “possibility” (*sambhava*);
with regard to that possibility, a word or a sentence functions—this is the link. “Functions” (*vattate*) refers to the distributive and the frequentative.
[The opponent] asks: "But surely the meanings such as substance (*dabba*) belong only to the word or the sentence separately;

how then can this [suffix], which has the property of expressing a speaker (*vattudhamma*) and the property of an action (*kiriyādhamma*), function in the sense of frequency (*abhikkhañña*) within that [word or sentence]?

With reference to this objection, he says: "By way of being the object," and so forth. The word or the sentence is the object of frequency—whether it be the property of a speaker or the property of an action—by virtue of its occurrence in a non-different sense.

The meaning is: by way of being the object (*gocarattena*), and by way of being the illuminator (*pakāsakattena*)—that is, by way of its non-occurrence therein and by virtue of that [non-occurrence], and by way of being the designator (*abhidhāyakattena*).
With the words "of that" (*tassa*) and so forth, he demonstrates the transformation of the case-ending of the nominative *yaṃ* (which was brought forward in the phrase *yaṃ vattataṃ*).
By this, he illustrates the following: "Even though the genitive is not explicitly uttered in the phrase ‘*vicchābhikkhaññesu*’..."
Nevertheless, the genitive case remains established. How so? The rule for substitution, “*dve* [is used] in place of *iccādi*,” requires a related term (*sambandhin*).

Furthermore, the statement “in cases of desire (*vicchā*) and begging (*bhikkhañña*)” is a specification of meaning (*attha-niddesa*); yet a connection between that meaning and a substitute (*ādesa*) is not logically possible. Therefore, the sense of the genitive is this:
“In cases of desire and begging, whatever word or sentence occurs, for that, *dve* [is substituted]. Thus, the genitive case is justified.
The connection is as follows: "it can be said" indicates that there are two forms (*rūpa*).

In the phrase "assigning the accusative plural ending to the number in the case of the word-forms *sadda* and *rūpa*," it is taught by way of its connection with the act of assignment (*paṭipādana-kiriyā*).

Regarding the statement, "the word *api*, even though its meaning belongs to another sentence, enters into a connection with something else [here]," the word "two" (*dvi*) is [to be understood] as follows in the subsequent [text]:
In both sentences, the word *dvi* is used in the sense of "twofold," yet it is not stated that the word *dvi* has a similar form (*sarūpa*) as its primary referent.
To the question, "If it has a similar form as its primary referent, why was it not so stated? he replies: "Because of the designation by means of the plural number.

Furthermore, since it is stated generally as "two" (*dve*), there might be a doubling of words (*dvibbacana*) in place of the words and sentences, or there might be a twofold application (*dvippayoga*) because those very [words] recur; such being the case, [the rule applies to] "that which recurs" (*yaṃ vattate*).
Regarding the word "tassā" (of that), he asks: "Why was an explanation made regarding subsistence based on [the previous] very first [statement]?
and thus says "evañca" and so forth. Now, in order to show that the position of two applications (*dvippayogapakkha*) is not accepted because it is faulty, he says "yadātu" and so forth.
The particle *tu* serves to distinguish the subsequent position from the preceding one; for in that [preceding case], there are two forms.

In the manuscript, the forms of words (*saddarūpa*) and their repetition (*āvutti*) are considered separately; however, here it is intended that the word itself (*so va saddo*) is repeated twice. It is thought thus:

"The word *dvi* is a term denoting a numeral (*saṅkhyeyya-vacana*), because of the statement: 'The numerals from one up to ten function [as adjectives] when they denote a thing to be numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*)'.
Therefore, in this case, the thing to be numbered may be either the form of the word or the repetition; thus the grammatical designation (*niddesa*) refers to both."
"Whether by means of the neuter gender or the feminine gender: therein, when the designation is by means of the neuter gender, then the phonetic forms (*saddarūpa*) are to be counted;

but when by means of the feminine gender, then the repetitions (*āvutti*)—that is, the action characterized by utterance—are to be counted, and thus here even the repetitions are to be counted. In that case, there is a double application (*dvippayoga*).

"‘The dual ending’—this is the alternative; this is the meaning here: when two repetitions (*āvutti*) are prescribed, then the dual usage at the end is indifferent (*sopekkha*), for there is no substitution of the base (*ṭhāny-ādesa-bhāva*) here. However, the alternative of dual usage does not apply in the case of a substitute (*ṭhāne*).
For repetition (*āvutti*) is an action (*kiriyā*), and here the word is its instrument (*sādhana*); and [the rule] does not apply to the instrument of an action."

"And since the state of being a substitute for *ṭhā* (the letter *ṭ*) is possible, when the rules (*vutti*) are prescribed, then the employment of *d* ending in double-consonants (*dvibbacana*) is that alternative (*pakkha*).
This alternative is also accepted by the Pāṇinīyas; however, showing that it is improper because it is tainted with faults, he says "But that...
and so forth. For they, having accepted even this second alternative, [do so] merely as a figurative convention (*upacāra*).
They establish that [the self] through merit by means of either difference or non-difference from the substrate.
To the question, "In what way does its being possessed of hatred not apply, such that it is not apprehended? he says, "For thus," and so forth.

Regarding the suffix *ṇya*, as in the rule "tassa bhāvakammesu tta tā ttana ṇya ṇeyya ṇiya ṇiyā" (4.59), when *ṇya* is prescribed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), it exists as a distinct word-form on the view that there is a doubling of the application.

Regarding *punappuna*: from the perspective of the collective nature (*samudāya-sabhāva*), the meaning is "occurring again and again" (*punappunabhāvo*). However, if it were taken as a collective [compound] in the sense of "again and again," it would not occur.

It is not only the suffix *-ṇya* that is excluded; rather, even the vowel *o*—which arises from the vowels contained within a single word, specifically from the *u* sound that is the initial of the vowels, according to the rule *“sarānamādissā yuvaṇṇassā eo ṇānubandhe”* (4.1.124)—would not occur. This is because of the rule *“manādyāpādīnamomaye”* [which applies to words beginning with *man*, etc., in the case of the suffix *-maya*].
And: "Thus (3-59), the vowel *o* occurs in both cases... because it is taken as the cause (*nimitta*) for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
For even in the former case, since two identical sound-forms (*saddarūpa*) are prescribed as the beginning, the division of the word (*padabheda*) certainly occurs; for he will say:

'even though the difference is inherent in itself' (*satīpi attagate bhede*). [Objection: Is it not the case that the difference is metaphorically attributed (*upacarita*) to the word by virtue of its quality of being repeated (*āvutti*), whereas in its own form (*sarūpato*) there is actually no difference?"
Otherwise, there would be no repetition at all; for it is said that "repetition occurs with respect to a single entity" in such passages as "not without an interval" (*nāntarena*).

If it is argued that "otherwise" means that the distinction is merely metaphorical and not real by nature (*sabhāva*), [the response is: the connection is that one cannot say "the effect comes to be" in that way.
However, since the non-distinction exists by nature, he emphasizes the distinction that actually exists in the entity (*vatthu*) through the absence of metaphorical usage.
"Otherwise" (*aññathā*) means: if there were a difference, there could be no recurrence (*āvutti*). This is the intended meaning here:

"If the difference were due to the very nature [of the word], how could there be recurrence for that which is differentiated? Regarding the phrase "because it resembles the original" (*ṭhānisadisattā*), it indicates the *paribhāṣā* rule: "The substitute is like the original" (*ṭhānīviyādeso*).

In the phrases beginning with "by the action" (*kiriyāya*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*); this is because the desire to express the object, agent, or instrument arises through the action and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "desādīti" (in the manuscript), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes time, location, and so forth.
He says "anekappakārayutte" (connected with many modes) because it is only that which is joined with various modes that is called "divided" (*bhinna*).

The connection is that this is stated because of the use of the plural number; "by that" means by that use of the plural number, through which the desire for simultaneous application (*sakiṃ byāpani*) is indicated, acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The connection is as follows: "by means of being a cause" or "with the desire to pervade successively," and "with the desire to pervade [the qualities] such as birth.
In that context, "this village is beautiful and this village is beautiful" is the desire to pervade successively;

although there is here a connection between the object (the village) and the quality of beauty, nevertheless it is a connection of the villages with the quality, as in "the entire village is beautiful."

Generally, because there is no desire to pervade [the object] entirely or successively—meaning there is an absence of the wish for total pervasion (*sakalabyāpana*)—there is no repetition [of the word].

Thus, the meaning should be understood by applying this principle further on. "Abundant barley" (*sampanno yavo*) expresses the desire to pervade the species of barley by means of its quality of abundance;

the species (*jāti*) has a single referent (*ekattha*), whereas the distributive repetition (*vicchā*) has multiple bases (*anekattha-nissaya*). This is the distributive repetition based on a single referent (*ekatthā-jāti*), which refers to a single object.

In the *Mahābhāsya*, it is stated that the word *jāti* (genus) is employed with the intention (*vicchā*) to make known [a thing] in its manifold aspects; and the intention is employed with the thought, "I shall make known [the thing] in its manifold aspects.
In the phrase "the beautiful *dhava* and *khadira* trees," there is the desire to pervade the substances such as the *dhava* tree with the quality of beauty.
By the word "object" (*attha*) here, substances and so forth are intended to be expressed; thus he says, "in the characteristics of substance, quality, and action."
But here, the word *visadda* has the sense of pervasion; thus he says, “to pervade, to connect. *Sāti* is repetition (*vicchā*).
It is the property of the speaker (*vattudhamma*)—that is, the property of the speaker who utters such [phrases] as “tree-tree” and so forth.
Because it is connected with that property characterized by desire, the word is “tree” and so forth. That which is the form, the very essence, of that word—[that is what is meant].
By the counter-argument (*paccāsatthā*)— namely, that "among what is heard and what is inferred, the connection with what is heard is stronger"—

because that form which is currently being uttered among those subject to reduplication is proximate to what is heard, the application appropriate for the dual number (*dvisaṅkhyā-yutta*) is extended by the word *dve* in the rule;
thus, the very same dual suffix (*dvibbacana*) is applied to the dual suffix itself, as in "tree, tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ*).
For in the manuscript there is a mention of "being joined with the number two. Now, what is this doubling of that which ends in the singular?
For indeed, since all these [words] here denote plurality through reduplication (*vichchā*), they attain the plural ending because of their multiplicity;

yet the singular does not succeed [in such cases], as in "he waters tree after tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati*), where there is a cognition of all trees individually despite the expression of a single referent—how then can there be a singular ending?

Suspecting [that] there might be a dual ending, he says: “*tatthe*,” etc. Because the sense is indicated by means of plural endings—according to the method that will be explained later with the words “by the employment of plural endings”—there would not be a dual ending there;
and since a dual ending must occur, it cannot exist without the presence of a singular ending. There is no opportunity for a dual ending [in this case].

The word *so* (he/that) is a term understood through its power (*balāvagata*) as having the sense of "that which"; the capacity (*sāmatthiya*) characterized by the impossibility of that meaning occurring otherwise is "capacity of the meaning" (*atthasāmatthiya*).
Because of the connection [in the rule] "from a singular form, there is a dual," the phrase "connection with action and so forth" refers to a connection with action, quality, and so on.
The word *mantvā* expresses the prior action of one who desires to pervade; "having brought together" (*abhisaṃharitvā*)...
Because of its unity. Since the word possesses the capacity to convey such a meaning, the power of the word resides in the word itself.

To show that when there is a desire for simultaneous expression regarding a common substratum (*sahavacanicchā*), only the plural number occurs and not the dual number therein, he says: "For this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means precisely because of the absence of the dual number, due to the manifestation of the desire through the power of the word ending in the plural. Thus it is understood.
Furthermore, here the application of *yoga* (conjunction) is twofold: the application of sound (*saddayogapajja*) and the application of meaning (*atthayogapajja*).

Among these, it is not possible for certain meaningful sounds to possess both the application of sound and the application of meaning simultaneously. That whose referent (*adhikaraṇa*)—such as a tree like a *dhava*—is simultaneous is "having a simultaneous referent" (*yugapadādhikaraṇa*), such as the word *sodhava-khadira-palāsa*;
the state of being that is so, and when that exists, [it is called *yugapadādhikaraṇa-bhāva*].

The simultaneous occurrence (*ekato pappatti*) of things that have distinct meanings but are expressible by a single word, occurring without the intervention of a phonetic connection (*sadda-yogapajja*), is "semantic connection" (*attha-yogapajja*).
This is shown by the phrase "desiring to speak them together.

And when there is such a desire to speak them together—as in "the beautiful *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāsa* trees" or "beautiful trees"—even when connected with the quality of beauty, the expression is made clear through the plural number itself.

Regarding the absence of reduplication (*dvivacana*): although there is a conjunction of sounds in the phrase "beautiful *dhava* and *khadira* trees" (*sobhanaṃ dhavakhadiraṃ*), because it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*), there is no conjunction of meanings (*atthayogavacana*) or conjunction of nouns (*nāmayogavacana*).

Since it ends in the singular number, even though there is occasion for reduplication, there is no reduplication because there is no desire to express the sounds [of the individual words] simultaneously; this was stated previously.

The author of the *Vāttika* stated, "In the case of *ānupubbi*, two [words] should be mentioned" (*ānupubbiye dve bhavantīti vattabbaṃ*). He expresses this with the words beginning with "even in the case of *ānupubbi*.

By means of the phrase beginning with "mānupubbi," he provides an explanation of the explanatory sentence beginning with "atthi yeveva," demonstrating that even in the case of *ānupubbi*, there is repetition (*vicchā*), and from that very fact, the doubling [of the word] occurs.
This is like [the case of] members of a village belonging to the same class, who are distinguished by differences of direction, location, and so forth.
There is no distributive repetition (*vicchā*) here; for the root and the tip are primarily one and the same, due to their unity as parts of a single whole from bottom to top.

Since the designations "root" and "tip" are applied in relation to the upper and lower portions respectively, these parts of the root and tip belong to different categories; yet there is no distributive repetition of things belonging to different categories.
For instance, when the word "cow" (*go*) is uttered, [the term does not apply distributively] to those who have gone to the Vāhīka country.
The teacher Jinindabuddhi has established that there is an absence of *vicchā* (poetic arrangement) in the sequence;
in order to refute that, he says "if indeed," etc., and then states "just as," etc., to elaborate on what was said in the commentary.
"Not established" means not fixed; it is said to be "non-existent. That which has an upper part is also called a "root."
It states that "being made" (*katatta*) is dependent on the designation of the root; "both" refers to the root and the path.
Likewise, by the phrase "other parts of the root and the tip," it indicates multiplicity when there is inclusion—as in the case below—of the various divisions of roots and tips.

By "as previously stated," it means according to the method explained before, beginning with "due to the abundance of trees, etc."; what is meant is that [the terms] such as *thūla* (large) and so forth apply to the roots and so on by way of their abundance.
"Considering the connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*), by means of the word *sabba* joined with the seventh case-ending and accompanied by words such as *mūla*,

one collects the referents beginning with 'root. Then, when there is a desire to pervade the subject (*vattuno*) in this way— namely, 'in every root it is coarse' (*thūlā*) and 'in every tip it is fine' (*sukhumā*)—
the dual number is used precisely for the sake of distributive repetition (*vicchāya*) of that which [otherwise] has a singular ending."
Since there would be no entry of the "eldesthood" for the absolute youngest when a distributive sense (*vicchā*) arises among the eldest,
[the author] stated "insert each eldest one by one" (*jeṭṭhaṃ jeṭṭhamanuppavesaya*) by that same teacher merely to express a sequence; however,
that is now being refuted by the words "the eldest," etc., because he states that a distributive sense also arises for the youngest, since the youngest is also inserted.
Regarding this, he states the reason: “*Yatheva hi*,” etc. In the phrase “of another” (*parassa*), the word “middle one” (*majjhima*) is the qualification;
the connection is that even for the youngest, there is the designation “eldest. He supports exactly what was stated above with the words “*Vatticchānibandhane hi*,” etc.
The compound *vatticchānibandhana* means “that which has the desire of the speaker (*vattuno icchā*) as its cause (*nibandhana*). This refers to the actual nature of the thing (*vatthusabhāve*).
The basis (*vatthu*) is therein; the adherence (*abhinivesa*) is its occurrence (*pavatti*). It does not attain, it does not reach. The author of the *Vārttika* stated:
"When the meaning of the suffix itself (*sakattha*) is being maintained, it should be said that two [suffixes] occur in the case of more than one.
Therefore he says ‘sakatthe’, etc.; in the meaning of a word that is independent of the distinction of meanings and so forth, which is the meaning of the suffix itself (*sakatthe*).

The meaning is that when it is being determined and understood as "only this much," and when many [items] are being given, the dual number is desired and accepted by the followers of Pāṇini; this is their intention:
in the phrase "Give two *māsakas* from this *kahāpaṇa* to you two," only two *māsakas* are intended to be given, for what is called a *kahāpaṇa*—
Four *guñjā* seeds make one *viha*; two *guñjā* make one *māsaka*.
Two *akkhā* make one *māsaka*, and five *akkhā* make one *dharaṇa*, which consists of eight [units].
According to the stated method, there is a collection of many *māsakas*; however, not all the *māsakas* connected to a *kahāpaṇa* are included in the act of giving.

Regarding the statement, “*byāpitā*, ‘only two’—this is not a distributive repetition (*vicchā*), but rather a dual number according to the rule already stated,” [the author] says, “having shown that,” meaning having shown that example of the dual number;
and in order to establish that the doubling occurs only in a distributive sense (*vicchā*)... the intention here is as follows:

in the phrase “give a *māsaka*, a *māsaka*,” etc., there is no desire to pervade the act of giving with the word “give”; rather, it is only in a distributive sense (*vicchā*) that the doubling occurs here.
“Because of the repetition, for it is from this that the desire for repetition is understood. Having asked what was intended by the mention of “another word” and so forth, he says:

“*Dehi*,” etc. When a restriction is being understood—namely, when there is a large quantity of *māsaka* coins related to a *kahāpaṇa*, and a specific selection of two *māsakas* is being cognized—the act of giving, “Give the *māsakas*,” is understood without distinction, that is, in its general sense.
The connection is with the phrase “malicious states of mind” (*byāpannā bhāvā*).

Starting with the words “with a word,” etc., he begins to explain the intended meaning through another word (*saddantaro*), namely, the word “māsakamiccādinā. Here, “with a word” means with the word “māsakamicca.
“From this kahāpaṇa” is the other word used here. “Of that which has been prepared” means of that which has been produced as “māsaka, māsaka. [This is] “through another word.”
He said, "Because of connection with another word," meaning that by this [rule] the connection with another word is included; this is the intended sense here:

at the time of applying the *dvitta* suffix, because there is no regard for a meaning expressible by another word, the *dvitta* is applied without distinction to the desire for a *māsaka* as in *māsakaṃ-māsakaṃ*;
however, subsequently, when there is a connection with another word such as *kahāpaṇa* from this [term], if it is connected with *kahāpaṇa*...
"One does not grasp the remaining two māṣaka coins as belonging to this [specific] kahāpaṇa; therefore, there ought to be a genitive case, such as 'of this kahāpaṇa.

However, because of the designation of the ablative fifth case in the sense of a limit—as in 'from this kahāpaṇa'—it is understood from the other word 'from this kahāpaṇa' that you are to give the two [coins] after having taken exactly two from the kahāpaṇa."
It has been stated: "When there is a desire to express an excellence of meaning for words that are 'prior' (*pubba*) and 'first' (*paṭhama*), two [suffixes] occur" (8-1-12-vā).

To that effect, he says: "Of *pubba* and *paṭhama*, etc."—that is, when there is a desire to express an excellence of meaning (*atthātisaya*) for the words *pubba* and *paṭhama*, which is the specific distinction (*pakaṃsa*) of the meaning;
[the suffix *mic* occurs] merely to denote the excellence of meaning consisting in the state of being absolutely first (*sabbapaṭhamabhāva*).
The intention here is not that there is a desire for speech; rather, even when "the act of blossoming" and "the act of ripening" are mentioned,
since the sense is possible as "the act of causing to blossom" and "the act of causing to ripen"— as in the case of "each preceding flower" and so forth—
it is by way of qualifying the action, meaning "they perform each preceding blossoming" and "they perform each preceding speaking."

The meaning should be understood as follows: by the phrase "the former is considered the first," he states the reason for the presence of distributive repetition (*vicchā*) through the extension of the plurality of those things intended as "former" and "first.

[It is said: "In the case of feminine declension, when expressing equality or comparison between two or more, it should be stated that the suffixes *-itar-* and *-tam-* occur twice to denote the state [of being]."
(8-1-12-vā) It has been stated: here, the word *itthiliṅga* refers to "feminine" because of its connection with the feminine gender; *nigada* means that by which something is expressed;

he whose nature (*bhāva*) is such that his expression is feminine is called *itthinigada*; in that state of being a feminine expression (*itthinigade bhāve*), it says: "in words such as *ratararata*, *mantānaṃ*, etc.";
and regarding *itthiliṅge*, that whose nature is feminine gender is *itthiliṅga*; in that state of being feminine gender (*itthiliṅge*).
The connection is that for those words occurring in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), the doubling of the word is intended when expressing "mutual delight" (*rataratamanta*).

To the question "In what domain? he says: "In the domain of equal comparison" (*samasampadhāraṇavisaye*). Equal comparison (*samasampadhāraṇā*) is the investigation, determination, or comprehension in the form: "These two are both wealthy" by means of an equal quality such as wealth (*aḍḍhatā*); that itself is the domain, and when that exists—
Their intention is that because there is no state of being "half" or "manifold," and because there is no absence of action and so forth, there is no ellipsis here.
By the phrase "when being asked," he shows that these two [words] and others function as interrogative sentences.

He speaks by way of another's conventional usage, saying: "the object-sphere of verbs (*ākhyāta*) and so forth"; by this, he indicates that only verbs, by virtue of being words that manifest action, [function in this manner].
The compound *puṇṇapuññasaṅkhātakiriyā* indicates that the object of the Dhamma is indeed like wealth;
by the word *atisayavisiddha*, it is shown that the prefix *pa-* in the term *papacati* is an upasagga signifying excellence (*pakaṃsa*). Regarding the form *hivi*:

from the root *lū* in the sense of "cutting," the suffix *hi* is added in the sense of "manner" (*vidhi*) according to the rule *pañhapattanāvidhīsu* (6-9); and *ossa* [is derived] according to the rule *yuvaṇṇānameopaccaye*.
(5-82) Regarding the substitution of *o* for *u*, [the rule] "only for those whose agent is the ancestors" (5-62)— by means of the particle *eva*,
it is shown that if this condition is prescribed even here as being non-repetitive (*ābhikkhañña*), then, just as in the case of *papacati*,
since the meaning of non-repetition is already expressed by the very condition prescribed as non-repetitive, there should be no doubling (*dvibbacana*). However, when [it means] "intensely"...
The desire for the expression "he cooks again and again" (*punappunaṃ pacati*) results in the form *papacati* even then.
In this example, by the rule "only in the sense of repetition" (*ābhikkhaññe icceva*), the grammarians of the Pāṇinian school establish a mere imitation;
there is no actual repetition here. There is no purpose for such a statement in this context.

This shows that it is indeed a reduplication (*ābhikkhañña*) of two syllables; thus it is understood: "The imitation [of sound] here, *paṭa*, occurs with respect to the action of becoming (*bhavana*);
therefore, it is said to be an expression of the action of becoming (*bhavanakiriyāmatī*). Thus, there is a repetition of the same action here. For this very reason, he will say:
"'Paṭapaṭā bhavati' is a reduplication of two syllables in the sense of repetition. It is not [the suffix] *-ti*.
When the sound *iti* is not present, the suffix *rā* is applied; thus, after first doubling [the syllable], the suffix *rā* is added.

Alternatively, he says "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth to establish the form by another method: since the lengthening is compulsory (*nicca*), after first doubling [it] as *paṭapaṭa-karoti*, the vowel is necessarily long.
Having shown the derivation here as *paṭapaṭā karoti*, he now addresses *paṭapaṭāyati*.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with *paṭapaṭāyati* has been commenced. 55.

When *ekassa ekassa* stands [as the base], and the preceding case-ending (*pubbavibhatti*) has been elided and the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) has been applied, it becomes *ekekekassa*; likewise, when *matthakena matthakena* stands, it becomes *matthakamatthakena*.

56. When *añña* stands as *aññaṃ aññaṃ*, by the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti-lopa*), the vowel *a* is replaced by *o* according to the rule *tadaminā* (1-47), resulting in the form *aññoññanti*. 57.
Up to...
In the phrase "yāvabodhaṃ," the compound *yāvāvadhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.1.8) is an *asaṅkhyasamāsa*. 58. The rule applies extensively (*bahula*);
in some cases there is occurrence, in some cases non-occurrence, and in some cases [the application of] another [rule], or in some cases [it occurs] here and there.
"By the word *bahula* (‘occasionally’), every rule [is understood] according to the tradition.
Thus ends the commentary on the First Section in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*,
the sub-commentary on Moggallāna’s *Pañcikā*.
2. Commentary on the Second Chapter 1. Regarding "the connection of pairs":
this refers to the connection of the parts that are spoken of as "pairs" with the whole (avayavisamudāya) of which they are parts.

In this matter, there must either be a *vutti* (commentary) conforming to the *pañcikā* (the fivefold analysis), or a *pañcikā* conforming to the *vutti*; yet here, no mutual conformity between the two is observed.
For in the *vutti*, it is stated merely as “from a noun (*nāman*) occurring in one or many meanings,” by way of specifying the base (*pakati*);
whereas in the *pañcikā*, it is stated by way of specifying that [base] and by way of specifying the meaning of the suffix (*paccaya*).
And the meaning has been shown; that very mutual compatibility of both is seen here. Therefore, we shall explain how the mutual compatibility of the two comes about.

[One might object: "If, in this context, there were a pentad compatible with the sequence, the side of the meaning of the conditions would have to be abandoned"—thus, because of the necessity of abandoning these [terms] such as "te... pe... ekānekatthesu" and "tena... pe... yojanīyaṃ," [the following applies].

"One incurs the fault of omitting many readings; however, if the usage were consistent with the *pañcikā*, there would be only a slight addition to be made within the usage, and thus there would be no fault of omitting much.
Therefore, since these two [terms] occur in various places as singulars and plurals, the usage must be 'from the noun' (*nāmasmā*).
