For if this were so, it would also be consistent with other teachers' traditions (*satthantara*).

It is consistent [with the rule], because it is stated in the Sutta: “In the case of two, two, one, or many, [the suffix] *nām* [is used]. Thus, the term “one or many” (*ekānekesu*) is appropriate either as a qualification of the condition (*paccaya*) or as a qualification of the base (*pakati*).
When this is a qualification of the condition, then by implication (*sāmatthiyā*), the phrase “one or many” is also understood as a qualification of the base.

In this context, “implication” refers to the power of the meaning; for indeed, when [suffixes] occur after “one” and so forth, they do not deviate from the singularity and other qualities of the very bases denoted by those words.

How could suffixes such as *syā-* and others—which indicate forms like the neuter singular (*rittattha*)—be anything other than names occurring in the sense of oneness (*ekatta*) and so forth? This is a reference to the specific names already mentioned.

Likewise, even though there is no distinct grammatical base (*pakati*) for suffixes such as the feminine marker (*itthiṇā-*) and others, they arise from that [base] through functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*), since the meaning to be expressed is not present in the root (*dhātu*) and so on; rather, it is expressed by the roots ending in *tyā-* and so forth.

In the manuscript, it is stated that case-suffixes (*vitti-paccaya*) do not occur, and likewise suffixes such as *ṇa* and so on [do not occur] because they are prescribed [only] after word-forms ending in case-suffixes (*vibhattanta*).

Furthermore, since that which qualifies the base (*pakati-visesana*) also occurs in the sense of singularity and so on by its own inherent force (*sāmatthiya*), how could the suffixes beginning with *si* (the nominative marker), which arise from a noun (*nāma*) to indicate that [number], occur elsewhere when it is impossible?
Thus, "two each" (*dve dve*) is applicable to both the singular and plural. Alternatively, even though it is not explicitly stated by its own form...

Since it is understood that "in the sense of singularity or plurality by virtue of capacity" is already stated [by the previous rule], one should understand that the phrase beginning with "te ca" (and those) has been stated.

As for the purpose of [the rule] "from a noun denoting a single or multiple [things]," he states another reason beginning with "yam panā" (but as for what...), because there is no connection with singularity and so forth in the case of an action that is not a sentient being (*asatvabhūta*), and because singularity and so forth have already been expressed by [rules] such as *kriyātthācca* (and from a verbal root expressing an action). Furthermore, [the suffixes] ending in *ti* and so forth would not occur [with such nouns] because they are not applicable to them.
Furthermore, the intended status of the meaning of the word "pañcaka" (fivefold) here is appropriate only for this particular position (*pakkha*).

For instance, number, object, and so forth are properties (*dhamma*) of the substance (*davva*) which is the denoted object; and a word that has its own primary meaning as a subordinate element (*sakatthopasajjana*) applies only to the substance.

Since designations such as "otherness" (*aññanaya*) and so on apply only to the substance, it is not improper that the inclusion of the properties of the substance within the substance itself occurs through a word expressing that substance by means of its name (*nāma*).

The [nominal] stems are the designators of the five [cases], while the case-endings (vibhattiyo) are their illuminators; likewise, the feminine suffixes (itthipaccayā) belong to the feminine gender, as we have stated in the *Sambandhacintā*:
"Having expressed its own meaning, a word [expresses] the meaning of the base, which is designated as a substance (*dabbasaññita*)."
"One should state the gender as combined [with the number], as well as the number and the action and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "by that" (*tenā*) was stated in order to show the application of *si* and the other case endings respectively to both singular and plural meanings;

"by that" means by which the fivefold nominal meaning is intended, and by which the case endings beginning with *si* will be prescribed for the meanings starting from one onwards when they are to be expressed; "in all cases" (*sabbattha*).
In all instances such as "aṃyo" and so forth, the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) of the phrase "by way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato*) and so on is this:

"Even though *syādi* [the case endings] occur in relation to both single and multiple entities, nevertheless, terms such as 'one' (*eka*) and so on function with respect to an object delimited by number (*saṅkhyā*), not with respect to mere number itself.

Because number is either present or absent in the thing numbered (*saṅkhyeya*), it exists in that which is numbered; thus, number is not the meaning of the *syādi* endings. This is not merely their own meaning (*sakattha*).
The meaning of nouns such as *dabba* is not only [the substance] itself, but number as well; this is the sense of the word "also" (*api*).

By this, the position that "number is the meaning of the case-ending" and "the fourfold set is the meaning of the noun" is refuted. In the view that "the fivefold set is the meaning of the noun," the case-endings are the indicators of number, object, and so forth;
however, in the view that "the threefold set is the meaning of the noun," number, object, and the rest are expressed by the case-endings.
Now, in order to demonstrate by way of its own form the meanings of the five [categories] intended here—beginning with the meaning of the self (sakattha)—he says "Therein," and so forth.
Therein, the meaning of the self is the qualifier (*visesana*); whatever is intended to be expressed as a qualifier, such as form and so on, that is called the "meaning of the self.
He demonstrates this by saying: "Form, genus, quality, and substance."

When the [individual] instances (gagādi) are broken down by means of the genus (jāti), that which persists is the cognition and the word for the genus, just as a thread is perceived when flowers are strung together.
Therefore, the substance (dabba) is distinct from its substratum (ādhāra); it is the cause (nimitta) for the cognition of that [substance].
That which has the nature of both existence and non-existence is considered a quality devoid of qualities.
Whatever distinguishes a substance—whether it be a genus, like the form of a word, or a specific property—is designated as a "qualifier.
Any such thing by which a substance is qualified is called a "substantive" (dabba).

Now, in order to show that the qualifier (*visesana*) such as "having the same form" (*sarūpa*) possesses its own meaning (*sakatthabhāva*), while the qualified object (*visesya*) such as "the distinction of genus" (*jāti*) possesses the status of a substance (*dabbabhāva*), he says "therein" (*tattha*), and so forth.
He says "by the same form of the word" (*saddassa sarūpena*) by means of a metaphorical transfer (*abhedopacāra*), as in the expression "the word functions with its own form.

Here, however, when the word "cow" (*go*)—which denotes the mere genus—is associated with the word "cow" which expresses the mere genus, that [word] expresses the mere genus; thus it [expresses] the genus.

It is called "qualifying. Since the words "staff" and so forth are taken metaphorically to refer to those things associated with a staff and so on, it is said that "the substance itself becomes a qualifier for another substance," meaning that by means of substances such as a staff, the persons associated with those staves are qualified.
Thus, "make him enter with a staff" means "make the person, distinguished by the substance denoted by the word 'staff,' enter."

The same method applies here as well for the phrase “he causes to enter into a spear” (*kunte pavesayati*). Since there is also a sense of self (*sakattha*) other than the fourfold sense of self already mentioned, he says “in some cases” (*katthaci*), and so forth.
“The cause of connection” (*sambandhanimitta*): the compound means that connection is the sign, the cause, or the reason for the arising of conditions;
for in this case, the word “possessing” (*assati*) refers to the owner, the person who possesses the staff (*daṇḍo assa atthīti assa*).
The connection with a substance such as a staff, which is conceptually determined, is a relation involving a basis (*sāmisa-sambandha*); that too is a condition (*paccaya*).
And so he will say: "The condition is 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍī*) due to the connection between the staff and the person.

Since even an action (*kiriyā*) functions as a qualifier of the word-meaning, its status as a self-referential entity (*sakatthabhāva*) must be stated in the very same place where it was stated for the category-meaning (*jāti*) and so forth. Thus, in the case of *pācaka* ("cook"), there is the relation consisting of the connection between the action and the agent.

Desiring to point out, by means of instruction from another, even that which is accepted by others as a *sakattha* (meaning inherent in the word itself), [the author] says here, “In some cases, even the action (*kiriyā*) [is included],” etc., in order to show the *kiriyāsakattha* at the very place where the *sambandhasakattha* was stated.

For, having subsumed the fifth meaning—known by its nature as a name and designated as a "name"—under the category of the "substantive referent" (*dabbapadattha*), [the classification is given as]: genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kiriyā*), and substance (*davva*).

The meaning of "name" (*nāma*) is fourfold. Furthermore, name is twofold according to its etymological derivation; it is threefold according to gender—masculine, feminine, and neuter—and thus becomes fourfold.
It is called "name" for the reason that it inclines toward the fourfold meaning as already stated, or because it inclines those [meanings] toward itself.
Others also state that name is fourfold according to commonality, quality, action, and desire.
In that context as well, the inclusion of *yadicchānāma* should be understood by its very substance-name (*dabba-nāma*).

The meaning established as "this is its state" (*itthattaṃ esa*) is proven by the passage beginning with "yampana," using the phrase "tatthe" and so forth; [it is proven] by way of being a designator (*abhidhāyaka*) and an indicator (*jotaka*), [derived] from the word *muni* ending in the vowel *i*.
"Otherwise" means if it were not [derived] from one ending in *i*, [it would be incorrect] because of the occurrence of the substitution (*ādesa*) of *ta*.

The connection is: "the result would not have been shown. In the commentary, by the word "evam" in the examples such as *kumārī kumāriyo*, he shows that just as in the masculine gender an example was given for the *sy*-suffixes etc.
ending in *ikāra* for the sake of showing the absence of an augment (*anādesatthaṃ*), so too in the feminine there is no ending in *ākāra*.

And this is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇaṃ*) of suffixes such as *-inī*, *-nī*, *-ū*, *-ti*, and so forth. By the phrase "if it were not... [etc. ...by the statement," [he indicates that the rule applies].
This demonstrates the existence of another rule among Pāṇini’s sūtras that prescribes the technical designation *vibhatti* (case-ending). For their rule is:
*vibhatti ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.104). Its meaning is: "The designations *syādi* and *tyādi* have the technical name *vibhatti*.
They are called by the word *vibhatti* according to their literal sense (*anvatthavasena*) because they exist; that very same meaning is expressed by the term *vibhatti*.
"Vibhatti" means "that which is divided" (*vibhajīyati*); this indicates that the word *vibhatti* contains the *ktin* suffix in the sense of an object (*kamma*).
How, then, is it among these [suffixes] beginning with *si* that there is an understanding of the meaning of the sentence "it is divided"?
Anticipating such a doubt, he says "For thus," etc., demonstrating both by what means and in what manner it is divided.
2. Regarding "in the activity of action" (*kammavuttiyaṃ kattukiriyāyā*): because of the agent's capacity for action, it refers to the two kinds of activity related to the agent and the object;
since verbal roots have multiple meanings, he says "it is done" (*karīyati*) in the sense of "it is connected" (*abhisambandhīyati*), meaning that "doing" (*karoti*) here has the sense of connecting.
The meaning is that whatever form of word-meaning is connected [to the action];
by this, he shows that the designation "object" (kamma) is established precisely through the sense of being "connected with" (anvattha).

Furthermore, although all factors (kāraka) possess a connection to an action, that which is intended to be expressed as being directly connected to the action itself should be understood as the object; even though the agent and other factors are connected to the action of the agent.

Just as there is no action (*kamma*) merely through the desire for speech, so too, since it is only through the desire for speech that the factors of action (*kāraka*) come into being, the absence of such factors in the case of one factor reaching another should be stated accordingly for all factors.

By the phrase "by a portion of the sentence," it indicates that "two [cases] for two [objects]" and "the second case for the object" (*kamme dutiyā*) belong to a single sentence; this refers to the entire treatise (*pakaraṇa*).

Because they take the form of a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), even sentences that are separate become a single syntactical unit through the experience of their mutual connection within the nature of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth.
For it is said: “Since expectancy, compatibility, proximity, and the presence of the seed [of meaning]—by these, even separate sentences constitute a great sentence.”

"By way of commonality" means by way of non-distinction such as the object (kamma) and so forth; it is said "the second and so on" by way of the conventional designation (*samaññā*) used by former teachers.

Therefore, although even *tyādi* could be designated as "second" because it completes a pair, nevertheless, since the terms "second" and "third" are conventionally established (*ruḷhi*) only for the *syādi* group, the groups of *tyādi* are not grasped by the words "second" and so forth. "In the specified" means in those [words] distinguished by the object and so forth.
"Threefold action": by this he states that action is threefold according to what is established in our own system (*sakasamaya*); others, however, maintain it is sevenfold.
How so? "It is considered threefold by way of production (*nibbatti*), transformation (*vikatti*), and acquisition (*patti*);
therein, the most desired [type] is 'action' (*kamma*), while other types of action are fourfold."

"Desired, undesired, neither desired nor undesired, and likewise that which was previously another and not previously another"—thus the other [type of karma] is fourfold. In this context, the "desired" and so forth will be explained further below;

here, by means of the threefold classification beginning with "desired," he shows karma according to its own nature. Regarding that, some conceptualize productive karma (*nibbattikamma*) in many ways; we shall clarify that here.
Whether it be nature itself that is non-transforming, or that which is dependent upon it, that is what arises as a manifestation; karma, however, is otherwise for others.
That which is non-existent is born, or that which exists is not made manifest.
“Or, through its manifestation as something produced, it is called ‘the production thereof’;

this is the meaning here: ‘The existing original material (pakati), designated as straw, which is subject to transformation, transforms itself into the modification of straw (kaṭavikāra) and is not discarded in that application...
in the expression ‘he makes a mat,’ there is merely the comprehension of the sense.”
Because it is intended to be expressed and because it is not being heard, [the verb] "kāseti" (he coughs) is used; for if it were naturally audible, it would be a modification (*vikāriya*).
For this very reason, one says "he makes a mat while coughing" (*kāse kaṭaṃ karoti*) or "he cooks rice while coughing" (*taṇḍule odanaṃ pacati*); thus, both "karoti" and "pacati" have a dual sense.

Therefore, in "he makes a mat while coughing" and "he cooks rice while coughing," there is modification (*vikāriyati*), whereas in "he makes a mat" and "he cooks rice," there is production (*nibbatti*).
The meaning is this: or rather, the nature (*pakati*) does not exist because it is non-existent; for that wherein [an action] is not dependent... (as in the case of) [the statement in a book]:

"it produces conjunction and brings about disjunction. Since there is no modification of the nature of anything whatsoever regarding conjunction and disjunction, they are produced from those very things which possess conjunction and disjunction while remaining unmodified. Such is that which has a non-dependent nature.
One [teacher] says that the productive action (*nibbattikamma*) is either a non-existent (*avijjamāna*) nature (*pakati*) or an effect (*kāriya*);

another, stating that it is otherwise, demonstrates this with the words "that which is non-existent," and so forth: that which is born while being non-existent and unmanifested is the productive action, just as [the action] produces pleasure or generates cognition;
or else, it is simply something existent and manifest that was previously unproclaimed.
Whatever manifests through arising or through becoming evident is also productive karma (*nibbattikamma*), just as the act of giving birth to a child makes manifest the commonality of being human.
Thus, according to the opinion of some, productive karma is of two kinds: that which has no inherent nature (*anissitapakatika*) and that which has no existing nature (*avijjamānapakatika*);

and according to the opinion of others, productive karma is also of two kinds: that which is non-existent yet arises, and that which, though existent, does not manifest. All of this [is productive karma].

He says that the cognition of what does not exist—that "what was never previously established arises"—is not distinct from [the process itself], stating: "The production of the non-existent is brought about.
This refers to another state, such as the characteristic of softening and so forth in the case of rice and other substances.
Some things arise through the destruction of their original nature (*prakṛti*), while others are subject to transformation (*vikārya*).
Thus, that transformation is twofold due to the emergence of another quality (*guṇantara-samuppatti*).
Some transformative action arises through the absolute destruction of the cause as it was in its original state (*pakati*), such as when one turns wood into ashes;
this is the "transformation by total reversal" (*parāvatti*) of the wood. However, some [action] arises through the emergence of other qualities.
Just as one makes gold into a bracelet or an armlet, so too that modification (*vikati*) is twofold—this is the meaning. "Not being manifested" means not being understood;
it is called "attainment" (*patti*) because it is "reached" (*pāpīyati*), that is, made an object (*visayīkarīyati*).
Where no distinction produced by action is perceived...
Whether through direct perception (*dassana*) or inference (*anumāna*),
that [excellence] is designated as "attained" (*patti*). Wherever no excellence, distinction, or superiority produced by action or accomplished through action is perceived or recognized—

either by the means of direct perception (*paccakkha-ppamāṇa*) or by the means of inference (*anumāna-ppamāṇa*)— as is the case with the excellence of produced or modified things, which is known through direct perception and inference.

It is to be understood as follows: for in that case, the attainment of excellence upon rebirth is well-established... because the agent of the action is not perceived when the excellence known as the "acquisition of wealth" is absent;
however, in some manuscripts, it is an object of direct perception in the case of a modification—as in "the wood burns," since states such as blackness are apprehended through direct perception;
in other cases, it is to be known through inference—as in "he offends Devadatta."
Or it "inspires confidence" because anger and so forth are inferable from the resulting effects, such as a distinguished facial complexion;
thus, where there is no establishment of a specific [fault], but merely a conviction (*patti*), that is designated and described as a "conviction.

The meaning here is: "one who meditates on the Dhamma as being like the *ādicca* tree. For how could there be anything [to be done] for one who is non-existent, or for one who exists but performs no act of conviction (*pattikamma*)? (Note: *santassa* is in the manuscript).
The status of being an agent [is established], for nothing that does not act can deserve to be called an agent.
Thus it is said: "The appearance of visibility, clarity, distinctness, and so forth—these specific qualities of the object are desired for the accomplishment of the action."

In this context, regarding the phrase "it is possible to see," such distinctions as "suitability for seeing" (*khamatā*), "coming into appearance" (*ābhāsopagama*), "coming into the state of being an object" (*visayattopagama*), and "manifestation" (*vyañjita*)—as applicable—are intended as the performance and accomplishment of the action of the patient (*pattikamma*).
Therefore, the meaning is that it possesses the status of an agent (*kārakatva*). For in the expression "he sees the sun," the sun is capable of being seen; therefore...
Thus, it is seen that because it "attains manifestation" (*abhi-vyañjanam upayāti*), its status as a *kāraka* (grammatical factor) arises from its being the producer of the action of seeing;

likewise, in other cases as well, its status as a *kāraka* should be understood through the accomplishment of the action by way of the specific distinctions conveyed by words such as "knowing" (*jānāti*).

Is it not the case that even the "object of transformation" (*vikāri-kamma*) is indeed an "object of production" (*nibbatti-kamma*), since it is produced precisely while being non-existent in that particular form? And even the "object of attainment" (*patti-kamma*) is likewise non-existent in the form of its connection with the action.
"It becomes so afterwards" means it is simply its production; this is true.
This is indeed the stability of the basis (*vatthuṭṭhiti*), in accordance with the conviction within the range of subtle intelligence.
In that regard, whatever is applicable there is due to the turning back of the meaning of the word "conviction" (*patīti*).
"Because there is no specific basis for restriction": this is stated because it was taught in general terms as "the second case [is used] for the object" (*kamme dutiyā*).

In cases such as *karīyati kaṭo* ("a mat is being made") and *kato kaṭo* ("a mat has been made"), the second case and so forth apply even to the substrata of the object and other factors—such as unity and so on—due to the absence of a restrictive rule.
For instance, in the *Pañcaka* (The Fivefold), regarding the meaning of nouns, the meaning of the object and so forth is related to that which is to be expressed by words such as "mat."

Regarding the phrase "beginning with *tyādi*": in order to express another meaning of a case ending—namely, number—which has not already been expressed, Pāṇinīyas apply the rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1) even when [meanings such as] the object (*karman*) and so forth have already been expressed by [words like] *kaṭa* etc., so that the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others may occur in rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2).

This is done for the sake of clarity, even though there is no possibility of applying the second case and others [to the word itself], because [the case endings] depend upon the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

In the case of those [meanings] expressed by the term *jotanā* (manifestation), the second and subsequent case endings may occur; however, in the triplet (*tika*), the number, the object (*kamma*), and so forth, are to be stated as case-endings (*vibhatti*).

In that regard, although the object and other [grammatical relations] are expressed by means of a suffix (*paccaya*), nevertheless, since singularity and the rest are not [separately] expressed, for the sake of maintaining the status of that other meaning of a case-ending called "number," the second and subsequent case endings occur even when the object and others have been expressed.
The followers of Pāṇini [hold that] the rule "the second case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2) governs the expression "when not already expressed" (Pāṇini 2.3.1). Indicating this, he says:
"In this regard, the following might be asked," and so forth. Therein, in that formulation of the second and other cases, this objection might arise.
To ask "What is it? he says: "In the group of five," and so forth. "Based on unexpressed objects and so forth" means that the objects and so forth are the bases when they have not been expressed.

The meaning of "in those" (*tesu*) refers to singularity and so forth; the sense should be understood according to what is appropriate for the purpose of indicating—that is, for expressing—the second and subsequent case-endings (*vibhattiyo*). By the word "also" (*api*), singularity and so forth that depend on an unexpressed object (*kamma*) and so forth are included, even alongside those that depend on an expressed object and so forth.
Since it was stated in the previous operation (*pubbakiriyā*) that they are "to be expected" (*āsaṅkiyā*), the subsequent operation should be understood [as follows]. In the pentad and the triad...

Having shown—by way of raising the suspicion that the status of the second case and so forth might apply to the state of being a trainee (sekha) and others, based on the support of the "unexpressed object" (abhihitakamma) and so on—and having set forth and refuted the position of those who maintain the theory of the fourfold [case-roles], he says "yadi ca" and so forth. This is his intended meaning:

"If this number, which has the sense of 'the first day' (pāṭipadika), implies that the object and other factors are to be expressed by case-endings when they are being undertaken, then [it would follow] by the rule 'when the object is unexpressed' (anabhihite kamme) and so forth..."

The inclusion of the term *anabhihita* (not already expressed) is purposeless with respect to the specific [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, because when [the relation] is already expressed, there is no function for the case-ending (*vibhatti*).

However, when this position—that "number is what is expressed by the case-ending"—is held, then the rules such as "the second case [ending] occurs in the sense of the object" (*kamme dutiyā*) should be understood merely as indications of the scope [of application].
This applies in all respects to both those who maintain the theory of five categories (*pañcakatikavādin*) and those who maintain the theory of four categories (*catukkavādin*).
In every respect according to its own power, it is merely the mere object (atthamatta) that exceeds the literal meaning of the word;
thus, "byatireka" means "that which is set apart" (*byatiritta*), where the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of an abstract state.

That from which no "byatireka"—meaning separation or distinction—exists is "abyatiritta," the meaning of which is "not separated. It is the mere object, the commonality of meaning, which is not set apart from the literal meaning of the word or from its own specific meaning.
That word *odana* and so forth, for which [the suffix] was stated in that manner, is used accordingly.

Although in the commentary (*vutti*) it is stated that what is expressed by means of the *tabba*, *iṇa*, and *na* suffixes is "unexpressed" (*avutta*), nevertheless, even when these are expressed, it should be understood in exactly the same way; showing this, he says:

"In this way," and so forth. [The word] *kato* is derived from *karoti* (to do) with the sense of the agent and the instrument, meaning "done"; [it is formed] by the rule "the suffix *kta* occurs in the senses of the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)."
(5-56) In the word *kamma-kto*, here [the suffix] *ito* is applied in the sense of the object (*kammatthe*) by the rule "other suffixes are also seen" (4-120).

The state of being an object (*kammabhāva*) is understood because suffixes such as *kita* are prescribed for the object; thus, since the Teacher has given only one example for *dhu* [ending] in this context, he says:
"Example," etc., meaning even without the statement "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*). The phrase "even without the statement" refers to the expression *vināpi*.

The word *eva* is used here in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), while the particle *api* expresses possibility (*sambhāvana*). The meaning is: "Even if there were no occurrence of the second case endings and so forth when [the object] is already expressed without [the use of] a verbal suffix, then certainly there would be no occasion for discussion regarding the presence of such suffixes.
Furthermore, one should understand that in this context, there is no possibility of the second case endings and so forth occurring when [the object] is already expressed;

for example, in "rice is being cooked" (*paccate odano*) or "a mat is made" (*kato kaṭo*), if the second case endings and so forth were to occur, there would be no scope for the prescription of the nominative (*paṭhamā*).

"Then, when the agent is not expressed by the [verbal] capacity, the second and subsequent case endings would occur for the object and so forth along with their respective actions, whereas the first case ending occurs only when [the agent] is expressed.

Is it not the case that the first case provides no scope for the agent? [For example, in the expressions] "the tree is a *pilakkhu*" (*rukkho pilakkho*) and "the tree is a *pilakkhu*" (*rukkho pilakkho*), the verbal form is not heard; thus, the *Bhassapadīpa* considers this to be the occurrence of another case ending.
What is this that is called "non-agent"? If it were a non-agent, it would not be fit for such usage;

therefore, where there is no hearing of a specific action, the understanding of existence—which is co-present with the referent of the word—is considered, as in "there is a tree," "there is a *pilakkha* [fig tree].
Thus, since the status of being an agent belongs to the tree and so forth themselves, in order to establish another object regarding that very meaning, [this is stated].

The word *ñāṇaṃ* is employed [as the subject], and *sato* [is used] where there is no application of another verb; in such cases, by the general rule (*ussagga*), the nominative case (*sattamī*) is understood as the fourth [case].
Since there is no occasion for the introduction of the third case (*tatiyā*) for the agent through the connection with a verb, this is the meaning of the first [case].
[This is illustrated by] the example *bhassapadīpo*, and not [by] *uccaṃ nīcaṃ*, because the sense of the locative is already expressed by the particle [in the phrase] "there is" (*atthi*).

Regarding the statement "there is no connection," it can be argued that the status of agent belongs only to the receptacle (*ādheya*) and not to the locus (*ādhāra*), and thus there is no scope for the locative case;
yet, the rule for the nominative case would have no scope [in such instances].

Furthermore, the reason stated—that [the relationship] is unestablished—is valid because, instead of prescribing the nominative from what is non-numerical (*asaṅkhyato*), the general rule [at 2.39] states "after [a word ending in] the nominative" (*paṭhamāttha matte*).
It is indeed established that the statement "because it does not state a reason" stands as meaning "it is purposeless.
As for the word *yañca* (and which), the particle *ca* serves to collect another thing to be stated; the meaning is: "there is something else further to be said.

The connection is: "and which result one conceives. In this context, when there is no governing topic (*adhikāra*) of what has been previously stated, it is like the expression "the mat is made," where [the agent] is understood by implication.

Because the object (*kamma*) is already expressed, the accusative case (*dutiyā*) does not occur; likewise, in the expression “he makes a large, beautiful mat” (*kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ dassanīyan*), because the object arising from the word *kaṭa* is already expressed, the accusative would not occur after qualifiers such as *vipula*.
Therefore, in compounds such as those ending in *tya*, *tabba*, or *ṇādi*, the accusative occurs only when the object is not already expressed; thus, it occurs even with qualifiers like *vipula*.

The meaning is: "In the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the word *anabhihite* (‘when not already expressed’) from the sūtra *dutiyāvidhānasaṅkhātaṃ anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1), one considers the result [of the action];

the meaning of *yuttassa* is ‘of the connection,’ and because it connects individually, as in ‘he makes a mat, he makes it large, he makes it beautiful,’ thus there is a connection for the verb *karoti* with each individual object."
The object (*attha*) is the remaining factor, namely "the state of being an object" (*kamma-tā*). Thus it is considered:
"The [state of being an object] exists even for 'vast' (*vipula*), 'beautiful' (*dassanīya*), and so forth, as these occur in such phrases as 'I am making it vast' and 'I am making it beautiful.
Since one easily perceives the other when one of them is expressed, the second case ending will also occur to express that [other factor]. This is an entry into another perspective.

Nor is it "not prohibited by the Teacher. We shall demonstrate this point as well: when the word *kaṭa* arises, the accusative case expresses the action (*kamma*) that is the second type of matting, not the action characterized by qualities such as "extensive" (*vipula*).

Therefore, for the purpose of expressing that [action], only the accusative occurs. Alternatively, the matting itself is the action; thus, even when [the matting] is expressed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "extensive," the accusative will still occur.
For when it is said, "Vipula makes a mat; he is beautiful," one would understand *vipula* and the others as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) only with the agent (*kattā*).
Therefore, in order to establish apposition with the word *kaṭa* (mat), the accusative case must be applied here. This is the objection beginning with "Is it not so?

etc. [The answer is: "So" means that when there is the status of an object (*kammatā*) for that which is endowed with such qualities, [the suffix] *-ta* is reached when the mat is to be designated as the object (*kamme abhidhāniye*).

"Done" (*kata*)—because of the suffix *-tta* in *katatta*, and because of its connection with "he does" (*karoti*) starting from "noble" (*udāra*), the accusative case is obtained; such is the meaning.

Thus, the resolution [to the objection] beginning with "it is thought" (*maññate*) and so forth is that it does not denote the object (*kamma*) by way of a part; this is the connection. "By way of a part" means individually. To the question "What then?", he says:
"It denotes the entire object by way of its intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato*). Let it be as you wish; even though it is stated starting from "noble" (*udāra*)...
Regarding the phrase "according to the rule" (*vidhinā paṭhamā*), he says "also from the word *kata*" (*katasaddato pi*) and so forth, asking:

"From what does it proceed based on the word *kata*? The meaning is as follows: the meaning of the noun (*nāma-sadda*) is "included within" (*antobhūta*) or "contained within" (*antogadha*). That meaning—namely, the characteristic of the object (*kamma-lakkhaṇa*)—is expressed, stated, and fulfilled in that [meaning] which is characterized by the object;
this is the sense. Is it not the case that in examples such as "the mat is made" (*kato kaṭo*), the function of all objects exists by way of their own inherent nature (*sabhāvato*)?

Because the first case ending occurs everywhere when there is the application of a name whose meaning is internal to the object, even in the mere sense of "the object," one might raise the objection that since the second case ending arises even from words such as *kaṭa* (in the expression *kaṭaṃ karoti uḷāraṃ sobhanaṃ dassanīyaṃ*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) of using the first case ending for words like *uḷāra*.
Keeping in mind this objection—which has reached the point of questioning the application of the first case to what is already expressed—the author says: "The word *kaṭa*, etc."
Regarding the phrase "tvi-ccādi" and so forth: "by way of generality" (*sāmaññena*) means by way of the commonality of each individual [object], such as a mat (*kaṭa*) and so on.

By the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.49), Pāṇinīyas establish the technical designation of "object" (*kamma*) for that which is most desired by the agent in relation to the action;
having thus established this, they prescribe the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) for objects such as "cooking" (*nibbatti*) and so on, expressed by the suffix *ti*.

And because it is the object of that action, there is the state of being most desired (*icchitatamatta*); for in such expressions as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) or "he milks the cow" (*gāvaṃ duhati*), the actions of cooking and so forth are undertaken for the sake of the rice and so on, and thus the rice, the cow, and so forth possess the state of being most desired. Demonstrating this, he says: "That which [is] by the agent," and so forth;

the connection is that [the case ending] is intended as the accusative after establishing the grammatical inflection (*vibhatti*). Furthermore, whatever serves as the cause for the production of the milk and so forth—

The factor such as a cow, which is intended [as the object] and is not mentioned by way of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, though connected with actions such as milking, is an *akathita* (unmentioned) *kāraka*. Even in that case, the designation of "object" (*karman*) is prescribed by the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51), and by that very rule the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is ordained. To illustrate this, he says: ‘when it is being employed,’ and so forth; and here the restriction regarding the *akathita* was established by the author of the Vārttika:

“[The *akathita* designation applies] when the agent intends the object through another *kāraka*. (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.51) This means: when the agent intends the object (*karman*) by means of another *kāraka*, such as the instrument (*karaṇa*), that object is called *akathita*. For example, in the sentence *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (“he milks milk from the cow”), the cow is the *akathita* because the agent intends the cow as the basis for the milk, which is the actual object. In this context, the cow is not mentioned as the instrument or any other *kāraka*; therefore, it receives the designation of object and takes the second case ending. Thus, the rule is formulated: when the agent intends the object through another *kāraka*, that object is *akathita*. This is the restriction made by the Vārttikakāra.
The term *nimitta* (cause/sign) is used in the sense of application (*upayoga*) for those [words] ending in the suffixes *pucchi*, *ci*, *bhikkhī*, *duhi*, and *yāci*;
it is also stated in the context of the preceding rule (*pubbavidhi*) for those ending in *brū*, *sās*, and *īna*, as well as for those not attached to a quality (*guṇa*).
It is called *upayoga* because it is applied—that is, it is employed—for the accomplishment of a desired meaning; it begins with the word *upa*. In that [sense], it is a *nimitta*.

In the case of *gavādi* and so forth, in a rule prescribing what has not been previously established (*apubbavidhimhi*), there is no prescription of prior technical designations such as ablative (*apādāna*) or locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

For if there were such a prescription, it would apply appropriately in cases such as *māṇavako maggaṃ pucchati* ("the boy asks the way") and *rukkhā phalāni avacināti* ("he gathers fruits from the tree").

"Connected with a quality" (*guṇāsattaṃ*) means connected with, or related to, a quality; here, by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), it is intended to express the primary instrument (*padhānasādhana*), such as a property (*dhamma*) and so forth, for the primary instrument is indeed [what is meant].

A quality (*guṇa*) exists in relation to an action (*kiriyā*) that is primary and beneficial—that is, helpful to the action. The particle *ca* is used here for inclusive conjunction (*anuttasamuccaye*).

Furthermore, since the primary [action] has that [quality] as its purpose (*tadatthattā*) in the occurrence of phenomena and so forth, and since that which is being employed is the source of what is employed (*payopabhuti*), one forms a descriptive compound (*visesanasamāsa*) of "the source of what is being employed" (*upayujjamānapayoppabhuti*).

Then, by forming a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) with "the cause" (*nimitta*), it becomes "the cause which is the source of what is being employed" (*upayujjamānapayoppabhutinimitta*). The word *pabhuti* means "source."
By the word *saddena*, there is the inclusion of *gavādi*; by the first *ādi*-word, *gomantādi*; by the second *ādi*-word, *adhikaraṇādi*; and by the fourth, *vinayādi*.
"The prescription" (*vidhāna*) refers to the prescription of the accusative case; it should be construed as "the prescription of the accusative is intended.

By the Pāṇinīyas, having established the designation of "object" (*kamma*) through the rule "That which is thus connected but not intended [as primary] is [called] object" (1.4.50), [they state] "In the object... (*kamme*).
By the very statement “the second case ending” (2-3-2), the second case is prescribed; to demonstrate that, he says “by which,” etc.

The meaning of the phrase “likewise, what is connected even if unintended” should be understood according to the reading of the *Pañcikā* beginning with “by which. It is connected to the verb “is joined” (*yujjati*);
“connected” (*yutta*) refers to the connection with the action. However, in this context—
If it is through lack of understanding that one does not desire [something], such as food and so forth, then that is "undesired.
But when it is due to shame, fear, and so on, that is considered the "most undesired.

Regarding the phrase "likewise, what is appropriate and undesired," because this sutta is stated by way of exclusion (*pariyudāsa*), "undesired" refers to something other than what is desired—namely, that which is not intended or favored.
Therefore, in the expression "going to the village, he approaches the foot of a tree," the designation of "object" (*kamma*) is established for the foot of the tree, whether intended or unintended;
thus, the second case ending (*dutiya*) is prescribed there by the rule "the second case is used for the object. This is shown by the phrase "from that which is intended or unintended," and so forth.
The foot of the tree is not "intended" because it was not previously desired, nor is it "unintended" because it is not repugnant to one who is going to the village.

For him, that [dwelling] is the primary concern; however, approaching the foot of a tree is mentioned as a secondary consequence (*pasaṅga*). Thus, there is indeed a connection between the action and the roots of trees as well.
Regarding this too: "Neither what is desired nor what is undesired is approached by one of great intelligence;
the root is for the sake of rest, and that would be the most desired."
To show that the word "and" (*ca*) includes the term *brūsāsinaṃ* as well, he says: “*Evaṃ*,” etc. Here, the designation *akathita* (unspoken) applies to the village, Devadatta, and the Ganges;
however, [in cases such as] “*ajādayo*,” the object is that which is most desired. By the word “etc. (*ādi*), examples such as “*pattheti gāvuṃ purisaṃ dvijo*” are included.
The roots *nayati* and *nī* mean “to reach”; *vahati* and *vaha* mean “to reach”; *harati* and *hara* mean “to take away”; *jayati* and *ji* mean “to conquer”—this applies in all instances.
In this case, the form [is derived] by the substitution of *ay* for the root; the form *daṇḍa* [in *daṇḍeti*] is from the *curādi* class with the suffix *ṇi*.

Then, having designated it as an object (*kamma*) by various rules such as "the object of *adhi*, *sī*, *ṭhā*, and *ās*" (1-4-46), the accusative case ending (*dutiyā*) is prescribed by those respective grammatical authorities according to the rule "the second case is used for the object" (2-3-2), as in the example "he will lie upon the earth" (*paṭhaviṃ adhisessati*).
In all these cases, the world’s desire for the object of the action (*kamma*) is preceded by the cognition of it as something other [than the agent];

thus, demonstrating that this action is preceded by such a cognition, he says "preceded by *adhi*," and so forth. The connection is: "How indeed could there be the status of an object (*kammatā*) through that very desire for the action by which [the case ending] the accusative (*dutiyā*) would be employed?
The phrase "are not found at all" connects with the possibility that this might occur for someone at some time. "Should be endeavored" means it should be undertaken by beginning another sutta.

The meaning is: "In that very case, why do you allow this to fester in your mind as a fault? Regarding the word *dhamme*, the meaning should be understood by applying the same grammatical construction;
just as there was a desire for the accusative case in the sense of a substratum (*ādhāra*), so too here there is a desire for the locative case in the sense of a substratum.
Therefore he said: "In *dhamme* there is a desire for the locative case. The connection is with the phrase "clinging to *dhamma*," because it shares the same meaning as the word *evaṃ*.
Likewise, since the meaning of the word *tathā* is understood by following its own sense, the meaning of *tathā* is not stated separately.

Furthermore, *pāna* (drinking) and *ācāra* (conduct) form the compound *pānācāra*; in that *tasmin tappānācāre*, which refers to the substratum (*ādhāra*) of that drinking and conduct—namely, the river or other such substrata connected to the verbal roots whose meanings are "drinking" and "conduct"—it is said:
"in the substratum of the roots whose meanings are drinking and conduct," because that very substratum is the locus of both drinking and conduct.

"Of some" (*kesañci*) means, without restriction, of some grammarians (*saddasatthakārānaṃ*). "In this" (*ettha*) refers to this case when there is a desire for a locative expression (*ādhāra-vacanicchā-pakkhe*).
By the rule "the suffix *pati* [is used] in the sense of 'part' (*bhāge*) after the prefix *pari*," he shows that the word *pati* is not connected with the verbal root (*dhātu*).

If it were so connected, there would be an absence of the genitive case; therefore he says "but when" (*yadā tv*), etc. In the commentary (*vutti*), by the pronoun "by that" (*tena*), that which is included by the particle *api* is indicated.
"Having taken [it] a third time also, [the word] *vācā* is a designation for the plural number. 3.
Time (*kāla*):

By such rules as ‘when [there is a connection with] time or distance,’ even in constructions with intransitive verbs—as in ‘he sleeps for a month’ or ‘he lies for a league’—[the accusative is used] for time, state (*bhāva*), distance (*addha*), and place (*desa*)."
It shows that others have stated: "And [the status of] being an object (*kamma*) is not authorized by all [grammarians] in every respect through [rules such as] *yadātviccādi*";

for if that were so, how could there be the status of an object? Furthermore, it shows that even the connection with the action of measuring (*māna*) is not dependent [on such rules]—just as in examples like *māsaṃ āsate*, the connection of actions such as sitting (*āsana*) with time periods like a month (*māsa*), etc., occurs despite the absence of such grammatical authorization. (Note: *āsanādīsu* appears in the manuscript).
And because the connection with qualities such as goodness enters the path of worldly conviction, it is said that "it is not accomplished. This means that actions do not exist;
since there is an absence of connection with action, there is an absence of the status of being an object (*kamma*). For example, "sugar-grains" refers to roasted barley mixed with sugar.
Because there is no connection between the action of reciting and the mountain, nor between the mountain and the entirety of the coin-purses, [the action does not apply].
In expressions such as *māsassā* (of the month), the second case ending does not occur because there is no absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
By the phrase *pubbaṇhe samayaṃ*, he shows that this is a locative-tatpuruṣa compound (sattamī-āmādi-samāsa) meaning "at the time of morning.

By the phrase *accantameva* (absolutely), he states the connection of the word *samaya* with the action of dwelling in its entirety; the connection is: "that one single time (*ekaṃsamayaṃ*) when he dwelt by means of dwelling in compassion. [The same applies] absolutely to the action of approaching.
By the word *yutto* ("joined"), he characterizes the absolute suitability of the morning time and so forth even for the acts of wearing and dwelling;
furthermore, by the phrase "But when... (*yadā tv*) and so on, he demonstrates that accomplishment is possible through another mode as well.

*Vibhattiyā vipallāso* (a transposition of case endings) is the occurrence of something otherwise than its natural state; here, however, the locative case (*sattamī*) is used in the sense of the locative (*sattamyatthe*).
By way of general rule (*bāhulaka*), the occurrence of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is established simply by the statement "the second case [is used] for the object" (*kamme dutiyā*).

The third case (*tṛtīyā*) is intended as that which is favored by the followers of Pāṇini through their detailed exposition (*papañca*) in the rule "the third case [is used] for the apavarga" (*apavarge tṛtīyā*).

However, having raised the doubt as to how time and distance can possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*), he says "nevertheless," etc., while establishing that very status of being an instrument.

"Even so" (*tathāpi*) means that although the instrumental case exists because the state of being an instrument is possible according to the sequence already stated, [the word] "might be" (*siyā*) implies that the instrumental case might be used;

and "that too" (*tañca*) refers to that instrument. Regarding the phrase "in the midst of the factors of action" (*kārakamajjhe*), this is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*), and by the word "factors of action" (*kāraka*), the factor of action as capacity (*sattikāraka*) is intended;
thus he says, "in the midst of two capacities of the agent. For even though the single agent, such as Devadatta, is indivisible, [the distinction is made].
Among the distinct capacities inherent in the agent, [the author] expresses the differentiation of time and duration itself by saying "for instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
"In a single object" (*ekattha*) means in a single Devadatta; "accomplishing two days" (*dvīha-sādhana*) is the connection [to the act of eating];

"two days" (*dvīha*) is the collective compound of two days, and in that [compound]. Alternatively, it is formed by the word *issāsa*, derived from the analysis "an archer (*issu*) who possesses an arrow (*asa*)," or "one who has an arrow in his hand."
The phrase "in the act of shooting" (*isvasane*) indicates an action currently being performed; the objection beginning with "But surely... (*nanu...iccādi*) follows;

"five hundred *dhanus* is a *kosa*" is the response, as is the subsequent passage beginning with "it is thus understood" (*evamaññateccādi*). Regarding the expression "having reached the sixth" (*chaṭṭhiyāsampattāyaṃ*), it means "having reached a portion of the *kosa*"; thus, "having reached the sixth" (*chaṭṭhiyā sampattāyaṃ*).

The phrase "this is equal to that which has its doubt released" (*muttasaṃsayenedaṃ samānaṃ*) means that this is similar to that [target] such as the *avadhya* where the doubt has been released (*mutto saṃsayo yasmiṃ avadhyādo*). Thus is the meaning.
In the *Vutti*, the term "intended" (*abhimata*) refers to the fact that the locative and ablative cases are intended to express the state of being an elaboration (*papañca*), according to the rule:

"The seventh and fifth [cases] are used for the middle of the factors of action" (2-3-7). Thus, in the example *dvīhe bhuñjissati* ("he will eat in two days"), the meaning is "he will eat when two days have passed";

here the locative case is used by the rule "the state of being 'yad' is a characteristic of a state of being" (2-3-6), for this [rule] depends solely on the desire to express each respective factor of action.
This is stated by way of abundance: "He will eat two days from the treasury" means that having gone out for two days, he will eat;
the limit is the object already grasped, such as a target situated outside the treasury. "He pierces the treasury" means he pierces a target situated within the treasury—this is the meaning.

4. *Gatikatacatthasamāsa*: Those compounds in which a *gati* (preverb) has been made into a *catthasamāsa* (compound ending in a past participle) are so called. Regarding the term *aññapadatthavutti*: it means those in which there is a function (*vutti*) with respect to another word-meaning (*aññapadatthe*);

thus, this is a *byadhikaraṇa-aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound of different case-relations as the external referent). This is because, within a *catthasamāsa*, the *gati* and other elements each possess their own distinct predominance.
He considers that when the word *attha* (purpose) is employed after those [words], it is connected individually with "going" (*gati*) and so forth.

Now, if only the word *payojje* (in the purpose) were stated in the sutta, how would it be understood that the "one who is to be employed" (*payojjo*) is himself the agent (*kattā*), such that the commentary provides the explanation "in the agent who is to be employed"?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "the meaning of going and so forth," and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [he includes] "understanding" (*bodha*) and the rest.
"Grasping" means "one who is capable of performing that action"; thus the connection is that only one capable of that action—such as going and so forth—is employed.
He says, "And he is the agent," meaning that one capable of performing an action is indeed the agent. Regarding the phrase "when the second case is established":

because the status of the object (*kamma*) is established for the instigator (*payojaka-kattā*) according to the method to be explained later, the second case is applied to the object by the very rule "the second case is used for the object" (*kamme dutiyā*).
When the second [rule] is established, he asks: "What is the characteristic of this restriction for which this [sūtra] is commenced?
and says: "For the purpose of [denoting] motion and so forth," etc. It will be illustrated by counter-examples with the words: "Of these very [verbs]," etc.

And thus, when it is accepted that "the instigator (prayojaka) is the agent and not the object," the meaning is that it is explained as "the instigator is the agent. Furthermore, by the words "capacity (sāmatthiyaṃ pan'... and so forth, he states the nature of that capacity.

The word division is *gati-ādi-atthānaṃ*. The meaning is that the one being enjoined (*niyujjamāno*), because it is connected with the activity (*kiriyā*) designated as the operation of the instigator (*payojaka-byāpāra*), becomes precisely the object (*kamma-bhūto*). This is the intended sense here:

although the instigated agent (*payojjo kattā*) is indeed an agent because he is the means (*sādhana*) for the activity of going and so forth, nevertheless, while being made to operate in the acts of going and so forth by the instigator, [he is the object] of the instigator’s operation characterized as activity.
The meaning is: "If that which is connected with an action were not the object (*kamma*), what else could it be?

By this implicit power characterized by the impossibility of its being otherwise, it is understood to be indeed the object. By the word "is understood" (*patīyate*), it is indicated that its status as an object is merely through the mode of cognition (*patītiva-sena*);

however, in its essential nature (*sabhāvato*), it is also made known to be the instigator (*payojja*) or the agent (*kattā*). Everywhere, the term "instigator" (*payojaka*) refers to Devadatta and others.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "it is an example for the purpose of understanding. Regarding the phrase “*ete sameva*,” etc.: because the statement has a restrictive purpose according to the sequence explained below, the particle *eva* is obtained.
Since the word *ete* expresses a relative [to something else], it refers by way of abbreviation to those very states of going and so forth as they were recited, acting as the qualified objects;
thus, one considers that it is formed as “*ete sameva*” and “*evosañca*” (as found in the manuscript). [For example: “Devadatta goes... and so forth.

By the phrase "it does not exist," he illuminates this meaning: "Even though, due to the connection with the action, the object-hood of the agent follows as it does for the instigator (*prayojaka*), nevertheless, because [the rule] states 'he causes to go' (*payojjeti*), the second case ending does not follow for the agent Devadatta.
This is because the rule *gati-buddhi-* etc. (Pāṇini 1.4.52) prescribes the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) for the agent who is the instigator.
In that [context], the word *payojje* is intended in the sense of the locative; the particle *cara* is used in the sense of a question.

Regarding the phrase "in this enumeration (*uddese*) where it says 'he employs' (*payojeti'), how should it be?"—the meaning should be understood as follows: at the end of the sentence beginning with "when *cara*" and so forth, in the proximity of the statement "he employs" in this enumeration, there is a remainder of the text (*pāṭhaseso*) consisting of the words "'then how should it be? This is the sense to be known up to that point.

The particle *tatiyanta* (ending in the third case) is a locative adverb (*nipāta*); because the sense [of the reason] proceeds from it, and because the second case is obtained, there must be the connection: "by Yaññadatta.
5. *Harā*.

By means of the words beginning with *niyamena* ("by way of restriction"), he states the purpose for commencing this grammatical rule. That [purpose] is to be expressed as "even the third case [is used], even the second case.
When, however, by means of the words beginning with *iccādi*, it carries [the sense of] "taking" (*harati*), it indicates that it does not mean "eating" (*āhāra*) nor "not eating" (*nāhāra*).

The phrase "in both senses" (*ubhayattha*) means in the sense of both the attained and the unattained second case; the meaning is that there is an option (*vibhāsā*) or alternative. In *kāreti*, the suffix *-ti* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kara*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*); the substitution of *la* for *tta* occurs because of the presence of *l*.

In this context, *ettakāyādessa* refers to the verbal root (*vacana*). Since one performs that which is called *abhivāda*—meaning "salutation" (*abhivadana*)—it is indicated in the nominal root (*nāmadhātu*) *abhivādi* according to the rule *dhātvatthenāmasmī* (5-12). Thus he says: *abhivādismā*, and so forth.
6. Nakhā.

*Khādayati*: from *khād* and *ad*, meaning "to eat" (*bhakkhaṇe*). *Avhāpayati*: from *vhe*, meaning "to call" (*avhāne*), preceded by the prefix *ā*. According to the rule "In the sense of the activity of an instigator (*payojaka-vyāpāre*), there is also the suffix *ṇāpi*" (Pāṇini 3.1.26), when *ṇāpi* is added, there is the elision of the preceding vowel.

*Kandayati*: from *kand*, meaning "to call out" or "to weep" (*avhānarodanesu*). Regarding the grammatical rule (*gaṇasutta*) "In the case of the root *vah* [meaning] 'to carry,' when the agent is not a driver (*aniyantuke*)," the meaning here is:

"The second case ending does not occur after the root *vah* when it has an instigating agent who is not a driver. A driver (*niyantā*) is one who controls the accomplishment of the action; having stated this, he says "the factor of the action" (*kiriyaṅga*) etc., in order to clarify that very point.
The "instrumental factor" (*kiriyaṅga*) is that which serves as the instrument for the action, such as a bullock and so forth;
"having restricted" means having established [the agent] in a specific task or sphere of action.

In the expression "he causes Devadatta to carry the load," Devadatta—being a wise man—carries the load even without a driver, and thus he is the agent who is "without a driver. [In contrast, one says] "he causes the bullocks to carry the load."
But here, since oxen do not pull [the cart] without a driver, they are "with a driver" (*saniyantukā*).

Regarding the phrase “*bhakkhissāhiṃsāya*,” this is the meaning of the rule concerning the group (*gaṇasutta*): “The second case ending does not occur after a verb root whose purpose is to eat when it is used for an agent who employs [another].
Now, how is there the sense of harming (*hiṃsatthatā*) here in *bhakkhissa*, since harming (*hiṃsā*) consists of volition (*cetanā*)?
It is possible that this [tree] is not sentient or possessed of volition; therefore, he said "all," and so forth. "All" refers to trees and other such entities, which are the referents of the word.
Now, in order to demonstrate the sense of "harming" (hiṃsā) that is conducive to the vision of all things, he said "or else," and so forth.
But is this grammar not based on the Buddha’s word? If that is so, then having demonstrated only what is accepted therein—

"One must go; what is the name of this [path] that leads to the vision of others?"—thus he remains silent. It is understood that for those who have departed from their cause, there is the state of going forth (*nikkhamissā*) from existence (*bhava*).
However, those of great merit and wisdom do not consider the hardship of being bound to the welfare of others as anything at all.
For by this, the welfare of others is achieved: "Even amidst death, there is success for disciples who know each respective way of dying."
"Or perhaps at some time or other they might find such an opportunity or such a means (in this book), and thus acquire confidence in the Buddha’s word through the acquisition of wisdom;
by that entry-point, they would gradually attain firm confidence in the Blessed Buddha.
In the same way, even in various contexts where specific explanations and examples are cited, [the same applies].
The purpose of this work should be understood precisely according to that [tradition]; one should not think, "This teacher is intent on useless talk.

This was stated by our supreme guru, the Great Lord (Mahāsāmi)—who is known as Ratanamati, the author of the *Pañcikālaṅkāra* and other works, who has been made aware of the various essential meanings of the Vedas through his great wisdom and proficiency, who is possessed of wisdom, and who is a benefactor of the jewel of the Sambuddha’s dispensation.
Having stated, “This matter here is to be investigated,” [the author] has drawn forth various alternative opinions and explained much;
we, however, shall clarify the meaning by taking as our basis only that which was intended by the Teacher.

Even though there are many different views, according to the usage established by tradition, wherever terms such as *padhānakamma* (primary action) and so forth are seen, and where terms such as *appadhāna* (secondary) and so forth appear—

Since this applies to both cases, he explains it here by following the sequence approved by the author of the *Bhāṣyakāra* and others, beginning with "duhādīnam" and so forth. Here, the word "ādi" (and so forth) expresses a manner;
by it, [verbs] such as *yācati* (he asks) and others are included. In the phrase "of those joined with two objects," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
Therefore, among those joined with two objects, even though [the verb] is non-primary (*appadhāna*), there are [cases] such as "in the object, such as a cow" (*kamme tyādippabhutayo*).

The construction (*yojanā*). By the phrase “*iccādi*,” there is the inclusion of such expressions as “he acquires a cow” (*avarundhati vajaṃ gāvaṃ*) and “the cow is acquired” (*avarundhīyate vajaṃ go*).

By the phrase “of meanings such as going” (*gamanādyatthānaṃ*), there is the grasping of meanings such as “understanding” (*bodha*). Regarding the question, “How is the status of being the instigator (*payojaka*) possible in the case of ‘Devadatta goes to the village’ (*gamīyate gāmo devadatto*)?
he says: “*Purise*,” etc. Even though the village is silent because it is devoid of activity...
Just as a person accomplishes the act of going, nevertheless, the characteristic of attaining the fruit of that act of going—which belongs to the person—is common to both the village and the person;

thus, because the fruit of the person’s action is the same, the intention is that even the village becomes a cause for the designation of the "agent" of the act of going. For instance, someone going to a village [might say] while near the village...

When one says, "The village has come; the village has arrived," there are others—namely *duh* and so forth—which are connected with two actions and have been cited as having the sense of going and so on; [the suffix is used] after these for others.

Furthermore, regarding the primary action (*padhānakamma*), in cases such as *ajā* (goat) and so on, when the primary action is present, the primacy of *ajā* and the rest is due to their being the purpose (*payojana*) for the action.
For the action of bringing is undertaken for the sake of the goat and the other objects. This, then, is the summary here:
“*Duhi*, *yāci*, *rudhi*, *pucchi*, *bhikkhi*, *ci*, *bruvi*, and *sāsi*;
*ji*, *daṇḍi*, *patthi*, and *manthi*—these are the verbal roots beginning with *duh*.
Those [roots] established in the sūtras on motion and so forth possess the meanings of motion and so forth.”
In the case of verbs having two objects, such as *nī* (to lead), *vah* (to carry), *hr* (to take), and *kṛṣ* (to pull), the forms *duh* and so forth occur when the secondary object is intended;
whereas the forms *nī*, *vah*, and so forth occur when the primary object is intended. The roots beginning with *tyaj* (to abandon) and others follow this same pattern.
“In both cases, the application [of the rule] is for roots such as *gati* (to go) and others.

Furthermore, the application should be understood in every respect according to what has been stated here and in the investigation of grammatical relations (*sambandha*). 7. *Dhy-ādi* (the group beginning with *dhyai*).
Since [the vocative case] was previously prescribed for the second case by virtue of its dependence on an action (*kriyā*) or its dependence on an agent (*kāraka*), he says "now," and so forth.
Alternatively, through the indication that the word *hi* emphasizes the meaning, or by means of the word *ādi*, there also occurs the form “*hā devadatta*.

However, in the expression “*hā devadatta-dukkhaṃ*,” because it is connected with suffering (*dukkha*), it is not connected with Devadatta; thus, in the case of addressing Devadatta, the first case is used.

Now, one might object: "If, when joined with the word *antarā*, the second case is used—as in *rājagahā nālandāhi* (from Rājagaha to Nālandā)—then why is the second case not used here in *antarā maggaṃ* (on the way), since it is both *maggā* and *antarāmaggā*? [The answer is: Because of the lack of connection (*ayoga*).
For those things whose middle it is that are connected with it; therefore, the second case is used only with those [words]. Alternatively, even if [the objection] were accepted...
In that construction (*taṃyoge*), because the path is primarily related to that [object] itself, the second case (*dutiyā*) does not apply to everything [in the sentence];
rather, even here, only the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) is obtained, as in *antarā tañca mañca kamaṇḍalu*. The meaning here is "the water-pot between you and me.
Now, why does the second case not occur after the word *kamaṇḍalu*, even though there is a connection with *antara*? Because that [word *kamaṇḍalu*] is the primary factor (*padhāna*).
For instance, [the suffix *ka*] occurs in its own sense (*sakattha*) in the case of *kamaṇḍalu*;
however, in your view, it occurs in the sense of another (*parattha*) because it functions as a qualifier for the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu-visesanatta*).

Since the suffix *ka* there functions in its own sense, it is understood as primary (*padhānatthena avatattā*), and because it does not deviate from the initial form (*pāṭipadikato accutattā*), it comes first according to the principle of Jinendrabuddhi. This applies to the relationship of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) such as censure (*nindā*) and so forth.
Because it exists everywhere, this word is formed with a genitive of relation; it belongs to the class of *ākati* (nominal stems).

Regarding the rule "in the sense of 'characteristic' (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth," since it is a specification of meaning for a noun ending in *-ka*, he says: "the suffix *-in* is appropriate," and so on.

"By that" means by way of the reason for the designation of the meaning connected with the prefix *abhi*; since it is intended to state the cause by means of a term denoting a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), he says "in that [context]" and so forth.
The cause is twofold; for it is said in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*: "Causes may be of two kinds: the generative (*janaka*) and the indicative (*ñāpaka*). (252).
It is "characterization" (*samupalakkhaṇaṃ*) because it characterizes thoroughly; it is the indicative, which is a mere conventional designation (*saṅketamatta*).
But it is not the producer (*janaka*). Even a convention (*saṅketa*) is called a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), because it is characterized (*lakkhīyate*) by that which is being produced.
The purpose for including even the producer here as a characteristic should be seen in the context of the phrase "by means of a [particular] aspect" (*anunā*, 2–10).

By the word "any particular aspect" (*kañci pakāraṃ*), he states the meaning of the term *ittham*. By the word "attained" (*patta*), he states the meaning of the root *bhū*; for here, the verbal root *bhū*—

The term *rukkholakkhaṇa* functions as a *pattiya* (possessive compound); "the characteristic of a tree" means that the tree is the indicative cause (*ñāpakahetu*). This is because [the lightning] is made known by means of the tree.
However, the teacher Jinindabuddhi explains it otherwise; his opinion is as follows:
"This [word] is not an indicator of an action, nor is it a designator of a relation."
Nor does it depend on another action; rather, it is a differentiator of the relationship.

This is the meaning here: it is not an indicator of an action like [the prefix] *abhi-* in such cases as *abhinandati*, nor is it a designator of a relationship like the genitive case, nor is it dependent on an action like the word *ni-* in *nikkhamati*.
Nor does it depend on another action; rather, it is that which differentiates and qualifies the relationship. To demonstrate this, he says: ‘But others... and so forth.

Here, the word *iti* indicates an illustration. The meaning is that [the lightning] is produced by the action of reaching—expressed as “having reached the tree”—which is the action of causing the tree to be reached by the lightning.
For indeed, in the absence of the tree being reached by the lightning, [the relationship would not be established].

By what means could the relationship—the state of being a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is characterized (*lakṣya*)—between lightning (*vijju*), a tree (*rukkha*), and the act of marking (*tallaṇa*) be established?
For if the relationship itself is not illuminated by the word *abhi*, how could the tree’s status as the object characterized be made manifest? To this he says:
“And the sense of the characteristic [is established] by way of its being the object (*visayabhāvena*). He explains this in that alternative view with the words beginning “And thus,” and so forth.
He brings forward a suspected fault; therein, with the words "this is not so," etc., he states the very rebuttal being advanced by the opponent in order to avoid the aforementioned fault.
By demonstrating this rebuttal, it should be understood that this position [of his] is also shown to be not defective, and thus that position is accepted.

For this very reason, it is explained further on based precisely upon the aforementioned position, regarding Devadatta’s attainment of the letter *itthaṃ* (or *ittham*), which is reckoned as correctness (*sādhutva*).
Because the mother exists there as an object, he said "of the mother" and so forth. The mother is present there in such a state as the object, while Devadatta is present there as the subject;

and the relationship between them, characterized by the relation of object and subject, arises from the action characterized by reaching that state. That relationship with the mother exists by way of being the cause.
"It shines by means of the fire that belongs to its mother"—thus he says, "yvāyam" and so forth. The construction is: "the connection with the mother.
"By means of such attainment" (*itthampattiyā*) means by means of the action characterized by such attainment, which serves as the instrument. He thinks thus:
"Even though that connection is inseparable from Devadatta and is therefore illuminated by his own fire, nevertheless, it is the connection with the mother [that is meant] by the word 'fire'."

"It is called 'conjunction with that' because it illuminates [the relationship]; for, by means of the function of the word, even when the second case ending refers only to that [first member], it illuminates a relationship that pertains to both.

Thus, in the phrase "tree, tree stands," there is a connection; and the construction is: "depending on the standing" (*ṭhitiṃ paṭicca*) means "on account of the standing," and "the connection which belongs to these trees.
By the word "of the trees" (*rukkhānaṃ*), it is shown that the trees are the correlates (*sambandhin*) relative to the action.

By the phrase "but [the action] depends on that which stands," it is made known that the action of standing (*ṭhitikiriya*), which is expressed by the word *tiṭṭhati* and is of a nature to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*),

is connected to something other than the tree. Even though insentient trees lack expectation, because [the connection] is understood through worldly convention— just as in the case of words like *pipatīsā*—
a relationship characterized by the means and the end arises for the action of depending upon a location that is merely implied.
That which is to be known is connected to the tree; because it is illuminated by the word *so* (he/that), he says ‘so’ and so forth.

Although there is a function merely in the sense of distribution (*vicchā*) through the dual number itself as that which is to be illuminated, one should investigate the statement “merely in the function of the case-ending in the sense of distribution,” because the particle *abi* lacks a function in the sense of distribution.
For [the particle] *lakkhaṇitthambhu* is unable to illuminate a specific base (*pakati*) as an adjective.
The intention is that the dual number must indeed be employed for the sake of clarity. 9.
*Pati upādiyamāno*:
being accepted; however, if it is the portion that is being accepted (*upādiyamāno*), how then is the portion not being accepted (*anupādiyamāno*)?
He said: “As for ‘whoever,’ etc., *tagara* and *kuṭṭha* are specific types of fragrant substances. ‘He shares with me’ (*maṃ ābhajati*) means he partakes of me;
the intended meaning is that he becomes my portion.
10. Anu.
"Natulakkhaṇaṃ" means that the performance of truth (*saccakiriyā*) is the cause for rain, but it is not a mere conventional sign (*saṅketa*); this is the meaning.

Since it is a cause, even though it lacks the status of a formal "mark" (*lakkhaṇa*), he establishes its status as a mark by employing a syllogism (*sādharmya-paryoga*) to show how the second [case ending] applies to the mark in the performance of truth;

thus he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the words "yaṃ sakimpi," etc. For here, the proposition (*paṭiññā*) is that the performance of truth is the mark; the subject (*pakkha*) is "even once."

The reason is that it is a conceptual construction (*kappanā*) by way of being a sign (*nimitta*). Whatever is even once conceptually constructed by way of being a sign becomes a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).

For example, in the statement, "Just as you saw the pupil with the water-pot in his hand," the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is to be seen through the application of the common property (*sādhamma*).

"Is conceptually constructed" (*kappate*) means "is capable" (*samattha*); "water-pot-in-hand" (*kamaṇḍalupāṇī*) means "one who has a water-pot in his hand"; and "api" (just as) is used in the sense of an example.
Once, a certain disciple was seen by someone with a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hand; taking that very sight as the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), he asks with the words "Is it not so?

and so forth. Now, although the state of being a defining characteristic exists even through the reason (*hetu*) as it has been stated, why should the instrumental case (*tatiyā*) not occur for the reason due to the negation of another? Thus he raises an objection with the words "Is it not even thus? and so forth, [referring to] the prior negation.

By way of a prior negation of the exception (*apavāda*); for there is an exception regarding the sixth case (*chaṭṭhi*), since the rule for the third case (*tatiyā*) is prescribed when a cause (*hetu*) is present...

because the prescription of the third case for a cause occurs once the sixth case has been reached through its connection (*sambandha*), the rule for the case-ending of the subordinate word (*upapada-vibhatti*) is also an exception to the sixth case... because when joined with a subordinate word that serves as the cause for manifesting a particular relation, [the third case] is prescribed for that very same relation;
