in that regard, the scope for the third case of the cause is "a family by wealth" (*dhanena kulaṃ*), while the scope for the case-ending of the subordinate word is...

In the phrase “*rukkham anuvijjotate*,” [the commentary] states, “it rained following the performance of a truth-act (*saccakiriya*). However, when there is a prohibition of a prior statement regarding a cause (*hetu*) or a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), the second case ending occurs by means of a prior negation.
11. *Saha*.
Regarding how the application [of the suffix] occurs when the object is conveyed by the word itself, he says "by the word *pabbatena*," and so forth.

By the phrase "in the sense of being inferior" (*hīne visayabhāvena*), etc., he indicates the locative case (*visaya-sattamī*) in the sense of "inferiority. He states the manner of cognition by saying "inferior," and so forth.
"By that" means by the inferior; how is it connected with "the superior"? Explaining this by way of the relationship between the inferior and the superior, he says "in that context," and so forth.

"In that context" refers to what was stated as "the inferior" and so on. "Which" refers to the superior, such as Sāriputta and others. "The inferior" refers to those excluded from wisdom and so forth;
[thus] that which is the object of the inferior sense arises for the superior, such as Sāriputta and others. Its superiority exists in relation to its own specific domain.
It should be understood that the "connection between the low and the high" (hīnukkaṭṭhasambandha) is established by some action such as "exceeding" (atisāyana) and so forth.

14. Regarding the seven [types of connection], he says that "excess" (ādhikya) is the "connection of the superior and the superior" (adhikādhikīsambandha); for one who has an excess is "superior" (adhikī), [as in] a khārī [of grain].

Now, regarding the exchange involving a surplus (*adhikī-vinimutte*), how is the relationship between the surplus and the surplus-donor determined? For it is not the case that some "surplus" is being praised here; thus he says, "In *na vine*," and so forth.

The word *iti* functions as a reason (*hetu*) to establish the aforementioned relationship. Since it is joined with a prefix (*upasadda*), the meaning is: "at that time, there is a connection with the prefix for the surplus.

Because the relationship is twofold and the surplus is also connected with the prefix, why is the seventh case (*sattamī*) not used there as well? To this he replies, "Because of the absence of the sense of 'surplus' (*adhika*)," and so forth.

Just as, because a single case ending can express a relationship pertaining to both [the preceding and the following], there is an absence of the seventh case (locative) for the term *vijju* which is characterized by the number [of lightning flashes], so too here, indicating the previously mentioned concentration (*samādhi*), he says: "there is an absence of the seventh case as if it were characterized," as in:
"a *māṇikā* is four *doṇas*; a *khāritthī* is four *māṇikas*."
15. Regarding the statement, “What is this ‘lordship’ (sāmitaṃ) called ‘relationship with a lord’ (sassāmisaṃbandho)? he says it is “produced by such actions as protection.
The neuter designation “tañca” (and that) is used in reference to lordship. Since relationships are of many kinds, he says, “in all cases.”

Regarding the term "in relation to" (*sambandhe*), its meaning is established as "it is being stated" or "it is being made known. Furthermore, it is well known that one who has been brought forward by way of an example is able to engage [with the teaching] easily;
thus, he states an example where that which is already established is restated and that which is not yet established is what is being prescribed:

"Just as 'he who wears earrings is Devadatta. He explains that wearing earrings is established while being Devadatta is not yet established, stating: "By way of restating the state of wearing earrings," and so forth.

Just as even when there is a dual substratum (*ubhayādhiṭṭhānatte*), the genitive case occurs only as a subordinate element—as in “the king’s man” (*rañño puriso*)—and not specifically as a qualifier—as in “the king of the man” (*purisassa rājā*)—so too, even in a construction with the particle *adhi* which expresses a relationship, it occurs only as a qualifier and not otherwise; thus he says, “In that case,” and so forth.

It is called “separation” (*byatireka*) because it is brought about as a separation from the sixfold set of kārakas (*kārakachakka*); since the relationship is distinct from those [six], it is “separation.”
The meaning of *taṃ āpādīyati pāpīyati* is "it is acquired as one's own"; *ubhayato* means "from both [sides]": from the possessor (*santā*) and from the owner (*sāmi*).

In the expression *adhibrahmadatte pañcālā*, the meaning is that the Pañcālas belong to Brahmadatta; for the Pañcālas are the property (*santakā*) of the owner (*sāmino*), not the owner of the property.
In *adhipañcālesu brahmadatto*, the meaning is that Brahmadatta is the master (*sāmī*) of the Pañcālas.
16. What is the characteristic of the agent? To this he says: "In the agent," and so forth. In examples such as "Devadatta goes," [the suffix] is established in the agent;
in examples such as "Devadatta cooks rice," it is established in the object. The connection is that he performs an action (*kiriyaṃ karoti*); thus, "he does" (*karoti*).
And by this very designation according to its meaning, it is made known that this is a conventional expression for the agent;
even when employed by something else, it itself experiences predominance in its own action. Thus it is said here: "Or [it is] 'employed' by way of being predominant.
That which, by virtue of its predominance, performs the action upon the object of the agent—[that is the instrument].
"That [agent] is either unconnected with the name of the agent (*appayutta*) or connected (*payutta*); thus it is twofold.
Therein, "done by a man" (*purisena kataṃ*) is unconnected; "Devadatta does by means of a man" (*purisena karoti devadatto*) is connected.

Now, is it not the case that this action (*kriyā*), without any intervention, establishes only the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), while the agent (*kartṛ*) is established only through a remote connection? If that were so, how could [the action] be accomplished by multiple instruments?
It is said that an agent performs an action primarily, while others perform it secondarily:
"Because [the action] arises from something other than the agent, there is the perception of distinction through the exclusion [of others], etc."—this is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*.

Furthermore, in the commentary on the *Tattvabodhinī* regarding the third reading of *naṃpāta* 100 and *naṃpāta* 243, it is explained that in cases such as "it exists," "it becomes," or "it is found" (*atthi*, *bhavati*, *vijjati*), there is an agent and an action even when the state of being a distinct factor (*kāraka*) is not explicitly manifested.
Even when [an instrument] is helpful from afar, it is the agent that possesses primacy.
This is the meaning here: because the arising of the other factors, such as the instrument, occurs through their emergence from the agent;
for even an axe, though its nature as an instrument is well-established, becomes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) by virtue of its functioning dependent upon the agent, as in "in the axe... (*pharasumhi*).
"Setting aside [the object], he cuts"—by means of the perception and seeing of the action performed by an agent who has become distinct through the act of making something separate;
and by this perception and seeing of the agent Devadatta, who has become manifest as "Devadatta exists, is, and is found," [one understands] "Devadatta exists, is, and is found.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the instruments] such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth are included.

"Because [the agent] is included in such things as 'occurring dependent upon that,' for this reason, even though [the object] is helpful from a distance, the primary effort must belong to the agent alone.

Furthermore: "But the status of being an agent belongs even to insentient things such as cooking pots and the like, because of the false attribution [of agency] through the function of a word in its conventional sense, as in the case of [calling a pot] 'cooking' and so forth."

This is the meaning here: "Even for non-conscious things such as a cooking pot or a sword, agency (kattubhāvo) arises even in the absence of the causes for the manifestation of a real snake, and so forth.
Why is that? Because the occurrence (vutti) or application (paṭipatti) of a word toward its own referent (abhidheyya) comes about through beginningless false habituation (micchābhyāsa);

therefore, [the statement] 'of the pot, etc. is established. What is meant is this: the referent of the word is one way, while the referent according to its intrinsic nature (sabhāvattho) is another."
For sound does not exercise its function upon an external object;
for instance: The verbal expression "burnt" is one thing through its association [with the object], while the meaning "burnt" is understood quite differently from the sound "burnt."

"However, by means of a beginningless, erroneous practice that functions while external objects are non-existent—acting as the instrument (karaṇa) like the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of an external thing—the status of being an agent (kattutta) arises for pots and other such items.

And furthermore: "When the desire to speak is covered over by the functioning causes which possess the quality of being primary, and when the properties of an agent are expressed, the word itself is known as the agent."

Through the singleness, the primacy, and the establishment [of the object], and through the conceptualization of differentiation, the status of the object (*karmatva*), the instrument (*karaṇatva*), and the agent (*kartṛtva*) arises.

By the words "when stated" refers to [the rule] beginning with "because of the arising of others from the agent," etc.; by the words "regarding the word" means that these three properties may or may not exist in the word itself.

The meaning is that, through the very sound [of the word] expressing the desire to denote the aforementioned dhammas related to the agent, the agent is understood from the word itself, and not necessarily from the underlying substance (*vatthu*);

for, by means of the states of transformation (*pariṇāma*) which possess the form of that [agent] due to the cognition "the substances are secondary," there arises for that very same self the status of being the object (*kamma*) and so forth, as in the phrase "he kills himself" (*attanā attānaṃ*).
For this very reason, even though the sprout is absolutely non-existent [prior to its arising], it exists for the act of generating.
One becomes the agent [in the sense that] "the sprout is born"; for it is said:
"Prior to its being produced and prior to its being born, entities are the objects of cognition and are bound;
remaining as something other than existence, one becomes the agent of birth."
"By another," such as Devadatta and so forth.
To the question, "What indeed is this called an instrument (karaṇa)? he says: "But that which... and so on. "That which" (*yo*) refers to the referent of the word; by this he illustrates:

"Even in the absence of another sutta [explicitly] defining the designation 'instrument,' the conventional usage of the term 'instrument' is established through etymological derivation (*anvatthato*) as 'that by which one acts is an instrument. Herein, this is the inspired response (*paṭibhāna*):
"That which is intended to be said or done, and that which is the ultimate instrument of an action—the instrument (karaṇa) is twofold, through the distinction between the external and the internal.
Therein, by the phrase "that which is intended to be said," etc., this is shown: "There is no such thing as an instrument in terms of a substantial entity."

"However, since we observe that even for well-known instruments such as axes and the like, there is the status of agent and locus in expressions such as 'the axe cuts' (*pharasu chindati*) and 'he cuts with the axe' (*pharasumhi chindati*);
and since even for well-known loci, when specific qualities such as being unpolished are possible,

there is the status of instrument in expressions such as 'he cooks in a pot' (*thālyā pacati*), it should be understood that the instrument as a causal factor (*kāraka*) arises solely from the speaker's intention."
And that [kāraka] is of two kinds; thus he says, "it is twofold," and so forth. Therein, "he cuts with a sword" refers to the external, while "he sees with the eye" refers to the internal.
By the statement "a kāraka because it is the cause of an action" (kiriyānimitta), he expresses that the word *kāraka* is a synonym for "cause" (*nimitta*).
Since beauty, height, and so forth do not exist within the action itself, only a relationship is understood; therefore, it is characterized by relation (*sambandhalakkhaṇā*).

The sixth case may occur; however, in expressions such as *samena dhāvati* ("he runs evenly"), although the action exists, the desire to express it as the object (*kamma*) arises, and thus the second case may occur, meaning "he runs on level ground" or "he runs on uneven ground.
Similarly, *dvidoṇena* means "he buys for two doṇas"; *pañcakena* means having made a group (*vagga*) of five—the measure being five—he buys livestock five by five.
The author of the Vārttika added a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the prescription of the instrumental case, stating that the meaning is "having done [something], one buys.

To demonstrate this, he said, "By means of *pakati* and so forth," and so on. The connection is as follows: "in which there is the state of being an instrument" refers to that action in which *sampakati* and the others function as instruments;
it is that action which he expresses. Since the existence (*sattā*) of every word-meaning is never absent, he said "the root *bhū*" and so forth.
“Naturally handsome” (*pakatiyābhirūpo*) means that he is handsome by his very nature (*sabhāvena*), but not by means of clothing, ornaments, and so forth; this is the meaning.

However, when the sense of “making” (*karoti*) is implied, one says “made naturally handsome” (*pakatiyābhirūpo kato*) and so on; in that case, the instrumental case is used for the agent (*kattari*) itself. The connection is:
because he was not of another clan (*aññagotto*) but became Gotama, therefore he is Gotama. [Objection: But surely, is it not in dependence upon the purchase of two *doṇas* of five [measures]...?

Since [the measures] such as the *dvidoṇa* become the instruments of action (*kammabhūta*) by means of the price, what then is meant by the statement, “In dependence on the price, the instruments of action such as the *dvidoṇa* and *pañcaka* come into being”?
To address this objection, he says, “For it is thus,” and so forth. This is what is meant: “By the word *dvidoṇa* and so on, the object that is to be acquired (*gahupaga-vatthu*) is not expressed;
rather, the price is stated for the sake of those [objects] by means of the *tādatthiya* (dative) case-ending. Therefore, there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault.”
17. In order to show the connection with the action of coming together in due order, with the quality of thickness, and with the *gomanta* grass, he says, "Just as that," and so forth.
Even while providing a mere illustration, he shows it with this underlying intention; thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase “or in all cases” (*sabbattheva vā*) and so forth: in examples such as *puttena sahāgato* (“he has come with his son”), two agents are involved in relation to the action of coming and so on, by way of being primary (*padhāna*) and non-primary (*appadhāna*).
Among these, the suffix occurs for the primary agent either by way of the rule for the condition of the object (*kāriyasampaccayañāyena*) or by way of the frequentative statement (*bahulavacanena*).

For the other [non-primary agent], the third case ending (*tatiyā*) is already established by the rule “the third case is used for the non-agent” (*akattari tatiyā*). Therefore, this specific formulation [of the present rule] is not necessary.
One gives while conceiving [the recipient] as "Is this not my father? and so forth; therefore, he is designated as "father" because he is the primary agent.

Even though the connection to the action is equal for both father and son, here the father is primary because he is prompted by the word, whereas the son is not primary because he is not prompted by the word. For the distinction between primary and non-primary is established in dependence upon the operation of the word;
in this case, the act of coming is [attributed] to the father alone, due to his grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "arrived."
The relationship is expressed by the word, and not by the other [the person], because that is the inherent power of the word;
for such is the power of the word that it is the father alone who can here convey the connection with the action, and not the son.
And thus, as it has come down to us, the singular number arises; otherwise, there would be a plural, as in "the father and the sons have come. According to the method stated...
The third [alternative] is established: "When [a rule] is already established, a restatement is for the purpose of restriction (niyama) or for the purpose of option (vikappa).

In this case, there is neither restriction nor option; therefore, what is the use of this grammatical connection (*yoga*)? With this intention, he says: "only when it is not the primary element," and so forth.

"This is not so," and so forth, is the rebuttal. The construction is: "or it is intended merely to state coexistence. This is because [the term] *sāmatthiyā* (by implication) refers to the basis of distinction (*bheda-adhiṭṭhāna*).
The connection with the action is understood even for the son of one who acts with his own hand (*sahatthayoga*), by the force of the meaning:
"How else could there be acting with one's own hand? Thus, "taking the meaning" (*atthaggahaṇa*) refers to taking the meaning as "with one's own hand" (*sahatthena*) in the Sutta.

"A figurative sense" (*pariyāyattha*): the analysis (*viggaha*) is "that which has a purpose (*payojana*) as its meaning," where *pariyāya* means that by means of which they go around to or understand the meaning.
And here, the restriction "only the meaning of *pariyāya*" is not intended;

for this very reason, even without the employment of the word *saha*, or the employment of its synonym, because the rule prescribes [the third case] in connection with *saha*, the third case occurs wherever that meaning is understood—even in the absence of the employment of words such as *saha*—due to its connection with the understood *saha*, just as in the example: "in the place of *syādi*. (3-1)
“By way of a synonym” (*saha pariyāyena*) means by way of a synonym for the word *saha*.

“Because no qualification is taken up” (*visesānupādānato*) means because no qualification such as “non-primary” (*appadhāne*)—as in the Pāṇinian sūtra “*sahayukte ’pradhāne*” (2.3.19)—is taken up. 18.
[The section on] Characteristics (*lakkhaṇe*).

That by which something is characterized (*lakkhīyati*) is a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), which is to say a sign (*saṅketa*). What is this? It is [an object] such as a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and so forth. Since a grammatical operation (*kāriya*) cannot occur with respect to the meaning itself, one who considers that the case endings belong to the words expressing that [meaning] has provided the explanation: "from that which is occurring in the sense of a characteristic" (*lakkhaṇe vattamānato*).

However, disregarding that, he states the actual meaning with the words "whatever meaning" (*yo attho*) and so forth; it is understood that [the suffix] occurs from the point of view of its being present (*vattamānato*). This is because the formulation of the rule for the suffix follows immediately after the noun (*nāma*).

“Appropriated” (*upātta*) means grasped. [The opponent objects: Why is the third case ending used for a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) when one has entered into a certain state (*kañcippaṇaramāpanna*), as in the example “the lightning flashes toward the tree”?
Lest this [usage] occur merely for the sake of a characteristic, the followers of Pāṇini added the term “characteristic of a particular state” (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*) in their rule 2.3.21.
Bearing this in mind, he raises an objection starting with “But surely,” etc.; for “the characteristic of a particular state” is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*).
"Of one who has fallen into [a state]" means of one who has become so; "distinction" (visesa) is said to be a particular mode that breaks the generality of the ascetic life (sāmañña).
For instance, in the phrase "he saw a wanderer with a triple staff," the state of being a wanderer is a particular mode of the generality of being human;

that wanderer attained it, and the triple staff is its characteristic mark (lakkhaṇa). By the term "in the sense of a secondary characteristic" (upalakkhaṇatta), he expresses the absence of a characteristic mark for one who is already in such a state.
"Upalakkhaṇa" (characterization) is a conventional designation. This [example] "rukkham pati vijjotanaṃ" (lightning flashing toward a tree) is not a valid counter-example;

for since there is no such thing as a lightning flash that has already reached its destination (itthambhūta) here, no purpose is seen in including the term "itthambhūta" (already so become), as it would exclude [such cases].

However, in the case of "rukkham pati vijjotate" (lightning flashes toward a tree), because there exists the referent called "lightning" which is in the state of having already reached its destination, [the inclusion of the term is justified].
In the case of the third objection, he says "necessarily" and so forth to make it known that there is no other recourse apart from the aforementioned method for its cessation.

He says "otherwise" and so forth, meaning: if one were to apply the term "itthambhūtalakkhaṇe" (the characteristic of being thus) without accepting [the aforementioned point], then, fearing a further objection from the proponent of such a view, he says "and not" and so forth, [meaning] it cannot be so.
The remainder of the statement is "co" (and), used for emphasis; it is said that [the third case] is not possible.

Because of the power of the rule prescribing the second case, why would it not be possible [to say] "patiparīhi bhāge cā" (2-9)? To this he says: "'atthi' etc. For the power [of a rule] exists only when there is no other purpose.
Then, why would the third case not occur in the sense of "there is a water-pot in the hand"? To this he says: "'kamaṇḍalu' etc."
The connection is: "because it is not the substrate (anupādāna) by virtue of being a characteristic mark (upalakkhaṇabhāva) of the white water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).

By this, he states that the substrate (upādātṛ) possesses its own continuity. "By means of a specific part as a locus" (visiṭṭhāvayavādheyyena): the hand is a specific part distinguished by the water-pot;
the water-pot is the locus (ādheyya) of that [hand]; such is the meaning. From whichever limb, when it is modified, the modification of the whole (aṅgin) is characterized, from that...
The third [alternative] is "as it may be" (*yathāsīya*). Others have begun with the rule *yenāṅgavikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.20);
thus he says "by which," etc. Therein, by the word *ya*, the disfigured member is indicated as the cause (*hetu*), and the word *aṅga* is employed as denoting the whole (*samudāya*);
therefore he says "by which," etc. But surely, since words such as *kāṇa* ("one-eyed") denote specific qualities, the use of the word *akkhi* ("eye") [is unnecessary]?

"It is not appropriate because there is no exclusion"—this is not a fault; for this is the conventional usage of worldly language, and in the linguistic application of the world, there is no consideration of heavy or light syllables and the like.
Thus, in common usage, one says "sīsapā" both for the tree and for the fruit;
however, one who has a specific regard for that [distinction] employs the word *okkhi*. Alternatively, when a general term is introduced, a specific term is worthy of being employed.
For when "akkhi" (eye) is stated, there might be doubt as to what is intended to be said of it; therefore, "kāṇo" (one-eyed) is stated.
One does not perceive that someone is beautiful by means of an eye that is [merely] "akkhinā" (by the eye); rather, what then is "kāṇo"?

Lest one should suspect, "Why should it not be the case that 'he has a kāṇa-eye' and so forth?", he says—pointing out the solution already stated in the case of "kamaṇḍalu pāṇimhi assa" (he has a water-pot in his hand)—that "as in the previous case, there is no possibility of such an objection."
19. *Hetu*:
The term *hetu* (cause) is conventionally established in the sense of that which has its causal efficacy observed in relation to a certain fruit.

For in one case, even if it does not produce the effect (*kāriya*) because of a lack of suitability for it, it is still called a *hetu*—provided a co-operative factor (*sahakārī*) is present and no obstructing condition (*vidhurapaccaya*) is absent.

It fell [to the ground]; therefore, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the effect. For this very reason, he says: "even without producing [the effect]. He states the reason for the absence of the instrumental case (*tatiyā*) in relation to the cause:
"merely by way of being fit for that action," and so forth. 21. [Regarding] quality (*guṇa*).
"Upādhi" means a qualification (*visesana*). "Being subordinate to another" (*parāṅgabhūta*) means being subordinate to that which prescribes the bondage and so forth of another;
thus, the meaning is "in the case of a cause such as insentience (*jaḷatta*), etc. By this, he states that the word *guṇa* expresses what is non-primary (*appadhāna*).

And since that which is non-primary is subordinate to another, he explains the meaning of this term *guṇa* as "subordinate to another" (*parāṅgabhūta*). For whatever is employed for the sake of another is non-primary.

Because it is apprehended in the form of a *vā* [particle], as in "He is bound because of his dullness," "The tree has leaves on its head," or "There is fire here because of the smoke," for that very reason he says:
"having attained the form of another. Regarding the rule "vāvidhānaṃ," this refers to the rule "vibhāsā guṇe-thiyaṃ" (Pāṇini 2.3.25);
by the phrase "itthiyaṃ" and so forth, he shows that even the form of the ablative case is intended.

For this very reason, he says "in both cases" (*ubhayattha*) and so forth. One might object: "By the rule *tato pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 4.3.95), how can that which ends in a taddhita suffix have the form of the fifth case?
Anticipating this doubt, he says "in the rule for the fifth case" (*pañcaminiddese*) and so forth.

The construction is: "by this rule, [the suffix] is prescribed after the fifth case. Alternatively, keeping in mind the objection that it ought to appear in the third case form because it is prescribed after the fifth case, he provides the explanation.
Showing that the reason for the fifth example is the same as for the third, and that the third example is to be understood according to the first, he said:
“In the fifth also,” and so forth; “by way of non-existence” means by the cessation of formations (*saṅkhāranirodha*). 22.
The sixth.

Fearing that the genitive case might be established here merely by the desire to express a relationship (*sambandha*), he says: "In the sense of a cause" (*hetumhi*), and so forth. He states the reason: "That fitness," and so forth.

"By the power of the word's inherent capacity" (*saddasattisāmatthiyā*) means by the capacity known as the word's inherent capacity. He clarifies this very point with the words "Wherein," and so forth;
the connection is with the words expressing the sense of a cause. "With coreferential [terms]" (*samānādhikaraṇehi*) means with those that are coreferential with the sense of a cause.
The connection is with the words “from the belly, etc.,” and “for the purpose of illustrating that” means “for the purpose of illustrating the sense of cause.

However, by way of contrast, he states its occurrence from the sense of cause with the words beginning “wherein...,” and the potentiality [of the suffix] is demonstrated by the words beginning “in the sense of cause”;
therein, the example is given in the phrase “under the sway of the cause, which is the Dhamma.”
23. *Sabbā nāmabhūtehi*:

if among the words beginning with *sabba*, some were names (*nāma*) for certain things, then [the rule would apply] by means of those which have become subordinate (*appadhānabhūtehi*), such as *piyasabba* and so forth. As for the word *payojana* in the phrase "for what purpose" (*kiṃpayojanaṃ*), etc., according to the *Nighaṇḍu*—"purpose (*payojanaṃ*) refers to the effect (*kāriya*) and the cause (*hetu*)"—it is a term denoting a cause. 24. *Catu*... [The text continues with grammatical analysis of the numeral four.]
Since neither for one who is conscious nor for one who is unconscious is right giving possible without the desire to honor or assist, he said "honor" and so forth.
By that—meaning by the sense already stated—it is the cause of giving, which is connected as the object of the act of giving for one who gives;
now, desiring to reveal the characteristic of right giving along with its classifications:
He says: “‘This very thing,’ and so forth. ‘Not rejecting’ is *anirākaraṇa*; ‘honoring’ is *ārādhana*; ‘granting permission’ is *abbhanuñña*.
By way of these, it is here stated—that is, spoken of—as the recipient (*sampadāna*). He says ‘tree-begging monks’ to indicate [the agent].
To show that recipient, such as the tree and so forth, by way of its classification, he says ‘for therein,’ and so forth, [referring to] through entreaty and through honoring.

The connection is that "it becomes the recipient" (*sampadāna*). By means of consent (*anumati*) through granting permission (*abbhanujānana*), even though [the object] exists, it is not rejected; with the intention that the monk is the one who has given consent, he says "he," and so forth. 25.

In the sense of "purpose" (*payojana*) within the term *tāda*, since the word *attha* is present, it is possible to refer to this purpose as "this"; thus he says "tasseda" (*of him, this*), and so forth.

It has been stated that here, by the word *tas*, there is a connection with the derivative (*vikati*), whereas by the word *attha*, there is a connection with the base (*pakati*). By this [statement], "What is this explanation of meaning?

he indicates that there is no compound in this intended expression. Or rather, in this analysis (*viggaha*), the compound should be understood as occurring precisely through this grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
That meaning, which is designated as a derivative, is implied by the sense of another word as its base; from that—

Regarding the term *tadattha* (having that purpose), he asks: "What is this state of having that purpose (*tadatthabhāva*)? and so forth. The *nimitta* (the sign) is the modification (*vikati*), such as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), while the *nimittī* (the bearer of the sign) is the material cause (*pakati*), such as the wood;
these are grasped by the word *ta* (that) and the word *attha* (purpose). The relationship between them is the basis for the application of the term *tadattha*;
the meaning is that this relationship is called the "state of having that purpose. This relationship is characterized by the connection between the cause and the effect.

The word "name" (nāma) is what is meant [by the term *nāmagotta*]. Since it is being predicated as a quality that delimits the exertion (*padhāna*), these are qualities that delimit—that is, distinguish—the primary subject, the person.
For that which is predicated or made known is the primary; the other is secondary because it is merely being followed along.
Having stated, "When it is taken up," he says "Just as... and so forth, in order to clarify by means of an example the manner in which it is taken up.

That wood for which the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the cause is expressed as such; it is not [expressed] by any other cause. When [the post] is taken as the delimiting factor of the cause, then the fourth case (*catutthī*) from the word *nimitta* itself expresses the relationship.

From that, [it is distinguished] as "from another cause" (*aññanimittato*). Because the relationship between the cause and the caused exists in a state of facing toward one another, the application occurs right there at the cause; thus, the relationship is expressed. Furthermore, the third case (*tatiyā*) may also be used from the word *nimitta* in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

The connection is with the word *nāsaṅkanīyā* (“not to be suspected”). He states the reason: “*nimitta*, *hetu*, etc. The phrase “in both cases” (*ubhayattha*) means in both instances, such as “for the sacrificial post” (*yūpāya*) and “for cooking” (*pākāya*). Regarding the expression *piṇiyamānā*: [the question is] whether it is to be expressed by words such as “sound” (*sadda*) and so on;
that which follows is the meaning (*attha*) such as “sweetness” (*sādu*) and so forth. That which has another agent (*añña-kattuka*) is one whose agent is different.

By the word *abhilāso* (“desire”), he explains that even though the word *ruci* has many meanings starting with “light” (*ditti*), here the word *ruci* is understood specifically in its conventional sense (*ruḷha*) of “desire” (*abhilāsa*).
That which is the object of desire (*ruci*) is the referent (*attha*); for those things whose purpose is that [desire], they are related to it as being what is being desired.
And although both—the one in whom this desire arises and the one who generates it—possess [a connection to] it, nevertheless, the one in whom it arises is its locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Even though he does not generate it, he is conjoined with it; therefore, it belongs to him alone as that which is being desired.

The designation "recipient" (sampadāna-saññā) indicates that [the action] does not produce a result and is not conjoined with exertion; by the word "here" (idha), he shows that the examples cited here are of a different form [from those previously given].
Furthermore, this very difference in form among the examples is the reason for the formulation of the fourth case (catutthī-vidhāna);

otherwise, the sixth case (chaṭṭhī) alone would have been prescribed even for those [examples], as there would be no possibility for a [different] reason. Indeed, he demonstrates that it is precisely because such a reason exists that there is this counter-example (paccudāharaṇa).
He states the reason for this state [of being]: ‘because it is the agent of the desire to act, having no other agent.
He says ‘here, however,’ and so forth, to show how this might serve as a counter-example here; ‘tvam’ is simply the first person singular pronoun used for the self.

He states another reason for its occurrence: ‘or else,’ and so forth. That which has no other agent is ‘anaññakattukā’; regarding that desire (*ruci*), for the one who is being enjoined, even though they are connected to that desire...
The connection is with the phrase "but those who desire the designation *sampadāna*"; the connection is with the phrase "but those who say.

Arising (*uppatti*) means the act of arising; of what is there arising? Of desire (*ruci*). The basis for that arising is the "basis of arising" (*uppatyādhāra*), as in "it pleases Devadatta" (*devadattāya rocate*).

Since it characterizes Devadatta and so forth, the statement is a "characterization of the basis of arising" (*uppatyādhāropalakkhaṇa*). In this context, it is precisely the characterization of the basis of arising for desire.
The word *vacanaṃ* (statement) should be understood as having a restrictive sense (*sāvadhāraṇa*), because all sentences have restriction as their result.
Therefore, the statement "let it be made concise" (*piṇiya māna*) does not aim at showing that desire has another agent; thus, [the possibility of another agent] is excluded.
The connection is: "for them, [the rule] of Kaccāyana applies here too. "Here too" means even in the case of the word "you" (*tvaṃ*). [This is so] because it is not established otherwise.

Because [the desired meaning] is already established by the first rule alone regarding the object (*atthamatte*), the phrase "of the statement" (*vacanassa*) refers to the statement prescribing the fourth case for both [the agent and the object].
"Excessive over-extension" (*atippasaṅgo*) refers to the occurrence of the undesired form *tava* in such instances as "To whom do you find the Dhamma pleasing? (*kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesi*).

Regarding "in the employment of the root *dhāri*" (*dhārippayoge*), he says "the creditor and the debtor" (*uttamīṇo adhamīṇo*), because these are conventional terms (*ruḷhi*) for the one who lends and the one who borrows. Thus: "The creditor... (*uttamīṇo*).
“Master of wealth” (*dhanasāmī*); “one who leads upward” (*uttamīṇo*)—this is said to have the meaning of “he carries,” derived from the root *dhṛ* (to carry/sustain).

Having prescribed the technical designation of recipient (*sampadāna*) for those various [words] restricted by specific rules in another Sutta, the fourth case ending is ordained by others; thus he says:
“*silāgha*, *hanu*, *ṭhāsa*, *pāna*,” and so forth, in all instances.

In the context of grammatical relation (*yogasambandha*), the genitive case is used. "To make known" (*ñāpetum*) means to inform regarding praise and so forth; "desired" (*icchito*) means highly esteemed.
The phrase "of those roots whose meanings are anger, malice, envy, and jealousy" is stated for the purpose of including roots that express those specific meanings.
By the words "anger toward whom," the object of the anger is stated; by the word "whose," one refers back to that which was already mentioned as "the agent"; and "whose" refers to the king or others.
"He asks" means he is questioned; for by that very [word] he will say: "The fortune-teller asks about the good and bad fortune related to someone.
And by the phrase "one who is born in accordance with that," this is shown: the verb *suṇoti* (he hears/accepts), preceded by *pati-* and *ā-*, functions in the sense of accepting and acknowledging;
when this acceptance is preceded by an aspiration (*patthanā*), then, by way of that aspiration—
"The fourth case form (*catutthī-rūpa*) occurs for the agent (*kattu*) who desires [to give].

However, when people, seeing even that which has not been requested but which exists merely through its favorability, accept what is to be given, thinking 'I shall show this or that,' or 'I shall give this,' then the fourth case form occurs for the agent of the action characterized by proceeding through such favorability. By this [statement], [the author] refers to the author of the *Pāṇini-vutti*.

He states a deviation from the opinion of Jayāditya; for he says: "What is called 'acceptance' (abbhupagama) occurs when something desired by another comes to pass; in that case, the dative case form belongs to the very one who desires it.

This is because [the dative] is used due to the authorization of the effort (ussāha) consisting in the performance of praise as prescribed by the Vedic statement, "he who is the agent of the prior action," which refers to the action that has already occurred.
Regarding the agent (*kattā*) and the reciter (*potā*), in all instances the word "of him" (*tassa*) should be connected with the rule: "The form desired for the dative case.
As for the genitive, it is extended by the statement "thus" (*evam*) and so forth, based on the principle that it pervades all cases.
However, due to the similarity of form and because the sense of the dative of purpose (*tādatthiya*) is present, the dative of purpose is also not contradictory, as applicable.

For he will say: “Let them choose the words for their own benefit,” and so forth. By the phrase “the desired king is the object (kamma), the choosing of the words,” he states that the choosing of the words is the primary factor.
Because all the factors of action (kāraka) are directed toward the choosing of the words;

because of its lack of frequent application—that is, because it is not employed extensively—he strikes away [the obstacle] and removes it. He attends upon [it]; he performs attendance, which is approaching. They long for it.
They long for; he becomes angry and harbors resentment. Since [actions] such as harming do not arise immediately following anger, terms such as *dūbha* (deceitful) and others are also cited.
Regarding the rule “in the case of a consonant, there is lengthening or shortening” (1-33), [the examples are]: *aparajjhāmi* (I offend); *issayanti* (they envy) and *nasahanti* (they cannot endure);
*ārajjhati* (he is attached); when questioned, the fortune-teller examines [the matter]; and one clarifies the meaning of the word *yassa* with the phrase beginning “of whom,” and so forth.
He examines and investigates: "What is the characteristic of this restraint and observance? He says, "Not from one who asks," and so forth;

the genitive case here is used specifically for the one who asks, as in "not from one who asks" (*nāvassamaya-niyamo*). From where does he say this? He says, "In connection with," and so forth; "from another too" means even from one who has not asked.
The donors (*hotāpotāro*), being the agents of the act of praising, are the ones who provide encouragement and permission.

He said, "It is *kamma*," [referring to the rule] "in the sense of *giṇāti* when it follows immediately. By the rule beginning with "after *hotu*, *potu*, etc.," the genitive form of the word *potu* is also shown;
however, in the commentary (*vutti*), the reading appears simply as "hotu pati-giṇāti. Even so, we remain indifferent here.
In the sense of "urging on" (*ussāhayati*), the root *giṇāti* contains the causative meaning (*ṇyattha*). "Except for *nāvā*" means excluding *nāvā*, *anna*, and so forth. But here, however—

Likewise, even in the absence of an explicit prohibition, by virtue of the governing rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikāra*), there occurs such usage as "he did not conceive that form" (*na taṃ nāmamaññe*) or "he did not conceive it as self" (*nataṃ attamaññe*).

For indeed, by virtue of the governing rule of "frequently," there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the suffix]. [The compound] "conceiving the form ending in the nominative case" (*paṭhamantaṃ rūpaṃ*) means "conceiving the form which ends in the nominative case.
And here, when the suffix *khika* is derived even from words beginning with *tiṇa*, then there is an understanding of censure (*nindā*). In that regard:

And because the application of the negative particle (*nañ*) necessarily results in the non-attainment of the intended meaning, the phrase ‘*na maññamāno*’ (not conceiving) is cited as an example involving negation.

Since the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs only when there is a limit (*avadhi*), and since the application of the negative particle necessarily conveys censure (*nindā*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*) alone;

or else, even though censure is understood, the second case is used for its own specific domain according to the speaker’s intention. This is the application of conventional designation (*sammuti*), regarding the word *sammuti*.
Regarding the phrase "they desire the fourth [vowel] in usage" (*payoge catutthiṃ icchanti*), they desire the fourth vowel here [in the word] *mattāya*. He states the reason for its repetition as:

"because it exists" (*atha sotivijjamānattā*). In the sutta beginning with "of the fierce dog" (*caṇḍassa kukkurassa*), because the reading "atha so" exists, the intention is that in the phrase "bhiyyoso mattāya," the vowel *o* is a repetition (*punarutta*).
By the inclusion of the particle *ca*, [the following is understood]: "Silāghahanu... [and so forth]."
By the inclusion of the particle *vā* in the rule *sattamyatthesu ca*, it is intended that [the suffix] is the fourth case (*catutthī*). This is established by the rule *namo yogādisvapicā*.
26. *Avadhi*: That from which something falls away or slips off is called an *avadhi*. It is derived from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ava*, according to the rule *dādhātvī* (5-45).
"Whatever object is delimited from something else, preceded by an action, whether it be moving, unmoving, or otherwise—that the wise call a 'limit' (*avadhi*).
Herein, this is the meaning: whatever object is delimited from something else—whether for the sake of conjunction or as a cause for an action—"
"An object that is subject to loosening—whether it loosens itself prior to actions such as going or giving, or is separated by another—is of such a nature, both moving and unmoving;
those wise ones who know its true nature call such an object a 'limit' (*avadhi*) characterized by loosening. This is illustrated, for example, by:
"The man falls while running," or "He causes the man to fall," or "A leaf falls from a tree," or "The leaf..."
It causes one to fall, it blows, and it is said to be threefold according to the distinction of its objects,
as follows: "One whose object is indicated, likewise one whose object is grasped,
and one whose object is inferable— thus it is declared to be threefold according to its scope."
In this context, that wherein the action indicated by the word is the object is called "the indicated object" (*niddiṭṭha-visaya*), as in ‘He has come from the village’;

that wherein the action taken up [by the speaker] and brought forward is the object is called "the taken-up object" (*upātta-visaya*), as in ‘It lightens from the cloud’, the meaning of which is ‘Having emerged from the cloud, it flashes with lightning’;
and that wherein the action is inferable is called "the inferable object" (*anumeyya-visaya*).
As in the example, "The people of Mathurā are more handsome than those of Pāṭaliputta," here the excellence [of the former] by way of the quality of being handsome is to be inferred;
for this very reason, it is understood that this very designation (*saññā*) is clearly manifest here, and thus no designation causing confusion is employed.

Now, when it is said "having a limit" (*avadhisamā*), from what is it determined that it means "having a limit of the word-meaning" (*padatthāvadhisamā*), such that this particular explanation was made? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of words," and so forth.
By the passage beginning with "Just as in a village," etc., this is illustrated:
"It is not only physical contact that constitutes a breach of decorum; rather, even mental association can do so. Indeed, there is such a case here involving mental association.
For instance, in the case of one who is fearful of thieves and so forth, thinking: 'If the thieves should see me, my death is certain.'"
"Reflecting with his intellect, he reaches them, and having reached them, he turns back from them.

Likewise, in the case of 'He protects [himself] from thieves,' if one who is a friend to someone were to see this person, [he thinks], 'If the thieves should see him, his death is certain. Seeing this, he reaches them with his intellect and turns back from them.
Thus, because of the sense of 'having reached' (avadhitvā), the fifth case ending is indeed used in all instances."—[said by] others.
However, in all such cases, elaboration was provided by means of the Suttas themselves for the sake of supporting specific modes of practice;
here, however, because it is established by the general statement alone, elaboration has been made by means of examples for the sake of supporting that.
"Bhītibhāyanatthānaṃ" means those for whom fear and protection are the purpose; the meaning is "those whose purpose is fear and protection. Is it not [the case] for those whose purpose is fear?
If it is argued that a cause of fear exists in usage but not for the sake of protection (*tāyana*), this is not a fault;
for protection is defined as guarding, and guarding arises from threats. Thus he says, "that which is a cause of fear," and so forth.
By this, he also rejects the Pāṇinian rule for the designation of the ablative case (*apādāna*) which states: "The cause of fear is the object of fear" (Pāṇini 1.4.25).
"From that" means from the cause of fear; "of them" refers to those who seek protection from fear. "Fear" means the apprehension of falling into what is undesirable; "terror" is its meaning.
"Protection" (*tāyana*) means guarding against falling into what is undesirable. By the very expression "as if seeing," he indicates its primary importance;
for who is able to transcend the conventional usage of words? Thus, all [the examples], such as *dabba* and so forth...
All [grammatical] factors are indeed connected with the capacity to act; therein, this classification of factors occurs solely according to the speaker's intention, as for example:

"The cloud flashes," "It flashes by means of the cloud," and "It flashes in the cloud. By the rule beginning with *parāpubbassa*, the technical rule for designation (*saññāsutta*) stating "*parājissāsayho*" (Pāṇini 3.1.26) is set aside;
"asayho" means an object that is incapable of being endured or overcome.
He explains by way of example with the words "ajjhena-sakāsa-icca" and so forth. [An objection is raised:

"But if this meaning is stated, then the state of being a residence (*āsayhatta*) has been predicated of Yaññadatta; how then can that be the state of being a residence of study (*ajjhena*), such that it establishes the limitation of what is not a residence? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The non-overpowering of Yaññadatta," and so forth.
He provides a counter-example for the term "not a residence" with the words: "But he who... and so forth. "It is desired in the sense of warding off."
(1-4-27) This has been stated; thus he says, "for the purpose of prohibition," and so forth. Those whose meaning is prohibition are "prohibitive" (*vāraṇattha*).

Regarding the phrase "when there is a desire for a word expressing a limit (*avadhi*) alone": specifically, this refers to when there is a desire for a word expressing a limit without a specific injunction (*vidhāna*). Regarding the phrase "in a specific injunction": it means when such is desired.
Furthermore, regarding the desire for a word expressing a limit of the mind, [the sense is] "one should ward off evil from the mind."
It occurs [as follows]: “*Rakkhanatthānam icchitan*” (Kacc 2-6-3) is the rule; therefore he says, “*rakkhanatthānan*,” etc., indicating that this applies to Kaccāyana and others.
“*Antaradhāne yenādassanamicchatī*” (Kacc 1-4-28) is the rule concerning the technical term *saññā*; therefore he says, “*antaradhāne*,” etc.
The connection is: “If this preceptor sees me”; [this refers to] the fault in being seen.
By the phrase "takketi ‘nūnan’" and so forth, *pesana* (sending) is an assignment preceded by honor; *ajjhesana* (requesting) is preceded by honor.

"Maññamāno" (thinking) refers to the thought, "How indeed might I, being a disciple, become separated?"—the term *antaradhāne* (in concealment/separation) indicates the cause of separation (*byavadhāna-nimitta*), which is that by means of which one desires one's own invisibility;
this is a locative case of purpose (*nimitta-sattamī*) in the sense of "in concealment. Therefore...
He said: "On account of an intervention. "Separated" means "intervened. He spoke [the example] beginning with "my preceptor" (*māmaṃ upajjhāyo*) for the sake of illustration;

it is for the purpose of intervention, for the purpose of being separated. Regarding the counter-example provided by others, "What does he not see when there is an intervention?"—in order to establish that, he said:
"Where there is non-perception," and so forth. [The phrase] "he does not see the thieves" is used here.
One who does not look at thieves desires that they not see him; thus, it is not for the sake of disappearance (*antaradhāna*), but for the purpose of averting injury.
Regarding "averting injury," he thinks as follows: "In this case, disappearance is not what is intended, but rather the averting of injury caused by that [disappearance];
for in the phrase 'the preceptor disappears,' even in the absence of actual injury, the mere act of disappearing is accomplished."
[The question is asked: “For what purpose is the inclusion of the word ‘desires’ (*iccha*)? [It is] so that [the rule] may apply even when there is no desire to see, despite the presence of seeing.

To establish this, he says: “Even when there is no desire to see,” and so forth. “Even when there is seeing” means even when there is seeing by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). “From him” means from the preceptor; “only the state of being a limit” means only the preceptor’s status as a limit.

The rule *ākhyāta upayoge* (1-4-29) is a subsequent statement; thus he says, "In the case of *upayoga*, etc. Here, *upayoga* is intended as the acquisition of knowledge preceded by a formal restriction (*niyama*).

By the force of the mention of *upayoga*, the conduct of a student (*sissavatta*) is understood as the restriction for the purpose of acquiring knowledge; therefore, it is from that [teacher] who has spoken (*ākhyātṛ*).
The technical rule (*saññāsutta*) *janikattuno pakati* (1-4-30) has been formulated; thus he says, "Of that which has the sense of being born," and so forth.

*Janyattha* means the meaning of that which is produced (*janya*). What is it that produces? It is from the cause that acts as the producer (*janikattuhetu*). By the word *pakati* (nature/cause), the mere cause is intended;

others [hold this] so that it may also apply to things like "sons" in such expressions as "joy is born from sons. For there are two kinds of causes: the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) and the cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*).
Among these, the lump of clay is the material cause of a jar, being non-different in location from the effect.

The material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is that very [substance], whereas the stick, the wheel, and so forth—which occupy a different location [from the effect] due to their being the product—are the cooperative causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
Since only the material cause is intended to be included here, there might be cases such as "an arrow arises from a horn," but not cases such as "delight arises from sons";

this is because the reading here is "when there is a desire to express another causal factor" (*kārakantaram icchāyaṃ*), rather than "when there is a desire to express another word" (*vacanicchāyaṃ*).
It must be so... because even the desire for a verbal connection within this interval is possible; "those who stand there" (tatraṭṭhā) means those standing there;
their "worldly" (lokiya) people—meaning the legal authorities who do not speak otherwise—are those existing therein.

But the speaker (vattā) is one who speaks according to his own inclination, saying "I alone speak," having transgressed the desire for worldly speech and being unbound to that; [the term] "bound to that" refers to those connected with it.
The meaning is "it does not exist. The rule "pabhavo bhavatissā" (1-4-31) is cited;
regarding that, he says "bhavatissā" and so forth. By explaining the meaning as "it is first perceived," he states that the sense of being produced (*janya*) is not possible here.
For the Himālaya is not the cause of the Gaṅgā; she indeed arose from other causes, while the Himālaya is merely where she is first [perceived].
It is found [in usage]. It has been stated: “The addition of *virama*, *pramāda*, and *artha* [is optional]” (1-4-24 vārttika). Therefore, he says: “In the sense of abstaining,” and so forth.

However, it is stated that when a verbal root is joined with *jigucchā*, *pramāda*, or *artha*, the desire for the accusative or locative case endings is observed. Furthermore, the desire for a term expressing a limit (*avadhi*) is also observed, as in:

“He feels disgust toward a snake for its wickedness” (*jigucchati nāhiriko pāpā*). Moreover, the expression “he neglects the dharmas” (*dhammā pamajjati*) certainly occurs as well, because there is no prohibition [against such usage].

The rule is stated as: “When joined with the words *añña*, *itara*, *itaro*, *disā*, or a word ending in *-añcu* [as the second member]” (Pāṇini 2.3.29). Regarding this, he says: “In connection with the word *añña*,” and so forth.
Since it is explained by others that “*añña* is taken here in its sense [of ‘other’], therefore it occurs even when used as a synonym,” he says:
“different from Devadatta. Because the word *ārā* has the meaning of “distance,” [the example is] “far from the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*)”.
The meaning is “he becomes distant”; thus he says, “the word *ārā* has the sense of distance.
Regarding the term “the correlative being indicated,” this means that when it is said, “Devadatta is brave,” whoever is the second person to that one being indicated is the correlative (*paṭiyogī*).

Because the words for direction, place, and time are subsumed under the category of “direction-words” (*disā-sadda*), he says, “in connection with those expressing direction, place, and time. [This applies to] “prior to the awakening,” and so forth.

Examples for the construction with words denoting time (*kālavācī*) are given; however, examples involving the suffixes *añ*, *uttarapada*, *āca*, and *āhi* have not been cited here. Regarding the Vārttika on Pāṇini 2.3.28, which states:

*“In the rule for the fifth case [ending], there should be an addition [of the object] when there is elision of the suffix *lyap*, and an addition [of the locative] in the sense of the locus,” this is expressed by the words beginning with ‘yattha’.
When there is the application of the suffix *lyap*, if its meaning is understood even though it is elided—that is the elision of *lyap*.

The elision of the suffix *tvā* and the elision of *lyap* are without distinction. In the phrase "having ascended the palace, he looks; having sat down on a seat, he looks," this is a compound with a qualifying action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), meaning that which has the act of looking as its prior [element].

To show that even in all the lookings about to be described, the palace itself is intended to be expressed in its primary form because of the presence of the act of stepping out from the palace, he says: "For thus," and so forth.
“*Apakkamati tato taṃ dassanaṃ*”: from that palace, the vision—that is, the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*)—departs or goes away; this is the meaning.
It is understood that the palace serves as the point of departure (*avadhi*). The word “of whom” (*yesaṃ*) refers to the Vaiśeṣikas, for they explain it thus:
“Among the faculties, the eye-faculty [is so called] because of its extremely subtle nature within the eyeball.”
"Having emerged and become expansive, it approaches the region of the object and sees everything seen by itself in the form of rays;

just as a trumpet is thin at the base and large at the tip, so too are the faculties of knowledge. Here, "the region of the basis" refers to the region of the eyeball which serves as the basis for the faculties.
"The occurrence of the object" refers to the engagement with the sense-field (*gocara*). "Continuity" refers to the succession of the faculties.
The connection is: "the mind-faculty does not reach the basis [of the eye]. "From there" means from the palace; "by departing" means by going away.
Even though the eye-faculty itself goes out from the eyeball, nevertheless, since it departs from the eyeball that remains within the palace, the palace also serves as the limit.
"But for those who" refers to the proponents of momentariness (*khaṇikavādin*); [for them], the faculty has reached its basis.

They are called "those that act by reaching" (*pattakārīni*) because they perform their function of cognizing an object by way of their own nature; the connection [of the sentence] is that they do not lead to the fault of being based on non-faculties (*anindriyādhiṭṭhāna*).
"From there" means from the palace. By the phrase "for those who," he shows that it refers specifically to the proponents of momentariness (*khaṇikavādin*).

For here there are four positions: (1) faculties that act by reaching; (2) those that do not act by reaching; (3) the eye and ear, which do not act by reaching; and (4) the others, which are the opposite of what has been stated.
The statement, "Only the eye is the producer [of the result]; the others are otherwise," presents and establishes only two of the four initial positions among those [four].
Because by establishing that [position], the others are also established, and because the science of grammar (*saddasattha*) is common to all systems (*sāmayika*), this appears somewhat inconsistent.
However, it is not so, because this science of grammar is employed within the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) and thus functions in accordance with the Sogata system.
However, this is quite appropriate for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*khaṇikavādin*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "attention and so forth," the non-difference from the eye and the reaching of the visual object (*rūpāpātha*) are shown; "in a suitable place" means in a location fit for seeing. It is stated [in the grammatical rule]:

"In cases of questioning and explaining, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) should be used" (2-3-28 Vārttika). Therefore he says: "from the word 'questioning' (*pucchanasaddato*)" and so forth; regarding questioning and explaining...

In order to show that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the formulation of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) by way of generality, he says: ‘*Avassaṃ*’ and so forth. ‘Of whom? is the question;

‘Devadatta’s’ is the statement (*ākhyāna*). ‘Kosa, Yajña, Datta’ is the question; this is of the nature of a rule (*vidhi-rūpa*). ‘He who [is] adorned with armlets,’ etc., is the statement of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda-rūpa*), namely:
‘the one with armlets, the one with bracelets. It is stated: “The fifth case should be prescribed after that from which the determination of time occurs. (Vārttika 2-3-28).

Regarding this, he says: *addha*, etc. That by which something is measured (*nimīyate*) or delimited (*paricchijjate*) is a measure (*nimāna*); that itself is the standard of measurement (*nimmāna*). It is stated [in the grammatical rule]:
"The first and seventh cases are to be employed for *addha*" (2-3-28). In this context, the meaning is as follows: "The word *taṃ* (it) is understood [from a previous rule];
when joined with *taṃ*, the fifth case ending is applied, and for the subsequent *addha*, the first and seventh cases are to be employed. Thus: *pāṭaliputtasmā*.
The fifth [case] is appropriate; however, to show that these [other cases] are not to be stated, he says: ‘seven yojanas,’ and so forth.
For here, when the non-difference between Rājagaha and the yojana is intended to be expressed, then [one says], “Rājagaha is seven yojanas from Pāṭaliputta.
But when there is a desire for a statement of difference, the seventh case is established by [the rule] *sabbhāve* etc. (2-34), as in “in seven yojanas.”
For instance, from the statement "Rājagaha is seven *yojanas* from Pāṭaliputta," this meaning is understood: that Rājagaha’s existence is related to the seven *yojanas*.

Thus, being related to the seven *yojanas* becomes the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of Rājagaha. By the rule "the sixth case [is used] for relation" (*sambandhe chaṭṭhī*), this rejects the statement [of the opposing school] that "the seventh case should be stated when connected with time" (*taṃ yuttā kāle sattamī vattabbā*). And [regarding the rule] "also in the sense of instrument" (*karaṇe ca*).
The rule is stated in the sutta as: *thoka-appakā-thokappakicca-katipayassa sattavacanassa* (2-3-33). Regarding this, he says: ‘When [the word] *iccādi*...
By the phrase ‘*kicchādayo* etc.,’ the words *thoka*, *appaka*, and *katipaya* are included. ‘*Asattarūpan’ti* means having the form of a non-number (*asamkhya*).

‘*Guṇe hetumhi*’ means that when the sense of a quality (*guṇa*) is the cause (*hetu*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) applies according to the rule ‘*guṇe*’ (2-21); such is the meaning. ‘By the aforementioned method’ refers to the previously mentioned grammatical procedure.

"By the rule stated in the sutta for the [suffix] *guṇe*," "by the rule stated in the sutta for the [suffix] *guṇe*"—this shows that there is no purpose in separately prescribing the instrumental case by means of [the rule] beginning with *yadā tu icc-ādi*, as is done for others. The connection is with "of the movement (*calana*) of the form to be made";

the construction is that it is an adjective (*visesana*) by virtue of being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇatta*), and by "by virtue of being in apposition" [is meant] "of the king... [etc.]
The phrase beginning with "puriso" (a person) is stated because it demonstrates that even a term not in grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) can function as a qualifier (*visesana*).

Furthermore, its status as a qualifier by virtue of being in apposition is shown by the word *thoka* ("little"), which, when applied to a movement possessing a slight quality, is a qualifier despite not denoting a sentient being;

for this very reason, it is explained that "because *thoka* functions as the object (*kamma*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object. While the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is being carried over [from the previous rule], [the rule continues] with "in the sense of distance and proximity..."
It is stated [in the rule] "the sixth case ending as well" (Pāṇini 2.3.34); therefore, he says: "'Dūraṃ' means 'by means of wood,'" and so forth.
"Characterized by connection with a limit" means that the fifth and sixth case endings are stated thus because their characteristic or cause (*nimitta*) is precisely the connection with a limit.

By the phrase "it is desired to be expressed," he indicates that the speaker's intention alone is the primary factor. In this way, indeed, other [case endings] may also occur according to the speaker's intention regarding the respective *kāraka* functions.
To the question, "Why should the case endings (*vibhattiyo*) not be employed here?", he says: "And these are worldly," and so forth.

The meaning is that, regarding the restriction of case endings here, the cause for the application of specific words is indeed the worldly convention. Furthermore, while the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is being carried over [from the previous rule], it is stated in the rule:

"In the sense of 'far,' the second case ending is used after words denoting place" (Pāṇini 2.3.35), and also in the rule: "The fifth case ending is used in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇe*)" (Pāṇini 2.3.36).
The author of the *Sārasaṅgaha* and others have stated that the locative case is used in the sense of "far" (*dūra*) as well as in the sense of the ablative (*pāṭipadika*).
To show that what was stated in the *Vutti*—namely, "some [say]... and so forth, regarding the rejection of this by means of another designation—is indeed the case, he says:
"'Some' refers to the *Sārasaṅgaha*, etc. The connection is: "This [usage], 'from afar' (*dūrāpādāvasecana*), is their refutation."

In this context, however, the word *iti* has been omitted; it should be understood that in expressions such as *na h’idaṃ*, the word *taṃ* is intended to refer to distant forms (*dūrādi-rūpa*) which are desired to be expressed.

For indeed, it is not understood [otherwise]: "for it is not gone," "for it is not gone from that," "for it is not gone by means of that," and "for it does not stand in that"—these connections should be understood separately.
The word *ca* in *patīyante ca* serves to connect another statement, while *ato ca* refers back to the reason that will be stated hereafter.

Since *yanti* is a particle (*nipāta*) used in the sense of "because," [it is explained as follows: "due to coreferentiality with that" means due to coreferentiality with words such as "far" (*dūra*);

"also due to connection with that" means also due to words such as "village" (*gāma*) being connected with "far" and so on; "rejecting" (*paccakkhanto*) is the statement of the author of the grammatical treatise (*vākyakāra*), for in this regard the reading of the *Mahābhāsya* is:
"In the rule prescribing the fifth case (*pañcamī*) for the meanings of 'far' and 'near,' there is a prohibition of the fifth case when it is connected with that."
It should be said that [the word] *dūra* (far) governs the village (*gāmassa*). Even there, the prohibition regarding "seeing" (*dassana*) is not purposeless;
for in that case as well, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is observed—as in:
"Released from a distant lodging, with water for washing the feet far away, Far from an angry teacher—thus should one be addressed."
In this context, the statement beginning with *dūrantika* and so forth is the formulation of the author of the grammatical commentary (*vākyakāra*); *dūrā gāmassa* is its illustration;

and the passage beginning with *tatrāpi ca* constitutes the explanation (*bhāssa*). Regarding the phrase *dūrasmā āvasathā*, Kyeṭa states in the *Bhāsapadīpa* that the meaning is "far from the dwelling" (*āvasathassa dūre*).
According to the Kaccāyana-sutta (2.6.5), *paṭhamapuriso* refers to one for whom the first person [is used], as in the rule for *dūrantikādi*.
The "pure and so forth" (*suddhādi*) construction is also included; therefore he says, "in the pure, the releasing, and the secluded measure constructions.

Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ca*) in the rule *dhātunāmānam upasaggayogādīsvapi ca* (2-6-2), the "starting from" (*pabhuti*) construction is also taken; therefore he says, "and in the starting-from construction.
By the phrase "and in the starting-from construction," the construction expressing the sense of "starting from" is also included; for this very reason, it is cited as: "From whom I withdraw myself."
27. [Objection:

"Is it not already established that contact (*yoga*) belongs to those things such as the sāla trees? What is the point of this question? Anticipating the objection, "To what, then, does contact belong by means of these?", he says: "'Vajjanaṃ hi,' etc.
The suffix *-ana* is used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*), so 'vajjanānaṃ' means 'by those characterized as contact' (*vajjanasaṅkhātehi*). This refers to those existing in relation to contact.
Regarding the phrase "from that which is connected" (*yuttasmā*): by the words "connected" (*yuttā*), it is meant "only from one that is connected," and not from anything else.

By the question "what is to be said here? he states that the establishment of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) after [words] connected with *apa* and *pari* is well-known (*pasiddha*). Having brought forward even this well-known fact in order to explain it, he says: "of the agent" (*kattuno*), etc.
"That for the sake of which" (*yadattho*) means that for which the act of uttering has a purpose, such as a village (*sālā*) and so forth.
That which is the purpose of Rambha. According to the rule *pañcamy apāparihī* (Pāṇini 2.3.10), the ablative case is prescribed even when there is a connection (*āyutta*) with other words;
thus he says ‘from the boundary’ (*mariyādāya*), etc., for here the raining has a limit.
28. Paṭi...
"Of one for whom the connection is seen" means of the primary [term] whose causal function is established by way of common consensus;
"for the sake of its function" means for the sake of that function belonging to that primary [term]; what is stated is "for the sake of performing the primary function.

The connection is with "he brings forward" (*pabhineti*), occurring in the sense of a substitute (*paṭinidhi*); "in exchange" (*vinimaye*) means for the purpose of bartering, and "in giving back" (*paṭidāne*).
And the word *ca* (and) should be understood as indicating the connection of the case-role (*saddassāṭṭhānappayutti*); the relation (*yoga*) is with that [word] by way of conjunction (*patinā*).
29. Regarding *rite*:

if the second case is used for the object (*kamme*) because that which is connected to the action of avoiding (*vajjanakiriyā*) functions as the object (*kammattā*), then for what purpose is it stated again?
He says, "the second case-ending," in the passage beginning with ‘paṭipadavidhāne,’ etc.
That which has a formulation (vidhāna) pronounced in its direct form is ‘paṭipadavidhānā’; the meaning is that it possesses a specific formulation.
He thinks that if there were no second case-ending here, then the fifth case-ending—which is directly prescribed in connection with the word *rite*—would be superseded by the second case-ending.
If the purpose here were merely the absence of sublation of the fifth case by the second case, then one should have simply formulated the rule as *rite vā*;

for in that case, the second case would apply in its alternative form (*pakkhe*), and the sutta would have been composed more concisely. Anticipating this objection, he states another purpose: “*uttaratthañce*.
The phrase *ato yevā* means precisely because it serves a subsequent purpose. To demonstrate yet another further purpose for the inclusion of the second case, he says: “*vibhatyantare*,” etc.
"Direct speech" (*āhaccavacana*) refers to speech that has been brought forth by striking the throat or other locations with the breath;

it is said to mean "straightforward speech. The change in case ending is from the sixth case (*chaṭṭhīvibhatti*); its purpose is for exclusion (*byudāsa*), while its purpose is for negation (*nirāsa*).
The phrase "another also" means another [case] besides the second, namely the sixth; the phrase "connected to the original" (*pakatasambandhana*) means connected to the original fifth case.
31. *Putha*:

Nor even for a second reason is it a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). This is how he considers it: "If, while [the rule] 'and the third' (*tatiyā ca*) were being stated, the word 'second' (*dutiyā*) were connected there by means of the particle *ca*, and if likewise the word 'fifth' (*pañcamī*) were [connected] by means of the particle *ca*—then, since no one would be excluded [in that case], [the rule] would apply as follows:

'except for *vinā*, *aññatra*, and *putha*.'"* *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a grammatical commentary (likely on Kaccāyana’s Pāli grammar) discussing the interpretation of specific rules regarding case endings.*

If it were intended that "tatiyā ce" (if the third case) and "jātu pañcamī" (sometimes the fifth case) formed a single compound rule (*ekayoga*), then by the power of the rule's division (*yogavibhāga*), one might ask:

"Since the meaning of 'without' (*vinā*) is already included in the sense of 'absence of accompaniment' (*asahāyatthatte*), why was a separate formulation of the sutta not made simply as 'vinātthe hi' (for in the sense of 'without')? To this he replies: "'Bhedo pādānantu' etc. 32.
Satta (Seven)
Because sounds are eternal, the word *yattha* (wherein) refers to the relationship; thus, that which is referred to as *so* (it) and *yo* (which) is explained as *tassa* (of it).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with *yo yattha* (which wherein) is an exposition of the textual sequence beginning with *kiriyādhārabhūte* (in that which is the locus of the action).

Therefore, *yo* (which) is intended as that which is the substratum of the action; this is precisely what is stated by the words *kiriyā ca* (and the action), etc.; thus, this [substratum] is supported by the agent and the object.
It should be understood as ending in the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), meaning "that in which actions are combined" or "that which supports that [action] in its locus.
Alternatively, it is the agentive *ghañ*, meaning "support" (*ādhāra*) because it supports both the agent and the object, which serve as the substrata for the action. For it is said:
"That which supports the agent and the object, which are the substrata for the action..."
They say that the support (ādhāra) and the agent (kāraka) are each fourfold.
Now, if it is asked: "Is it not the case that 'support' is defined as the sustaining of an action? Why then is it described in this way?"—there is no fault here.
For that which is the sustaining of an action for it is precisely the sustaining of the agent and the object, which serve as its basis; there is no other kind of sustaining for it.
From that [locative case], an action arises by means of a cause; "support" (ādhāra) means "that which supports" (ādhāreti), which is precisely this meaning.
An action is not directly grasped through a support that excludes the agent and the object. For this very reason, he will say:

"The locus of action," and so forth. But is it not the case that the agent directly supports the action inherent in the agent, while the object [directly supports] the action inherent in the object, such as the act of cutting or the sensation?

That being the case, they would indeed be the support [of the action], and not... because in common worldly usage and in the grammatical treatises (*sattha*), the status of being a support for those [actions] is not established;
rather, it is shown that only the status of agent (*kattū*) and object (*kamma*) is established for them. Thus he says, "If it is an action," and so forth. And so it has been stated:
"The agent and the object are separated [from the verb], while the action remains close at hand."
And that which assists in the accomplishment of an action (*kriyāsiddhupakāri*) is considered the locus of the object (*adhikaraṇa*).
"Separated from the agent and the object" means separated from the agent and the object by way of being inherent in them; that is, indirectly.
"Assisting in the accomplishment of an action" means assisting—that is, acting as an aid—in the successful completion of the action inherent in the agent and the object.

Now, bearing in mind the objection that one might define this substratum (ādhāra) not only by its supporting [an action] like a container, but also by its supporting the agent and the object—since it can indeed be established as such—he says “na ce” and so forth.
[The phrase] “only the cause of the action” means only the cause of the action inherent in the agent and the object.
Thus, in order to show that such a substratum is fourfold, he says “ādhāro.”
"Such as 'cloth,' etc. It is "fourfold" because it has four kinds of support.

An "opasilesika" (contact) substratum is so called because it possesses the characteristic of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) together with that which is supported (*ādheyya*), as in "he sits on a mat" or "he cooks in a pot," where the mat and so forth are the substrata.
For instance, the mat, while supporting Devadatta, supports the act of sitting inherent in Devadatta, [supporting it] as mediated by Devadatta; the same applies to the pot.
