The mat and other such objects possess the state of being a proximate support (*upasilesika-dhāratta*) because they sustain the action of moistening and so forth, which is inherent in the rice grains.

That wherein the supported object does not exist at all, or exists to a greater degree elsewhere, is the *visayika* [support]; for "object" (*visaya*) means the non-existence of the supported object elsewhere.
Just as color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest are called the objects of the eye and so forth because the functioning of the eye and so forth does not occur elsewhere, so it is with space.
In the case of "birds" (*sakunaya*) and so forth, because birds and the like do not exist elsewhere than in the sky and such places, those [locations] are called their "domain" (*visaya*).
That which belongs to the domain is "domainal" (*vesayika*). Regarding that which pervades the relationship between the container (*ādhāra*) and the contained (*ādheyya*), it is the contained;

for it is the pervader. Thus, in the expressions "oil in sesame seeds" (*tilesu telaṃ*) and "ghee in curd" (*dadhimhi sappi*), the sesame seeds and so forth are the pervasive containers, because they remain pervading the oil and so forth which are the contained.
That which exists in proximity, or that which is itself proximate, is "proximate" (*sāmīpika*). That for whose vicinity the contained object (*ādheyya*) resides is thus called [the container].

An example here is: "He dwells among his teachers; there is a hamlet on the Ganges. But surely, even here, the locative case is prescribed for the locus (*ādhāra*), and a locus is said to be a support (*nissaya*).
Furthermore, a support occurs through either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). Yet, students and the like do not possess [conjunction or inherence] with their teachers and so forth.

There is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as in the case of Devadatta with his bird and so forth through such means as a side-glance, nor inherence (*samavāya*), as in the case of oil with sesame seeds and so forth;
therefore, it is improper for you to say that [the support] is its substratum (*ādhāra*). This is not so;

for when the stability of one thing depends upon another, that [latter] becomes its support even without conjunction or inherence. For example, there is no conjunction or inherence of a man with a king.

Just as a king’s dependent is designated a "king's man" because his existence is dependent upon him, so too, since the existence of disciples and others is dependent upon their teacher and so forth, this dependence of theirs on the teacher and others is logical. (In the manuscript: This dependence of the teacher and others is appropriate;
[Jinindabuddhi says: "the state of being a support for the teacher and others is logical. However, in this regard, even if...

Although there is a mutual proximity (*upasileśa*) between the substratum and the superstratum for those things that pervade their objects, nevertheless, because it is distinct from other modes [of relation], it is designated as such;

it is not otherwise. Since the pervaders of the object are not grasped by means of either the proximate or the proximate itself, and since proximity (*upasileśa*) is clearly manifest only as proximity, it is designated accordingly; thus, there is no confusion, nor anything to be confused with.

33. Regarding the phrase "by the mere state of being a sign" (*nimittabhāvamattena*): this indicates the occurrence of the locative case even in the absence of a connection with karma, and not merely in the case of a connection with karma as is the view of others.
For this very reason, he will say later: "it is so conceived," etc. For according to outsiders, [the rule is] "signs [are connected] by means of karma."
This is the sutta (Pāṇini 2.3.89). Therein, the meaning is that the seventh case ending occurs when there is a connection with a "purpose" (*payojana*) through an object (*kamma*).

For example, in the phrase *ajinamhi haññate dīpī* ("a leopard is killed for its skin"), the skin is the purpose for the killing of the leopard; thus, he kills the leopard for the sake of that [skin].
Regarding the mention of "object" (*kamma*) in the sutta, he begins to state the purpose [of this rule] with the words "But not... (*na pana...*), and so forth.
34. *Yabbhā yassa kiriyā*:
the action such as milking that belongs to a certain object, such as a cow; "of another action" means of another action such as walking;
"by this" refers to the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*); the explanation of that is "possessing action" (*kiriyāvato*).
“*Kālabhāvesu ce*” (2-6-43) is the sutta formulated by Kaccāyana; thus he says: “*Kālatthehi cā*,” and so forth. 35.

Regarding the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*): When used in connection with [words expressing] ownership, lordship, and so on, the sixth and seventh cases may occur, as stated in: “*Sāmissarādhipatidāyādasakkhipatibhūpasutehi*.”
And since [the rule] beginning with "iti" (2-3-39) was initiated by others, he says: "sāmi," etc.

Here, Jinindabuddhi, having cited the statement—"Let there not be here the separate mention of *sāmi* and so on for the purpose of excluding other synonyms, as in 'the king of the village'"—and having made it an object of laughter, spoke while demonstrating its logical inconsistency:
"'sāmissare,' etc. What is it that prevents [this]? The meaning is: nothing at all.
In order to show that even the expression "the king in the village" (*gāme rājā*) must be possible when there is a desire for the word to denote the object, he begins with the rule:
“*Āyutta-kusalehi āsevāya*” (2-3-40). To explain this, he says: “*Āyutte*,” etc. *Āsava* means devotion to that;

*byāvaṭo* means appointed. Here, one might object: “Since I shall say ‘*āsevāya*’ [in the next rule], this present rule must necessarily be commenced; otherwise, even in the case of slight connection, [a word] would be called *āyutta*.”

Having raised the doubt, "He asserts [the word] *go* [as a noun] because of the [compound] *gosakaṭassa*," [the author] says "even without" (*vināpi*) and so forth, in order to show that even this purpose does not exist.
The *Kaccāyana-sutta* beginning with "sāmissarā" is cited; "by that very [rule]" means by the very definition of the word *kusala* following the word *pasūta* in the *Kaccāyana-sutta*.
"Here" refers to the *Moggallāna-vutti*. According to *Kaccāyana*: "In the senses of object (*kamma*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and cause (*nimitta*)..."

The rules "sattamī" (Pāṇini 2.3.37) and "pañcamyatthe ca" (Kaccāyana 2.6.41) have been stated; therefore he says "in the sense of the object," etc. The connection is that "the arms are the objects of grasping.
For the Kaccāyanas, "among the bhikkhus" and so forth are examples in the sense of the object; "in the hands" and so forth are examples in the sense of the instrument;
"among the plantains" is an example in the sense of the ablative. [And there is the rule: "The third case ending is used for 'maṇḍita' and 'ussukka'."

(2-6-45) The *Kaccāyana-sutta* states this: "In the sense of being adorned," and so forth; "in the sense of being adorned" means in the sense of being embellished; "in the sense of zeal" means in the sense of exertion. 36.
Since selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is a separate operation, the teacher Jinindabuddha [asked]: "For what purpose is this statement, given that..."

"A part being extracted remains within the whole; when one wishes to express the whole as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then the locative case is established, as in 'the branch on the tree' (*rukkhe sākhā*);
but when there is a relation with the part, then the genitive case is used, as in 'the branch of the tree' (*rukkhassa sākhā*).
This is true, but the statement was made for the sake of elaboration. Showing that this is not properly reasoned, [the author says:]
He says: "Grains such as *sāli* and so forth that are joined with husks are 'husked grains' (*sūkadhaññāni*).
'Placed' (*āhitā*) means established; what is meant is that they have become the receptacle. 'From which' (*yato*) means from the cause of their being placed;

'therefore' (*tato*) means because the speech of the Lord of Jinas, the Buddha, is thus inconsistent for that reason. This refers to the Pāṇinian rule, *pañcamī vibhakke* (2.3.42); hence he says: 'from the whole' (*samudāyato*), and so forth."
The connection is that virtue (*sīla*) is "far superior" (*atisayena seyyo*) to learning (*sutato*). Regarding this, others explain:

"When the sixth and seventh cases (*chaṭṭhī-sattamī*) are encountered in a context of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), this [use of the fifth case] is an exception (*apavāda*) to them. To this we reply: first of all, there is no selection here at all;

how then could there be the occurrence of the sixth or seventh cases? Therefore, demonstrating that this [rule] is commenced for the purpose of setting aside those two cases, he says: "Not here... (*nātra*).

"By birth and so forth," etc. By the phrase "not by [specifying] birth and so forth," he shows the absence of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). In the expression "of birth and so forth" (*jaccādīnaṃ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of selection.

He asks, "Why is it not so? and replies with "by connection with birth and so forth," etc. "Because of that designation" means because of the absence of designations such as "virtue" (*sīla*) and so on.
Again, he states another reason for the absence of selection with "And of equals," etc. [This applies] when there is association with those who are good and skillful, in the sense of honor.

This locative case (*sattamī*) is being discussed; likewise, it occurs in connection with the word *asādhu* (unskillful), and likewise, the instrumental and locative cases occur in connection with the words *pasita* (attached) and *ussukka* (zealous).
Furthermore, the Pāṇinīyas have prescribed the elision of the final syllable of the word *nakkhatta* (constellation) according to various grammatical endings.

All of this is intended solely to establish the desired expression for each respective grammatical factor (*kāraka*), as in the examples "skillful toward his mother" (*mātari sādhu*) and so forth, and "attached to the hair" (*kesesu pasito*).

"Attached" (*pasatto*) means "bound" (*avabaddho*). The meaning is that one has become attached by means of the hair acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*), or else, with the hair acting as the agent (*kattā*), the meaning is "one who has been made attached.

By the word *phusse*, which is connected to the moon (*indu*), time is characterized; this is because of the non-differentiated relationship [expressed as] "this is that," [meaning] "by that which touches.
Thus, it is by that [moon] acting as the instrument.

37. Regarding the first [section], although it is stated merely as "the first," neither the meaning of the sentence nor the meaning of the individual words is understood; thus, to show that this follows from the inclusion of the term *nāma* (name), he says: “Two-by-two, one-by-many, etc., according to the Sutta,” and so forth.
When the meaning is being demonstrated by means of a name, it is contained within that which is designated as a name.
Having superimposed [the quality of] being denotable [upon the name], it presents [it] without regard for specific case-endings; thus he says, "It is denoted," and so forth.

By the phrase "by its own form" (pakatirūpena), he means by way of the name. By the words "of that which is denoted" (tassa abhidheyyassa) and "of the word *matta*," etc., he shows that this is a statement of the general meaning of the word *matta*.
This is what is meant: by the expression "the mere denotation of the name," that which is about to be stated is expressed.
It occurs thus: “The nominative case is used for the mere expression of gender, measure, and number on the first day [of the lunar fortnight]” (2-3-46).
Having understood that the nominative is prescribed with a distinction regarding gender and so forth, he says: ‘liṅgaparimāṇe,’ etc. Gender (*liṅga*) consists of feminine, masculine, and neuter;

measure (*parimāṇa*) is delimitation; number (*vacana*) consists of singularity and plurality. Since even that which possesses these [categories] is indeed the referent of the word (*saddattha*), [the rule applies] even to that which possesses gender and so forth.

The referent of a word (*saddattha*) is indeed distinct from its form (*sarūpa*). Because it occurs by taking as its primary focus the commonality of highness and lowness, the nominative case (*paṭhamā*) is used with the words "high" and "low.

Since that which is connected to them also possesses the status of a word-referent, in expressions such as "high houses," the quality of height is made the cause (*nimitta*), and thus [the nominative] applies to the houses through a relationship of non-difference (*abhedasambandha*) expressed as "this is that. This is seen in examples such as "he approaches" (*ajjhāgacchati*).

Regarding the phrase "asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ" (2-119), by the power of the rule for elision (*lopavidhāna*), the nominative case is indeed established even after [suffixes] beginning with *p* that do not have the sense of *anatthaka*. 38.

By the statement "addressing (*āmanta*) means making [something] face-to-face," etc., he demonstrates the result of the commencement of this grammatical rule (*yoga*). "In the sense of a noun" (*nāmatthe*) means in the sense of a word (*saddatthe*); "from a word" (*padato*) means from a word that expresses merely the additional sense of addressing. And here [the following examples] occur...
The "making present" (*abhimukhīkāra*) or the state of being present (*abhimukhībhāva*) of one who has attained success (*siddha*)—this may be a mere address (*āmantaṇa*).
For when the meaning is made present, it is then employed in the action. Address is not the meaning of the sentence, because it is understood from the word itself.
In the world, there is no such thing as addressing someone with a name that is not established by a referent (*vatthu*) that must be brought into being;
for example, "O King, may you exist" and "may you become one whose purpose is accomplished. Regarding the word *siddhassa*:

it refers to one who is already established by means of a name such as Devadatta; "purpose" (*attha*) refers to Devadatta and so forth; "accomplished" (*kata*) refers to the act of bringing [the name] into presence or establishing it.

*Yena* is a compound; it is employed in the sense of an action, as in "go" or "eat. There is no address [here]. Because that which is being enjoined lacks the capacity to be directed toward [an object] since its power has not yet been acquired, it must be brought about—that is, it must be accomplished. 39.
The Sixth Case.
He begins the commentary on the meaning of the grammatical treatise beginning with “Kiriyākārakeccādi” with the words “This relation is called one,” and so forth.
By the phrase “produced by action and by factors of action” (*kiriyāya kārakehi ca nipphādito*), he states that relation has action and the factors of action as its antecedents;
for this very reason, it is not accidental, and thus it does not belong to just any two things whatsoever, but only to those that are specifically distinguished.

However, there is no over-extension [of the term *sambandha*] to the case where it exists between two [entities], because a relation other than the *kārakas*—such as the relation of owner and owned—is preceded by a relation between an action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*). And so it has been said:
"A relation other than the *kārakas* is preceded by the relation between an action and its factors."
"Whether this action is heard or not heard, it is that which is designated as the 'action' (kriyā).

In this context, regarding an unexpressed action—as in "the king's man" and so forth—the relation of possession (*sassāmibhāva*) and the like is understood as being distinct from the relation between an agent and its object (*kārakasambandha*), even though it is preceded by such a relation.
However, in cases such as "he remembers the kingdom," where the word for action is actually heard, [the relation is understood directly].

In this context, however, although an action (*kamma*) exists, it is not intended to be expressed; rather, only the state of being a qualifier (*visesanabhāva*) is assigned to the refuge with respect to the kingdom, as in the expression “the refuge connected with the kingdom.

For everywhere, the relationship between action and its factors (*kiriyākārakasambandha*) exists by way of the persistence of the underlying substance (*vatthuṭṭhitivasena*), and from that [relationship] arises the state of having an owner (*sassāmibhāva*) and so forth.
In that regard, when there is an intention to express the state of having an owner, even though the relationship between action and its factors is present...

A relation is not intended to be expressed [in such cases], as in the expression “a girl with no belly. Furthermore, this relation should be understood as being of many kinds, characterized by the states of owner and owned, knower and known, producer and produced, part and whole, and so forth.
Among these, in the relation of owner and owned: "the king's man"; in the relation of knower and known: "the seed of the *nigrodha* tree";
in the relation of part and whole: "the branch of the tree. Now, regarding this very relation...

In order to demonstrate elsewhere as well how the state of being produced by the relationship between an action and its factors arises according to the specific case, he provides an illustration beginning with ‘For thus’ (*tathā hi*).
By the statement “their relationship is due to the action of protecting,” he shows that this relationship is characterized by the protected and the protector;
furthermore, this action characterized by protection is the cause for the state of "thisness" (*idambhāva*) which constitutes the relationship.

Having produced [the understanding], it ceases; however, through the exposition of the meaning (*atthappakaraṇa*) and so forth, the specific distinction that "this action is connected to this" is understood.
There is no capacity for the genitive case (*chaṭṭhī*) to convey such a distinction, because it is uniform in all instances.

Or rather, even when the word for the action is actually heard, there is an absence of the desire to utter the cause of the factorhood (*kārakabhāva*), which consists precisely in the relation of "this belongs to that" (*assedambhābhāva*).

Because it is intended to express the fruit (the object), the relationship arises in that very same way and is expressed by the genitive case, as in "he remembers the rope" (*rajjussa sarati*). For it has been said:
"Having first produced a relationship, some action then ceases;
in other cases, the relationship arises while the word for the action is being heard."
"He protects" means he protects men; therefore, the action—which has the nature of assistance consisting of protection and so forth—belongs to both of them as its relata.

For when it is performed by the king, that action belongs to his related men and is connected to the state of being men; thus, the action is possible for both. Consequently, because that action belongs to both, [the suffix] *ase* occurs by virtue of being the cause for the cognition [of the agent].
Because this relation, whose nature consists in mutual dependence, exists, it is produced by an action; its characteristic is mutual dependence.
For if there were total independence, the relation would be non-existent, since the cognition of the relata—such as "the king's man" and so forth—would not be possible.
Thus, for the cognition that proceeds in this manner, the existence [of the relation] is established. As others say: "The genitive case is used for qualities."
Since there is no other statement [to the contrary], he says ‘nanu ce’ and so forth in order to demonstrate that the application of the sixth case occurs in both instances (in this very manuscript).
Taking the objection as stated to be true, and having applied the aforementioned nature of the relationship to something other than that [the agent] as well,
he says ‘Devadatto’ and so forth in order to urge the objection regarding the application of the sixth case in that case.

Having introduced here the intention of the objector—that even when non-existence (*asatī*) is expressed by "not" (*athaiva*), the desire for the word itself is the cause in a relationship characterized by mutual dependence—the author then states "If this is so, here too...
and so forth, specifically to apply that same principle to the absence of the genitive case. In that context, *atha* is a particle used to introduce the clarification of the objector’s intention;
*evaṃ vattabbaṃ* means "it should be stated thus," by way of "if this is so" (*yadi evaṃ*) and so on.
This demonstrates that it should be stated according to the method to be explained, beginning with the phrase "because of the necessity of being presented [in order]," and so forth:

"Because it is not dependent on another due to its state of being that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), it is distinguished from its subordinate status; therefore, it is established as *tat* (that) itself and does not assume another form, as in ‘of the man’ (*purisassa*).
However, the qualifier, such as ‘the king,’ being mentioned as a subordinate member of that [man], is distinguished from the form of the agent (*kāraka*) because of its own subordination."

Then it resorts to another form, namely "of the king" (*rañño*); from that, there arises a relation characterized by distinction (*byatireka-lakkhaṇa*), because a single [referent] cannot possibly possess the state of being related [to two things].

Thus, although [the relation] is seen as twofold in its objective basis (*vatthu*), it is understood through its having entered into the state of being a qualifier (*visesanagatattena*). Therefore, the genitive case-ending (*chaṭṭhī*) follows after the qualifier alone;

for the application of words occurs within the sphere of cognition (*patīti-visaya*). Indeed, that which is the object of conceptualization (*vikappana*) belongs to words; for this very reason, there is a relation.

It invariably conforms to the distinction of the qualifier... even when [the object] is seen as two from the standpoint of its substance, because it is understood as being contained within that [qualifier], it does not necessarily follow that "the wealth of the brothers" implies "the wealth of the non-brothers";
likewise, even though there is a distinction in the qualified, it conforms to the distinction residing in the qualifier itself, as in "Devadatta’s horse. All of this is as follows:
Because it is understood through its relation [to the qualified] by way of being situated in the qualifier (*visesana*), it is metaphorically attributed [to the qualified];

likewise, because it is situated in the qualified (*visessa*), there may necessarily be a conformity to the distinctions residing therein, just as there is a conformity to the distinctions residing in the qualifier.

However, the state of being "seen twice" (*dviṭṭhatta*) is not contradicted by the fact that the object (*vatthu*) is fourfold; for those who propound this [theory], the state of being "seen twice" is considered solely in connection with the verbal expression (*vattu*).

A relationship is expressed as being between two [terms]; for this very reason, this is understood as an ablative case (*byatireka-vibhatti*). It functions as an expression of a relationship characterized by the distinction residing in the related term that serves as the qualifying attribute (*visesana*) which is being distinguished.
However, a qualifier such as "blue," even if it is subordinate because its referent is external, is not distinguished from the status of being a *kāraka* (grammatical participant).
This is because words such as "blue" denote a substance such as a lotus; as in: "his lotus is blue," or "it stands with a blue lotus."

Regarding the phrase "the fragrance of a blue lotus," when there is no occurrence of distinction, then the relationship of the agent and the state—characterized as "the blue quality having the lotus as its substratum"—is indeed distinct; thus, the blue and so forth are distinct from the primary state.
Therefore, the qualifier itself remains in its manifold variety, and consequently, the qualifier exists in some form as an agent.
It should not be suspected that because [the word] is distinguished merely by being set apart from its primary state (*padhānabhāva*), all the rest would likewise become so.
"Even both" means even two royal servants; in the third case, it is connected with what is designated as "home.
By the phrase "even depending on what is associated," this demonstrates precisely the subordinate status (*appadhānatta*) of the person; "intended" means intended according to another Pāṇinian rule.
Since, in his own opinion, the sixth case [the genitive] expresses both relation and support, he said: “The relation also,” and so forth.
Regarding this, some say that the relation here is the cause for the mother’s acts of taking refuge, such as her remaining steadfast;

others, however, maintain that because taking refuge is itself an action, a relation with a substance is possible even without another intervening action, just as there is a joining together of two pieces of lac.
But in the case of *jatunā* with *kaṭṭha*, the joining occurs with the lac itself, not through another substance containing lac.

When the suffix *kita* is employed in the sense of the third case, the second case, and—excepting other instances—in the sense of the fifth case and the seventh case, the sixth case is considered [to be used] by virtue of the rule “*chaṭṭhī cā*” (Pāṇini 2.3.38) and the rule “*dutiyāpañcamīnañcā*” (Kaccāyana 2.6.29). This [sixth case usage] also occurs solely according to the speaker’s intention.
To demonstrate that the state [of the rule] has been established, he says "yathā cettha" and so forth.

Here too, in the first two examples, because there is an absence of the status of a recipient (sampadāna) without another sutta, the genitive case for others occurs only when there is a desire to express a relationship; therefore he says "ettha" and so forth.
He shows the meaning of this [rule] as being "predominant" (bahulanta) by saying "yathā dassanaṃ," [referring to] non-deceptive light, truth, and so on, in the sense of an object (kamma).

As for the examples: regarding the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*), one should understand that all instances such as *daṇḍassa atthāya* ("for the sake of the staff") and so forth are examples based solely on the speaker's intention.

40. Regarding "equal" (*tulya*) and "unintended" (*anabhimata*): by the rule *tulopamāhi tatiyāññatarissa* (Pāṇini 2.3.72), [the third case ending is used] after words meaning "equal" (*tulya*) or "comparison" (*upamā*).
Because [the use of] the third case is prescribed when joined with other words having the sense of "equal" (*tulya*), it is not favored by the followers of Pāṇini;
for since similar entities do not constitute a simile for them, it is said, "There is no scale (*tulā*) for Arjuna," and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning of *tadevaṃ* should be understood as "in the manner just described"; or alternatively, *tadevaṃ* is a collection of particles used in the sense of indicating what has been previously stated.
"In similar ones" means in those that are alike; "stated in that manner" means stated in such a way as "there is no balance for Arjuna," and so forth.

41. Therefore, regarding what is stated in the Sutta as "from this" (*ato*), one might ask how it is stated as "from that which ends in the vowel *a*. To this he says "from this," etc.; [the meaning is] that the substitutions (*ādesā*) occur.
The remainder [of the rule] would apply only to the *yakāra*s... because the substitutes *ā* and *ē* consist of a single phoneme (*ekavaṇṇa*).

When the elision (*lopa*) has been made—that is, when the *okāra* has been elided—the phrase "in that case" (*tatra*) precludes the previously mentioned [application of the rule] beginning with *dhacādi*. He states the reason for this preclusion: "because of the elision of the subsequent [element]" (*paralopassa*), etc. Then he begins to state another reason: "furthermore" (*kiñca*), etc.;
there would always be only the elision of the subsequent [element], and not even the elision of the preceding one, in accordance with the suitability for the application of the augment (*āgama*).
He says ‘nacā’ and so forth, meaning “it is not possible to apply [the rule]”; the connection is that since the elision of *pa* is constant, it is not possible to maintain [the form].
With the words “evam santeti” and so forth, he states the contradiction therein. Regarding “atosambhavā,” this means because of the impossibility from the perspective of the substitute vowel *ā*.

He states the reason for the absence of the purpose already mentioned—namely, that the prescription of the vowel *ī* for *jhissa* in the rule “yosu jhissa pume” (2-93) serves as its sole purpose—with the word “aniṭṭhattā.”
The meaning is "because it is not desired. To demonstrate precisely that it is not desired due to the absence of a purpose, he says:
"for this very purpose," and so forth. "Of this" refers to the rule *ato yo naṃ ṭāṭe*.
"Only from *jhismā*" means either the rule itself, namely *jhismā*, or the rule *jhismā yonaṃ ṭāṭe*. "From *ata*" refers to the rule *ato*.
“Of such an application” means “of the foremost,” that is, of the application [expressed by] “foremost.
42. Regarding *nīnaṃ*:

since only one form is cited, the distinction between *rūpa-arūpāni* and *rūpe-rūpāni* should be understood; for by that, it is shown that in the plural, through the plural [form], only one single form—namely *aṭṭhīni*—is cited in both the first and second cases.

44. Regarding the question, "What is the purpose of the letter *ñ* in [the term] *sassāya suñ*?", it is said: "The letter *ñ*," and so forth. For if the letter *ñ* were not present, then by the rule "that which has *ñ* as its suffix" (*ñānubandho*), the letter *s* would not be qualified by the qualifier *ñ*;
only when that [letter *ñ*] exists can it be qualified by it. Therefore, [it is stated]: "Those beginning and ending with [roots] having *ñ* as their suffix."
In the Sutta, the qualification "with a different consonant as an adjunct" (*aññakānubandha*) has the sense of being a qualifier; that which has this sense is "that whose purpose is qualification.

Since much is established by the rule even when not intended or left incomplete, the author begins with the words "by way of generality" (*sāmaññena*) and so forth, in order to show that [the term] "furthermore" (*bhiyyo*) and so on is taught in the Vutti.
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is in the genitive case; for is it not a compound where the sense of the word *attha* functions as a different referent (*aññapadattha*)?

How is it stated that the meaning of the fourth case (catutthyattha) is determined? It is said: regarding the rule "the singular of the fourth case [expresses] one's own purpose" (*attattha*), the meaning here is that the hearing of the True Dharma (*saddhammasavana*) and so forth serve as the cause (*nimitta*).
That same meaning—though it is the referent of another word—is also the purpose (*attha*) or motive (*payojana*) for that which has become the referent of the other word, by way of being its cause;

thus, there is no difference in meaning. Therefore, the phrase "of all [words] beginning with *sa* etc., excluding these two" refers to those words beginning with *ta* and *eta*, excluding the words *ima* and *ava*.

To show that even among those [words] beginning with *sabba* which are excluded from this rule, the substitution of some [other form] is observed even when [the original] is prohibited, he says: “and of the word *ta*.
45. *Ghapa*:
*itthiyā*, *vadhuyā*—these are examples of the substitution of *ī* for *gha* and *pa*. *Ūna* is an example of the substitution of *ū*.
46. *Ssāvā ghapasaññehi*:

this [term] should be understood as a qualifier of *teti* and *māmūhi* through a compound where the meaning of another word (*aññapadattha*) is predominant. The phrase "vuttiyaṃ katan" and so forth is provided for the purpose of illustrating the agent and other grammatical roles. "Tāyā" is an example of an alternative form (*vikappa*) in all instances.
47. *Namhi*.
“The maxim ‘that which has become subordinate to it is included by the inclusion of that’ is a statement of grammatical convention.
In this context, ‘subordinate to it’ means subordinate to that augment; being subsequent [parts] by way of their constituent members, they are non-primary.
‘By the inclusion of that’ means by the inclusion of the augment; that is, because of the inclusion of *naṃ*, which has become the augment.”
It should rather be stated as ‘namhi vibhattimhi’; or else, a transposition (*vipallāsa*) should be understood here.
He explains what was already stated by the words ‘ikārass’eva vā’ and so forth, using the words ‘tissa’ and so forth. [The phrase] ‘tassa tissa’ means ‘of that which is designated as *tissa*’.

[The phrase] ‘niddiṭṭhattā’ means ‘because it is designated as *tissa*’. By the rule “*namhi ticatunnamitthiyam tissa catassā*” (Pāṇini 7.1.20), there is the substitution of *tissā* when *na*-locative follows. “*Namhi*... [is the rule].
Regarding "of the seventeen beginning with *nuka* and *dvā*" (2-47), there is *nuka*; [it applies] to three.

51. In the *Suña Vibhattisutta*, in the rule beginning with "in the dual and singular, and in the plural" (2-1), he states the singular number together with the plural suffix *-ssan-*; this rule is "of *suñ* and *sassā*"; "when the rule exists" means when the rule "of *suñ* and *sassā*" exists.
55. *Rati*, *ratti*, and so forth constitute the group beginning with *rati*; [the compound is] by means of those.
56. *Sukhī*.
"By way of imitation" (*anukaraṇavasena*): imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is the act of making something similar, that is, speech that imitates.
57. *Ltu tena*:
"By that which has *ltu*" means that by the qualification "*ltu*," there is the grasping of the suffix intended to be expressed; the sense is "by that."

When there is the mention of a condition (*paccaya*), the inclusion of that which begins with it is obtained... according to the rule: "In the mention of a condition, there is the inclusion of that which begins from where it is prescribed.

Because it is intended to be expressed as a qualifier (*visesana*), there is the inclusion of that which ends with it... bearing in mind the statement: "A prescription applies to that which ends in a qualifier" (1-13), he says: "from where," etc.
That which has the sense of an action (*kriyattha*) is the beginning of it; thus, it is "that-which-begins-with-that" (*tadādi*).

The term *tadanta* means that which belongs to a composite whole (*samudāya*) ending in that [suffix]; the meaning is that there is a grasping of such a specific composite whole as it is seen, and not merely of that which ends in it. Now, one might object:

since the intention is to speak of a qualifier (*visesana*) such as *ltvī*, let there be a grasping of the "end of that" (*tadanta*) by means of the rule "of the end of a qualifier of an injunction" (*vidhibbesanantassa*);
however, by the mention of "affix" (*paccaya*), [the reference is] to that which begins with it (*tadādino*).
To the question, "How can there be a grasping [of the cause]? he says: "Because of its inseparability from that" (*tadavinābhāvitā*).

Since it is prescribed by that [cause], and because it does not exist without that moral habit (*sīla*), it is "inseparable from that" (*tadavinābhāvī*); the state of being such is "therefore" (*tasmā*).

According to the principle that "when a condition is grasped, there is a grasping of that which begins with it," since the grasping of the condition occurs wherever this applies, the term "that which begins with it" (*tadādino*) is used because of its common applicability.

It has been stated; however, no distinction is seen here in the inclusion of a collective group beginning with that [word], because it is impossible to see a distinction in cases such as *adhikattā* (from *adhigatantāva*) and so forth.
But a distinction is seen in the rule *tuṃsmā lopo cicchāyaṃ te* (5-4), for there he will say:
"The forms *tuṃ*, *tā*, and *itave* occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) and in the future tense (*bhavissati*) when referring to an action."
(5–61) “He will state the suffix *tuṃ*,” and so forth. 58. Regarding *ge*:
“It should be stated as *gea* alone” means it is said that it should be stated as *gea* alone; [this is] because in the alternative view, the rule for the long vowel (*dīgha*) is already established.
When this substitution of *a* has been made, the long vowel occurs by the very rule prescribing lengthening in the alternative case (*pakkhe*).

Regarding the phrase “because of its meaning being established elsewhere” (*aññatthacaritatthatāya*), it means that in examples such as *bhopurisā* and *bhopurisa*, the meaning is established through the basis of the nominal stem (*jātipadatthanissayena*) in a sense other than [the original compound], which is to say, by the mere fact of its being a group (*parisamattatthatāya*).
He states the reason for the necessary presence of the long vowel with the words “*yadica ākāro*,” etc.; here, the word division is *yadi ca ākāro*.
60. In [the examples] such as *ghabrahmā*, *ghaitisaññā*, *ghasaññā*, and *tāsaṃ kaññāsaññā*, there is a plural designation because of the multiplicity of those [words] having the phoneme *gha*.
In *gharūpassa*, [it means] "of the form of the word *gha*. Likewise, in *bho brahmā*, by the word *tathā* (thus), [it refers to] the form of the word *brahmā*.
By the very fact that it is demonstrated in the *Nirutti*, it shows its state of being included here. "They explain thus" means they explain in this way:
"Therefore, from the sound *sa* [comes] the vowel *a* and *ā*," and so forth.

For they describe the *ettupasaṇiddesa* (the designation by elision) after forming a *dvanda* compound of *aca, āca, ica, īca, ecā*; and "the general rule" refers to the phrase "by Brahmā as the agent."
"By way of similarity" (*sakhato*) means speaking generally (*sāmaññena*) without such specific distinction. "For what purpose" (*kimatthaṃ*) means that for which there is a purpose or motive;

thus it is "for what purpose. Regarding the general formulation "for what purpose," having kept in mind the consideration of the doubt as to the motive—since it was stated [in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*] that "the group is the arrival"—he says "by way of meaning" (*atthato*), and so forth.
"By way of meaning" (*atthato*) means by way of its significance (*sāmatthiyato*).

By this statement, “the group of those who have come,” the following is intended: by means of this expression “the group of those who have come,” which reveals that the group is primarily characterized by birth (jāti) in that specific form, if there were no purpose for including terms such as *isi*, *sakha*, *muni*, and *bhadanta*—which possess the singular endings *-o* and *-e* when used in the vocative—then it would be otherwise inexplicable;
thus, [the meaning is established] through the power of the definition of "otherwise-inexplicability" (*aññathānupapatti-lakkhaṇa-sāmatthiya*).
He states the purpose for the rule on common application (*sāmaññavidhāna*): by the word "they suffer" (*sōyanti*), he indicates the statement found in the *Vutti*:

“The group [of suffixes] beginning with *ā* is called *gaṇa*. 63. *Ghossaṃ*, *ssaṃ*, *ssā*, *ssāyaṃ*, *añca*, *tiñca*: this is a compound in the fourth case (*catthasamāsa*) formed by mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*) of these six terms; they occur in the forms *ssaṃ*, *ssā*, *ssāyaṃ*, and *tiṃ*.
64. "A *gho* [suffix] ending in *oka*, *gha*, *ghanta*, or *okāra*; there is no *gho* where there is *yesa*;

because of the rule for general application (*sāmaññavidhānato*), due to the non-appropriation of any particular gender, it is prescribed generally; 'not in the singular of *nādi*' means not in the singular of *nādī*."
The meaning [of the first example] is: because there might be such a corrupt intention in someone regarding the cause;
therefore, it is the second example. The meaning [of the second example] is: because it is for the sake of including all [cases], even though it is not intended as such.
Since there would be no inclusion of all the singular forms, he states the manner of composing the suttas with the words “otherwise,” and so forth.

The intended meaning [of the author] regarding the subsequent rules and so forth is as follows: "Because the sutta was composed as ‘*aṃyosvaghona*’, there is the understanding of the word *agha* in its general singular form;
since there is no negation of that [shortening], one might say that the rule ‘*sismiṃ napuṃsake*’ would apply shortening in the case of ‘*daṇḍi kulaṃ*’.
Therefore, the phrase ‘*aghona*’ is a negation of the vowel-ending *o*; it is a substitute for another [suffix]."
Regarding the substitution of *gāvā* for *go* and so forth, as prescribed by the rule beginning with “*gossā gasihinaṃ sugāvagavā*” (2-67),
it is not cited here because [the forms] such as *daṇḍi* and *kula*, which end in the neuter singular, will be discussed later. However, in the feminine dual (*yosu*),

although the rule “*yolopanisudīgho*” (2-88) prescribes lengthening even for what is not already long, this serves as proof that there is no short vowel at all in the first place where a long vowel occurs.
It has not been cited; rather, it becomes *daṇḍī-daṇḍīni*. However, the reading *nossavāti* is seen [in some manuscripts].
Since there is the risk of the fault of the vowel *o* becoming short when followed by the suffix *ge*, the reading should be *nossā*. 67. *Gossā* (of the word *go*).
The forms *gāvena* and *gavena* are identical in the instrumental case; likewise, *gāvassa* and *gavassa* are identical in the genitive case.
69. Because *senā* is heard following *gavaṃ*, the letter *se* is postulated as the cause for the grammatical operation (*vutti*) [of elision].
72. The connection is that "there is some fault because of the substitution of *gāvu* for *saddanta*"; the substitutes (*ādesā*) are those which are to be indicated and must be made.

The term *īpī* is joined with the suffix *paññā*; or, by taking it as a non-distinct [collective] reference, it means "that which cooks" (*pacati*) or "that which drinks" (*pivati*), hence *vāpī*. Regarding the phrase "of another," this refers to the substitution of the vowel *i* for the vowels *u* and *ū*. 77.

Because one observes the use of a collective designation for a part—as in "Devadatta is Datta" in the world—the meaning of the locative case ending *smin* is shown by this [term]. Thus he says, "by this word *smin*," and so forth.
81. Regarding *jhalā* in the rule for *brahmādi* and others: the connection is with the reading "from this [point] onwards, in some cases, there is the suffix *ṭā* as an *anubandha*.

In the phrase "in *brahmādi* and others," it refers to the *brahmādi* group mentioned in the sutta *ghabrahmādite* (2-60). "From the reading" means from the reading of the group-sutta beginning with "from this [point] onwards" (*ito*). "*Ṭā* as an *anubandha*" means...
By this [word], he indicates the substitution of *e* for *eta*.
That whose end is *bhasma* is a compound ending in that; of such a [compound], [the rule] "what is drawn forward does not follow further" applies.
*Viññū-vacanaṃ*: *viduno* and *vidū* are examples of the *kūpa*-suffix; *viññuno* and *viññū* are from "known by one who knows" (*vito ñāto*) according to [Kaccāyana 5.39];
*sabbaññuno* and *sabbaññū* are from "the all-knowing" (*kammā*) according to [Kaccāyana 5.40].
“Because it is established by the word *lopotī* itself in the *voma*-group” means that because it is established by the very word *lopotī* in the *voma*-group [of the *Kaccāyana-vutti*].
87. In “*nano amuyā*,” there is the substitution of *yā* for the feminine; this is a counter-example (*paccudāharaṇa*) for the word *nanoti*.

88. Regarding the first and second *yol* [sandhis], the examples for them occurring together are "aṭṭhī aṭṭhīni"; these are shown specifically by way of the elision (*yol*) and contraction (*panil*), and other cases are to be understood in the same manner. 92.
Of that... [ntassa]

"Ṭamuttapakkho" means "the alternative where there is no substitution of Ṭ for *nt*," referring to one who performs what is non-existent (*asantaṃ*). Because [the form] "ntussa ceva" is well-established, it is compared to the alternative where there is no substitution of Ṭ; this follows from the rule "sañjātaṃ tārakāditvito" (5-45). 93.
Why is it said that "the substitution of Ṭ applies to *yo*"? Is it not the case that when the entire compound ending in that [suffix] is reached, the rule "chaṭṭhiyantassā" (6-108) should apply?

(1-17) [Objection: “It is internal (*antasseva*)”; if this were so, there would be no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*). Therefore, why was it stated, ‘why does it undergo over-extension (*kasmā atippasajjati*)’? [Response: True.

Nevertheless, since it could have been said ‘it will elide (*jhissā*)’, it was stated as ‘*issā*’ because it is capable [of that function]. By virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmatthiyato*), the substitution of *ṭā* occurs for the final *i*;
thus it was stated as ‘it undergoes over-extension (*tippasajjati*)’. [Objection: But even if ‘*jhissā*’ had been stated, would there not still be that same over-extension?
"It remains in that very state" is true; nevertheless, if the substitution of *ṭā* for the whole [suffix] were intended, then since that would be the case, one might ask:
"What is the purpose of including the mention of *jhā*? One could simply say 'in the sense of *issā*. Thus, there is no over-extension.

However, this [objection] is appropriate only if one does not wish to state it as a qualification that, upon the mention of *jhā*, the vowel *i* at the end of the name [of the suffix] alone receives the designation *jhā*.
94. *Vevo sahacaritañāyassā* means: according to the principle that "those things associated with it are included by the mention of that [principal thing].

Regarding the words *hetu* and *kuru*: when the substitution of *ṭā* [for the feminine suffix] is reached by this [rule], and the elision [of the feminine suffix] is also reached by the rule "there is elision" (*lopo*), then—since the elision of the suffix is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on a grammatical condition (*paccaya-nissita*), while the substitution of *ṭā* is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on the base word (*pakati-nissita*)—and since among internal and external operations "the internal operation prevails," the elision does not occur first because its cause is absent once the substitution of *ṭā* has taken place.
To demonstrate this, he says: "By the words *hetu* and *kuru*," and so forth.
99. One might ask: "Are not all words such as *katara* and so forth the referents of the word *sabba* and its synonyms when expressed by a compound, rather than the word *sabba* itself?
To this he replies with the words "by way of a part" (*avayavena*), etc. Even if [the analysis] were "those for which *sabba* is the beginning," it is by way of a part...
There is a dispute; nevertheless, the meaning here is that of a collective whole... [the sense being] "those by whom there is a grasping of this collective whole.
The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). [The question is: "Which one among you two or many is Devadatta?

or, regarding meanings such as Kaṭha and others, when there is a selection (*niddhāraṇa*) of one from two or many, in what kind of selection? [It occurs] in the selection of the best (*ratara*) or the very best (*ratama*), according to the application of the suffix *ṇādi*.

Regarding the phrase “ekatthatāya” (in the sense of having the same referent): after the elision of the case ending, the form of the word *kiṃ* is established by the elision of the final vowel and following consonant according to the rule “rānubandhentasarādissā” (4-132). To demonstrate this, he says “katamā” and so forth.

In the sense of “one who has both shoulders,” the form is established by the application of the suffix *aya* according to the rule “ayubhadvitīhaṃse” (4-49), followed by the elision of the vowel according to the rule “saro lopo sare” (1-26); thus he says “ubho aṃsā” and so forth.
He says, “The body is called ‘definition’ (vavatthā),” and with the words beginning with “having a denotation” (sābhidheyyā), he clarifies its meaning through terms such as “limit” (avadhi).

Non-destruction, non-deviation, and remaining fixed within the state of being a limit—this is what is meant by “having a denotation” (sābhidheyyā) in the phrase “one looks at that which has a denotation.

Here, “that which has a denotation” is understood as one’s own denotable object, such as the directions and so forth; thus he says, “of the east and so on,” etc. The term “having a denotation” is used here in the sense of the accusative case.
Regarding the word *parā*, [it is derived] from the root *īkṣ* meaning "to see," with the suffix *aṇ* applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.28 (*kvaciṇa*). This suffix depends on the expressed object;

thus, in order to show that it is indeed a restrictive rule (*avadhiniyama*), he says: "it looks toward that" (*tam apekkhati*), and so forth. He explains the intended meaning therein with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
And here, the meaning expressed by the word *parā*—namely, direction such as the east—is [the object] of the meaning expressed by the word *pubba* (east), which is direction.

The intention here is this: either a direction such as "east" functions by way of restriction through its status as a limit (*avadhi*), or that very status as a limit which functions by way of restriction depends, when functioning as a restriction, upon a direction such as "east" expressed by words like "pubba" (east).

Thus, it is said that the restriction of the limit is defined as being "dependent on the denoted object" (*sābhidheyyāpekkha*) because it depends on the direction expressed by the word; however, it is not [defined] merely by the denoted object itself.

Showing that [the occurrence] is impossible, he says "yo hi" and so forth. "By means of skillfulness as the cause" means by means of the skillfulness that is the cause for the application of the word *kusala*.
"Uttarakurus" refers to the inhabitants of the continent of Uttarakuru, or the region itself. He asks:

since the application of the *sabbādi* rule is already prohibited in the case of a technical name (*saññā*) by this very rule, "And no other [term] except when it is the primary [meaning]" (2-136), what is the purpose of stating "not in the case of a non-name" (*asaññāyam*)? To this he replies:

‘Not another,’ and so forth: with reference to something such as priority and so on, a designation that conforms to the meaning—such as being prior or subsequent—is an “anvatthasaññā” (a designation according to its meaning).
Regarding the phrase “vānekaññatthe” (3-17), it shows the absence of impropriety because [the rule] follows an alternative option (*vikappa*); that is, it shows that "this is not improper.
Furthermore, since its propriety is demonstrated by showing an exception (*byabhicāra*) in the recitation (*pāṭha*), he says “napuṃsake,” etc., to state this.

For the composition of the sutta follows the recitation; thus, while this very statement is non-neuter (*ananapuṃsaka*) due to following an alternative option, there is an exception to it in certain instances.
To state that [the sutta] is an indicator (*ñāpaka*), he says: "And of that," and so forth. One must necessarily grasp the meaning here in this way;

otherwise, if the meaning were taken according to the sequence of the text as it stands, because each individual sutta would be understood as primary (*mukhya*), how could it be an indicator of another?
For if it were primary, the sense of being an indicator would not be tenable.

108. Now, one might suspect that by the maxim "among those stated as characteristics and as paths, only that which is stated as a path is to be taken," the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (in *lakkhaṇika*) would not be applicable;
therefore, he states the proof beginning with "in the case of the short *ā*," etc., and the meaning of this maxim is as follows:
“By means of this it is characterized, thus it is a *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic). Because it causes one to know what is correct and what is incorrect, the *sutta* is called a treatise (*sattha*).
A word that has returned [to its root] is a *paṭipada*; the meaning is ‘the straight path.

Both the characteristic and the path are the *lakkhaṇapaṭipadāni*. Forms expressed by those are *lakkhaṇapaṭipadavuttāni*. In these [compounds], the word *vutta* is understood with each individual member: ‘in those expressed as characteristics...’”
Regarding the phrase "stated by way of a characteristic" (*lakkhaṇavutta*):

therein, that which is not indicated directly (*añjasā*)—but rather, through the demonstration of a characteristic, it is established by means of that characteristic that "when this characteristic exists, it must exist in this form"—is called "stated by way of a characteristic.
However, that which is established by the word itself directly is called "stated by way of a method" (*paṭipadavutta*). In that case, regarding what is stated by way of a characteristic...

"When there is a form occurring both as a grammatical rule (*paṭipadavutta*) and [as a general characteristic], only that which occurs as a grammatical rule is to be taken, not the other"—by this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), "only that which occurs as a grammatical rule," it is understood that this is a restrictive maxim (*paribhāsā*).
And that restriction stands firm only when there exists a doubt preceded by the absence of such a restriction;
therefore, where there is only that which occurs as a characteristic (*lakkhaṇavutta*) and not that which occurs as a grammatical rule, this maxim does not apply.
Even where there is only a statement of the grammatical procedure (*paṭipadā*) and not a statement of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), that too is not within its scope;
for it is a matter of established logic that this maxim (*paribhāsā*) reiterates only that which occurs where two forms are possible, by way of removing doubt.
Thus, in cases of doubt, even if a single form is thus both non-different and different—
Nevertheless, matter described by way of its characteristics (lakkhaṇa) is inferential when its characteristics are being deduced—just as fire is inferred from smoke or water from a crane;

however, matter described by way of its mode of presentation (paṭipadā) is established through direct perception (paccakkha). And between direct perception and inference, direct perception is the stronger means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
therefore, only that which is described by way of its mode of presentation is accepted here.
110. In the neuter gender, there should not be [the substitution] of the vowel *e*; this is the connection [of the rule].
114. Elision (*lopa*).
He states the reason for the status of *akāra* as *antaraṅga* with the words ‘because it depends on the base’ (*pakatinissitattā*);

here, *pākataṃ* means this is evident from the base, namely the [substitution] *ṇo* (by rule 4-34). He states the reason for the status of the elision (*lopa*) as *bahiraṅga* with the words ‘because it depends on the suffix’ (*paccayanissitattā*).
By the phrase ‘among the *antaraṅga* and *bahiraṅga* [rules], the *antaraṅga* rule is stronger,’ he indicates the *paribhāṣā* [sūtra]. The word *aṅga* denotes a constituent part (*vayava*).

The word *ante* is used in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*). *Aṅge bhavaṃ antaraṅgaṃ* (“that which exists within a constituent element is *antaraṅga*”) is a compound formed with a numeral (*saṅkhyasamāsa*) according to the rule “*eonama vaṇṇe*” (1.3.37), and it takes the suffix *atta*.

*Aṅgato bahi bahiraṅgaṃ* (“that which is outside a constituent element is *bahiraṅga*”) is a compound not formed with a numeral (*asaṅkhyasamāsa*) according to the rule “*paryapābahitiro purepacchā vā pañcamyā*” (3.5.2).
In this context, however, *antaraṅga* and *bahiraṅga* do not mean “that which exists within a constituent element” and “that which is outside a constituent element.”
Furthermore, an operation dependent on what is internal (*antaraṅga*) is itself internal; nor is a composite whole that stands outside its constituent parts external (*bahiraṅga*).
Rather, an operation dependent on what is external is external—just as when people sitting on beds make a noise, it is said, "the beds are making a noise.
It is for this very reason that even in a numeral compound (*saṅkhyā-samāsa*), there occurs a connection with a different gender, case-ending, or number.
Regarding the expression “internal, internal”: this *asaṅkhyasamāsa* is indeed conventional (*saṅketika*), for it does not have the meaning of the prior member as its primary referent.

Just as, for the purpose of making known that direct perception (*paccakkha*) depends upon the sense faculties (*akkha*), the distributive compound (*vicchā*) “it functions by means of each sense faculty” (*akkhamakkhaṃ pati vattate*) is formed—even though an *asaṅkhyasamāsa* has been made—this *asaṅkhyasamāsa* is formed by way of convention in order to indicate that knowledge of direct perception depends upon the sense faculties.
It is not the case that the primary meaning of the prior member [of the compound] is dominant;

rather, the connection of gender, case-ending, and number—such as in "paccakkho paccakkhā"—is established by convention for the purpose of making known that this [compound] depends on the whole (samudāya) just as it depends on its internal members.

Thus, the connection of gender, case-ending, and number is not contradicted in this "innumerable" (asaṅkhyasamāsa) compound. Alternatively, it means that this grammatical operation (kāriya) has an internal member as its object.

Regarding "being characterized by faith, etc. (4-84), [the text] speaks of the external (*bahiraṅga*) as well as the internal (*antaraṅga*), and both the external and the internal—namely, the internal and the external.
Among these, the internal is stronger. To establish the strength of an internal grammatical operation (*kāriya*), it was stated that "[it must be applied] first of all," and so forth;
however, this is not the reason for establishing the strength of an internal operation, because it is internal.
Indeed, the state of being stronger (*balavabhāva*) alone is the very first cause for subordination (*vidheyyatta*); thus it has been said:
"He who states that the elision of the vowel *a* occurs first because of the inherent strength (*antaraṅgattā*) of the vowel *a*"—therefore, that reading is not tenable.

However, since the proof of the state of being stronger through its inherent nature is desired based on common usage (*lokato*), this very reading is appropriate in this context: "It is precisely the inherent (*antaraṅga*) [rule] [that prevails]."
"The internal [cause] is powerful in the world because it is seen as such; for the world sees it thus," and so forth.
"Because it is seen as such in the world" means that the state of the internal cause being powerful is seen in the world according to the method about to be explained.
Alternatively, even if it is sometimes impossible to act due to the occurrence of some adverse condition or due to the incapacity of the causal factor, the internal cause must necessarily be obeyed.

To demonstrate this, he said: “Because it is to be applied first. Regarding “when there is the possibility of the operation”: when there is the possibility of the grammatical operation because the cause (the *nimitta*) has not been destroyed.
116. Regarding “because it is stated as ‘ye’ for the vowel *i*”: because in the rule “*ye* for the vowel *i* and *passi*,” it is stated as “for the vowel *i*.”

118. Regarding the term *asaṃ*: because they are devoid of grammatical case (*vibhatti*), the ancient masters have designated indeclinables (*abyaya*), possessives (*vantu*), participles (*upasagga*), and particles (*nipāta*) as such, even when there is a difference in gender and number.

Since they lack number, he says "those which have no other number," beginning with "in singularity" (*ekatthe*) and so forth; for it is stated that [they apply] "to the singular and plural" (*ekānekesu*), thus referring to specific numbers.

With the intention of asking how [grammatical operations] such as *syādi* (the suffixes *si*, etc. being prescribed can possibly arise when there are innumerable [words], he says: “How is the occurrence of *syādi* possible with innumerable [words]?
Then, thinking that if there were no innumerability, the occurrence of *syādi* would necessarily follow—as in the case of “uccaṃ rukkho” (tall tree) and so on—where number is present—he says:
“But when number is present,” and so forth. This is the intended meaning of the *Vutti* text.
He explains this with the words beginning "otherwise," etc. [The question is: what is the purpose for their arising, such that their arising is not inferred from the [other] numbers?

To address this doubt, he says "and when that exists," etc. For if the arising of *syādi* (the verbal suffixes) did not exist, there would be no basis for the numbers of *ucca* and so forth being assigned to the words;
thus, in the case of the words beginning with *yo*, the word-signs such as *vo* and *no* would follow the words *tumha* and *amha* along with their case-endings.
The sense is this: if there were no *kāriya* (grammatical operation), applications such as “uccaṃ vo” and “uccaṃ no” would not be established;

however, when there is the occurrence of *syā*, even in cases of elision (*lutta*), because the status of a word (*padatta*) is accomplished through the very production of that [form], and since the status of a word is thus established, the grammatical operation characterized by being a word is indeed accomplished.
Others here state that when there is a desire for the expression “tassaṃ sālāyaṃ,” it becomes “tatra sālāyaṃ.”

Regarding the phrase *yathā siyā*: according to the rule *abyayatvā syādino* (Pāṇini 2.4.82), the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *āp* is prescribed after an indeclinable (*abyaya*) even when it follows the feminine suffix *si*.
Therefore, he says "by the asaṅkhyas," etc.; the meaning is that this is incorrect, for the prescription of the elision of the suffix *āp* is improper.
Now, by what rule is the suffix *āp* here prescribed, such that its elision is also taught [by the rule] *itthiyamatvā* (Pāṇini 4.1.26)?
This [suffix] *āp* has no purpose here, because the suffix *āp* is prescribed for the feminine gender, and because numbers (*saṅkhyā*) lack gender.
Therefore, since the suffix *āp* cannot possibly occur after non-numerical [bases], the statement regarding its elision is purposeless;

thus, in the rule "in the feminine" (3-26), the description is primarily focused on the possessor of the quality (*guṇī*), and the suffixes *āp* and so forth are prescribed for that which possesses femininity. In that [feminine base]...
Regarding the word *sālāya* (in that sense of the base), the term *tatra* occurs as an indefinite number (*asaṅkhyā*) within this state of being (*itthattavati*).

Therefore, some might think that since there is the suffix *āp* after this [base], the elision of the suffix *āp* must necessarily be prescribed; to address such a person, he says "even if," and so forth.
This collective indefinite number (*asaṅkhyasamudāya*), occurring in the context of accepting the expression of a specific distinction, is the "designation" (*aniddesa*).

Since both [the terms] are understood as "occurs," he said, "for the suffixes such as *āp* occur when there is femininity (*itthattavati*)," in order to establish that in the definition [of the term], the quality (*guṇa*) is predominant.
In this context, because this number occurs in the hall (*sālā*), he said, "and when there is femininity.
The connection is that this also does not occur in the form of a derivative (*apasiddhi*). If this also were to occur in the form of a derivative...

From where, indeed, does this determination of "thisness" (itthattāvasāya) arise? He says: “‘Determination of thisness,’ etc. Now, having brought forward the words of Jinendrabuddhi, he speaks in order to demonstrate their logical consistency:
“‘Even though,’ etc. Even though there are the words of Jinendrabuddhi, such as “even though,” etc., the connection is as follows:
“of that” refers to “thisness” (itthatta), and the meaning of the word is that “thisness might be”; thus, “even though [he] says” is the construction, because the sense is already understood.
The phrase “the application of the word *iti*” means that the statement of that proponent, Buddhindo, is “inappropriate” (*ayutta*); the sense is that his speech is illogical.

From where [does he say this]? From the passage beginning with “For if,” and so forth. The meaning is: if the status of being a woman (*itthatta*) were the meaning of the sentence, and if it were the exclusion of the feminine suffix, then in cases such as “in the hall” (*sālāyaṃ*), the cognition of being a woman would have to occur there, because of the dependence on other words like *iti*.
The sense is that it is not understood in that way. To clarify this very point, he says “tathā hi” and so forth.

“Aviddasū ayanti” is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the singular number used here in both instances—“avidvasu” and “ayanti”—the meaning is that the unity [of the referent] is understood independently of any other word;
there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word “sālā” (hall) and others, which functions in the feminine gender.
In this context, showing that it cannot be said that the suffix *āp* arises merely by virtue of the word *tatra*, he says: ‘Even because of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatta*), etc.

The phrase ‘even because of having a common substratum’ means even the state of being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as *sālā* when used in the feminine; the connection is that [this] is not a cause for the suffix *āp* and so forth.
The word *eva* follows [from the previous context]. That collection of bases and so forth which has a single meaning is "ekattha" (of one meaning).

Regarding that word *ekattha*, he states its basis for application (*pavatti-nimitta*)—namely, the rule for the suffix *ī* and so forth—as "the state of having a single meaning (*ekatthatā*) is the rule for the suffix *ī* and so forth. "In the occurrence of *ī* and so forth" means "occurrence" (*vutti*) is the act of occurring;

thus, it means "when there is the occurrence of *ī* and so forth," i.e., when there is the rule for *ī* and so forth. "From the compound" means "from the state of being a compound. "By that very [reason]"...
“By the very sutta ‘dissantaññepi paccayā’ (4-120). 120.
And when there is the employment of the prefix *adhi* here, since the meaning of the case-ending is already expressed by that [prefix] alone, the seventh case is not employed.”

When there is the locative case (*sattamī*), the prefix *adhi* is not present; therefore, the analysis must be shown by the word itself as "the discourse proceeded among women" (*itthīsu kathā pavattā*).
He states the reason for the occurrence of the locative case after the word "women" (*itthi*) as "because of its having the same referent" (*taṃsamānādhikaraṇattā*);
the meaning is that it has the same sense as that prefix *adhi*.

121. "And this *am*-substitution is not [applicable] from here on; it is only for the *ā*-substitution" means it is only for the *am*-substitution. "Except in the fifth case" means excluding the fifth case.
Since this *am*-substitution is prescribed elsewhere, and because the fifth case is prohibited, the prohibition of the fifth case implies that this [substitution] itself is also prohibited.

He says, "It is called [the negation] of the substitute itself," meaning that this negation applies to the substitution, while the negation of elision—which was stated by the preceding rule "nāto"—does not apply here;

this is the connection. Now, one might ask: how is this connected specifically with the substitute for the fifth case-ending (pañcamī) and not with the negation of elision? To address this, he states the paribhāṣā: "A rule or a negation applies to what is immediately preceding. In this context:
Although the word *antara* has multiple meanings, here it does not signify "interval" (*antarāla*). [In the term] *anantara*, there is no interval—that is, no middle—between [the two].

There is no purpose in negating a mere interval; therefore, because there is neither a prescription nor a negation regarding what lies within an interval, the term *anantara* is used figuratively, just as in expressions such as "villages that are non-adjacent" (*anantarā gāmā*).
However, in its primary sense (*diṭṭhatte*), there exists no interval for that which is in the middle. Thus they say: "there is no interval for me."

In the *Viggahe-sutta*, because both the immediately preceding [element] and the immediately following [element] are seen, even though there are two, one is called "immediately preceding" (*anantara*).
For that very reason, the singular form "of the immediately preceding" (*anantarassa*) is used in the *Paribhāsā*. The word "iti" has the sense of "this"; thus, the meaning is:

"by this *paribhāsā*, it is connected by means of substitution. "By that" (*tena*) means by way of the aforementioned *paribhāsā*; the meaning of "by that" (*tena*) is: "for the reason that it is connected by means of substitution."
"Alopa" means the prohibition of elision (*lopa*); since [the elision] is obtained through the force of the context, two sentences are required for the prescription of the two meanings.

Among them, "not from this" (*nāto*) is one sentence that prescribes the prohibition, and "except in the fifth case" (*amapañcamiyā*) is the second, which pertains to the substitution of *am*. Therein, it connects specifically with the phrase "except in the fifth case" (*apañcamiyā*);
it does not connect with the previously stated prescription by way of the prohibition of elision. Such being the case, this expression "except in the fifth case" (*amapañcamiyā*)—
If a sentence does not rely on a specific meaning because it is otherwise untenable without it, then what [meaning] is obtained by the force of that [context]?
This is the sense. "The elision (*alopa*) indicates" is the connection; the explanation is made by splitting the sentence, not as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).
The distinction is that if it were a single syntactical unit, there would be a prohibition of the ablative case for both operations. [Thus, one must] avoid the ablative.
The connection is: "those two operations are to be understood as established," even though [they] are already accomplished. By the rule "yena nāprāpte...
(Pāṇini 1.4.2), one observes the maxim that "an operation which is enjoined when something else has not yet applied serves to sublate that [other].
For what purpose is this maxim recited here in this treatise? Therein, the restriction is that exceptions sublate general rules. In that regard:

Exclusions (*cussagga*) are of two kinds: those whose application is certain and those whose application is uncertain. Those which enter even the scope of every exception are called "those whose application is certain";
those which penetrate the scope of an exception only in some instances are called "those whose application is uncertain.
Among these two types of exclusions, it is only the obstruction of those whose application is certain that is intended [to be avoided], not...
For those who hold that [the rule] is fixed, this censure is recited for the purpose of demonstrating that very point.
The word *yena* is an indication of the general rule (*ussagga*), while *na* is a particle expressing negation. The phrase *appatte asamphuṭṭhe visaye* is to be supplied;
the meaning is: "by which general rule [it applies] not when the object is unattained, but only when it is attained, and only when it is touched."... "Two negations lead back to the original sense."
"Having made [the rule], it is enjoined"—this means that both a prohibition and an injunction are commenced;

"is commenced," "is enjoined," and "is recited" are its meanings. By this, he demonstrates the injunction as an exception (*apavāda*). Regarding the phrase "of that": by means of what has been pointed out as the general rule (*ussagga*), there occurs an annulment by the exception;

however, the meaning is that there is no annulment of that which is commenced in a domain where [the general rule] does not apply. If one asks why? It is because there is no opportunity (*anavakāsatā*).
For if, by way of a general rule (*ussagga*), the entire domain were grasped, what other domain would remain for the exception (*apavāda*)?
Therefore, it should be understood that because there is no room [for the exception], there can be no sublation of the general rule by the exception;

since some portion of the domain of the exception regarding deities might not have been reached by the general rule, but not the whole, the disciples are said to be sublated with respect to that [portion].

In the expression *pañcapūlimānaya* (“bring five bundles”), there is a descriptive compound (*visesanasa-māsa*) meaning “the collection of five bundles,” according to the rule *nadāditovī* (Pāṇini 2.4.7).

Since a collection (*samāhāra*) is a bringing together (*samāharana*), and because a collection is also of the nature of an abstract state (*bhāva*), he says: “even though it is predominant as a state (*bhāvappadhānattepi*).
The bundles, being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), are the substances.

125. Regarding the statement "these [words] are not feminine" (*anitthī*) in this sutta, what is the purpose of the prohibitive expression? Having considered that this very [sutta] provides a description by means of the non-feminine gender (*anitthiliṅga*), he says:
"In the mention of a name," and so forth; namely, "in the mention of a name, there is the inclusion of even that which is distinguished by gender."
In this commentary, "distinguished by gender" (*liṅgavisiṭṭha*) refers to a name that is distinguished from what is indicated in the Sutta by its gender through some other [attribute].
Where there is reliance on the commonality of the word-form, when the term "name" (*nāma*) is used, there is the inclusion of even that which is distinguished by gender...
the intention is that within the general category, all specific instances are included; thus, "this very [term]" means "not feminine."

The meaning is this: the very word "prohibition" (*paṭisedha*) is the indicator (*ñāpaka*). Since there was previously a prohibition [of the feminine], that [prohibition] might have been applied even when there is a feminine *patti*, as in "not-feminine" (*anitthiya*);
therefore, the statement of the prohibition "not-feminine" indicates this maxim (*paribhāsa*).
By this, he shows that this maxim is established through its own inherent power (*sāmatthiya*).
127. "Of one who is not a neuter" (*anapuṃsakassa*) means "by way of exclusion" (*pariyudāsa*); here, the word *nañ* has the sense of exclusion. 129.
Of a man (*massa*).
By the words *taṃ neti* and so forth, it is indicated that in some instances the substitution is irregular (*anica*). 130.

Let there be the substitution of *s* for *ta* when [the condition] other than *ke* is present; however, in the case of the locative singular (*simhi*), the substitution of *s* for *m* was already effected previously by the suffix *kappaccaya*.
When that condition exists, one might wonder: "Why [is it said] 'by what'?"—fearing that this might be a general rule for the substitution of *sā*.
To demonstrate the fruit of this sutta’s general application, he says: "'By what, because of having the same referent,' etc. Regarding "'by what, because of having the same referent'":

this refers to the occurrence of *ṇa* and so forth together with the *ka* suffix; and regarding "'of the prior part'": because the prior portion (*asubhāga*) lacks the status of being a word (*pada*), [it is said] "'because of having the same referent'" (2-119).

Because of the disappearance of the case-ending that establishes the status of being a word (*padatta*), there is an absence of word-status; thus, it is "dependent on the conditioning factors of words" (*padasaṅkhāranibandhana*), meaning it has the accomplishment of words as its cause.

This is the meaning of the principle: "In the absence of the sign, that which is indicated by the sign (*nemittika*) is also absent. Here, "sign" (*nimitta*), "cause" (*kāraṇa*), and "reason" (*hetu*) are not different in meaning.

The "absence of the sign" (*nimittābhāva*) is the non-existence of the sign; in that absence of the sign, the meaning is "upon the destruction of the cause. [The suffix] *-ta* is derived from the sign (*nimitta*).
"Phenomena that have become results are 'caused by signs' (nemittika), or the existence [of a result] within a sign is 'caused by a sign.

In the absence of the sign, there is also the absence of the result caused by it, which proceeds from that cause. For instance, the shadow caused by the sign of an umbrella ceases when the umbrella is removed;
the perception caused by the sign of a lamp does not shine when the lamp is gone; so too here, for those things that proceed from a sign...
In the absence of a cause, non-existence itself appears logical; thus one conceives [it], and being attached elsewhere, one [thinks] "elsewhere.
131. Therefore, for the sake of dropping the letter *t* from these [words], it is stated as “*tatassā*.”

132. Regarding this [rule], in the case of *atyi* and so forth, although it is possible to include the forms beginning with *ssāya*— since the forms beginning with *i* are included by the rule "ssaṃ ssā ssāye" (2-52),

and because of the paribhāṣā "the substitutes for *ta* behave like *ta* itself," which leads to the inclusion of the substitutes for *sā* and so on— why is there no inclusion of *ssāya* and the others, and why is the sutta made more cumbersome?
Fearing that [the rule] might be over-extensive, he says "nanu ce" and so forth in order to show that the *vutti* text has been stated:

"Is it not the case that... and so on. The [suffixes] beginning with *ṭas* and *smā* should be stated as "ṭasasmāsminnannāsvimassa ca"; for the purpose of including the rules for *nam* and so forth, and for the purpose of excluding the rules for *na* and so forth, [it is said] "tassā" [in the manuscript].
*Desina-ādeso* means a substitute for that; *taggahaṇaṃ* means the inclusion of that [substitute] which is the substitute for it; by that [means].
134. *Dutiya*:
