"In another way" (*aññathā*) means when there is a description by another light mode rather than a description as heavy; because it is described with a single case-ending, [the rule] "of the second case, *ssā*" (*dutiyāyossā*) applies.
It should be understood that by this phrase ending with "nekadeso" (not a part), namely "aññathā" and so forth,

the intended meaning of the paribhāsa rule "na tvekavibhattiyuttānam" (but not for those joined in a single case-ending) is revealed; however, by the statement "etadevānuvattati" (only this [word] recurs),
it is shown that while "a part of those stated in a single compound recurs," a part of those joined in a single case-ending does not recur.
This is an explanatory exposition (*yojanā*); "it makes known" means it makes known by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmatthiya*), as in the previous case.
139. *Nāññaṃ*:

Since there is a negation of that which is not primary, there ought to be an application of the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) to [the group] beginning with *sabba*; otherwise, in the inclusion of the group beginning with *sabba*, [the rule would not apply].
What occasion is there for [the application of] *piyasabbādīnaṃ*, since it is the negation of the subordinate [element] that is performed?
To show that by means of this, forms such as *paramasabbe* arise, he says: ‘The negation of the subordinate,’ and so forth.
140. Third.

"Yattha" means "in which," whether referring to the agent (*kattar*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the agent, he states the establishment of the third case in the phrase beginning with "karoti.

When the verbal root *kar* (to do) is understood from the word "karoti," there should be the reading "māsena katā" (done by the month). This is because it must be stated as "of the previous [actions] done by the month" (*māsena katānaṃ pubbānaṃ*).

In the sense of "prior existence" (*pubbabhāve*), the month functions as the instrument (*karaṇattaṃ*); however, in this context, it is by means of the month acting as the instrument (*karaṇabhūtena*).
The meaning is "those who existed previously"; for that very reason, the reading here should also be *bhavantī*.

141. Regarding *cattha*, the meaning of *ca* is *cattha*; in the phrase *soyeva*, there is a reference to the compound (*samāsa*). The reading should be: "The meaning *cattha* occurs here, but *sabbādi* is not within the scope of the *cattha*-compound."

144. Regarding the statement "What is the purpose of the frequent mention of *manā* as 'absence of growth' (*avuddhibhāvo*) or 'absence of arising' (*otthābhāvo*) [in the Pañcikā]?"—for that very reason, the reading "and the non-growth of Sumedha and others" was made in the list of word-groups (*gaṇapāṭho*).
He says that by the word *hema*, things made of gold are understood without distinction.

Regarding the phrase “made of gold”: by the word *kappana*, head-ornament nets are understood; those very things are called “garments” (*vāsasāni*) or “cloths” (*paṭā*) because of their similarity to them.

The connection is that even in its own primary sense, it occurs according to the tradition. The construction is that [the words] do not apply to the objects denoted as arrows and so forth, nor to the mind and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “in arrows and so forth,” this refers to the meanings of the word *bāṇa* such as arrows and the like; for the word *aha* cannot have the function of denoting the mind and so forth.

The word *aha* should not be understood as belonging to the class beginning with *manas*; and because the vowel *i* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) and is not a consonant (*asabba*), the word *rahas* also should not be understood as belonging to the class beginning with *manas*.
Thus, the elision (*sajjhāhāra*) and the connection (*sambandha*) should be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the substitution of *i* for *smin* in the case of the word *rahas*, as prescribed in the *Kaccāyana*, and regarding the replacement of the vowel *i*, he stated "in secret" (*rahasi*) and so forth in order to demonstrate that the word *rahati* is an indeclinable by its very nature.

Regarding the phrase *rahosaddeti*, it should be understood here that the reading is *raha-saddo*. By "by that" (*tena*) is meant: because there is no possibility of applying the *man-ādi* [substitution] to the word *raha*, it is therefore a particle (*nipāto*), namely *rahasi*;
[this applies] in cases such as *iha-man-ādi*. 146.
*Bhava* (existence).

When others perceive it as a particle (*nipāta*), [the question] "Whence indeed, O Sir? (*kuto nu iccādo bho*) ends in the plural; such being the case, the expression “*tayojanā*” (of those three) is appropriate. And since that [plural ending] establishes its status as a particle, he says “in the sense of plurality,” etc., in order to show that it is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*). 148. “The seventh case ending occurs” is the remainder [of the rule].
But surely, when “ending in *nta*” (*ntassa*) is stated, one understands that the suffix *nta* itself is intended, not the rule for designating what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*).
Since it is not determined that [the suffix] is only the *nta* affix, there must be a reading stating "also by way of the *tadanta* rule";
thus he says, "only for the *nta* affix," and so forth. "Because it has been heard" means because it has been grasped by auditory consciousness; what is meant is "because it is directly perceived.

Regarding the inferred [suffix], the meaning is: "of that which is known through inferential cognition—which consists in the demonstration of the sense designated as *tadanta*—by virtue of the grammatical gender [in the rule] ‘vidhibbesanantassa’ (1-26)."
154. “The king is firm; the bow is of strong material.
When suffixes such as *ima* are mentioned, [the word] ending in *-ta* is included by the paribhāṣā rule regarding the mention of suffixes. Thus he says: “By this, etc.”

162. By the rule beginning with "Ltu-paccaya-iccādi," it demonstrates the principle that "in the apprehension of a grammatical condition (paccaya), there is the inclusion of that which begins with what [the suffix] is prescribed for, as well as that which ends with it.
In this context, by the principle that "a condition does not exist without that for which it was prescribed," the very same meaning [as previously stated] is established.
It is explained that, because it is prescribed in the section on the apprehension of suffixes (*paccaya*), there is the apprehension of that which begins with it;

and it is explained that, by the rule "the prescription applies to what follows a specific term," there is the apprehension of that which ends with it. That which has such a specific beginning or end is a specific aggregate (*samudāya*):

that aggregate which has the suffix as its beginning is "that-beginning" (*tadādi*), and that aggregate which has the suffix at its end is "that-ending" (*tadanta*). Of such a specific aggregate, whether beginning or ending with it...
The meaning is that it is not merely the suffix *tu* itself that is included, but rather that the inclusion of the suffix ending in *tu* is appropriate here;

to demonstrate this, he says: "By the rule *kattari ltuṇakā* [Pāṇini 3.4.69], etc. However, the result of including the entire aggregate beginning with and ending in *tu* should be seen in examples such as *byajigisī*;
and he himself will explain that in the rule *tuṃsmā lopocicchāyaṃ te* [Kaccāyana 5.4].

165. Sālo Kaccāyana states in the rule "sakamandhātādīnañce" (2-3-44). He says that this [rule] was cited in the Vutti in order to show that even that [word] ends in -l, thereby establishing the desired form;
thus he says "sakamandhātu," etc., [meaning] that there exists a word *mandhātu* ending in -l.
The word *sakamandhātu* is also a term ending in *-tv-*, so it should be understood as a compound word (*sajjhāhāra*) connected with the preceding term. Therefore,

by saying “also,” he means not only from the perspective of the agent (*kattū*), but having established that the word *mandhātu* ends in *-tv-*, he says “of all” (*sabbesaṃ*) and so forth in order to introduce the word *sakamandhātu*.
169. Although the word *saṅkhya* (number) refers to the act of counting, it nevertheless refers here to the objects to be counted by means of that counting; thus he says, "by fourteen numbers.

There should be the reading *cuddasahi saṅkhāhi*; for the numbers five and so forth are precisely what is expressed by the word *cuddasa* (fourteen), since the word *saṅkhya* is not included [in the compound] here.
175. From *divā* and *divasato*, when [the word] *smin* follows, there is the elision of the preceding *sa* and *ra*, resulting in *divi*. 181.
Of the *yo* [sounds].
"By the inclusion of the accusative case" means by the inclusion of the accusative in the formulation of the rule as *dutiyāyossa ne vā*.
185. "Because the substitution of *en* is impossible in the [ablative] *nā*" means that because *nā* is a substitute for *smā*.

187. Regarding the phrase *gassaṃ ubhayavikappo*: this refers to the formulation of two sides—the compound and the non-compound—intended to reveal the error of the author of the *Kaccāyanavutti*. He says, “In the *Kaccāyana*,” and so forth.

As for the expression “the collective of feminine, masculine, and neuter,” the sequence of its grammatical derivation (*sādhanakkamo*) among those who follow this [work] is as follows: “In compounds formed with *dvanda* and the genitive case, there is the collective of feminine, masculine, and neuter.”

In the case of the word *ṭhita*, by the rule "optionally in a compound" (*samāse ca vibhāsā*, 2-2-35), there is the substitution of *am* for the masculine ending; then, by the rule "a guttural may optionally [replace] a guttural at the end of a group" (*vaggantaṃ vā vagge*, 1-42), the *niggahīta* is replaced by a guttural.
Regarding the phrase *kammādittā enassāpi abhāvapakkhehi*: it is stated as *nāsse no* (Pāṇini 2.4.32) because, starting from the word *kamma*, the substitution of *en* for *assa* is not applied.

197. *Ādesa* means "speaking" (*kathana*). *Anvādesa* means "subsequent speaking" (*anukathana*). Thus it is said: "*Anvādeso kathitānukathanaṃ*"—the subsequent speaking of what has already been spoken.
"Repetition of what has been stated" (*kathitānukathana*) does not here mean merely the subsequent utterance of that which was already expressed;
rather, it refers to the restatement of a single referent that was previously presented by means of a preceding word.

Therefore, this [definition] does not apply to such cases as "Feed Devadatta, and this Yajñadatta," because in that case there is a repetition of what was stated with reference to a different distinction.
The connection is with the term *anvādeso* (repetition). How, then, is the association with another qualification understood?

To this he says: “by implication” (*sāmatthiyā*). Implication is the impossibility of repeating what has already been stated if it were not associated with some particular qualification; for this very reason he says: “otherwise,” and so forth. 198. Of what?

By the phrase "it is not contradicted" (*navirujjhati*), he states that because of the general rule "after *itthi* [the suffix] *amat*" (3-26), the suffix *itthiyaṃ* is not contradicted even in the midst of forms ending in case-suffixes (*syādyanta*).
204. Regarding *naṃ*:
Is it not possible for *naṃ* to follow the order of the case-endings (*vibhattikkama*) as well? If that were so, there would be two substitutes for two words.
To address the doubt as to why it was stated specifically "according to the order," he says: "Not even according to the order of the case-endings. He states the reason: "Because of its independence.

By this, he shows that the act of providing a basis (nissaya) is one method consistent with the *satthi* (the grammatical treatise). To explain how it would be [possible] if there were dependence, he says:
"For if," and so forth. It depends according to the sequence; thus it is understood: "Even though both [types of bases] are not [explicitly mentioned] by the description of the genus (*jāti*)."

Although forms are grasped, nevertheless, as in the case of the expression "three or four," it is the specific designation of proficiency that is helpful according to the sequence, because for a person of intelligence it is understood in that way;
thus one might say "only this much," yet it is not stated so. From this it is inferred that "the sequence is not intended here."
205. [Objection:
"Is it not the case that by the paribhāṣā rule regarding the inclusion of suffixes (*paccayaggahaṇaparibhāsā*), those ending in *nt* are understood?

That being so, since they are understood precisely as having *kāriya* (grammatical operation) status, why is there a suspicion that only those ending in *nt* are meant? To this he says: 'teyeva' etc., [meaning] 'on account of their being directly perceived' (*paccakkhatāya*)."

The connection is that because the *sutathāya-pañcikā* (the fivefold group beginning with *suta*) are [verbal roots] that are established (*sutattā*) and possess strength (*balavattā*), they alone are understood as having the status of being the action (*kāriyittena*), and not those ending in *-tad*, because they are weak;
having stated this distinction (*byatireka*), he states the reason for their weakness: "because they are inferred" (*anumitattā*). To establish that they are inferred, he says:
"by those which are inferred," and so forth. The reading *bhavibhattīnaṃ* is more appropriate; the connection is that when there is the substitution of *-anta* for it, the vowel *a* [is applied].

219. Regarding the term *yomhi*, because it is a designation of a genus ending in the locative case (*sattamī*), it is stated in the *Vutti* as "individual" (*pacceka*) according to its available meaning;
for this very reason, the *Pañcikā* asks: "How is it determined that this is a designation [of a genus]? and now, in order to clarify its meaning:
It is said: “‘Paccekam’ means ‘in each one,’ and so forth. Since two substitutions are possible for each *yo* [suffix], there is also the possibility of a plurality of substitutes;
therefore, the plural designation “of two” (*dvinnam*) is used in the Sutta.

However, in the Vutti, because the word “two” (*dvi*) occurs individually for each *yo*, it is stated as “of the two” (*dvissā*). Furthermore, in the second case as well, it is “two, two” (*duve dve*).

228. "Not by way of their natural state" (*nāsmā pakatavasena*) means not by way of the predominance of the substitutes for *tumhaṃ*; the connection is that they do not occur without exceeding their proper order.
230. *Caṃ vā*.
The teacher Kaccāyana, by means of the rule "sassaṃ" (2-3-3), which prescribes the substitution of *am* for the fourth and sixth case endings following the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhe*,
establishes the plural forms ‘tumhaṃ’ and ‘amha’. He states ‘tumhaṃ amha’ and so forth in order to demonstrate that even when referring to a single person—
such as oneself— or in the presence of elders and others, the plural form is used out of respect (*gārava*).
Because that [explanation] was inappropriate, he stated, "That is inappropriate," and established its inappropriateness with the words beginning "For thus...

In this commentary, however, in order to demonstrate the method for establishing the forms of the plural number in every respect even when [the context] refers to a single entity, he began with the words "But here...
"By the letter *na* [in the word *nāma*], even in the absence of a case-ending, there is the designation of a 'word' (*pada*).

This means that although there is no sutta from the Pāṇinian system—such as "that which ends in a suffix is a word"—which prescribes the designation of a word for those [forms] ending in a suffix, if one were to accept "word" based solely on its etymological meaning (*anvattha*), there would be an over-extension (*atippasaṅga*).
Therefore, he says: "Because of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), there is no over-extension. And: "A sentence (*vākya*) is a verb together with indeclinables, kārakas, and qualifiers."

Some say that a sentence consists of a single verb (*ākhyātika*), while others [say it consists of] all [the elements] taken together; in order to show that the author of the *Vutti* stated, “a collection of words is a sentence,” he says:

“*sābyaye*,” etc. They call a verb (*ākhyāta*) that which ends in *-ti* and so forth; an indeclinable (*abyaya*) is that which has no number. The meaning is that a verb, when accompanied by an indeclinable, a case-factor (*kāraka*), and an adjective (*visesana*), receives the technical designation “sentence” (*vākya*). As for the term “adjective” (*visesana*): [The text continues: ...it is that which qualifies the primary noun (*nāmika*).

An indeclinable is that which does not change its form. A verb is that which expresses action. When these are combined with their respective adjuncts, they constitute a sentence. Thus, a sentence is defined as a group of words consisting of a verb along with its indeclinables, factors, and qualifiers. This concludes the explanation of the definition of a sentence.

There is a general inclusion of both the qualifier of the *kāraka* (participant) and the qualifier of the action (*kriyā*). With an adverb: "He cooks together with [his] attendants" (*sābyayaṃ pacati*). With a *kāraka*:

"He cooks rice" (*sakārakaṃ odanaṃ pacati*), "Devadatta cooks" (*devadatto pacati*). With a qualifier of the *kāraka*: "He cooks soft, clear rice" (*sakārakavisesanaṃ muduṃ visadaṃ odanaṃ pacati*), "The handsome Devadatta cooks" (*dassanīyo devadatto pacati*).
With a qualifier of the action: "He cooks softly" (*sakiriyāvisesanaṃ muduṃ pacati*), "He cooks slowly" (*mandaṃ pacati*). [This constitutes] a collection of words (*padasamūha*).
When it is said, "they speak" (*vākyanti*), he says "it should be stated" (*vattuṃ*) and so forth, in order to explain that even this specific intention (*adhippāyaviseso*) can be understood.

By means of the phrase "according to one's wish" (*yathecca*) and so on, he states that a sentence (*vākyaṃ*) becomes one through the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇappadhānabhāvo*) among its various expressions (*anekākhyāti*), rather than by mere proximity. He asserts that a collection of words (*padasamūho*) constitutes a sentence because it has been so stated;
the connection is that there is a diversity of sentences (*vākyanānattaṃ*). The phrase "here too" (*ihāpi*) refers to the intended meaning and so forth as well.

233. In the rule regarding the inclusion of the fifth case (pañcamī) within the term *higgahaṇa*, it would follow that the fifth case is also included; therefore, it is stated in the Sutta as "not the fifth" (*apañcamyā*).

In the line of the verse, "By you, merit has been performed, not small," because of the presence of forms such as *tumhehi* and so on, there is no substitution with *vo*. [For example: "You stand in the city."
Because it is a separate sentence from the preceding statement, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

Having debated that "they are seen like you" and "they are seen like us," [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule "In the sense of 'seeing' (*disa-pekkhaṇe*), when the word *disā* is used as the object (*kamme*) following a common term such as *bhavanta*, the suffix *ka* is added" (5-43).
Then, by the rule "When *kā* follows, there is elision of the *anubandha*" (5-85), the *ettābhāva* occurs.
In the compound "syādisyādinekatthan" (3-1), there is "ekatthatāyaṃ" (2-119); in the elision of the case-ending, there is "sabbādīnamā" (3-86);
and in [the formation of] "tumhādisānaṃ," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "anvādesa" (subsequent reference) is understood as a restatement of what has already been said after it has been grasped, he asks: "How is this known? and replies: "Because it is considered to be a subsequent statement that depends upon what was previously stated.
236. *Sapubba*:
That which has a preceding part existing along with it is called *sapubba*.

237. "And not for the purpose of practicing a continuous connection" means for the purpose of not grasping the continuous connection mentioned by the words "the leaders of villages and towns," and so forth.
240. Not that...
"One who has matted hair (*jaṭā*) is a *jaṭila*; he himself is a *jaṭilaka*. The term *jaṭilaka* is an example of a word expressing a specific distinction within a single referent (*ekattha*);

it is not a general term (*sāmañña-vacana*), unlike the word *māṇavaka*. Regarding the statement ‘this [term] refers to a non-existent [person] when [the quality] is attained,’ this was stated because the sutta ‘an address (*āmantaṇaṃ*) that was previously non-existent’ (Pāṇini 2.2.39) is a general rule;
by the phrase ‘a negation of a general term,’ it is indicated that this applies to a specific term."
In this context, the address by those with matted hair (*jaṭilaka*) indicates either a previously non-existent name or a past name;

it refers to a common noun such as "Devadatta. In that common noun beginning with "Devadatta," when the word *māṇavaka* (youth) follows—as in the case of the youth Devadatta—both [the preceding and following words] are non-existent. By this, he illustrates the following: "Devadatta..."

"Because it is a term of distinction and because there is no negation, this [rule]— 'the vocative, whether preceding or following, is elided if not already present'— applies to both the preceding and the subsequent.
Thus ends the commentary on the Second Chapter in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*, the sub-commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*.
3. Commentary on the Third Section.
1. It might be asked: regarding that collection of syllables beginning with *yassātikamāvaṭṭhita* and so forth, what is it? To this he says: "‘This’ and so forth; ‘this’ [refers to... etc.
The form consisting of the aggregate beginning with *si*, as previously stated, is the analysis (*viggaha*) by way of its members; the aggregate is the meaning of the compound (*samāsa*).

Since words that function with respect to an aggregate also function with respect to its members, the word *syādi* applies even to the individual members beginning with *si*. This is according to the principle of the inclusion of the rule (*vidhiggahaṇañāya*), which states:
"When a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with it and that which ends with it. Thus, *syādi* [refers to those] having *si* at their end.

Regarding that which ends in a *syādi* suffix: one might object that if it were stated in general terms as "a word ending in a *syādi* suffix [forms a compound] with another word ending in a *syādi* suffix," then any word ending in a *syādi* suffix would be eligible for composition (*ekatthībhāva*) with any other word ending in a *syādi* suffix.

For instance, just as in examples such as *gāmagato* ("gone to the village"), so too would compounds such as *passa devadatte gāmaṃ* ("see Devadatta go to the village") and *gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃ* ("Yaññadatta went to the teacher's house") be suspected of being valid. To this, he says: "In general..."

Even when stated as "vuttepi" and so forth, it is understood and determined from the context that a word ending in a *syādi* suffix which has a connection with another word ending in a *syādi* suffix becomes a single meaning (*ekattha*) together with that *syādi*-ending word; this is the meaning of "yassātyādi.

Likewise, in the case of *gāmagato*, there is a connection characterized by mutual expectancy between these two, and this constitutes their state of being a single meaning (*ekatthībhāva*); for this very reason, they say here:
The means of accomplishment is restricted to that which is to be accomplished, and the action has its means of accomplishment restricted;
if it is thought that this restriction of theirs exists by way of proximity, [it is] because of their non-existence.
This is the meaning here: "Since 'village' and so forth—this means of accomplishment—requires the action to be accomplished, which is capable of being known through its designation."
Because it is said "gone," the means (sādhana) is necessarily connected to the action (kiriyā) in the sense of that which is to be accomplished (sādhya);
and because the action itself requires a means, asking "by what has it gone?", the action is also necessarily connected to this means.
Thus, this aforementioned rule, occurring by way of mutual dependence, exists through the mere presence of these factors—the thing to be accomplished and the means.

"...it makes [them] manifest to one another. Consider the example: *passa devadatta gāmaṃ gato yaññadatto gurukulaṃ* ("Behold, Devadatta! Yaññadatta has gone to the teacher's family from the village").

Here, "the village" (*gāmaṃ*) as the instrument (*sādhana*) requires the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), while "gone" (*gato*), which is the action of going, requires the teacher's family (*gurukulaṃ*).

Consequently, there is no mutual expectancy between the components of these two distinct sentences (*vākyantara-avayava*), such as "those who have gone to the village"; thus, no compound (*samāsa*) occurs. This principle should be applied in all similar cases.
For a relation, characterized by mutual expectancy, excludes what is not established from the other related term and establishes [the term] in its specific distinction;
and thus it has been said:
"But for one who desires that [relation], there is a state of wavering regarding the difference."

"Establishing that [general term] in a particular sense, it cuts off the connection"—thus, in the case of a distinction or particularity, this general term such as "village" (*gāma*) depends upon a particular specification, as in:

"he sits in the village," "he leaves the village," or "he has gone to the village. Likewise, for one who desires or longs for such expressions as "gone to the village," "to the forest," or "to the teacher's family," there is the relationship between that primary word and its subordinate word (*upasañjanapada*).

And that state of wavering and instability, when being established and fixed upon a specific related term (*sambandhin*), delimits—meaning it distinguishes [the term] from other related things—a relationship which is of various kinds:

in some cases characterized by the relation of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), in some cases having the nature of original state and modification (*pakativikārabhāva*), and in some cases having the form of a master-and-possessor (*sassāmi*) relationship; for this [delimitation] is dependent upon that.

It is determined precisely within the Vākyakāla; therefore, the meaning is that where there is a mutual expectancy (*apekṣā*) between words, there is the comprehension of a compound (*samāsa*), whereas where such expectancy does not exist, it does not occur—thus the division of domains is understood even without being explicitly taught.

Relying on this for the sake of instructing the ignorant, there is a manifold means consisting of various methods, such as the rules for compounds and elisions, for the purpose of thoroughly understanding correct words through practice.
This is possible [conventionally], but in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), because they are different words, there is an absolute difference between sentences and compounds;
for the words seen in a sentence do not exist within a compound. And thus it has been said:
"This means of support for the foolish is manifold through its various modes of practice."
The separation of sentences and compounds, the ending in *cc*, the change of *ñ* and *ṇ*, and that which is another word (*saddantara*)—this is what is meant.

"For this very reason" means: although it is stated in a general sense, because its connection with the [preceding] word is understood through its relation—that is, because it becomes co-referential (*ekattha*) with it—therefore nothing undesirable occurs here; the meaning is "for this very reason" as a cause. This is the mutual expectation (*byapekkhā*).

Regarding the phrase *sāmatthiyapariggahāya*, there is a mutual expectancy (*aññoññākaṅkhā*) among the words; that very [expectancy] is the "capacity" (*sāmatthiya*), and it is for the sake of grasping that.
The term "capacity" (*samattha*) has not been employed here as it is by the Pāṇinīyas, who state: "The rule for words applies when there is capacity" (*Pāṇini 2.1.1*).
In the paribhāṣā "The rule for words applies when there is capacity," this meaning is established: "it is prescribed."
"Vidhi" means that which is prescribed (*vidhīyati*); "padavidhi" refers to the prescription of words, such as compounds and so forth.
Whatever word-prescription exists here in this science [of grammar] should be understood as having the capacity (*satti*) to express the meaning of the analytical sentence (*viggaha-vākya*).

Because of the operation of such a rule, there is no undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha*) in cases such as "Look, Devadatta, go to the village; Yaññadatta has gone to the teacher's family. And here, the capacity is...
In a sentence, two things are admitted: syntactic dependence (*byapekkhā*) and unification of meaning (*ekatthībhāva*).
[The manuscript reads: "either unification of meaning in a compound or syntactic dependence in a sentence.

Therein, having demonstrated the inclusion of the first [alternative] without using a formal statement, he now demonstrates the inclusion of the second with a formal statement, saying: "Unification of meaning," and so forth. Unification of meaning...
The distinction in the mode of occurrence [in a compound] is by way of the common meaning of distinct meanings; for in a sentence, there is no common meaning because the meanings are distinct.

Precisely for this reason, the genitive case arises here based on that distinction, as in "the king’s man" (*rañño puriso*). In a compound, however, there is a common meaning because it expresses a meaning delimited by both members.
This is what is meant: "In a compound, the qualifier enters into the qualified and becomes one with it."

"A qualifier, however, remains distinct from the qualified in a sentence. But in the case of a *dvanda* compound, although there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between its constituent members,
because it has all the word-meanings as its primary referent, the compound "the king's cow, horse, and man" differs from the sentence "the king's cow, horse,
and man" by virtue of its being a single unified meaning (*ekatthībhāva*), which is the defining characteristic of a compound.

It is indeed so; for in that sentence (*vākya*), the word *ca* is employed to express a conjunction based on distinct meanings, whereas in a compound (*samāsa*) it is not employed because of the expression of a single meaning (*ekattha*).

This is indicated by the rule “*syādi* [is used] with *syādi* [when there is] a single meaning” (*syādisyādinekattha*), which refers specifically to the expression of a single meaning. The remainder of the sense is that “only the state of being one (*ekattībhāvo*) occurs.
The particle *eva* (indeed) demonstrates that this is not the case in a sentence. To explain how it is in a sentence, he says: “In a sentence,” and so forth.

Regarding the term *vākye*: in the analytical sentence (*viggahavākye*), it is specifically understood; that by which something is known is an analysis (*vigga-ho*). That [analysis] and that sentence together constitute the "analytical sentence" (*viggahavākyaṃ*).

Alternatively, analysis (*vigga-ho*) is specific apprehension; the sentence for the sake of that is the "analytical sentence" (*viggahavākyaṃ*), and in that [sentence], it pervades the body [of the compound].

Thus he says: "characterized by dissolution (*bheda*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of both conjunction (*saṃsagga*) and the conjunction of dissolution (*saṃsaggabheda*).

In this context, "separation" (*byāvutti*) is the exclusion [of one thing] by means of its own negations and the negations of others; "conjunction" (*saṃsagga*) is the connection between specific qualities and specific subjects.

He states this with the words beginning "for thus" (*tathā hi*). "The differentiator" (*bhedaka*) is that which excludes; it is "taken as a meaning" (*atthagahita*), meaning it is taken by the proponent of differentiation on the basis of a cause.
With the words beginning "when," he states the intention of the proponent of conjunction; and with the words beginning "but when both," [he explains further].
The term *abhimata* refers to what is intended by both proponents; it is desired by Pāṇini through the rule “*pākkaḍārāsamāsaḥ*” (2.1.3).
By the rule “*kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye*” (2.2.38), the word *kaḍāra* [and those following it] are placed first; this is the meaning.
Those words whose meanings are distinct are *puthagatthāni*; for in a sentence, such as “the king’s man,” there [is a distinction].
The word *rāja* denotes only the meaning "king," and the word *purisa* denotes only the meaning "man.
However, when they occur in the compound *rājapurisa*, even the word *rāja* denotes the meaning "man"; thus, there is a unification of meaning (*ekatthībhāva*) between the two.

Since a distinct collective meaning (*samudāyattha*), endowed with the meanings of its constituent parts, becomes manifest, the unification of meaning is spoken of in relation to that [collective meaning], having accepted the abandonment of the individual functions of their own respective meanings.
It is stated: “In the case of the relinquishing of its own meaning by the qualifier,” and so forth; for this very reason, another will object with the words “Is it not indeed...?
By the term *ekatthībhāva* (becoming one in meaning), which is synonymous with *samāsa* (compound), it is demonstrated that there is no difference in meaning.
That [compound] is so described because the constituent words relinquish their own meanings; it is not thought that they abandon them entirely.

“‘One who abandons for his own sake’ is said with reference to mere relinquishment, but not because there is total relinquishment for the benefit of others, since that [relinquishment] involves grasping;

and if there were total relinquishment of one’s own sake, it would result in no benefit to others, so in the absence of such a purpose, there would be no grasping at all”—thus says the Master Vaḍḍhati.
“Sake” (sakattha) means the referent of the word *rāja*. Even in the case of absolute relinquishment, it is not...

Regarding the fault... [the author] says "atha vā" and so forth, demonstrating that when there is the application of a word seen in a sentence to a subordinate element, it is understood as having that very meaning because of the determination of identity (*anvaya*).
This determination of identity (*anvaya*) is the thought "this is indeed that";

for those who employ conventional usage, there is a determination of oneness based on the notion that "this word *rāja* is the very same one that was seen in the sentence," even though such [oneness] does not exist in reality.
The intention is that [the word] *rāja* will serve as a qualifier for the person (*purisa*) in the sense of "king. To this very point, he provides an illustration, beginning with “Just as,” etc.

2. Regarding the term *asaṃ*, it is called an indeclinable (*abyaya*) because it is well-known among others; and because they are devoid of change (*byaya*), prepositions (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*) remain the same despite differences in gender and number.
Because it is designated as "indeclinable" (abyaya) by others on account of its indeclinability, it is well-known among others as "indeclinable.

For them, this compound is established as an *abyayībhāva* because it is preceded by the sense of an indeclinable, such that "that which was not an indeclinable becomes an indeclinable. Since the term "numberless" (*asaṅkhyassa*) is heard [in the rule], it is understood that its very case-meanings and so forth function as qualifiers by way of being the domain [of the compound];
thus he says "in the numberless," etc., by which he indicates that this is the meaning of the compound for these [words].
Regarding the word *tāva*, he explains its meaning when used in a distributive sense (*kamavutti*) with the words “*vibhattatthe*,” etc.

Having illustrated an example for the sense of a case ending (*vibhattattha*), he says that for the numeral *asaṅkhyā* occurring in the domain of the sense of a case ending, a feminine compound is formed with the word *itthi*.

He states that a compound with the suffix *-ni* is not appropriate, or rather, a compound of separate words (*asakapadaviggaha*) is more suitable; otherwise, there would be the consequence of violating the rule of permanence (*aniccatā*). Thus he says:
"Because it is always associated," and so forth.
"Analysis by means of separate words" (*asakapadaviggaha*) refers to an analysis performed using separate words such as *anattaniya* (not belonging to self) or *añña* (other).

By this [method], here, just as in the sentence "in the vicinity of a jar" (*kumbhassa samīpam*), because the word "vicinity" (*samīpa*) expresses that which is denoted by the prefix *upa*, [the prefix is understood].

The prefix *adhi* is not employed [separately]; for example, in the phrase *itthīsū*, because the locative case expresses the sense of the substratum (*ādhāra*)—the referent of the word *adhi*—there is no separate word *adhi*.
Thus, the compound sentence *itthīsū* is stated; however, the progression of the discourse reveals the thing supported (*ādheyya*).
In this way, it should be inferred in all instances: the meaning alone is expressed through a compound analysis that does not include its own constituent parts.

However, in order to show that the word *adhi*—which stands before [the noun] and functions as a locative modifier—is compounded with a feminine word ending in the locative case that shares the same grammatical core (*samānādhikaraṇa*), he says:
"The word *adhi*," and so forth. "Elision of *syādi*" means that there is elision of the locative plural endings following both the word *adhi* and the word *itthi*.
"Attasampatti" (perfection of self) is intended here as the perfection of the body; thus, the meaning of the word *brahma* is "body."

He said: “Regarding the phrase ‘brahmaṃ sarīranti,’ because in some instances the meaning of the final member of a compound is predominant, the analysis (viggaha) for this asaṅkhyasamāsa is stated as ‘sampannaṃ brahma.

‘From the case-ending of the compound’ means from the case-ending that arises from the compound; ‘the whole [is] the part and the whole’ means ‘expecting inclusion,’ that is, expecting acceptance. For even in the sense of acceptance, the word *pariggaha* [is used].”
"Oath, retinue, and roots; acceptance, and when the sun is seized by Rāhu;
and 'pariggaha' refers to wives"—this is the Nighaṇṭu.
The state of being whole is "sākalya," which is the cause for the application of the word *sakala*; furthermore, that [state] is considered to be without remainder (*nissaesa*).

In the manuscript, it says "separate from grasping," to which he replies: "grasping without remainder. The analysis (*viggaha*) is "the totality of grasses. For by the word "grass" (*tiṇa*), those things accompanied by grass are included;
for this very reason, he will later say in the method of distinction: "He swallows all that, together with the grass.
To express the intended meaning here—that he swallows it along with the grass—he says "as far as" (*yāva*) and so forth.
The word *tiṇa* (grass) is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) for other non-edible things; therefore, he said, "even grass and so forth.

For the purpose of including that which is contained within the scope of the requirement for a governing relation (*pariggahāpekkhā*), Pāṇini cited the example *sāgyadhīte* in the rule beginning with *avyayaṃ vibhattisamīpādi*;
however, that was cited in its entirety in order to include everything, and thus *sāgyadhīte* was cited as a complete example.
The passage beginning with “tato” was stated in order to demonstrate this. The connection is as follows:

“Tato” means from that point where [the term] “sakala-sakala” (all-in-all) does not apply; because of the requirement for a circumscription (*pariggaha*), the completeness (*sākalya*) is not broken even at the limit (*anta*) of its own scope. The remainder is that even in the case of a capacity (*samatthiya*), there is an illustration at the end.

“Aggipariyantaṃ” means: the fire is the purpose of the text; by virtue of the sense of “for the sake of that” (*tādatthiyā*), it is “fire”; that which has fire as its limit is the subject matter (*ajjheyya*), thus it is “bounded by fire” (*aggipariyanta*).
The analysis is as follows: "the whole" (*sakala*) means that which is accompanied by a limit (*pariyanta*) consisting of fire, [a limit] defined by however much of the fuel (*ajjheyya*) is grasped;
or alternatively, it means the entirety (*sākalya*) of the fire.

"Of those who know grammar" (*saddikānaṃ*) refers to those who are experts in grammatical analysis. In the phrase "in the absence of meaning" (*atthābhāve*), the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*attha*) is intended to refer to mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and the non-existence of phenomena (*dhammābhāva*).
And [the thought] "may I not be" is precisely why it is called "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*) and so forth; for mutual non-existence is the non-existence of one thing in another.
Indeed, in the case of "a cow is not a horse," it is the state of being a different entity that is negated, not the existence of the substrate itself.

Likewise, in the case of "he is not a brahmin," it is the property of being a brahmin that is negated, not the existence of the substrate itself. This is indicated by the phrase "otherness" (*parattā*) and so on.
He states the object of the negation.

Regarding the phrase "atikkamābhāve," he says "atikkamā" because it is a compound designation in the ablative case; however, by the words "not after what has arisen," he shows that "non-existence after" means the non-existence [of the cause] subsequent to what has already arisen.
*Nittiṇa* is a numeral compound (*saṅkhyāsamāsa*) where the meaning of the final member is predominant. Although the word *sampati* is a general term...

In order to show the time intended here, he says: “of enjoyment,” and so forth. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: “this is not the time for enjoyment (*upabhoga*) of a light garment (*lahupāvuraṇa*), where *upabhoga* is used as the object of the action.
To demonstrate the grammatical derivation (*rūpasiddhi*) of the term “light garment,” the commentary states: “of a light garment,” and so forth.

Regarding the analysis “a suitable form” (*yoggaṃ rūpaṃ*), which yields the compound “appropriate” (*anurūpa*), one might suspect that because it is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*), there ought to be an analysis with the particle *sa-*; therefore, he says: “in the sense of a distributive repetition (*vicchāya*),” and so forth.
For when joined with the sound *anu*, the second case ending is prescribed as *anunā* (2-10) in the sense of distribution (*vicchā*);

and since its usage occurs only in a sentence and not elsewhere, it is considered that this is also a sentence. In the word *sakikhi*, here too, by the rule "for *saha* in the sense of itself [is substituted] *sa-* when not at the beginning of a compound" (3-81), *sa-* replaces *saha*.
In the phrase *sadiso kikhiyā*, here, because *kikhi*—which has become well-known—is taken as the instrument for the sake of establishing similarity (*sādhiya*), [the comparison is established].

Regarding the statement, "Is anyone superior or equal by virtue of possessing the same dhamma?"—what is meant here is that the "equal" (sadisa) is itself the primary factor (padhāna), not a subordinate one.

If that were the case, then in the compound *sakikhi*—which is an *asaṅkhyasamāsa* where the meaning of the first word is primary—it would not be possible [to analyze it as such]. Therefore, he says, "But is it not so...

and so forth. In the phrase *kikhiyā*, the genitive case is used in connection with the word; however, because the state of being similar (*sadisatta*) is not dependent upon the *kikhi*, it is the subordinate factor (*appaṭibaddhattāppadhānattaṃ*).
With the words "Netadatthī" and so forth, he addresses the objection stated previously.
If there were a compound in the expression "yathā devadatto," it would have to be "yathādevadatta," meaning "one similar to Devadatta";
however, because it is prohibited, it is not a compound. "Kikhī" is a name for a monkey. "In order of seniority" means...
Because it is stated [as such], "the eldest" is understood as being in the third case. "With the wheel" means simultaneously with the wheel (*sacakka*).
4. *Yāva* is used in the sense of limitation.
"As much as the measure of the vessels" means the extent of the limit of the vessels.
5. Regarding *payyapābahitiro*: Why was it stated as "with the fifth case" (*pañcamyā*)?

One might suspect that even if that [word] were not stated, the compound would be understood to consist only of words ending in the fifth case, because of the manner in which it will be explained later.
Anticipating this, he says “*yadipi*,” etc. He resolves it with “*tathāpi*,” etc., saying: “Let it be so, if you wish.”
The phrase “it shines upon the surrounding mountain” serves as a second negation; in order to exclude other cases, he says “if here,” and so forth.
In the expression “or four [villages],” the prefix *ā-* functions either within the sentence or as a marker of direction (*saraṇa*); the meaning is “the village stands outside.

By saying “he sees the village ahead,” he shows that the demonstrative pronoun *yaṃ* (in *purato*) is primarily expressive of meaning (*atthappadhāna*), rather than being primarily expressive of grammatical form (*sarūpappadhāna*); the meaning is “he sees the village facing him.”
These are illustrative examples of what has not been explicitly stated; therefore, it is also said, "he sees even across the village" (*tirogāmam-pi passā*).
The meaning is: he sees across the village, or he sees behind the village.

Because of the connection with the word *apa*, the rule for forming compounds (*samāsavidhāna*) does not apply as an option due to the constant presence of the suffix *-pañca-*. An example is given here: although there is no functional purpose for the ablative case (*pañcamī*), when it is employed for another reason, it becomes meaningful in this context as well.
6. *Samī*:
Regarding the two statements of Pāṇini, namely "anu yaṃ samayā" (2-1-15) and "yassa cāyāmo" (2-1-16), this is their meaning:
when the word *anu* expresses proximity (*samīpa*) to something, it forms a compound with that [word], and likewise when it expresses effort (*āyāma*). *Anu*...

“And that which has ‘āya’ as its suffix is compounded with a word ending in ‘syā. Thus, showing that although words ending in ‘sāmīpya’ and ‘āyāma’ are not explicitly mentioned [in the rule], they are implied by the force of the context, he says: “of those near and long,” and so forth.
The term *sambandhittā* means that relational words denote their own referent as well as a specific correlative; without that [correlative], [the relation] would not be established.

Because they lack their own referent (*sakattha*). *Āyāma* means length; the phrase "in the vicinity of which there is length" (*yassa samīpāyāmesu*) refers back to the two previously mentioned sūtras by way of implication.

*Anuvanaṃ* means "in the vicinity of the forest. Although [the form] is established by the rule "after *asaṅkhyā*, when there is the attainment of case endings or in the sense of vicinity" (3-2), the repeated mention of "vicinity" (*samīpa*) is for the sake of providing an option (*vikappa*);
therefore, the expression *vanassa anu* should also be possible.

Regarding the term *anugaṅgaṃ* (along the Ganges), the word *āyāma* (length) is understood from the rule *bhāgavuttikāro*, and the word *lakkhaṇena* (by way of a characteristic mark) is carried over [from the previous sutta]. That which has *anu* signifying length is characterized by that [length];
thus, Bārāṇasī is "along the Ganges. By means of the Ganges—which serves as the characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*)—being well-known for its quality of length, Bārāṇasī is characterized [in this way]:
"As long as the Ganges is in length, so long is Bārāṇasī. Thus, by its very nature, there exists the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameyya*).
"In the compound, it is understood as being long like the Ganges," thus he describes the relationship between the characteristic and that which possesses the characteristic.
Thinking that if this were so, the nominative case in "Bārāṇasī" would not be appropriate, he says: "'Joined with the Ganges,' etc.
The meaning of "Bārāṇasī along the Ganges" (anugaṅgaṃ bārāṇasi) is that the length of the Ganges is the characteristic of Bārāṇasī.

7. By the phrase "tiṭṭha akatasamāsā ca," he indicates that [the preceding rule] applies when a compound has been formed; and in order to show that "tiṭṭhanti" is a word ending in the suffix *nta*, he says:
"when the agent (*kattari*) is expressed by the suffix *nta*" (Pāṇini 3.2.124), and so forth. Furthermore, "āyanti" is the plural form of the word "āyati."

The absence of the masculine gender is due to grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), as is the case with the vowel *a* in the rule "In the sense of 'cow-nature' (*gotva*) and in the elision [of the suffix], etc. (3-46), because of the continued application of the phrase "not in other numbers or meanings" from the preceding rule.

Here, by irregularity, words such as *lūnayava* ("where the barley has been harvested") possess the neuter gender even when referring to time; thus, *saṃhaṭayavaṃ* means "the time when the barley is gathered.
Furthermore, in the technical name *ummattagaṅga*, there is a compulsory compound (*niccasamāsa*) despite the governing rule regarding other word-meanings, for a sentence is not a technical name.

By the word *ādi* (and so forth), there is the inclusion of such terms as *‘samassa sobhanattaṃ susamaṃ’* ("the beauty of the even is 'well-even'"), and so on; *pabhāvanaṃ* means "making manifest" or "explaining. 8. Regarding *ore*:

when the compound *oraṃ gaṅgāya, pāraṃ yamunāya* ("this side of the Ganges, the other side of the Yamunā") is formed, the vowel *e* occurs by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātanā*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vutti* (Commentary): "The state of ending in *e* is due to an irregularity. The analysis of the compound [in the phrase] *vuttivikappanattho* is: "that whose meaning is a modification of the *Vutti*. Thus, *vuttivikappanattho* means that its purpose is the modification of the *Vutti*.

10. "The state of being a single-minded seeker of peace is considered distinguished"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. "For a moment" (*muhuttaṃ*) takes the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*).

"Having formed a *pādipada* compound" means that the word *āsadda* [is compounded] with the word *vutti*, which is expressed by the word *harasadda*; thus, according to the *Pañcikā*, the action is to be expressed.

In the absence of an action such as sprinkling and so forth, there can be no agent of formation (*saṅkhāraka*) nor an object of formation (*saṅkhāriya*); since both exist here, it is considered that the action which has become a compound for the sake of their very occurrence is understood.

For instance, when "curd-food" (*dadhibhojana*) and the like are mentioned, the status of being the agent of formation is recognized in the curd and the like, and the status of being the object of formation in the food and the like; and this does not occur without the sprinkling and other such actions.
The state of being that which conditions and that which is conditioned is established by the very capacity [of the words], such as sprinkling and so forth.
"In dependence on that" means in dependence on the implied actions of sprinkling and so forth.

According to the Pāṇinīyas, in the sense of "this belongs to that," a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*) is intended, along with the quality of having all genders; likewise, disregarding the absence of number here, [the author] says "how," and so forth.
Having cited the statement of the objector (*codaka*), the commentary (*vutti*) clarifies the intended meaning there with the words "it is thought thus" (*evamaññate*) and so forth.

The connection is: "a rule (*vidhāna*) has been made; it is thought thus. By the phrase "there" (*tattha*) and so forth, while clarifying the intention that [the suffix] will occur in the sense of another word (*añña-padatthe*), it establishes both its status as a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*) and its possession of all genders (*sabbaliṅgata*). [The phrase] "only by the completion of the sentence" (*vākyanivattisiddhāyeva*) [is used].

Since its meaning is already understood through the word *attha* itself, it would be improper to say "of this [there is]"; thus, the syntactical resolution as “the meaning of this” (*etassa attho*) is indeed established.

Furthermore, even if a compound were formed with a word ending in the dative case whose meaning is distinct [from the other members], he states the contradiction therein with the words beginning “of that which ends in the dative” (*catutthyantassa*), and so forth.

The statement as well—referring even to the established rule by the author of the *Vākya* that "there is always a compound [with a relative pronoun] with its referent (*atthena*), and it takes all genders" (Pāṇini 2.1.36)—is shown by the words "yo" and so forth to demonstrate that for the Pāṇinīyas, when a compound is formed in the sense of "this belongs to that," the resulting suffix *-ya-* occurs; and that this very same sense applies even in compounds with other meanings.
Or rather, [the passage] should be connected with such terms as "exertion" (*vāyāma*) for the sake of attaining *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupādāparinibbāna*).

Regarding the phrase "because they have that as their cause" (*taṃnimittattā*) [in reference to] "exertion and so forth" (*vāyāmādīnaṃ*), and "of those [things such as] speech and so forth" (*tesaṃ kathādīnaṃ*): here, it should be stated as "of those [things such as] exertion and so forth" (*tesaṃ vāyāmādīnaṃ*).
Since this has been stated by way of "exertion" (*vāyāmo*) and so on, that [speech, etc. indeed has that [exertion, etc. as its cause; this is the intended meaning here.

In the sentence "this belongs to this" (*etassa idaṃ*), when there is a compound with a substantive (*atthena samāse*), there is the state of having all genders (*sabbaliṅgatā*). Thus, in the forms "having this as its purpose" (*etadattho*), "having this as its purpose" (*etadatthā*), and "having this as its purpose" (*etadatthaṃ*), [the words] "exertion" (*vāyāmo*) and so forth [are used].

And they possess a combined meaning; this is the meaning, the purpose, of this [word], of that [word], or of these [words]—even when there is a different referent (*aññapadattha*) for these words, the meaning remains the same, so there is no difference in meaning.

And this: "The wholesome states, Ānanda, have non-regret as their purpose; non-regret has joy as its purpose... [and so on] ...the knowledge and vision of liberation... [has the purpose of non-regret].

This was stated based on the canonical passage beginning: "For the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging; for this purpose is effort, for this purpose is discourse, for this purpose is consultation, and for this purpose is the application of the ear" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.107, Ānanda-vagga).
This is because the grammarians [of the Pāṇinian school] prescribe a compound with the instrumental case by means of a *kit*-affix ending, according to the rule:
"The instrumental case is frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kit* affix" (Pāṇini 2.1.32).
By including the term *bahula* in that very [rule], compounds such as *gāmaniggatā* and others are stated;

therefore, the absence of a compound is intended for these two internal examples (*antodāharaṇa*), as is accepted by the Pāṇinīyas in the sūtra *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayataddhitābhavasamānādhikaraṇena* (2.2.11) through the mention of the word *guṇa*.
For them, the technical term *sat* refers to those [words] ending in *nt* and *mān*.

The meaning is: "How is it?"—here, because the prohibition of composition is prescribed specifically by the *bhāva*-suffix in the rule "with [words ending in] *bhāva*, *taddhita*, and *ittha* suffixes," how is that prohibition of composition established in cases such as "the white of a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇassa sukkā*)?

"Only when they possess the nature of a quality" (*guṇattaniyeva*) means only when they have the intrinsic nature of a quality; or rather, it is what is intended by the author of the *Vārttika* in the rule "and with qualities that reside in that" (*tadavaṭṭhehi ca guṇehī*). By the word "that" (*tad*), there is a reference back to this quality; thus, "residing in that" (*tadavaṭṭhā*) means those which remain fixed in that very quality.

The meaning is as follows: qualities (guṇa) reside only in a substance (guṇin); they never exist independently [of it], such as the expressions "white" and so forth, because there is no distinction [between them].

These qualities, such as fragrance and the like, remain fixed within that [substance]. Therefore, it should be stated that the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) is appropriate for the qualities that remain fixed within that [substance].

Regarding the word *ābhimata* ("intended"), although the genitive in "Devadattassa" is dependent upon something else (*gurumhi sāpekkhatte*), it is included by the mention of indeclinables (*abyayaggahaṇena*) in the sutta beginning with "pūraṇā."

Because the word *guru* is a relative term, just as in a sentence used in its own sense (*sakattha*), its presence in a derivative formation (*vutti*) is established through the non-abandonment of its expectancy;
to prove the existence of this formation by means of another statement, he says: "And so they have said.

The phrase "as if in its own sense" (*sāttheva*) means "just as in its own sense"; "of it" (*assā*) refers to the relative term; and "its capacity" (*sāmatthiya*) means its quality of being indicative.

The meaning is that there exists either the capacity characterized by mutual dependence between words, or the quality of making the meaning of the analytical sentence understood even in the absence of such capacity.
For example, in the analysis "the family of the teacher is the wife of the slave," one might ask:

"How is it determined that in cases such as 'the high [caste] of the Brahmin,' there is neither capacity nor the quality of making the meaning understood, on account of which the absence of capacity here is described as the reason for the absence of a compound? To this, he says: "But [it is not so] due to capacity, etc. and so forth.
The absence of compound formation is intended because, in the rule beginning with *pūraṇā*, even a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is included.

By the statement, "In the case of *sehi* [meaning] 'one's own,' a prohibition of the sixth-case compound must be stated for those that are not in apposition and are not compounded," this explains the application of *micca* as having a distinct meaning—that is, a different meaning—just as in the case of non-compounded words such as *go* and so forth; and it is the same for *assa* and so on.

The connection is with the word "alanti" (it is sufficient) in brief. "Yogīnaṃ" means "of those joined together" (*itarītarayogīnaṃ*); by this, he indicates the *itarītarayoga* type of fourth-case compound (*catthasamāsa*). The phrase "vuttihoti" (a usage occurs) is an explanation of "chaṭṭhīsamāso bhavati" (it becomes a sixth-case compound). The phrase "ekatthībhāve" (in the state of unified meaning) is an explanation of "gavādīnañca catthasamāse sati" (when there is a fourth-case compound of cows and so forth).
"Ruḷhittā" (because of conventional usage) is because the compound itself is well-known as denoting play and as being the cause for one's livelihood. It is not... [the sentence continues].

Regarding the statement "vākyassāti": one considers that in cases such as ‘uddālapupphabhañjikā’, there will be a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*) by virtue of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), so what is the need for a specific rule?
The analysis (*viggaha*) is: “remembering [the word] *ruḷhī*.
Furthermore, this *amādi*-compound—along with all others, including *kammadhāraya* and *digu* compounds—is similar to the *tappurisa* compounds of other grammarians.
Regarding *tappurisa*: just as the term *tappurisa* is one where the meaning of the latter member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, so too would those [compounds] be.

A *digu* is so called because it "goes" or "proceeds" by way of two characteristics, namely, having a numeral as its prior member (*saṅkhyāpubbatā*) and being neuter (*napuṃsakatta*). 11. *Vise* (The section on *vīsa*).
Regarding the question "What is the qualifier? he says "that which [is called] 'this'," etc.; the connection is that it is called the qualifier because it establishes [the object].
Regarding the question "What is the qualified? he says "that which [is called] 'many,'" etc.; the connection is that it is designated as the qualified because it is established by [the former].

Now, when it is stated "by means of a single meaning," how is it understood that it refers to the "qualified"? Anticipating this doubt because it has been explained in such a way, he says "Even though," etc.
"Because they are words denoting relations": this is what is intended. "Words denoting relations attract their respective correlates as if they were their own meaning...
for without those [correlates], their own meaning would be impossible. [The form] *vivaritvā* means "having opened";

thus, by the rule "with one meaning," there is a compound with a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). In this way, the meaning should be understood as including the elided portion (*sājjhāhāra*), because the word *attha* has multiple meanings.
It qualifies [the term] by stating: "The meaning (attha) is that which is to be expressed. To the question, "How is the meaning expressed by that?

he says: "'It is made the locus' (adhikarīyati)," and so forth. The connection is that the state of having a common locus (samānādhikaraṇatta) of the qualified (visessa) depends upon the qualifier (visesana).

The state of having a common locus of the word denoting the qualified with the qualifier depends upon the word denoting the qualifier; in this way, the meaning here is to be understood. In that regard—
He states the reason: “Because of the connection” (*sambandhā*). What is called the commonality of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) belongs to distinct related things (*sambandhin*);
and since related things do not exist without a connection, the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is understood.
Thus, the meaning is: “because of the connection,” since it is understood in this way.
For here, apart from words, the relationship of qualifier and qualified between meanings is not possible;

for instance, in the phrase "a blue lotus" (*nīlam uppalam*), five entities are present: "blue" refers to the common quality of blueness (*nīlattam*), the quality of blueness (*nīlo guṇo*), and its substratum, the substance (*dabbaṃ*)—these three;
"lotus" refers to the genus of lotus (*uppalattam*), and the substance which is its support—these two.

In this regard, it is impossible for there to be a relationship of qualifier and qualified between "blue-ness" (*nīlatva*) and "lotus-ness" (*utpalatva*), because a genus (*jāti*) lacks qualities (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, since "blue-ness" inheres in the quality of blue, while "lotus-ness" inheres in the substance of the lotus, they do not share a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇya*).
This is because the genus "lotus-ness" and the quality "blue" [inhere in different things].

There is co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇattaṃ*): the lotus and the blue [color] share a single substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) or support for their respective grounds for application (*pavattinimitta*), namely the lotus-universal (*uppala-jāti*) and the quality of blueness (*nīla-guṇa*).
However, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*visesanavisessabhāva*) between them, because the universal is not blue.
But the relationship of qualifier and qualified is possible between the quality and the substance, since the substance possesses multiple qualities; yet, they share a further common substratum.

There is no third [element] by which there could be grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*). Thus, even in the case of the words *nīla* (blue) and *utpala* (lotus), when they are intended to be expressed in mutual exclusion, there is neither the relation of qualifier and qualified nor grammatical coreferentiality.
Why? Because they lack a mutual connection due to the absence of mutual expectancy (*apekṣā*), and because they are the opposite of what has been stated.
However, according to the method that will be explained, grammatical coreferentiality belongs to words alone.
The relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) must also be understood; for this very reason, he says:
"For this very reason," and so forth. "For this very reason" means: because the coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) of the qualified depends upon the qualifier, it is for this causal reason.
[The phrase] "only of those connected by different causes" refers generally either to the word *nīla* applied to a substance that is the locus of the quality blue, or to the quality itself.
And because the word *uppala* generally refers to a substance possessing a quality, it is the very conclusion (*niṭṭhāna*) of words employed for various distinct causes for the application of sound;
this is what is meant by "having a common substratum" (*samānādhikaraṇatta*).
For if the words *nīla* and *uppala* were used separately, it would be impossible for them to express a qualified substance.

When the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "blue" and "that lotus" is established, their identity of referent (*samānatthatā*) occurs precisely because they function with respect to a qualified object;
thus he says "not [in] non-distinct [objects]" and so forth to show the meaning excluded by the particle *eva*. The objection beginning with "But is it not...
refers to the *sīsa-pāti* (Sīsapā tree), which is a specific type of tree; the resolution begins with "This is not so," and so forth.

Now, with the words "But it is said," etc., he anticipates an opportunity for the opponent's objection. "Specific application" (*visesavutti*) means that because both "fruit" and "tree" are general terms (*sāmaññasadda*), their application is to a specific instance by way of their inherent nature. "Of these"—namely, the *sīsa* trees and so forth—they are not "aggregated" (*samodhārita*), meaning they are not determined [together];
the intention is that only a general application (*sāmaññavutti*) is aggregated. Those whose application is "concluded" (*avasita*) are those whose application is determined.
The connection is: "Those [trees], such as the *sīsa* and others, whose existence was determined, then attain [the state] even without effort (*payatana*).

Regarding "effort," there is the statement: "Even when excellence is obtained through capability. This is a resolution for cases such as "non-existence" (*anatthitta*), because it is said to be for the sake of stating the mere form (*sarūpamatta*).
Just as in the example, "Bring many cakes," which is used to state the mere form of things of that same class, so too here it is connected to the manner of stating the mere form.
He states the summary: “*Tadevaṃ*,” etc. This is a collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāyo*), and it functions in the sense of “in the manner already described.
To show that the statement exists even when only one of the two [qualifier or qualified] is possible, he says: “*Atha pi*,” etc.

“*Aññatarasambhavepi*” means even when there is the possibility of either the qualifier (*visesana*) or the qualified (*visessa*). Furthermore, although the relationship between qualifier and qualified may exist for both.
In that case, the formation of a compound is generally prevented by the mere mention of the word itself; however, to show how it might otherwise occur through some other possibility, he says:
‘Just as Puṇṇo,’ and so forth. Here, since there are others who also bear the name Puṇṇa, there is the possibility of ambiguity (vyabhicāra);

thus, when both [words] can stand in the relationship of qualifier and qualified, the mention of the word “generally” (bahulaṃ) alone prevents the compound from forming even in such instances. Thus it is said.
"Even when there is another [type of] relation"—that is, not only when there is the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), but also when there is such another relation;
this is the meaning of the word "even" (*api*).

If it were as stated in the passage beginning with "yajjevam," etc., then the objection regarding the production of an undesirable consequence would apply to each [term] individually when they stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified. Individually...
The qualifier (*visesana*) might apply to both because of their shared status as qualifiers; regarding this, he states the fault: “The prior placement of the qualified (*visessa*) [should occur].

Here, *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), or for the conjunction of another statement. From what [does this follow]? He says: “When not grasped,” and so forth; here *iti* indicates the reason. Therefore, he asks:
“What undesirable consequence follows? and answers: “Even ‘blue lotus’ (*uppalanīla*) could occur. Thus, in this case, what does he say? “Blue lotus” (*nīluppala*).
"Ceccādi. He states the refutation: "nesadoso ccādi. He states another argument: "atha ce ccādi.
"Aññamaññānupakārittā" means that there is no mutual assistance in their relationship as qualifier and qualified; the sense is that they possess predominance [over one another]. Then he asks:

"Why should there not be non-predominance for both? and answers: "appadhānattepi ccādi," meaning "even when there is non-predominance, [they are] those possessing dependence upon their respective predominances."

[This refers to] those who have expectations regarding their respective efforts (*padhāna*). Now, one might wonder: "Whence is it that effort belongs only to the substance (*dabba*) and not to the quality (*guṇa*)?
Anticipating this doubt, he introduces the following reasoning with the words "But if... and so forth. A *chāga* is called a goat;
"you should sacrifice" (*ālabhetha*) it means you should kill it, or touch it—the root *labh* preceded by *ā-* indeed signifies killing.
"It is appropriate for touching" means it is appropriate for the instruction; "codanāyanti" means "codanāvākya," which in this context means a Vedic statement (*vedavākya*).
Why? Because nothing other than a goat can be obtained; thus he says, "Indeed not," and so forth.

"In the absence of a goat" means in the absence of a goat endowed with white qualities; "a lump of flour may be sacrificed" means one should sacrifice a lump of flour by way of its association with the quality of whiteness. And since it is not the case that [the goat] is not sacrificed, therefore the word "quality" (*guṇa*) must be supplied as subordinate (*appadhāna*).
Challenging again, he said: "Is it not so? and so forth. He suspects the intended meaning [of the opponent] and points out an undesirable consequence:
"The same would apply even to the word 'blue'. From where does he say this? From the words beginning with "For that too," and so forth. This is what is meant:

"The word *uppala* (lotus) denotes a genus (*jāti*), not an individual substance (*dabba*). If it is claimed that it denotes a substance because the genus qualifies the substance, then the word 'blue' (*nīla*) would likewise [denote a substance]."

"There is no difference between these two [cases]: 'because it expresses a substance qualified by qualities' and 'it arrives at the expression of a substance,'" he said, offering a rebuttal with the words "this is not so," and so forth.
It is understood that "substances" (dabba) are those that depart, meaning they are liable to fall away. From what? He says "even though," and so forth; thus, it refers to the cause.
Although the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] in a single sense" (visesanaṃ ekatthena) is already established, he provides many examples to avoid prolixity and for the sake of clarity.
The followers of Pāṇini have cited many rules; however, in order to show that all of them are subject to rejection, only a mere example was shown in the *Vṛtti*.
Now, wishing to explain this, he says: "In the sense of 'prior time,' etc. The connection is with the rule *chinnañca visesananti* (2-1-49):

"The words *pubba*, *kāla*, *eka*, *sabba*, *dhura*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* [form a compound] when combined with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). These [words] are to be applied here.
In the Sutta, examples for the application of "eka" and the others have not been shown there;

rather, it is stated—beginning with "eke" and so forth—to demonstrate that they are understood through their function as indicators (upalakkhaṇa). The analysis (viggaha) is "eko ca so puriso ca," and because they serve as indicators, one should also understand examples such as "satta ca te isayo ca = sattisayo."
That by which something is compared or delimited is the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison); that which is compared is the *upameyya* (the object of comparison).

That quality which is common to both the *upamāna* and the *upameyya* is the *sāmañña* (commonality). The meaning is: "by means of the word [expressing] that which distinguishes the *upameyya* through that commonality. The remainder [of the sentence], "for what [purpose] does a compound (*samāsa*) occur for the *upamāna*, the *upameyya*, and so forth?"—he states the reason:
"in the case of a distinction (*visesa*), etc."; for there is no apprehension of a distinction [other than the commonality]. It is precisely the qualifier (*visesana*) itself.
"By way of commonality" (*sāmaññena*) means "of such a kind" (*evambhūtassa*), that is, even of the form of the object of comparison. [Objection:

Is it not the case that the word *satthi* functions with reference to a ploughshare (*satthi*), whereas the word *sāmā* refers to Devadattā? Therefore, because they have different grammatical bases (*byadhikaraṇattā*), how can a compound (*samāsa*) be suspected here?

To this he says: "That which... and so forth. That which has a common property (*sadhammo*)—such as being a measure (*sāmatta*) and so on—is "possessing a common property"; the state of that is "commonality of property" (*sādhammiyam*), namely, the state of being a measure.
Therefore, the word *sāma* functions with reference to Devadatta by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Even though the compound word *sāma* is a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), it refers to Devadatta either by expressing the quality of "evenness" (*sāmatta*) or through the metaphorical designation of non-difference based on his possession of faith and other qualities.

But is it not the case that if the word *sāma* denotes Devadatta, there would follow the undesirable consequence of an indefinite perception of qualities—since he is the substratum of many qualities—on the grounds that the quality [of evenness] is indicated as being "by means of a quality" (*guṇena niddiṭṭhā*)? This is because [Devadatta] is the locus of multiple qualities.
Suspecting [the opponent] might object, he says, “Even if,” and so forth.
Here, *iha* is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*), meaning “in the midst of these qualities”; or, it means “in this army” (*satthiyaṃ*).

Because of its possession of the quality of harmony, it is understood as *sāmāya*. By way of common usage, the army (*satthī*) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and Devadatta is the object of comparison (*upameyya*).
That which is well-established (*pasiddha*) serves as the analogy (*upamāna*), not that which is unestablished.

Since an analogy is defined as the means of proving (*sādhana*) the subject to be proven (*sādhya*) by virtue of its established similarity (*sādhammiya*), it is the *sāli* (rice) itself that is well-established through its constituent qualities, not Devadatta; therefore, the meaning is "by way of the establishment of the qualities of the *sāli*.

It is called an analogy (*upamāna*) because by it something is proven (*sādhyate*) or compared (*upamīyate*); it is called the subject to be proven (*sādhya*) because it is proven or compared (*upadhīyate*).
The establishment of something that is unestablished by means of something already established that shares its properties is "proof of the probandum" (*sādhyasādhana*).

Having stated that a compound exists even with a general term through the power of common usage— as in the passage beginning with "wherever..."— the examples "like rice [is separated] by ploughshares," and so forth,
were introduced to clarify, by means of another example, that it does not exist in other cases.

The phrase "the word *taṇḍula*" refers to the word *taṇḍula* as that which is being illustrated (*upameyya*). The connection is as follows: even after stating its quality as rice (*taṇḍulatva*), it does not become a general term (*sāmaññavacana*) applied to the substance (*dabba*). "To the substance" means to both the substance of rice and the substance of a ploughshare.

"In the absence of the application of words denoting qualities common to the simile and the thing illustrated" means in the absence of the application of words such as "courageous" (*visārada*), which denote qualities like courage common to both the simile and the thing illustrated, as in the expression: "This sage is courageous like a lion."
The meaning is that, among certain words, it clarifies the state of being a qualifier (*visesana*) alone.

By the phrase “If it were so,” etc., the intention is that since the qualifier and the qualified exist according to their respective natures, there would always be a contingency for the prior placement (*pubbanipāta*) of the word because of the qualification of lions and so forth.
He states another supporting argument: “Of the qualifier alone,” etc.; even though the lion is indeed a qualifier and not the qualified, [the rule applies].
Nevertheless, the intention is that because of the predominance of frequency, there is even the posterior placement of the qualifier (*visesana*).

Now, here too, when forming a compound with the qualifier at the end— as in "this man is like a lion, being courageous" (*sīho va visārado*)— even though a compound would otherwise be applicable by implication through the force of the context,
