it does not occur unless there is an expression of a common attribute such as courage shared by both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
He raises an objection with the words “Is it not so? (*nanu ce*) and so forth, suggesting that the statement should be commenced for the purpose of avoiding its connection with that [fault].

Regarding the phrase “by virtue of its capacity” (*sāmatthiyato*): the meaning is that because there is a state of expectancy when a general term (*sāmānyavacana*) is employed, a compound (*samāsa*) would otherwise result; therefore, it is by virtue of that capacity.

The phrase “the meaning of the non-employment of the general term” (*sāmaññappayogatthaṃ*) means the sense of not employing the general term—such as *sūra* (heroic) and so on—in a compound sentence; for it is thus, by means of the words beginning with “for indeed” (*tathā hi*), that the general term is employed.
By virtue of its capacity and the presence of a compound, it establishes that another sutta is not subject to being commenced [as a separate discourse].

Regarding "the absence of a distinct subsequent state": even though the general term is included within the compound, because the specific quality to be expressed—such as "heroic" which is distinguished by qualities like sharpness—is not included within the compound, there is no occasion for the objection that "that which is dependent is incapable. Now, [he quotes] "This is true," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: [the rule] must be undertaken for the purpose of making known that a compound may be formed even when there is apprehension of a contrary statement, for the sake of establishing such cases, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of the principal" (*padhānassa*): in the expression "the king’s man is handsome" (*rañño puriso abhirūpo*), the word *purisa* (man), which depends on *abhirūpa* (handsome), is itself the qualifier;
it is the principal because, as a constituent part of the compound, it does not lose its own inherent meaning by being subordinate to the king (*rājānaṃ*). Thus, it remains the principal.
[This refers to] a man who is the primary factor (*padhānabhūta*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes examples such as “the king’s man’s house to be seen.

For here, even though the master of the house is subordinate (*appadhāna*) by virtue of being a qualifier, a compound still occurs with respect to the man who is the primary factor in relation to the king, even though that [man] is itself dependent (*sāpekkha*).
This is stated for the purpose of making this known and to show the motive for beginning the rule; he states the reason: “because it is indicative,” and so forth.
"Because it is indicative": since the meaning of the analytical statement (*viggahavākya*) is understood even within the compound (*vutti*), it is therefore "indicative.

As for the phrase "there is no indicativeness here," the meaning is that the sense which is understood from the sentence "The sage is like a lion, [he is] a hero" is not understood from the expression "The sage is a lion, a hero";

thus, there is no indicativeness. For instance, by the word "muni-sīha" (lion-muni) alone, the cause for the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—[namely, the quality of being brave]—is indicated.
Because [the word] *visāra* is derived from its own inherent nature (*sabhāva*) as "grasping" (*upādāna*), there is no connection between it and the word *datta*.
[The author] points out the meaning excluded by the particle *eva*—namely, that *apavagga* is *nibbāna* and nothing else—by stating, "it excludes other occurrences" (*vutti-nivatteti*).

This is understood through the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*). But would this not result in the undesirable consequence (*appasaṅga*) of there being no possibility of a qualified relationship (*visessabhāva*) here? Indeed, it would.

He challenges [the opponent] with the words beginning "But surely," and so forth. "Non-deviation from fullness" means that because the specific states such as being a fool—which are designated as "fullness"—do not occur without [the underlying essence], there can be no deviation;

for only that which deviates [from its substrate] can be a qualifier, just as a blue lotus [deviates from the general category of lotuses]. He refutes this with the words "This is not so," and so forth, regarding the sons of Mātaṅga.
"Multiplicity" (anekatta) refers to the fact that they are not merely Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī, but rather their plurality;
thus, the multiplicity of householders (gahapati) is evident from the term "protectors of their respective households.

By the particle "eva" in the phrase "vuttiyeva," he expresses the meaning excluded [by it], namely, "it restricts the sentence. They are called "words expressing distinguished classes" because of the distinction between the class of black snakes and the class of red rice.
The woodcutter is explained as being like a snake; having been challenged by the presentation of the argument, he says, "Is it not so," and so forth.

"Not devoid of the state of a woodcutter" means he has not departed from the state of a woodcutter defined by such factors as childhood or youth. "Possessing that name" means there is someone named 'woodcutter' who bears that name.
It is a verbal noun (kiriyāsaddo), for it is derived as "one who cuts" (*tacchati*) is a "woodcutter" (*tacchako*), thus being grasped as the causal basis for the occurrence of the action.

The word *tacchaka* [carpenter] is synonymous with *vaḍḍhakī* [builder]. Thus, one might think: "Since there exists a qualifier and a qualified according to the method already stated, a compound ought to occur;
if that is so, why has this counter-example (*paccudāharaṇa*) been given?

To refute this objection—which is being raised here by someone who thinks that [the rule] beginning with "not after a name" and ending with "does not occur"—the author says: "In the case of *yo-pā-he*, etc."

The intention here is this: "Since, according to the method stated, the word *tacchaka* lacks dependence on the sphere of meaning of the word *kiriyā* (action), and because there is no qualifying attribute (*visesana*), this has been made a counter-example.

Why does he say it is "inappropriate" with the words "since" (*yato*) and so forth? [He asks this] in order to investigate whether the capacity to express a meaning is equal or not for both a proper name (*nāmadheyya*) and a word denoting an action (*kiriyāvācin*), and whether the establishment of the whole (*samudāyappasiddhi*) is stronger than the establishment of the parts (*avayavappasiddhi*).
Since there is no purpose for an additional string [of commentary], why then does he speak with an additional string, beginning with "But rather" (*api tu*)?
The construction is as follows: one should investigate whether the word *tacchaka* has multiple meanings or not;

thus, he employs an additional string. He thinks thus: "In this investigation into the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, it is an investigation into the capacity of words to express their respective meanings."
It is not logical that a qualification is purposeful only when there is the possibility [of confusion] and the existence of deviation;
rather, a qualification is sought out precisely where there is no impossibility and no deviation, as in the case of "cold snow" or "hot fire.

Therefore, the consideration of possibility and deviation is useful only in the context of considering the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. Thus, the question remains whether the word *tacchaka* has multiple meanings or not.
Even if it is argued that "a compound occurs whenever there is the presence of a qualifier and a qualified,

regardless of whether the former is more extensive," and even though names and words expressing actions denote their meanings unequally and possess greater strength through conventional usage (*samudāyappasiddhi*),
nevertheless, he says "And here... and so forth to show that there is no deficiency whatsoever because a compound is possible according to the method that will be explained.
The connection is as follows: "In this case" (*ettha ca*) refers to some alternative views, and it brings about a certain pressure [on the opponent].

Why? He says: "For thus" (*tathā hi*), and so forth. He thinks thus: "Even if, when there is the establishment of a collective whole (*samudāya*), no expectation regarding the object of the meaning of a verbal noun arises, nevertheless, the fact that the word *tacchaka*—like a proper name (*nāmadheyya*)—has multiple meanings remains exactly as it is... [in the case of] a particular kind of snake."

"And because the word *tacchaka* exists as a designation for humans of that same name, the possibility of a compound [of the form *manussa-tacchaka*] remains exactly as it was, due to the existence of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*visesanavisessasabbhāvato*).
The meaning of the particle *pi* is that the word *tacchaka* is a designation not only for the specific type of wood-cutter (*sappavisesasseva*), but also for humans.
Even though the word *tacchaka* has multiple meanings, [the compound is not formed] because the conventional usage of the whole [term *manussatacchaka*] is not established.
In order to show that there is no sublation (bādhā) due to the non-establishment of the members [of the syllogism], he says "And not" (na ca), etc. The particle *co* is used for emphasis.

To the question "From where?", he says "In the case of action" (kiriye), etc. The construction is as follows: "That which is the establishment of the meaning in sequence—that too cannot be understood. "That" (yaṃ) refers to the proof;
"in sequence" (kamenā) means by way of successive order because of the absence of sublation. And by the phrase "and thus" (evaṃ ca), he refers to the passage beginning with "And not" (na ca).
"Vuttaṃ paccāmasati" means "he recalls what was said"; the sense is, "what might have been provided, what might have been carried away?
For this reason, the counter-example "the woodcutter-snake" (tacchaka-sappa) is not appropriate; the intention is that it is because of the existence of the compound "woodcutter-snake.
He resolves [the objection] with the words "this is not so," etc., when there is the possibility of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified as stated.
To this he asks: "How then? and says: "When [there is] a qualifier," and so forth. To the question, "Even then, how should there be a sentence?
he says: "And this," and so forth. The intention is: "Precisely because of the statement that it is 'mostly' (bahulaṃ).

Regarding the word "of another" (aññassa), the genitive case is used when there is a desire to express a relationship with the object (kamma). In the phrase "because of being a delimiting factor" (avacchedakattā), [the agent] is connected with the agent (kartuṇā).
In the phrase *bhavitabbaṃ kāḷassa*, the genitive case is to be supplied [to *kāḷa*] because it expresses the agent (*kattar*) in connection with the action (*bhāva*).

Regarding the compound *jīvikappatto*: when used with words ending in the accusative, such as *jīvikā*, the compound *jīvikappatto* (one who has attained a livelihood) is prescribed by the rule "The agent is frequently [compounded]" (*Candaviveka* 2.2.19).

However, others have formulated a separate sutta for the purpose of compounding those [words] with the accusative, and they also provide the meaning for those [forms] even when they are feminine gender.
In brief, through the cessation of the cause, [the compound] "māso jātassa" (a month of one who is born) is analyzed as follows:

when time-words denoting a measure are combined with words expressing that which possesses the measure, ending in the sixth case, it is said: "of those that have reached [the state]," and so forth. That which possesses the measure—such as a month—is the limit;
because one who is born possesses that [measure], he is called "parimāṇī" (that which possesses the measure).
For here, "month" (*māsa*) is the measure (*parimāṇa*) because it is the delimiter (*paricchedaka*), and "born" (*jāta*) is the measured (*parimāṇī*) because it is the delimited (*paricchejja*).

Regarding the reading *patta-jīvika*, it should be understood as "one who has obtained a livelihood" (*pattā jīvikā anena*); thus, according to the intended meaning of the word, there must be a compound of two words (*aññapada-ttha-samāsa*).

To demonstrate that this [rule] applies even in such compounds of different words without departing from the intended meaning of the rule, it was stated in the *Vutti*: "It shall apply when there is another word's meaning (*aññapadatthe bhavissati*)."

Desiring to explain that, he says: *“vānekaññatthe icceva,”* etc. When another compound (*aññattha-samāsa*) has been formed, in all instances there is masculinization (*pumbhāva*) according to [Pāṇini 7.1.74], *itthiyaṃ bhāsite,* etc.

To show that in the phrase *“māso jātassa”* (a month since birth), the suffix *-ya-* (yo) which occurs when such a desire for expression exists remains unchanged even in an *aññattha-samāsa*, provided there is no difference in the desire for expression, he says: *“yassa jātādino,”* etc.

He states the meaning of the word *jāta* as "accomplished" (*sampanna*), which means "complete" (*sampuṇṇa*). By this, the meaning of the analysis (*viggaha*)—namely, "the month has been completed for him"—is shown.
"Otherwise" means that if the month does not appear to be complete for that other referent (*aññapadattha*) such as the person born, [the compound is not formed].

Having prescribed the technical designation "termination" (*niṭṭhā*) for words ending in *tta*, *ta*, and *vantu*, [the rule] "in a compound whose final member is designated as 'termination'" (*niṭṭhā*) applies. (Pāṇini 2.2.36)

The *pubbanipāta* (prior placement) was stated by the Sutta; thus he says, "If not," and so forth. The connection is that there would be no occurrence of the *pubbanipāta*. From where [does this follow]? He says, "Because of the genus" (*jāti*), and so forth.

To whom does he refer with the word "of some" (*kesañci*)? He refers to the author of the sentence. The connection is that it is not appropriate. He states the reason: "Because it is a qualifier" (*visesana*), and so forth.
By the phrase "for instance" (*tathāhi*), and so forth, he shows that when the qualifier has a meaning, there is the presence of the compound, and when it lacks one, there is its absence.
He establishes [the point]: because an adjective becomes meaningful when there is a possibility of ambiguity (*byabhicāra*) in the absence of a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*).

"Even if it is not stated" means even if the restrictive statement is absent; for otherwise, according to the method already explained, there would be the undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) of a genitive compound.
If it were argued that because there is no exclusion [of other meanings], the qualification would be redundant and thus the compound should not exist, then it would likewise not exist as a sentence;
therefore he says, "But the sentence," and so forth. Furthermore, this qualifying compound (visesanasamāsa) is known by others as a *kammadhāraya*.
Just as a deed (*kamma*) bears both action (*kiriyā*) and purpose (*payojana*), so too this compound bears a twofold nature like a deed.

12. *Nañ* [is added] "right here" means precisely in the sutta *ṭa nañssa* (3-74). Regarding *pāmanaputto*: since he has a particular kind of leprosy (*pāma*), the suffix *na* is applied to the word *pāma* by the rule *dissantaññepi paccayā* (4-120);
thus it is *pāmana*. [The compound] is "the son of one who has leprosy. If, in this case—
The letter *ñ* would not have been used for the sake of specification; in that case, the rule would have been formulated as “*ṭa nassā*” (let *ṭ* take the place of *na*).
And if that were so, there would be the possibility that even the *n* in the word *pāmana* would become *ṭ* when followed by a subsequent member of a compound.
Is it not the case, then, that in this rule for compound formation, the pronunciation of the letter *ñ* indicates that there is no compound formation for that which lacks the elision of *ñ*?
It is appropriate to say that it "exists," but not that the letter *ñ* has the purpose of specification according to the rule “ṭa nañssā.

It must indeed be true that the letter *ñ* here serves the purpose of specification; however, in this rule for compound formation (*samāsavidhi*), no exclusion (*byavaccheda*) of the letter *ñ* is observed.

As for the term *pariyudāsavutti*: *pari* means having thoroughly considered and grasped; *udāsa* means the non-eating, the casting aside, or the avoidance of that which is to be negated; thus, *pariyudāsa* [refers to] a statement of exclusion.
"Paryudāsa-vṛtti" (exclusionary function) is the function [of a term] in a sense qualified by that exclusion;

"prasajya-pratiṣedha-vṛtti" (negation-by-implication function) is a negation that, having first implied (*prasajya*) the very thing to be negated, proceeds to negate it without regard for anything similar to it;
the function belonging to that is "prasajya-pratiṣedha-vṛtti."
In the statement "wherein a brahmin becomes someone else," because it prescribes a different meaning through the phrase itself, the primary function is that of a prescription (*vidhi*);
by the very power of prescribing a different meaning, the negation of the brahmin is understood.
Since the prescription of another occurs in dependence upon the exclusion of the brahmin, the negative particle (*nañ*) participates in the function of prescription by its own word.

It is not so stated; rather, it is because of the employment of the word *añña* (other) itself as a *pariyudāsa* (presuppositional negation) based on a support within the sentence—as in "one other than a brahmin is a non-brahmin" (*añño brāhmaṇā abrāhmaṇo*)—and because the negative particle *nañ* possesses syntactic force (*sāmatthiya*) with that which ends in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*), not with that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tyādyanta*).
Thus, there is a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatā*), since in each instance the expression functions as a *pariyudāsa*, as in "one other than a brahmin is a non-brahmin."

Because the negation is the primary element for the purpose of negating the path, the sentence "he is not a brahmin" constitutes a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) where the negation of the brahmin is understood as a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, by its own word—the negative particle (*nañ*)—it is connected with that which expresses the state of being subject to negation.
To the question "Who is he other than a brahmin?", it is said: "one who does not adhere to brahminhood," and so forth.

"In the other" (*itarasmiṃ*) refers to the negation of a categorical assertion (*pasajjappaṭisedha*). "By some cause for doubt" (*kenaci saṃsayanimittena*) means by some reason for uncertainty, such as the sight of a sacred thread (*upavīta*) and so forth.
Every word, when used in its own sense, depends upon knowledge; and that knowledge is twofold:
right knowledge (*sammāñāṇa*) and wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*). Both of these bring about the application of the word "brāhmaṇa. Among those, right knowledge...
In the case of ancient usages of the term *abrāhmaṇa*, there is no function for the negative particle (*nañ*); for in those instances, nothing at all is effected by it.
However, in cases preceded by wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*), its function does exist; for in such cases, it expresses that the other [the object] originates from wrong knowledge.

And since wrong knowledge is caused by the sense faculties (*indriya*) and does not occur without a similarity [to the object], when there is a negation, [the result] is similar to the meaning of the subsequent word.
He states that the compound meaning arises here: "In that regard, 'similarity' [is the cause]," and so forth. For the cognition of a snake in a rope occurs due to similarity.
And "due to the capacity of the expression" means due to the capacity of expressions such as "bring a non-Brahmin.

One thinks thus: "If in this case there were merely the bringing of any Brahmin, the utterance of the first member of the compound would be purposeless; therefore, it refers to no one [other than a specific type]."
"Even this bringing forward [of the example] serves to show that the entire word 'brāhmaṇa' is devoid of meaning; therefore, by the power of the application, there is a similar practice.
"Taggata" means gone to a similar meaning.
This statement of the wise is offered for the purpose of further elaborating upon the very meaning already stated.

“For this very reason it is said,” and so forth. And here the meaning is as follows: that which is joined with the negative particle (*nañ*) and the word *iva* produces an application toward another object similar to the referent of that [original] word;
for such a correspondence of meaning is seen in common usage, as in “bring a non-Brahmin” (*abrāhmaṇamānaya*), where a Kshatriya or similar person resembling a Brahmin is brought.
That in which a word is placed or employed is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

And what is intended to be established by the explanation just stated? He says: "That very [thing]," and so forth. However, some here describe it as having the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) as predominant.
"Of those who maintain the capacity" means of those who maintain that "the rule for compounds applies to words that are semantically capable" (*samattho padavidhi*, Pāṇini 2.1.1).

The connection is: "for those who maintain the capacity, a compound is to be prescribed. "To be prescribed" (*vidheyyo*) means that which is to be enjoined by another statement; for instance, in the case of *apunageyyā* ("not to be sung again").

The negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with "singing" (*gāyana*), but not with the sense of the word "again" (*puna*). In the phrase "having made no space," there is a connection with the act of "making" (*karaṇa*), not with "space" (*okāsa*).

In "having gone from root to root" (*amūlamūlaṃ gantvā*), the connection is with "going" (*gamana*), and not with "root" (*mūla*); this indicates a lack of semantic capacity. Regarding the view that it conveys meaning (*gamakattavādin*):

even where there is a lack of semantic capacity, if there is the quality of conveying meaning (*gamakatta*), a compound (*samāsa*) certainly occurs; therefore, the quality of conveying meaning belongs to the compound itself.
"Nibandhanaṃ" means "of him who says [this]"; this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "even here," it refers to the rule *apunar-geyya* and so forth. One might object:

"Is not this teacher also one who maintains that [the suffix -ya] is productive (*gamaka*)? If that is so, why did he not state 'because of its productivity' instead of saying 'by virtue of the governing rule of *bahula*'?
To this he replies with the words beginning 'If he...'. He says 'only by some, not by all' in order to show that the meaning is delimited by the specific wording of the grammatical treatise."
*Apunageyyā* is formed by the elision of *na* according to the rule *ṭa nañssā* (Pāṇini 6.3.74). This is because there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*);
for even though a compound is not prescribed by another sutta [in this specific case], there is no apprehension of an unintended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "in the rule for *syādi*," since the case endings (*kārakavibhatti*) are prescribed separately from the rules for [the suffixes] such as *itthambhūta*, it refers to the rule for *syādi* which has attained the designation "rule for *syādi*.
By stating "in the rule for *asyādi*," he suggests that this is a *pariyudāsa* (exclusion) rather than a *natthakā* (negation), and says "Is it not...

and so forth, [arguing] that it would be meaningless because the meanings of the grammatical markers (*lakkhaṇa*) and so on are subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) within a compound; therefore, from the compound, there is no meaning for a case ending that conforms to a connection with an action.

By way of its primary function, it avoids [the fault] through such expressions as "this is not so" and so forth. Regarding the term *anunā* (2-10), because of the power of the rule prescribing the accusative case when joined with *anu* in the sense of diminution (*vicchā*), it also functions as a sentence;
otherwise, in a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*), the prescription of the accusative would be purposeless—this is the intended meaning.

He concludes with "therefore" (*tasmā*) and so forth. The reading of other authorities for the root *ku* is "in the sense of evil" (*pāpatthe*); likewise, in subsequent instances such as "du in the sense of reproach" (*nindāyaṃ*), it should be understood in this same manner.
14. Regarding *cīkri cīsaddo*:
here, by the word *cī*, it refers to that which ends in the suffix *cī*; thus, the meaning is "a word ending in the suffix *cī*.
15. *Bhūsa*.

*Pītisambhamo* means the agitation caused by rapture (*pīti*). It is a state of haste—preceded by rapture—regarding such matters as rising from one's seat or giving a gift; it is having eaten enough, having eaten to satiety and completion.
16. *Aññe*: having come forward, having come to the front. *Tirobhūya*: having become invisible, having disappeared. Regarding *anaccādhāne*, the meaning of this is "from above" (*upariyādhānato*).
"Except for" means setting down or placing; "those who desire" refers to Pāṇini and others who so desire;
"having placed the hand on the breast" means having placed the hand upon the chest.
17. In the forest.
He proceeds to state the purpose of the inclusion of the term *aneka* with the words "here" (*idha*), etc.

"The commonality of the intended singular number" (*vivacchitekasaṅkhyāsāmañña*) means the commonality of the singular number that is intended to be expressed. He thinks thus: "If there were no inclusion of the commonality of the singular number intended to be expressed by saying 'of this' (*asya*) and so on, then the inclusion of *aneka* here would be purposeless;
therefore, it is precisely by the power of the inclusion of *aneka* here [that the purpose is established]."
By the phrase "‘syādi-syādine’ti... pariggahitan" (the commonality of the number intended to be expressed by "syādi" and "syādi" is grasped), he shows by means of this and so forth:
"Therefore, every compound previously mentioned according to what was stated occurs only between two [words] ending in 'syādi' suffixes, namely the preceding and the following."

If this is so, how is it that “*tadahujāto*” (*born on that very day*) is established either by the rule of plurality (*bahulādhikāra*) or by a compound containing a qualifying factor (*visesana-samāsa-gabbha-kāraka-samāsa*)?

This is an *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound of a different referent). Because the plural is desired in the sense of the fourth [case], there is the inclusion of the word "many" (*aneka*) for that purpose;

thus, when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is connected to the womb (*yoni*), the preceding member [becomes plural], as in “*hotu potu pitā puttā*” (“be there sons, grandsons, fathers, and children”).
By the rule "putte" (3-65), [the word *putta*] is attracted [to the preceding term].

Otherwise, since a compound of two and two [terms] would be possible everywhere due to the existence of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), it would result in the form "hotā potā pitā puttā" by being attracted by both rules:
"vijjāyonisambandhānamā tatra catthe" (3-64) and "putte" (3-65). Because [the word] "anekaṃ" ends in the nominative case, the word "syādi" is understood to follow here; therefore, it is "anekaṃ".

It is stated that [the compound] consists of words ending in case-suffixes (*syādyanta*). Now, when it is said "of another meaning" (*aññattha*), why is it stated as "of a word" (*padassa*) rather than saying "of the meaning of another sentence" (*aññassa vākyassa atthe*)?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of that which ends in a case-suffix," and so forth. The connection is that by the force of the context (*sāmatthiya*), the compound is understood to belong specifically to the word ending in a case-suffix.

The term *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa* means that the other referent (*aññapadattha*) is indicated by its qualities (*tagguṇā*) through its own expression. "Its qualities" refers to those attributes or qualifiers belonging to that other referent;
the "cognition" (*saṃviññāṇa*) or apprehension of these is *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*. Alternatively, it is that which has such a quality (*guṇa*), thus "possessing that quality" (*tagguṇo*);
the cognition of that other referent as being endowed with that quality (*tagguṇa*), and not [the cognition] of one devoid of that quality.

Regarding *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa* (the cognition of its own quality): here, however, it is stated as a grammatical maxim (*paribhāsā*) that "in the case of another word-meaning [in a compound], there is also the cognition of its own quality.
In this context, the meaning is: "In a compound where there is another word-meaning, that other word-meaning is understood together with its qualifier, and not devoid of its qualifier.

In some instances, the particle *api* is used even when there is no cognition of its own quality; this occurs where the analysis (*viggaha*) is by means of a part, and the whole is the meaning of the compound.
In that very case, there is the cognition of its own quality (*tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*); other than the cognition of its own quality is the non-cognition of its own quality (*atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*).
In that instance where the meaning of the compound is merely the constituent parts themselves, there is the non-cognition of its own quality.

Here, however, the word *bahudhana* (possessing much wealth) is used because it serves as a characteristic mark for the person. It is "approved" (*abhimata*) by the followers of Pāṇini in such sentences as "near ten" (*dasannamāsanne*) or "close to ten" (*dasannamiccādi*).
"Number itself is the countable" means that the characteristic of number itself is the countable; and that characteristic of number is also the countable.
"The nature of counting" means having the essential quality of counting.
"By number" means by the number called 'countable' which is delimited by the number five.

"Functioning as a number" (*saṅkhyānavutti*) means that which has its functioning in "numbering" (*saṅkhyāna*)—that is, in that which is reckoned as a form of numbering which delimits and is not exceeded by it;

such is the "functioning as a number" [of the word] *pañca* (five). By this example he illustrates this: "Just as in the case of *pañcakā* (groups of five), where the base-meaning (*pakatiyattha*) is the nature of a collection consisting of distinct parts whose measure is five, and the meaning of the suffix is the possessors of that collection, so too it is here in the case of *tidasā* (the thirty-three). This refers to the *ka*-suffix.
By the phrase "due to the possibility of a distinction between the base meaning and the meaning of the suffix" (*pakatippaccayatthabhedasambhavena*), he indicates [that this applies] to Pāṇini.

By the phrase "due to the possibility of a distinction between the base meaning and the meaning of the suffix," he shows that the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*) for the technical term (*saññā*), because others maintain that there is no such distinction between the base meaning and the meaning of the suffix in their system.
By the phrase *syādyantassāti*, he shows that the word *vā* possesses the status of a grammatical term (*pada*).
Regarding the expression *tadatthe pi*: it means "even in the sense of that [word] *vā*," which is another term.

Here, its meaning is the sense of "option" (*vikappa*), such that when there is the inclusion of two, there are not three; and when there is the inclusion of those [three], there are not two. Or, it may mean "doubt" (*saṃsaya*); in that case, however—
Because doubt has the nature of taking two objects, when "two" is stated, three are implied; and when "three" is stated, two are implied.
Thus, five meanings that are objects of the intellect become the referents of the compound.

By the term "name-only" (*nāmamatta*) means by way of conventional designation (*ruḷhināmamatta*); this is what is intended by the followers of Pāṇini, as it is established by another sutta through the rule for the designation of all nouns (*sabbanāmasaññā*) by means of the option (*vikappa*) known as *vibhāsā*.
"By the nature of its parts" means by the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) designated as the parts.

Now, it might be argued that according to Pāṇini, a *bahubbīhi* compound is taught for terms in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), such as "one whose meal was eaten by five," but not for those in different grammatical relations (*byadhikaraṇa*).
Likewise, excluding the sense of the nominative case, it is desired [that the compound be formed] in all other case-senses, as in "the high place where it rained."

Thinking, "It should not be [interpreted as] 'one who has emerged from the rain' (*vuṭṭha-deva*)," he asks: "How then is a compound of words with different grammatical bases (*byadhikaraṇa*) explained here in the sense of the first [member]? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Even of those with different bases," and so forth. Since a compound exists even for words with different bases according to their specific expression—as in "pañcahi bhuttam assa" (it is eaten by five)—it will not occur [in such cases] either due to the rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikāra*) or due to non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).
And for that very reason, it does not occur even for words with the same grammatical base (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in "pañca bhutta vanta-ssa."
"In some places it will not exist; likewise, in the first instance as well, it will not exist in some places when the rain has fallen.
The meaning is: "when a coordinate connection (*tulyayoga*) is implied.

"In other cases" (*aññatra*) refers to cases other than a coordinate connection, such as in *salomako* ("one who has hair") and so forth; [it means] "one for whom hair exists," "one for whom [something] exists."

The analysis [of the compound] is *pakkhā assa* (“whose wings are”). It is added [to the rule] under the heading of *syāt-* by the Vārttika: “There is an addition for *itthi*, *khīra*, and so on” (2-2-24-vā).

This exclusion occurs by its very nature (*sabhāvato*) and not from another sutta; for even when the meaning has already been conveyed, there might be a lack of restriction in usage, as in the case of placing flour [on the fire].
How indeed could it be otherwise? For example, in the expressions: “Bring many Brahmins,” or “I am cooking. It is not necessarily the case that [the suffix must be applied] in this way alone.
In some instances, however, the employment [of a term] does indeed occur when there is a purpose such as the elegance of expression.
"Sambhava in the throat" means the occurrence in the throat of the sound *kāḷa*. "The meaning of the word *ṭṭha*" means the meaning of the word *ṭṭha* within the compound *kaṇṭhaṭṭha-sadda*.

By the phrase "the word *oṭṭha* itself functions for the mouth," he indicates the non-employment of the second word "mouth" (*mukha*), because its meaning is already understood through that implication.
Therefore, having analyzed [the compound] as "that which has lips for its mouth," it is a *oṭṭhamukha* (lip-mouth) compound. Furthermore, one hand is not the mouth of another hand;
and since similarity to a "hand-mouth" is well-established by means of the mouth itself, by implication it remains in the sense of "that which has a mouth like a lip-mouth.
"Upanyāsā" means "introductions"; by the phrase "for the purpose of showing the scope," [it refers to] "on the neck."
He shows that the phrase "kāḷo yassā" and so forth is indeed a single sentence. "In the case of a collective and a modification" means in relation to a collective and in relation to a modification.
"Of that compound" means of that genitive compound; "expressing that" refers to those [words] expressing the collective and the modification, such as the sentence of others:
"the collection of hair," and so on. "Born from an element" (*dhātuja*) means produced from an element; it is the subsequent member [of the compound], with words such as *patita* understood.
Its application (*payoga*) refers to the application of the word *patita*.

Regarding the Vārttika rule “*nañ-smāt-ty-atthānam*” (Pāṇini 2.2.24), this is stated as: ‘[The compound] with the suffix *ñ* as its attendant,’ and so forth. For the followers of Pāṇini, however, the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is the word *avijjamāna*;
in another [grammatical] system, there is no *bahubbīhi* for this [compound], nor is there elision of the final member (*uttara-pada-lopa*), as in *avijjamānā*.
They establish that "his son" (*puttāssa*) is "one who has no son" (*aputto*) when a son is actually present; this is desired by the followers of Pāṇini.

Because words such as *dakkhiṇa* and *pubba* have different meanings and are in different grammatical cases (*byadhikaraṇa*), even though the rule *vacane pi* exists, this is called a *maññapadattha-samāsa* (compound based on a conceptual object) by others, while it is called a *bahubbīhi*.
For instance, "he whose birds are many" is a *bahubbīhi*, just as [the term] *bahubbīhi* itself [is used].
Likewise, this [compound] also has as its primary meaning something other than its constituent parts. 19.

Regarding the term *catthe* (in the sense of a collection): *samuccīti* means "bringing together. Asking "What is it?", he says: "A single means," and so forth. A single means (*sādhana*) is a single action (*kiriya*).

The connection is that [the action] is accumulated (*cīyamānā*) in dependence upon [the factors]. To the question "Of what?", he says: "Of the means of accomplishing the action" (*kiriyāsādhanānaṃ*). To the question "By what?", he says:

"By way of the distinction of their own forms" (*attarūpabhedenā*). In this context, in such expressions as "Devadatta eats," "he stands," or "he cooks," the accumulation of actions in dependence upon the means of accomplishment should be understood by way of the distinction of their own forms. And [in the example]: "Cut the *dhava*, the *khadira*, and the *palāsa* trees."
The accumulation of the means of accomplishment (sādhana) should be understood as occurring through the differentiation of their own forms, dependent upon the action (kiriyā).
The word "he" (so) refers to the remainder [of the sentence], namely, that "there is a conjunction" (samuccayo bhavati). To the question "Of which?", he says:
"Of those of equal strength," and so forth. By the phrase "of equal strength," he indicates their mutual independence, since they are connected to the action individually as primary factors.
"Aniyata-kama-yogapajjānan" means those words whose order (*kama*) and simultaneous application (*yogapajja*) are indefinite. By the words "as follows" (*yathā*), etc., he shows an example therein.

Herein, this is the intended meaning: because the actions of leading are connected here with cows and so forth as individual primary factors, there is an equality of strength among the cows and so forth;
for, due to the absence of leading [them] according to the stated order, [the sequence is not fixed].
"Indeterminacy of desire (*aniyata-kkamatā*) arises from the impossibility of leading cattle and other such animals simultaneously, as well as from indeterminate simultaneity (*aniyata-yogapajjatā*);
the same applies to others of that kind. Subsequent accumulation (*anvācaya*) is the piling up (*cayaṇa*) following the primary [element] in accordance with it;
this is indicated by "wherever," etc. "In accordance with that" means conforming to that; he illustrates this with "just as," etc. Here, the going for alms...

The exertion (*padhāna*) is internal because it is primary, whereas the other is external because it is secondary. If that [exertion] were the instrument, then even if one sees a cow, one would bring her as well;
however, in this case, the bringing of the cow depends upon the wandering for alms, but not the latter upon the former...

because the former can be carried out even without the latter. As for the mutual connection of the one with the other—the *itaretarayoga*—that too is of such a nature; thus he said, "mutually," and so forth.

And because it is "predominant in its members" (*avayavappadhāna*), it is not coarse due to the inherent capacity of its own expression; furthermore, by way of conventional usage, the word *Sāriputta* has the meaning of *Moggallāna*, and the word *Moggallāna* has the meaning of *Sāriputta*.
Thus, when there is a simultaneous expression of two substrates (*adhikaraṇavacana*) through predominance in their mutual meanings, it is a fourfold compound (*catuttha samāsa*).
This aggregate of substrates is fourfold according to the meanings of both members that follow both words.
When grasped simultaneously by the intellect, it is sometimes perceived as having its constituent parts manifested; and by that very capacity for natural denotation, it thus emphasizes the parts.
Now, an objection is raised: how can contradictory things such as "birth" and "death" be expressed by a single term?
It is said in reply: every word being employed functions through mutual exclusion (*avadhāraṇa*); therefore, each individual word [denotes] a single specific meaning.

Although it is the designator [of the whole], nevertheless—just as in the case of "Sāriputta and Moggallāna," where simultaneous expression of the substratum occurs because the plural number would otherwise be untenable—so too here, by the force of the implication characterized by the unavailability of the plural number, there is expression even by a single [term].
Thus, regarding the cause: "because it is thus predominant in its parts" is the meaning.

"Plurality" (*bahutta*): Although there is no separate plurality of meaning for these [words] within the sentence itself—just as when it is said, "Bring Sāriputta," Moggallāna is not thereby included—nevertheless, since their plurality of meaning occurs separately only when they are co-present within the scope of the statement, therefore, in that context, the plurality is determined by the number of the meanings to be expressed. This is "aggregation" (*samāharaṇa*).
“Combining” (*samāhāra*) is the act of gathering together by way of making into a single mass (*piṇḍīkaraṇa*); he says “mutually,” etc., to show that this is how it should be understood.

And here, although the mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*) and the combining (*samāhāra*) are of the nature of abstract entities (*bhāva-rūpa*) and thus lack a physical form (*adabbarūpa*), nevertheless, in the case of mutual conjunction—as in the examples of words expressing qualities such as “a white cloth,” “a white blanket,” or “a white cow”—there is a distinction based on their respective substrates (*nissaya-bheda*).
The establishment of gender and number: thus, the establishment of gender and number should be understood from the perspective of the denotation and the support of those properties.

Regarding "because the aggregate is predominant" (*saṃhatippadhānattā*), the meaning is this: when a collection of many things is treated as a unified whole (*saṃghāta*) in which the distinction between its parts is obscured, then, because the aggregate itself is predominant, there is the singular number. "From the non-performance of that" (*tadanuṭṭhānato*).

Because of its performance. "Intermingling" means mixture; it demonstrates intermingling through the terms "breath," etc., and it demonstrates a multiplicity of sentences for each individual completion with the words "In that regard, indeed," etc.
"The eye and the ear, the mouth and the nose, the jaw and the neck, the skin, the flesh, and the blood."
“Name-and-form,” “aging-and-death”—these are compounds formed by resolving [the respective terms].

In all such cases, the neuter gender is applied according to the rule “in a collective sense, it is neuter” (Pāṇini 2.4.17). In forms beginning with *si* (nominative singular), as in *mukhanāsikaṃ* and so on, the vowel is shortened according to the rule “before endings beginning with *si*, there is shortening” (Pāṇini 6.1.93).
A *gomukha* is a type of drum; a *ḍiṇḍima* is a specific kind of kettle-drum (*bheri*); an *āḷambara* is a small drum (*paṇava*); a *muraja* is a *mudaṅga* drum; and a *maddava* is...

*Mudaṅgo*. The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: *maddavavādanaṃ* (the playing of the *maddava*), *paṇavavādanaṃ* (the playing of the *paṇava*), and his craft is that of a *maddavika* (drummer) and a *pāṇavika* (tambourine player);
*sammaṃ* (a cymbal), *kaṃsatāḷaṃ* (a bronze gong), *tāḷaṃ* (a hand-clap), *alasatā* (a type of drum), and *āḷambaro*;

*murajo* (a clay drum), *gomukho* (a horn-like drum), *saṅkho* (a conch), *ḍiṇḍimo* (a kettledrum), *maddaviko*, and *pāṇaviko*; and *gītaṃ* (song), *vāditaṃ* (instrumental music), *sammaṃ*, and *tāḷaṃ*. [This refers to] a yoke.
“Yogga” means oxen fit for work; this farming labor is their work, and it is a component of that. Therefore he said “of the farming implements” (*kasibhaṇḍānaṃ*); the analysis is:
the plowshare (*phāla*), the plow-handle (*okasaka*), the goad (*pācana*), the yoke (*yuga*), and the plow (*naṅgala*). “Piṇḍa” refers to a specific type of weapon; the analysis is:
the sword (*asi*), the spear (*satti*), the javelin (*tomara*), and the club (*piṇḍa*). “Camma” is a shield made of hide; “kalāpa” is a quiver.
The analysis is: "weapon and shield. The analysis is: "snake and mongoose, cat and mouse, crow and owl, and nāga and supaṇṇa.
"Number and measure" (*saṅkhyāparimāṇa*) means number and measure;
therein, for those terms designated as measures, it is like "long and medium" (*dīghamajjhima*). The analysis is: "the single and the pair" (*ekakañca dukañca*).
This same method applies to the triads of offenses and so forth as well.
A "small creature" may be one that does not have bones, or it may simply be small;
this includes those measuring a hundred or a *paṣata* [of weight], and even some from the *ānaka* family.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "the worm and the moth, the ant and the termite, the gadfly and the mosquito, the fly and the termite.
"Butchers of sheep" (*orabbhika*) is a conventional designation for shepherds and the like. One who lives by killing sheep is a butcher of sheep;
the same applies to the others. One who cooks dogs for them is a *sapāka*. *Vena*s are carpenters; *rathakāra*s are leather-workers.
“Common” means shared; this word *caraṇa* is taken here—this is the connection.

Just as those by which one conducts oneself (*caranti*) according to their own recitation are called *caraṇas*, so too the Vedic recitations of the Kaṭhas and others, known as the branches (*sākhā*), are [called *caraṇas*].
Because the noble disciple conducts himself (*carati*) by means of these—that is, he goes toward the direction of the Deathless—they are the fifteen *caraṇas*, beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
[These are] the Dhammas. Therefore he said: "By Kaṭha and others," and so forth. The phrase "by Kaṭha and others" is stated even by transposing the order for the sake of conventional usage;
thus, by the word "and others" (*ādi*), Ātisa and the rest are included. [The suffix] *Ṇa* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.121]:

"When [the teaching] was spoken by another [teacher], [the suffix] *Ṇa* [is added]," and according to [Pāṇini 4.3.123]: "There is elision. Thus, from *Atisa Bhāradvāja* and *Kaṭha*, we get *Ātisā Bhāradvājā* and *Kaṭhā*. By Kalāpin...
They know or study what has been spoken; by that very [suffix] *ṇo*, [the term] *kaṭhādayo* means those such as the Kaṭhas and others.
The connection is that there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of these [names] to both the specific recitations and the persons. By the word "etc.
in the phrase "virtue and so forth" (*sīlādayo*), the restraint of the sense faculties and other such qualities are included. Virtue and wisdom, and calm...
The analysis is: "insight (vipassanā), true knowledge (vijjā), and conduct (caraṇa). Those in which there is a single recitation are "single-recitation texts" (ekajjhayanāni).
The "words of the Teacher" (pāvacanāni) are the well-spoken words, the True Dhamma.

Of those [which are] both single-recitation texts and words of the Teacher—namely, the Long Collection (Dīgha Āgama) and the Long Discourses, the Middle Collection (Majjhima Āgama) and the Middle Discourses, the Numerical Collection (Ekuttara Āgama) and the Numerical Discourses, and the Connected Collection (Saṃyutta Āgama)—[this applies].
The analysis is: "the Khandhaka and the Vibhaṅga.
By the word *tesam* (of them), he indicates the genitive case-ending (*chaṭṭhiyantata*) for the specific genders:
woman and man, female slave and male slave, and robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites as support for the sick.
The analysis [of the compound] is: *tiṇañca kaṭṭho ca sākhā ca palāso ca*. The analysis of *cheko dakkho* is according to the rule beginning with *pubbā ca parā ca* (Kacc 264).
In compounds such as *pubbadakkhiṇa*, the vowel is shortened by the rule *byañjane dīgharassā* (Kacc 1.33).
The analysis of *kāso ca kuso ca usiro ca bīraṇañca, muñjañca babbajañca* is according to the rule beginning with *gajo* (Kacc 265).
And by such examples as "the ox and the cow," "the elephant, the cow, the horse,
and the mare," "the swan and the crane," and "the heron and the stork"; "gold and silver," "the jewel, the conch, the pearl, the beryl, native gold,
and wrought silver," "rice and barley," and "vegetables and roots."
The analysis [of the compound] is by way of *kāsiyā ca kosalā ca*, etc., and it ends in the plural because it denotes countries (*janapada*).

Regarding *ekavīsati* and so forth, there may be either a descriptive determinative compound (*visesana-samāsa*)—meaning "one and that twenty"—or a distributive compound (*catuttha-samāsa*)—meaning "one and twenty.
However, it does not attain the neuter gender in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), for "gender is not prescribed by rule, because it depends on convention (*soka-nissayatā*)."
Regarding the phrase "liṅgasse" (of the gender): the intention is that because this [word] is not designated as having the neuter gender in common usage, it will not possess the neuter gender.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the neuter gender in a collective compound (*samāhāra*) deviates from the rule, based on the indicative authority (*ñāpaka*) of the example "sabhā-parisā.

The expression "pubbappayogo-abhimato" (intended as the prior application) refers to the first case (*paṭhamā*) specified for the suffixes *syādi* which bear the designation of a subordinate member (*upasajjana*) within a compound.

Regarding the rule *pubbanipāto* ("the prior placement"): by the rule *upasajjanaṃ pubbaṃ* (2-2-31), it is desired that what is intended (*iṭṭha*) be stated as having the status of the primary (*padhānabhāvena*).

Thus, in the rule *syādisyādinekatthaṃ* (3-1), because that which is indicated by the nominative in *syādi* is established first, and that which is indicated by the instrumental in *syādinā* is established later, it is desired that they be stated in sequence as the primary factor in the sutta *syādisyādinā*.

"Desired as a compound with the final member first" (*parappayoga-bhimata*) means that, according to the sutta mentioned below, the posterior placement (*paranipāta*) is intended for those words listed in the *Rājadantādi* group under the opening section [of the *Kaccāyana-vutti*], by virtue of the rule "in the case of *rājadanta* and so forth, the final member comes first" (2-2-30).
By the expression "frequently" (*bahula*), it is intended that when joined with a preceding *kāla*-word, the compound has the final member first;
this is intended precisely from the reading of the *Rājadantādi* list.

By the phrase "disregard for the sequence," he expresses the intended meaning of the sequence being disregarded due to its primary importance. "Sarādi" (vowel-initial) means that whose beginning is a vowel (*sara*).
The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: conch (*saṅkha*), drum (*dundubhi*), lute (*vīṇā*), mortar (*udukkhala*), pestle (*musala*), the Lord of Wealth (*dhanapati*), Rāma, and Kesava.
The words *jaṃ* and *daṃ* have the same meaning as the word *jāyā* (wife); they are *jaṃ* and *pati*, and *daṃ* and [pati].
*Paṭicā* is a compound; *Avantayo* and *Assakā* is a compound; *Aggi* and *Indo* is a compound.
When those inhabitants are taken, the compound *Avantī ca Assakā ca* is also valid through the use of the singular (*ekatta*). As for the *dvanda* compound:
it is called *dvanda* because it resembles a pair (*dvanda*); for the word *dvanda*—meaning "two and two words"—is predominant in both its senses.
21. Number (Saṅkhyā).

Now, one might raise an objection, suspecting that since the rule "In a collective compound, the neuter gender" (3-20) already exists, what purpose does the rule "Number, etc. (3-19) serve, which shows respect for the Teacher?

Thus he challenges [the author] with the words "But is it not so," and so forth. By the phrase "For thus," and so on, he demonstrates that the formation [of the desired forms] is accomplished by the rule "In a collective compound, the neuter gender" alone.
He refutes [the opponent]. Imagining that the intention of the other [opponent] is to move the aforementioned objection, he says, “*cattho*,” and so forth.
By the word “no” (not), he shows that the hypothetical construction made by the phrase “*cattho*,” etc., is not established; he states the reason for this as:

“because the connection depends upon the person (*purisādhīnattā*). Then, with the words beginning “*sati ce*,” [he refers to] the inclusion of the qualifier in the rule “*samāhāre napuṃsakan*” (a compound denoting a collection is neuter).
Having stated the purpose (*payojana*), he further confirms the pointlessness of the term "number and so forth" (*saṅkhyādī*). Regarding "purpose":
it refers to the purpose of brevity (*lāghava*).
"It is connected" means that the inclusion of the qualifier (*visesana*) is connected [to the subject].
"In this" means in this sutta beginning with "number, etc.
By the word "therein," he sets aside the aforementioned objection.
By stating "of the sutta beginning with 'number, etc. and so forth, he declares that the sutta is purposeful. [He states: "The designation as a unity..."

"Should be made": having prescribed the technical designation *digu* for a compound preceded by a numeral according to the rule "A compound preceded by a numeral is *digu*" (Pāṇini 2.1.52), the singular designation of its meaning should be made by others using the rule "A *digu* compound takes the singular number" (Pāṇini 2.4.1).
By the rule "The bringing together is *samāhāra*," this word *samāhāra* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
If it is [derived] as "that which is brought together," [it is derived in the sense of an action].
*Samāhāra* may be used in the sense of the object (*kamma-sādhana*);

in that case, the application of the term would be according to the meaning of the sentence "five maidens have been brought together," and because the primary referent here is the individual members of the compound, the plural form *pañca-kumārī* would apply.

Furthermore, by the rule *ghāpassantassāppadhānassā* (Pāṇini 8.2.7), the non-emphatic nasalization (*anunāsika*) would not occur, because it is the maidens who have been brought together that are the primary referents; therefore, [it is] *pañca*.
In the sentence *gāvo sa māhaṭā* ("The cows have been brought by him"), there is no compound (*samāsa*) because the formation of the accusative case is not accepted.
However, in the sentences *pañcannaṃ gunnaṃ samāhāro* ("the collection of five cows") and *catunnaṃ pathānaṃ samāhāro* ("the collection of four paths"), there is [a compound].
Because the collection is a single entity, it indicates that the singular number is established as natural, just as in the expression *sataṃ yūthaṃ vananti* ("they enter a herd of a hundred").
22. Regarding the purpose of restricting the usage of the word *kvaci*: it should be understood according to the method stated in the rule *paro kvacī* (1-27).
Even in the examples given without distinction, one should apply the sutta *chāyā* (2-2-73) as others have done, and then optionally [form] *kuḍḍacchāya*.

Regarding the term *kuḍḍacchāyā* (“wall-shadow”), although the rule *bāhulle* (Candavuttasaṅgaha 2-2-74) has been applied and examples such as *niccam ucchucchāyam* (“the constant shadow of sugarcane”) and *salabhacchāyam* (“the shadow of locusts”) have not been cited,

and even though the general examples *salabhacchāyam* (“locust-shadow”) and *sakuntacchāyam* (“bird-shadow”) have been shown, [the word *aññattha*] means “in other cases,” that is, in cases other than those occurring frequently (*bahulabhāvato*).
The phrase *viggahasamattassa* refers to the general state of being a compound (*viggahasāmaññassa*), according to what is possible, as in the case of a palace (*pāsādassa*).
By means of *chāyā* (shadow), *iccādi* (and so forth), and by not exceeding what is possible, [the word] *saddā* is [to be understood] as being subsequent to *sadda*.

23. With the words beginning with *syādi*, he refutes the objection stated by *nanu ce* and so forth, saying “That is not so” (*tanne*). He states the reason for this: “Because of the technical designation *gha*,” and so forth.
"Regarding 'aghoṇanti gha-okāra-vajjitānaṃ' [etc.]: Is it not the case that the letter *ya* is a *gho* in the feminine?
If that were so, one might assume that in the neuter it would not exist [therein], thinking: 'Because it is neuter, there is no *gha*-sound at all. That too is not so;
having rejected what was stated above, he says 'chaṭṭhī-samāsassa iccādi' in order to show that the neuter indeed possesses *gha*-sounds, as in the word *napuṃsakatta*."
The word *napuṃsake* establishes the very existence of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakatta*) of the term *ghatta*, by means of the phrase "for the neuter gender," and so forth.

Regarding the term *pāribhāsika*, it is the sutta itself that is intended here; the meaning is that it is "derived from a technical rule" (*paribhāsā*), thus "technical" (*pāribhāsika*), namely a sutta.
This sutta must indeed be commenced for the purpose of prescribing the shortening [of vowels] even in the case of the neuter.

The intended meaning (*adhippāyo*) is as follows: even a grammatical operation (*kāriya*) dependent on *ghan*—such as the substitution of *e* and so forth prescribed by the rule "ghabrahmādīte" (2-60)—is what is meant here.

The connection is: "this grammatical operation dependent on *ghan* is not applicable. Even though it is inapplicable, this fault would indeed follow; therefore, anticipating an objection regarding the structure of the sentence, he says: "This is not a fault," and so forth.
This is because the short vowel (*rasa*) has already found its opportunity right here; thus, when [the rule] has first entered [into the word], the operation dependent on *ghan* [is applied].
Nor is this a fault; it should be understood as a mere figurative expression (*paribhāsā*). The word division is *salabhacchāye*.
24. *Ghama*.
The phrase "for this very reason" (*ato eva ca*) and so forth is stated by relying on the method explained below.

25. By the phrase “Gossu sakatthapariccāgena kule pavattattā” (because it occurs in the family through the sacrifice of the meaning of the word *go*), he expresses that the sixth-case compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) has the meaning of the final member as its predominant factor (*uttarapadatthappadhāna*).
26. Itthi...

In the rules for feminine suffixes (*itthivibhatti*), such as "from *puthu* [comes] *pathavī* and *puthavī*" (3-39), which conclude the section on sūtras, the term *itthiyaṃ* may be either a qualifier of the noun (*nāmavisesana*) or a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*paccayatthavisesana*).
To show that this is indeed a qualifier of the noun and not a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, he says: "From a noun ending in *a*," and so forth.
This means: from a noun ending in the vowel *a* that expresses meanings such as singularity (*ekatta*) and greatness (*mahanta*).

Not for me. Regarding the term *itthatta*: here, *itthī* refers to the feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*). For it is that by which she is characterized (*liṅgīyati*) and designated (*saṅketīyati*) as "she" alone;

thus it is a "gender-mark" (*liṅga*). That which belongs to her—namely, the state (*bhāva*) or commonality (*sāmañña*) of a well-known entity, such as the characteristics of childhood, youth, and so forth—is "femaleness" (*itthatta*). What, then, is meant here by "gender-mark"?
"That this is such-and-such" and "establishment in those meanings known to the world"— these are the feminine,
masculine, and neuter genders.
These are called "names" (nāmāni).

The meaning is that those things in which the world’s conventional usage (*pasiddhi*) occurs as "this," "that," or "it"—these, respectively, are called by the world "feminine," "masculine," and "neuter" genders.
And having established this, it is said: "The gender is not to be taught [by grammar], because it depends on the world."
Regarding the phrase "of the gender" (*liṅgassa*): therein, in words such as *go* (cow), it is feminine gender by virtue of the conventional usage "this is she" (*esā esā*);

in words such as *acci* (flame), it is feminine-neuter gender by virtue of the conventional usage "this is it" (*etam etam*); in words such as *taṭo* (bank) and *bhaṭī* (servant woman), it is masculine-feminine-neuter gender by virtue of the conventional usage "this is he/she/it" (*eso esā etam*);

in words such as *mālā* (garland), it is feminine gender by virtue of the conventional usage "this is it" (*esā*); and in words such as *rukkho* (tree), it is masculine gender by virtue of the conventional usage "this is it" (*eso*).
In the phrase "kulamiccādo," the neuter gender is due to conventional usage (*pasiddhi*). The same should be understood for the compound as well;
the connection is that [the word] "jotakā" indicates [this]. From the context, it is understood that "jotakā" refers to the state of femininity (*itthatta*).

By means of the suffix *ve* and so forth, he shows that there is no room here for those faults that arise from the meaning of the suffixes. The connection is that there is both coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatta*) and the plural number.

This illustrates the following: when *itthatta* (femininity) functions as the condition (*paccaya*), because it is the primary factor, there would be a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatta*) with the genitive case characterized by distinction—such that one might expect "the femininity of Devadatta" (*kumārittaṃ devadattāya*)—and consequently, [Devadatta] would not be the "girl" herself.
Likewise, the plural form "girls" (*kumāriyo*) would also be inappropriate, because femininity is a single entity (*ekatta*). This is the meaning of the base form (*pakatiyattha*).
"But in the case of the qualifier (*visesanapakkhe*), it is the substance itself that is expressed as distinguished from its feminine state by the base;

since *ā* and so forth are merely indicators (*jotaka*), there is no distinction [between them and the base] therein, and thus the application of the genitive case does not arise. Furthermore, the plural number is appropriate because the substance is manifold;
therefore, since there is no opportunity for the aforementioned faults, the desired meaning is established. By the word "others" (*aññe*), he indicates Jayāditya, Jinendrabuddhi, Ācārya, and others.
"In 'itthiyam abhidheyyāya'" means in "femininity" (*itthatta*), which is the actual state designated by the feminine gender.

By the passage beginning with "yatheva hi," he clarifies the aforementioned meaning by way of a simile. Therein, by the words "itthattam iccādi," he refutes the position described by others as being illogical;
[the phrase] "no papajjate nopapajjeyya" (it does not follow, nor would it follow) is used because even that which is denoted by the word "Devadatta" is not distinct from femininity (*itthatta*).
The claim that “‘itthattaṃ devadattāya’ [is an example of] a different grammatical core (bhinnādhikaraṇatā)” is untenable; the phrase beginning with ‘devadattāya’ actually supports the very opposite.

There must indeed be a common grammatical core (samānādhikaraṇatta), because that which is expressed by the word *itthī* is not other than that which is expressed by the word *devadattā*; thus, "the woman Devadattā."
"Ato evā" means precisely because of the teaching regarding femininity (*itthatā*). Regarding "tabbatotthassa," this was stated by the follower of Jayāditya and others;
for they have thus described the characteristics of gender (*liṅgalakkhaṇa*) [in the *Kāśikā* on Pāṇini 4.1.3]:

"Femininity and so forth, like lineage and so forth, are specific qualities of universals (*sāmañña*) that manifest in many ways; and they are 'universals' (*sāmaññāni*) because they are common to word-meanings (*padattha*) of a similar class."
Those [particulars] and the generalities are "general- and particular-characteristics" (*sāmaññavisesā*) because they distinguish one from another, are of different kinds, and exclude one another.
They are "manifestations" (*byattiyo*) because things are manifested by them; they are the supports for the general- and particular-characteristics.
Those general- and particular-characteristics which possess many modes of manifestation are spoken of in that way—(from the *Kāsikāvivaraṇapañjikā*). For they think thus: "Just as..."
Lineage and the like persist among all those of the same genus but are excluded from those of a different genus; likewise, femininity and the like [behave].

However, because the manifesters—the bases for generalities and particularities—are diverse, only a certain generality or particularity is manifested by a certain base, and not every [generality] by every [base], because the capacities of entities have restricted domains. In this regard:
"That which manifests only femininity, and not masculinity nor neuterness, is female only, not male nor neuter.
That which manifests only masculinity is male only. That which manifests neuterness is neuter only.
But that which manifests two or three [of these] is of two genders or of three genders."
(Pāṇini 4.1.3, Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā): Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows:

"from that" refers to the mountain, which is the object (*artha*) to be expressed (*abhidheya*) possessing the aforementioned nature of "thisness" (*itthatta*). By means of the phrase beginning with "athecca," Jinendrabuddhi postulates each [of the alternatives] in order to avoid the faults already mentioned.
Thus, by means of such words as "carahiccha" and so forth, he utters a reply preceded by mockery. "Like a cock smeared with soot":
when one cock is afraid of another, they then smear the mouth of the victorious cock with soot and bring it forward;
although that [defeated] cock was initially afraid of him, thinking "he is another," he again exerts himself to fight, considering [the victor] to be someone else.
Just as the cock itself was not shown here under the suffix *byā*, so too [the meaning] is "I am this. 29.

Since the suffix *inī* occurs in the sense of a wife through its connection with a masculine noun (*puṃyoga*) according to the rule "The suffixes *mātulādīni* occur in the sense of a wife" (Pāṇini 4.1.43), which is restrictive, he states by way of this non-restrictive [usage] that *inī* occurs in the sense of both a wife and one who is not a wife: "the wife of an ārāmika," and so forth.

31. Regarding the statement "after *tti*," although this much has been said, he states the reason for the rule "after a suffix ending in *tti*" as follows: "because there is no application of the suffix alone in the sense of another word (*aññapadatthe*).

By this, he demonstrates that even without the governing rule (*paribhāsa*) concerning the inclusion of suffixes, this specific meaning is obtained through the very force of the context (*sāmatthiya*).
32. *Ghara-taṃ-sanniyogā*:

Through that suffix *nī*, there is a conjunction (*sanniyoga*), which is to say a unification; this is the intended meaning here: "Wherever the suffix *nī* occurs, there the elision of *ya* takes place.
33. *Mātu*.

Regarding the phrase "to a wife" (*bhariyāya*): because it is a specific natural state (*pakativisesana*), he did not say "of a wife" (*bhariyāyaṃ*) and so forth. "Masculine names" (*punnāmadheyya*) means those that have become conventional designations for a man.
"By connection with a male" (*puṃyogena*) means by reason of a relationship with a male. "They apply to a female" (*itthiyaṃ vattanti*):

when there is a desire for non-differentiation expressed as "this is that," and they apply to this female designated as a "wife," it is understood from the mention of the list beginning with *nadi* that this is due to their belonging to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class.

This shows that the reading [of the word] as *nadādi* is indeed so; the meaning of "because of its connection with a masculine name, it is *apālakantā*, thus it is a *nadādi* reading" is the remainder [of the explanation].
And this should be understood as a rule (*gaṇasutta*) among the *nadādi* [groups]; he states its meaning with the words "a masculine name," etc.
As for "not ending in *-pālaka*," examples are *kiṃpālikā* and *khettapālikā*.
39. From the word *puthu*, the suffix *-vī* is employed to form a noun (*saññā*): “The earth (*pathavī*) is called ‘mahī’ because it has become broad (*puthubhūtā*).
By the phrase “has become broad,” he makes known that the word *pathavī* is derived from the word *puthu*; thus, it is called “mahī.”
By this [rule], the reading of *nadādi* [is established] for the purpose of the technical designation (*saññā*) when the suffix *vī* is applied; the meaning is "become manifold" or "spread out. 40.
Regarding *samā*:
because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *parā*, since proximity is already established by the subsequent rule (*paravidhi*) concerning the suffix, the word *santa* expresses proximity.

Thinking that "the inclusion [of the word] might lead to an undesirable consequence," he says "tassa anto" and so forth, showing that the word *anta* is taken here as denoting a component (*avayava*).
The word division is *avasānavati avayavo*. He states the reason for including it by means of the mention of the compound (*samāsa*) with the words "because it is a component.
To show, by way of an analogy, that there is no fault in the objection stated above, he says "this is not a fault" and so forth. Of that which has blossomed...

The meaning is that, just as the sprouts of a tree possess the status of being constituent parts [of the tree], so too, from the perspective of a compound, there is no contradiction in the letter *a*—which is prescribed at a subsequent time—possessing the status of being a constituent part of the compound.
*Atikkantamaṅguliyo* is the analysis (*viggaha*). By means of the analysis *dve aṅguliyo samāhaṭā*, it expresses the meaning [of the first type];

by the analysis *dve aṅguliyo pamāṇam assa*, it shows that this is a compound [of the second type], and then, after the suffix *matta* or the suffix *taggha* has been added, when the elision (*lopa*) is applied to that by the rule "there is elision" (*tassa lopo*, Pāṇini 5.2.58), it is shown that the vowel *a* is the result of a descriptive compound (*visesanasaṃāsa*) by the phrase beginning with "how" (*katham*).
In order to show what was stated [in the previous rule], the phrase beginning with “*aññapadatthe*” and so forth was spoken. The formation of the compound (*samāsavidhāna*) occurs from this as well;

that is, after eliding the suffixes such as *-matta*, the formation of the compound takes place by means of the rule “*visesanamekatthene*” (3-11). Now, this is not a compound formed with the word *aṅguli* alone;

rather, considering that the final form is achieved without a suffix (*appaccaya*) even without the elision of the suffix in the sense of measurement (*māna*), [the author] says “*aṅgula-saddo vā*,” and so forth.

Regarding what was stated in the *Vutti*, he raises a doubt with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth. Since the word *dvaṅgula* excludes that which possesses a measure, there might be a case where it functions as a *aññapadattha* (compound denoting something other than its members) in some way;
thus it is said, "let it function as a *aññapadattha* in whatever manner. One might object:

"Is it not possible to establish all such forms as *niraṅgula* and so on by means of the word *aṅgula* alone? If that were so, what is the purpose of prescribing a suffixless form for the word *aṅguli*? Anticipating this doubt:

To state the subsequent purpose, he says: “In all cases,” and so forth. He shows that the purpose here is to exclude [the application of] the suffix *ap* when it has not been prescribed after the word *aṅguli*, which would otherwise result in forms such as *niraṅguli*; thus he says: “for the purpose of excluding the word *aṅguli*.
45. Long.

Because no specific gender has been taught [in the grammatical rules] for a long time, one might suspect that the neuter gender is intended; thus, he raises an objection with the words "But is it not so...

and so forth. He resolves this with the words "This is not a fault... and so forth. He states the following as his supporting argument: "Gender is not subject to formal instruction, because gender is dependent upon worldly usage," beginning with the words "In the world...
and so forth. The particle *athavā* (or) is used here in the sense of indicating an alternative position.
“Vibhajja” means having analyzed. “Kvacī” (in some cases) is intended [to mean] by way of splitting the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*).
“Ahorattaṃ” (day and night): this neuter gender arises from a collective compound (*samāhāra-samāsa*). “Atiratto” (exceeding the night): this masculine gender is a *pādika* compound;

because a word denoting a whole can also function to denote a part, the word “ratti” (night) in the preceding phrase “pubbarattādi” (early night, etc. expresses a portion [of the night]. “Pubbā... [etc.]...

"And that night," and so forth. Thus, it should not be read as *ekaratti* (one night), because there is an absence of compound status (*samāsatta*) through its [the word *ratti*] being a collective [term].
Furthermore, the neuter gender is to be understood according to worldly convention.

In the alternative where there is no compound suffix—that is, in the view that the compound suffix affix is absent—the word *pubbarattī* (early night) is formed with the word *ratti* denoting a specific part [of the whole], and thus there is an absence of a compound suffix.

46. By means of the phrase "If it is argued that it is 'gotva' (cowness)," he addresses the fault previously established, asserting that this is not a fault. By the rule "syādilopassi ccādinā," he demonstrates that even though the elision of suffixes such as *su* and *la* is easily obtained, the elision of the *taddhita* suffix is more difficult to obtain; therefore, it is appropriate to refer to it by the term *alopa*.
47. Night.

Regarding the expression *rattindivaṃ bhuñjati* ("he eats day and night"): when the object to be placed (*ādheyya*)—namely, that which is designated as "eating"—is expected, the terms "night" (*ratti*) and so forth are dependent on what is to be placed (*ādeyyasāpekkha*).
Showing that even for these, the formation of the compound is established by this very particle (*nipāta*), he says:
"*rattandivan*" and so forth. The analysis (*viggaha*) is *ratti ca divā ca*; however, in a *catutthī-samāsa* (dative compound), it would be *ra(tti)ndivā*.

50. Regarding the meaning of the compound *dārusamāsa*: here, [in the phrase] *dāru*, a connection with the primary fingers (*mukhyāhi aṅgulīhi*) is not logical. Is it not the case that two fingers are its measure?
[One might argue: "In the expression *dārunocchādiṃ*, the primary word 'fingers' (*aṅguli*) is understood; thus a connection is possible. Why is it so?

To this, it is said in response: "Even if," and so forth. By the phrase "by a word expressing a measure" (*pamāṇavacanena*), it is meant by a word denoting a measure that serves as the meaning for suffixes such as *matta*.
Since the word *aṅguli* denotes the measure of a piece of wood, it is stated that "there is a connection with the wood.

Following a descriptive compound (*visesanasaṃāsa*), in relation to its object—that is, in the domain of that sense of measure—the suffixes *matta* and others must be applied according to the rule beginning with "in the sense of measuring" (*mānematto*, 4.4.66). This is the meaning.

The connection is "it should be understood as [the word] *lopena*. Regarding what was stated in the rule *asaṅkhyehi cāṅgulyā naññāsaṅkhyatthesu* (3-44), he extends that same principle here by saying "established as before. The term *anakārantānam* refers to [bases] such as *bhūmi* and so on;

the connection is that when those [suffixes] are prescribed—that is, when that *ap*-suffix is prescribed—the purpose is that the vowel *i* [is the augment]. By this, [the rule applies] to the followers of Kaccāyana.
The purpose [of the treatise] has been shown. Furthermore, regarding this point, the author of the *Vutti* stated what follows in order to demonstrate the irrationality of the following supposition:

that by the rule “in some cases, for those ending in a compound, there is the suffix -a” (*ka*, 2-7-22), when the suffix -a is applied at the end of the compound, then by virtue of the implied capacity (*sāmatthiya*), the substitution of -i for -ā as prescribed by “*syāca*” (*ka*, 2-3-29) does not occur, and thus the form invariably ends in -o. This is what was stated by the author of the *Vutti*.

To demonstrate this, he says “even for that which ends in *a*,” and so forth. To show that because the capacity to prevent the substitution of *si* for *ā* by means of the letter *a* is absent, the substitution of *si* for *ā* is not barred, he says “if not,” and so forth.

Because its purpose has been fulfilled through its having been employed, it was cited as ending in a suffixless form (*appaccayanta*) precisely according to the method of Kaccāyana’s *Vutti*, following the tradition of the Sakkata (Pali) texts.
By the phrase "having the final consonant [of the word]," this indicates that only those three words possess a final consonant;

"meaningless" (*niratthaka*) refers to being meaningless because they previously lacked the vowel *ā*, as stated in the rule for the insertion of *ā*: "by the very rule for the insertion of *ā*," namely, by the rule "and after *dhenu*" (*dhanumhā ca*).
51. *Civī*.

"Mutual action" (*aññamaññakiriyā*) refers to the exchange of actions; this shows that even though the word *kiriyā* (action) does not appear in this sutta, the phrase "exchange of actions" (*kiriyābyatihāra*) is understood through the word *vītiharaṇa* (exchanging).
52. *Latvī*:
