then, by the rule "tiye dutāpi ca" (2-8-43), he effects the substitution of *du* for *dvi* and *tī*, resulting in *dutiyam* and *tatiyam*. Furthermore, by the rule "catuchehi thaṭhā," [the suffix *tha* is prescribed after *catur* and *cha*].
(2-8-41) By means of the *sutta*, the suffix *thap* is prescribed after the fourth [case], and by means of the *dvitta*, the form "fourth" (*catuttha*) is produced.
Here, fearing how those [forms] could be established through such a state of being, it is said in the *vutti* "How... and so forth;
to show this, he says "In number," etc. In the *vutti*, portions of the *sutta* such as "of the second" (*dutiyassa*) and so forth are shown; these...

These [rules] were stated by means of the phrases “of the second” (*dutiyassa*) and so forth, as well as “of the fourth and third” (*catutthatatiyānaṃ*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate them in their complete form.
55. What fault is there in taking [the word] *saṅkhyā* (number) as a synonym for number? To this he says: “*saṅkhyāvāci*,” etc. There is no application [of the term] in the sense of plurality.
The word *siyā* is stated because the numeral expression is restricted to the singular sense. By the phrase "even when alone," etc., he explains the meaning of *ekākī*.
It refers to a usage in the plural sense regarding those who are reborn (*upapajjaka*).
56. *Vacchā*.

Even when it is stated "there is *taro*," it is understood from those [words] that "there is *taro*"; however, because "by calves and so forth" (*vacchādīhi*) is heard, it is also understood as "of calves and so forth" (*vacchādīnaṃ*).

Thus, the phrase beginning with "of calves and so forth" (*vacchādīnaṃ*) is a demonstration of the wording of the grammatical rule (*vutti*). [Objection: Is it not the case that the suffix is prescribed by calves and so forth when there is thinness?
And since calves and so forth are thin by virtue of their bodies, would it not follow that the application [of the suffix] occurs there without distinction?

Because no specific distinction is mentioned in the *Payogasajjana* (the manuscript), how then is the thinning of the inherent nature (*sabhāva*) understood here, such that it is said, "thus it is revealed"?

[The author] says: "of words such as *vaccha*," etc.; when the suffix *i* is prescribed after words such as *vaccha* to form the base, the occasion for their application (*pavatti-nimitta*) is a specific stage of life (*vayovisesa*) and so forth, in the presence of which the words *vaccha* and others [are used].
When [words] are applied to a substance (*dabba*), that is the condition for the cognition; however, the words "calf" (*vaccha*) and so forth do not apply to the state of thinness.

Therefore, it is considered appropriate for that very cause for the application of the word (*saddappavatti-nimitta*)—when it is attenuated—to be the condition (*paccaya*), and not merely the state of attenuation itself.
The terms "cause for application," "related," and "proximate" are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
A calf (*vaccha*) is in its first stage of life; its becoming thin (*tanutta*) is the attainment of the second stage of life.

For when a calf reaches the second stage, only a mere residue of that which serves as the basis for the application of the word "calf" remains; this very point is stated by the phrase beginning with "of one well-suckled" (*susuttassa*).
A young tree (*ukkhataruṇa*) is said to have reached the second stage of life; its becoming thin is the attainment of the third stage of life. For at the time of reaching the third stage...

In the second stage of life, the manifestation of the sound "ukkha" as a sign will remain only slightly, because of the mixing of breeds—due to the intermingling of the Gaddhabha breed and the Vaḷava breed.
Furthermore, one who is capable of carrying a load is called an ox (*usabha*);
however, when his capacity for carrying loads becomes weak and exhausted, [he is no longer so designated].
He says that it then becomes attenuated: "The attenuation of capacity is its weakness. 57. From what [is a collection]?
A collection may consist of two parts or many parts; therein, from a collection of two parts, there is selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
By virtue of its capacity, the selection (*niddhāraṇa*) of only one is understood, and it follows that very [one].
Even in the case of a collection consisting of many parts, although the word "of one" (*ekassa*) does not appear in the rule *ekassa niddhāraṇe*, the selection of only one must be understood;
for this very reason, he gave the example: "Which of you, sirs, is Devadatta?"—*kataro bhavataṃ devadatto*. "Which of you, sirs, is Devadatta? (*kataro bhavataṃ devadatto*).

By means of the frequent citation of examples such as "Which of you is Kaṭha?", it is stated [in the commentary] that although the word expresses selection (*niddhāraṇa*), it does so by virtue of the plurality of the thing being selected.

A lineage (*gotta*) is a family line (*vaṃsa*) that proceeds through a succession of descendants; and even words denoting that lineage which end in the suffix *-vappa* are called "lineage" through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*).
Furthermore, these words for descendants proceed with respect to the ancestors by way of their connection to those ancestors; thus, they are "relational terms" (*sambandhisaddā*).

There are words for conduct (*caraṇa-saddā*) such as *kaṭha*, which are words for action (*kiriyā-saddā*). Just as the words *kaṭha* and others function toward the Vedic recitations (*ajjheyya*) taught by them—
by virtue of being the cause for the performance of one's own conduct and actions—

even though the referents of certain related words and the referents of words for action lack the nature of a genus (*jāti*), in the world, grammatical operations (*kāriya*) are desired based upon that genus.
Thus it was said: “The lineage together with the conduct. Therein, even birth is censured;
therefore he said: “Because of Kaṭha’s conduct, there is birth; because of lineage, there is birth. By this—
"Lokiyā" (worldly) is said with reference to other grammarians; however, here it is stated without distinction—this is the connection.
The construction is: "because it is stated generally in the *Nirutti*. To show the manner in which it is stated generally, the words beginning with "How? are spoken.

"Given by the gods," "given by Brahmā," and so forth, are analytical sentences (*viggahavākya*) referring either to the agent (*kattar*) or the instrument (*karaṇe*). [The derivative forms are] "Devadatta" and "Devadattika."
The derivative expressions (vuttipada) such as *deviyā*,

*devala*, and so forth. In this context, having demonstrated the different derivations of derivative expressions found in the *Niruttipiṭaka* such as *devadatta* and *devadattika*, [the author] now says "given by the gods" (*devehi datto*) and so on,
in order to show that even for words like *devala* and *devī*, their derivation occurs through a different verbal root (*vacanantara*).

It has been stated. In order to show the derivation and the mode of derivation for even the authors of other grammatical treatises (*parasaddasatthakārā*), such as the words *devala* and *deviya*, the passage beginning with “some say” (*kecīhi*) was stated.
They desire the suffix (*paccaya*) from only one part [of the base]; therefore, for them, forms such as *devala*, *deviya*, *datti*, and *locca* arise.
As for *kappanāgāravo*, it is *kappanāgāravo* by way of retaining only one part after the elision of the word *datta*.

59. Regarding the phrase "na ca sabba" and so forth, the result is stated in the context of frequent occurrence (*bahulādhikāra*). The word *bhāva* (state/being) is used in some instances to denote an action, as in: "this rule applies to the state [of the action].
In other instances, it denotes intention (*adhippāya*), as in: "this is their state; this is the intended meaning. In yet other instances...
"In the sense of a word-meaning (*padattha*): 'these are entities' (*bhāvā*). In some cases, it is used in the sense of mere existence (*sattāmatta*), as in "the existence of grasses.

Therefore he said: "Of the word *bhāva*, etc. "By way of the grammatical derivation of the form": by way of the grammatical derivation of the form of the word *bhāva*. It is called *sadda* (word) because it makes known (*sappanti*) or manifests its meaning (*attha*).
That very thing is the designation (*abhidhāna*), considering that the meaning is designated (*abhidhīyate*) by it. One understands the nature of the meaning (*atthasarūpa*).
Regarding *buddhi*: it is understood that by means of this, the meaning is cognized; thus it is called "meaning" (*attha*) or "condition" (*paccaya*).
Now, since it was stated that "from this [condition], the words for cognition arise," the ground for the occurrence of both [the word and the cognition] is the same.

This being so, why is it said that "it is the ground for the occurrence of the word" specifically as the ground for the occurrence of the word alone? To this it is replied: [It is because the word is the primary factor in linguistic usage].

Having stated that the relationship between the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheyya*)—by virtue of its being manifest—is the very cause for the operation of the word itself, [the author] says "on account of the cause" (*nimittavasā*) and so forth, in order to illuminate that this [relationship] is the cause of operation by distinguishing it from the form (*rūpa*) which follows after the object of a separate cognition. The connection is:

"The quality (*guṇa*) in a substance (*dabba*)," meaning the quality is the cause when it functions within a substance. Two examples are given because the word *guṇa* itself possesses the nature of a genus-word (*jāti-sadda*).
"Given... [is said] because for a quality (*guṇa*), there is no separate cause for its arising apart from birth (*jāti*), and because it possesses the nature of being stored.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "action and so forth," substances (*dabba*) and other categories are included; however, some say that for verbal roots (*kiriyā-sadda*), action itself is the cause for their occurrence.

For those [words such as] Devadatta and others, the commonality by way of a specific state—that is, through the distinction of states—is "the commonality of that specific state. Therefore he says: "Of Devadatta," and so forth.

The meaning is that the characteristic of the genus (*jātilakkhaṇa*), which serves as the cause for the occurrence of those designative words (*saññāsadda*) such as "Devadatta" whose objects—the referents—actually exist, has been explained and established.
By this, it is stated that even though words like "Devadatta" are designative words, they are nonetheless genus-words (*jātisadda*). And if, indeed, they are designative words...
"They may be words denoting a genus (*jāti*); among these, the fivefold [classification] is excluded. This should not be understood in that way...
Words such as *kaṭha*, *govīhi*, and *yava*, which denote well-known genera, are separately grasped as being words for a genus (*jātisadda*).

"Due to the difference of the related" means due to the difference of the related things, such as pots and so forth. "Due to the difference of the absence" refers to [the absence of] pots, cloths, and so forth.

The construction is as follows: although there is no difference [in essence] due to the non-existence [of space and so forth], differences are metaphorically attributed (*upacarita*) based on the difference among their related entities.
"By virtue of which generality" means: by virtue of that generality [of non-existence] which applies to those things—space and so forth—in which differences are metaphorically attributed.
"Of those words whose objects are partless and non-existent" means: those words whose objects are partless like space and non-existent like non-existence (*abhāva*). This is the meaning.
"Sāmañña-bhāvo" means the state of being common to ordinary people and so forth. "Alasassa bhāvo" is the state of being associated with activity;
"brahmaññaṃ" is birth; "cāpalyaṃ" is fickleness; "nepuññaṃ" is either skill or a virtue.

In the commentary, regarding the rule "sakatthe ekanta," the meaning of "sakatthe" (4.122) is that it refers to suffixes added in the sense of identity with the base itself. It is to be connected with "na daṭṭhabbaṃ" (it is not to be seen). "Pattakālo va" (only the time has arrived).
It is appropriate. *Karuṇā* itself is *kāruñña*.

62. Regarding the phrase “of those taught as being joined by a single [suffix], there is co-occurrence (*sahavāpavatti*) and co-cessation (*sahavā nivattī*),” the term “in the sense of state and object” (*bhāvakammesu*) follows. Nevertheless, he says “in the sense of state and object,” etc., to show that even here, the inclusion of the word *bhāveti* serves a specific purpose.
64. Tārā:
Although the term *sīgha* (swift) occurs even in the case of a simple (*kevala*) action, it nevertheless occurs in its highest degree (*ukkaṃsa*) when preceded by the prefix *ati*.
Therefore, he says: "The excellence (*atisaya*) is the highest degree (*ukkaṃsa*). And as to whose this excellence belongs, he says: "And that [excellence] belongs to actions and qualities."
How does he state their superiority? By saying, "by virtue of the substance that serves as the substratum.

From where does he say this? From the phrase beginning with "when disregarded" (*anapekkhite*). The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom the support of actions and qualities is reckoned as substance, and which [support] is disregarded.

He says, "the secondary locus" (*paccadhikaraṇa*), etc., in order to state that even though the excellence of the substance—which is the substratum—exists, it can only occur by way of the actions and qualities dependent upon it, and not otherwise.
Now, if it is only the excellence of functional qualities (*kiriyāguṇa*) that constitutes superiority, then the term "better ox" (*gotara*) would not be established; yet this is not a fault.

For here, it is not the excellence of the genus (*jāti*) [that is meant]. Of which quality, then, does this "ox" possess the excellence, such that it is called "better ox" because it draws the cart, while the other is merely an "ox" because it draws the cart on its head?
Indeed, since a genus is eternal and uniform in nature, a connection with increase or decrease is impossible; therefore, it must be the substance (*dabba*) as well.
There is no occurrence of an excess [of quality]. For instance, even in the case of a multiplier of equal magnitude, an excellence is seen from the very root;
for although the length and breadth of a cloth may be the same, whether it be Kāsika or another, its value differs—being one thing for a cloth from Mathurā and another for other types.
Because the state of being superior is established merely by the fact that the substance is endowed with superior qualities, it is said: “Therefore he said,” and so forth. To the extent that...
Because of the excellence of the qualities dependent upon it, even the substance (*dabba*) which serves as the support is said, in some way, to "function" (*vattati*) within that excellence;
likewise, the root (*pakati*) which is expressed by that [term] also functions there solely by virtue of its own denotable meaning.

Therefore, it is stated with reference to a specific root (*pakativiśeṣaṇa*) as "because it functions in the sense of excellence" (*atiyaye vattamānato*); for this very reason he said: "by this root..."

"And it is called a qualifier (*visesana*)," he says. The connection is that for those who hold the sense of the base word (*sakatthika*), the meaning of the base word (*pakati-attha*) must be made manifest.

"Of those who hold the sense of the base word" is a genitive in the sense of the agent, used because of a desire to express a relationship; the meaning is "by those who hold the sense of the base word.

He states the reason: "'Because it is a qualifier of the base word. The word *iti* indicates the reason; because [it is] 'a qualifier of the base word' occurring in the sense of excellence (*atisaya*)."

The meaning is this: because it is born from a quality (guṇa) that constitutes the primary sense (pakatyattha), the quality constituting the primary sense must be illuminated by its own meanings (sakatthika) according to the method already stated.

In that context, he states the distinction [of the suffix] by saying "it is not the denotable" (nābhidheyyo); and so he will say later: "the words *atirā* and so forth are illuminators of excellence" (*atisayajotaka*). Now, one might ask:

if there is a difference in the primary sense, why is it said to be "not denotable" and "to be illuminated"? To this he replies: "by the primary sense itself," and so forth. [This refers to] excellence (*ukkaṃsa*).
In common worldly usage, it is observed that [a term] enters into a domain of objects possessing similar qualities;
therefore, even in the case of a general term (*sāmaññavacana*), it functions as such precisely because of that same cause. To demonstrate this, he says: “*atisayena*” and so forth.
By means of the phrase “*dvinnaṃ ekassa atisaye*” and so on, he clarifies the intended meaning of the rule *sakattha* (Pāṇini 5.3.96), namely: “*dvibahūsu kammaṃse taratamā*” (Kaccāyana 4.3.45).
*Tarai* is stated by its own technical term (*sakavohārena*); for these [words], the suffix *īya* applies. Thus, the connection here is: “the state of being more comfortable than this.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāyo*): because there is no superiority (*ukkaṃsa*) between two things when based on the meaning of the sūtra as previously stated, the suffix *tara* does not occur in such cases as “The people of Mathurā are more delicate than those of Pāṭaliputra”;
therefore, one is from Mathurā and the second is from Pāṭaliputra.
Of these two delicate ones, one is more delicate than the other by three times; likewise, of another pair, one is superior to the other, and so on for another pair—one is superior to the other.
In this way, the comparative suffix *tara* occurs after each member of pairs of two.
In both cases, however, the plural number is used with reference to the individual members; for it is in terms of delicacy that they are being compared.
The parts of a collection are many; for instance, when the Mathurans and the Pāṭaliputtakas are compared, their respective parts are likewise many.
Thus, by means of the *tarap* suffix, it is established that "the Mathurans are more delicate than the Pāṭaliputtakas.
In this village, the merchants are wealthier; according to the principle already stated, the *tarap* suffix is applied to express the superiority of each over two or two.
[The suffix] *bhavati* [is used]; however, as for the plural number, in some instances it depends on the individual parts, and they accomplish the entire [meaning] with difficulty.

But here, because such a rule is prescribed—and because *tara*, etc., are prescribed generally for the sense of excellence (*atisaya*) by the rule "in the sense of excellence, *tara*, *tamap*, *iṭṭha*, and *isi*"—it becomes easily accomplished everywhere by means of the *tara* suffix.
"By way of difference in state" (*avatthābhedena*) is said because of the distinction between a sharp state and a state that is even sharper;

for indeed, others speak of that very same person when he is joined with another state as "Your Honor is in a different state. He states the reason for establishing [the term] in another manner: "or because it is prescribed merely for the sake of excellence" (*atisayamatte vā vidhānato*).
He speaks of its instability: "even though there is excellence," and so forth. "In these five" refers to these [five].
Among the five suffixes beginning with *tara*, as previously stated, examples of their application to adjectives (*guṇavacana*) have been illustrated by forms such as *rūpītarā*.

However, for a word expressing an action (*kriyāvacana*), the forms are *atisayena pācakataro* and *pācakatamo*. According to the rule *issika iyaiṭṭhā sarādī tato*, the suffixes *issa*, *ka*, *iya*, and *iṭṭha* do not follow those [suffixes] beginning with *sa*, except by virtue of the general injunction (*bahulādhikāra*).

66. Although the word *tassa tassa* is stated in a general sense, it is understood as a genitive case related to a modification (*vikāra*), and the modification is understood as being related to that genitive case by virtue of their connection;
thus, he says "of which," etc., to demonstrate this. [This refers to] specific types of silk-worms (*kosakāraka-pāṇi-viśeṣa*).
The *kosa* has been completed. "Breathing beings" refers to sentient beings; "plants whose fruit is their ripening" refers to trees that bear flowers and fruit.
They state this as the definition of trees and plants; however, by virtue of that definition, trees and plants are not included here.

Rather, by the word "plant" (*osadhi*), creepers and the like are also included, and by the word "tree" (*rukkha*), forest-growers (*vanappati*) are also included, for forest-growers possess fruit but do not possess flowers.
"How is it that regarding the transformation of a cow, people say 'in another' and so forth? [The answer is: "This is the cow-dung (gomaya) of a cow.
67. *Jatu* means "another birth" (*upapattyantara*); due to the elision of the conditional suffix (*paccayalopa*), it becomes "another state of existence" (*yutyantara*).
68. The connection is that [the suffix] *tīsuttara* also functions [in this sense].

Since it is prescribed that for the clans of *rājañña* (royal nobles) and other humans, the suffixes for expressing a collection (*samūha*) are applied, he says “ending with the suffix *gotta*,” as in “a collection of *rājaññas*,” and so forth. *Ukkho* means a bull.
By such examples as "a herd of camels" (*uṭṭhānaṃ samūho*), "a herd of rams" (*urabbhānaṃ samūho*), and "a herd of sheep" (*mesānaṃ samūho*), [the author] refers to the sentence.
The analysis (*viggaha*) is "a collection of crows" (*kākānaṃ samūho*). By the rule *ṇika-acitta-*, it is made known that the suffix *-ṇika* is seen only after words denoting non-sentient beings.
*Apūpa* is a cake made of flour; *saṃkula* is a specific kind of mixed snack containing sugar.
69. Regarding the Kaccāyana-sutta rule, “*tadassaṭṭhānamīyo*,” this is its meaning:

“In the sense of ‘that is the place for it,’ the suffix *īya* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case. By that [rule], the place for intoxication (*madana*) is *madanīya*; the place for bondage...
They establish [the argument] beginning with "the place is binding," and so forth. However, since such a thing does not exist here, one might wonder how that [binding] is established;

having raised this doubt, he said "intoxicating" (*madanīya*), and so forth. To show that, he said: "By the establishment of 'intoxicating' and so forth," etc. To show the sequence of the proof, he said:
"It is understood thus," and so forth.
“*Ṭhāna*” means a cause. Regarding the Kaccāyana-sutta rule “*upamatthāyitattan*,” this is its meaning: “The suffix *āyitatta* occurs in the sense of ‘resembling.

Thus, it establishes such forms as *dhūmāyitattaṃ* (“smoking-like appearance,” because it appears like smoke) and *timirāyitattaṃ* (“darkness-like appearance,” because it appears like darkness), according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, the presentation of the two modes of derivation for *tampihacca*, etc., is shown here.
That which is shown as "it is seen like smoke" (dhūmo viya dissati)—that object of the action (kamma-attha)—can also be conceived by way of the agent (kartr) as "that which smokes" (dhūmāyi).

Therefore, because it is established as an agent, even when the suffix -ita is applied to the word *dhūmāyita* in its own sense (*sakattha*), there is no difference in meaning; rather, it should be understood that while the suffix -ita expresses the sense of "being seen like smoke," there is no difference in the intended expression other than the desire for a different wording.
However, the abstract state (*bhāva-attha*) [of these words] arises through the predominance of the state itself (*bhāva-padhāna*).
"It is obtained; it is the very sight of smoke"—this is the application [of the word] due to its being derived from the root *i* (to go) in the sense of "vigraha" (analysis). 70.
Regarding "Iyo aññasmiṃ": the construction is that the word *iya* occurs even in another sense.
74. One who travels far on a journey is well-suited for being away from home; one who observes a fast is well-suited for abstaining from food at night.
75. On the path...
On the road, provisions (*pātheyya*) that are beneficial and helpful are good; for one with a wife, wealth (*sāpateyya*)—that is, property and riches—is good as a means of support.

77. "Wealth (*rāya*) for the purpose of performing incantations (*tumantakiriyā*)," meaning for the purpose of performing spells (*mantakiriyā*) in order to kill (*ghātetuṃ*). The word *vā* is a conjunction (*samuccaya*); it is to be connected with the phrase "or for the purpose of killing," and so forth.

78. By means of the word "tame" (*tame*), indicating the meaning as delimited [from others], and considering that it requires a conceiving (*maññanā*) and possesses exertion (*sappadhāna*), he says, "herein this exists for him," thus showing that these two meanings—such as "snake" (*sappa*) and "effort" (*padhāna*)—function as a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
Now, is it not the case that whatever belongs to someone also exists in that person? (Whatever...)
In whatever [locus] it exists, that [quality] belongs to it as well; for this very reason it is said: "There is no distinction between the genitive and the locative.
Since this is already established by the description of one or the other [case], it is asked: for what purpose is the separate mention of the genitive and the locative made here? It is replied:

wherever there is a relationship of part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*), only there is the non-distinction of the meaning of the genitive and the locative in terms of the substance (*vatthuto*), as in: "The branch in the tree" (*rukkhe sākhā*).

"the branch of the tree. However, because the relationship of owner and owned (*sassāmibhāva*) or producer and produced (*janakabhāva*) does not necessarily entail the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheyyabhāva*), only these two meanings are taken.
But is it not the case that a qualifier is meaningful only when there is both possibility and deviation, as in "blue lotus"?
There is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the existence of that which exists; and thus it has been said: “The category of being (*satta*) does not deviate from its referent.

Therefore, because there is no possibility of exclusion (*byavecchejjābhāva*), he says “of the referent” (*padatthassa*) and so forth, in order to avoid the redundancy of the qualifier “exists” (*atthi*).

The connection is: “even though there is no deviation in the case of being. He says “at a [different] time” and so forth to show that the qualifier “exists” serves the purpose of precluding deviation at another time.
But surely, in the Suttas, time is not the primary factor; for by such expressions as "done by him" or "bought by him," the sense of a grammatical relation (paccaya) is shown.
Likewise, in cases such as "bodily" or "verbal," there is no temporal relation. Thus, here too, it should be understood merely as existence;
how then can it be determined that the word *atthi* ("is") refers specifically to present existence, such that it could serve as a temporal qualification?

True; however, although the meaning of the word does not deviate from existence (*sattā*), because of the force of employing the qualification "exists" (*atthi*), it is understood here that a qualified existence exists—that is, existence is taken as a qualifier, and not mere existence (*sattāmatta*).

Yet, that qualified existence is present existence, and since there is a deviation of that [qualified existence] from general existence, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is indeed appropriate.
It is so conceived. "Upādhi" (limiting condition) is a qualification.
Regarding the phrase "na bhuñjati cādi viyā" (like "he does not eat," etc.):

just as in the case of "he does not eat," because the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses negation, the understanding of the opposite meaning—the sense of prohibition—is not obstructed by the injunction (*vidhi*) which is based on the word and is present in proximity to a term with a contrary meaning.
This is the meaning of the words. Regarding the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*), he says: "The restriction of that which is the object of the desire for the word *atthi*.

However, when several meanings are possible, the construction is not "one who possesses cows" (*gomā*) or "one who protects trees" (*rukkhavā*); rather, it is by means of those [qualities] that are abundant and praiseworthy.
"Kakudāvatta" means one who has turned toward the hump (*kakuda*); "Kakudāvattī" means one who possesses a censured turning toward the hump. How is it that he is censured? He says: "Kakudā..."
"Vatto" and so forth. He says that one who possesses a staff (*daṇḍin*) is not designated as such merely because a staff exists, even if it is present in the house through being attached to it.
"In a substance to be denoted" means when the substance to be denoted—consisting of a genus, a support, a mass of cow-dung, a lump of horse-dung, and so forth—is to be expressed;
"you might be" means if you were to exist at any time whatsoever.
79. Having elided [the vowel], the wise one [should know that] in the case of "long and short" (*dīgharassā*) regarding the consonant (*byañjana*), it is short (*rassa*).
80. *Daṇḍā*.
"Two become" means that *ika* and *īca* become two; "each one" refers to both. The word *vā* (or) should also be understood here after "two become.
He explains the rule for the class (*gaṇasutta*) beginning with "the *ika* [is added] after *uttama*, *īṇa*, and *dhana*" by saying "after *uttama*, *īṇa*, and *dhanā*," and so forth.

To the question "What is the compound here? he replies: "The compound is formed according to the rule 'with *syādi* [words], with *syādi* [words], when there is a single meaning. Thus, *uttamīṇo* is the owner of wealth (*dhanasāmī*). [This applies] when the object is not present.
The *gaṇasutta* [explains] the meaning of *asannihite* as “*appatte*. The meaning is “not having reached” (*asampatte*). And the meaning “not present” (*asannihite*) is its qualification.
The meaning of *atthanaṃ* is the wishing for an object that is not present; one who has that [wish] is *atthiko*. From that ending [the suffix *-ika* is added].
The *gaṇasutta* [applies], and *asannihite* is carried over [from the previous rule]; [this refers to a word] characterized by the condition of being not present.

The meaning is that the suffixes *ika* and *ī* occur after words ending in *attha*. "Only those ending in *vaṇṇa*" is a rule from the *gaṇa*-sutta; alternatively, it is a compound meaning "the praise (*vaṇṇa*) of the Brahma-devas.
"In the sense of birth (*jāti*)" is a rule from the *gaṇa*-sutta regarding [words ending in] *hattha* and *danta*.

"In the sense of birth" is a qualification of the suffix. "From *vaṇṇa* in the sense of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*)" is a rule from the *gaṇa*-sutta. A specific restriction is established by the word *brahma*.

It is said: “He who knows,” and so forth. Regarding that practice of the specific rules, he says “And if that,” and so forth, showing that the entitlement belongs only to the three castes beginning with the Brahmin, and not to the Śūdra. The connection is: “He who exists within those three castes is called *tevaṇṇiko*.

The suffix *-ika* is used here in the sense of existence (*bhavatthe*), as in “existing within those three castes” because he is included among them. The word *vaṇṇa* denotes the castes such as the Brahmin and others.
In this context, by the term *brahmacāri*, the *sudda* (the low-caste person) is excluded.

Alternatively, "Brahma" refers to Nibbāna, and the scripture (*gantha*) which has that as its purpose; one who practices (*carati*) that Brahma—Nibbāna—or the Dhamma consisting of the Three Pitakas, is a *brahmacārī*, a recluse (*yati*).
For even recluses are called *brahmacārins* because they are "virtuous" (*vaṇṇī*). [As it is said: "The virtuous one is the one with the mark."
The meaning is: "it is indeed stated [that it applies] to those having the three genders. Here, however, the word *vaṇṇa* refers to the aforementioned Brahman.
The rule for the *gaṇa* begins with *pokkhara*. In this context, "place" (*desa*) means that place where there are lotuses and the like.

By the phrase "of that which denotes a cluster of lotuses (*padumagaccha*) or a lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*)," he shows that a lotus pond is also called *paduminī* because "there are lotuses (*padumāni*) in it."

The *nāvika* (boatman) exists because of the boat (*nāvā*); the *nāvāyika* (boat-merchant) [exists] because of the coming (*yāga*). The suffix *-ī* occurs after words for happiness and suffering (*sukha-dukkha*), as well as after *bala*, *bāhu*, and *ūru*; these are the rules of the group (*gaṇa-sutta*). 82.
Here too, one might apply it to "mouth" (*mukha*); in the usage "there is honey in this jar," the suffix *-ra* would also be reached [to form *madhura*].
The intended meaning is that [the word] "madhu" (honey/sugar) is the object of expression. They do not go, thus they are "nagā" (mountains).

Even though there is the possibility of the existence of words such as "pahūta" (abundant) when applied to objects like sugar and so forth, nevertheless, because there is no desire for verbal expression in the sense of being a condition (*paccayattha*) for that which possesses the quality of being "ñūsa" (sour/fermented) and so on, compounds such as *ñūsava* or *ghaṭa* and the like are not established.

Therefore, even if the existence of objects such as "abundant" is possible, [the compound is not formed] because of the absence of the condition (*paccayattha*) for that which possesses those qualities.
To say that "this is the sequence" would be incorrect as a condition; rather, the meaning should be understood as "just as otherwise, there is no light," thus he says "iti" and so forth.
Regarding "kuñjavāti": here, the word *kuñja* refers to a single part of a mountain covered by grass, creepers, and the like.
87. *Picchā*.

By means of the words "parehi" (by others), the author demonstrates the objection that "reproach has been introduced here, but it is not so," using the phrase beginning with "nindāyaṃ" (in reproach). 88. Regarding "sīlā":

the analysis of the compound is "one who possesses sīla" (sīlam assa atthi) and "one who possesses hair" (kesā assa santi). The rule for the *gaṇa* [of nouns] is established by the suffix *aṇ*, which signifies permanence (*nicca*).

They are recognized by means of the *gāṇḍī* [arrow]; the rule concerning the group (*gaṇasutta*) is for the purpose of restricting the scope of the designation. This belongs to the *gaṇḍa*, the horn of the *gaṇḍa* deer;
thus it is *gāṇḍī*. That which possesses this is *gāṇḍīva*.
"One who has *sāma* is a *suvāmī*; [this refers to] his own kin (*sakkiyan*). 91.

By the rule 'there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for *lakkhī*, concomitant with the suffix *ṇa*', it is shown that this substitution of the vowel *a* occurs precisely where the letter *ṇa* is present."
By the phrase "as a material cause" (*upādānato*), it is shown that providing a support (*nissaya*) is one way of understanding the term *satthiyo*.

By the phrase "due to the capacity for not prescribing the internal [vowel]," it is shown that although the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbalopa*) occurs, even when the letter *a* is prescribed for the completion of the grammatical formation, its subsequent elision is purposeless.
One who possesses *lakkhī* (fortune) or *sirī* (glory) is called *lakkhaṇo*.
94. *Kappiya*:
one who has fitness (*yogyatā*) for this [practice] is *kappiya*. The analysis of the compound is: "the matted hair (*jaṭā*) is his portion of decline (*hānabhāga*); he possesses an army (*senā*).
95. *Topa*.
In the rule ‘ohāka cāge,’ although the suffix *to* is prohibited when used with the root *hā* containing the letter *s*, the examples ‘satthā hīyate’ and ‘satthā hīno’ are shown.
Therefore he says: ‘To show this, the third example follows. The connection is that [the examples] end with the suffix *cī*, according to the rule:
“*cī* is added after a word denoting a modification when it is joined with *kar* or *asabhū* in the sense of becoming what it was not” (4-119).
The suffix *cī* has been stated [to apply] to those [stems] that exist at the end [of a word]; this is the analysis. Regarding the phrase "excluding the suffix *jātiya*":

by the rule *tabbati jātiyo* (4-113), it refers to those [stems] excluding the suffix *jātiya*. However, in the *Kaccāyana*, because case endings such as *to* and others are designated as case-suffixes (*vibhatti*), there is no further arising of a case ending from them.

96. Regarding the rule *vuttiyaṃ ‘etassa ṭa eta’*: the meaning is that in the case of *ato* and so forth, there is the substitution of *ṭā* for *etassa*, while in the case of *etto* and so forth, there is the substitution of *eta* for *etassa*. 97. *Abhyā-*...
[text fragment]
Now, one might object: "What is the use of this sutta? For those [words] ending in the fifth case, the rule ‘to pañcamyā’ (Pāṇini 5.4.45) will suffice;

as for those not ending in the fifth case, the rule ‘ādyādibhyaḥ’ (Pāṇini 5.4.48) will apply. This is not how it should be viewed. Since the rule ‘to pañcamyā’ (5.4.45) does not specify particular bases, let it apply to whatever ends in the fifth case;
however, regarding those not ending in the fifth case, in the sutta ‘ādyādibhyaḥ’, the word *ādi* is accompanied by a numeral (*sa-saṅkhya*).

It should be understood that by the mention of "gahaṇa" (grasping), those [words] similar to it, including their numerals, are indicated; therefore, [the suffix] "to" would not occur after words such as "abhi" when they do not end in the fifth case (pañcamī).
Thus, forms such as "abhito" and so on would not be established. Consequently, the rule "abhyādīhi" (after "abhi" and others) must be regarded as the governing sutta.
98. Ādyā.

[Objection: But surely, since it has been stated by way of a general rule (*sāmānyena*) that "from whatever [source], whether ending in the fifth case or not ending in the fifth case, the desired result is mostly established by the suffix *to*", what is the purpose of the rule "from *ādi* etc.
(*ādyādīhi*)? [Response: True; nevertheless, when it is shown through specific divisions, there may be a determination of particular distinctions according to those divisions—thus there is no fault.
From the nominative singular (*paṭhamantā*) "ya," [the suffix] *to* occurs after the word "yato" (from which).
100. *Kattha pubbeneva*:
by means of [the rule] beginning with “*sabbādito*” (4-99), etc. *Etassa*: of the word *eta*; *imassa*: of the word *ima*.
*Vāvidhānaṃ* means the prescription of the suffix *ya* by way of option (*vikappa*). 102.
When *yā* or *yattha* is stated, it would already be implied that *yattha* [is used]; therefore, it is not explicitly stated. The same applies to what follows.
104. Where is *hiñcana* prescribed? It is by the rule (*sutta*) "hiṃ haṃ hiñcana" (2-5-9). "Of *hiñci*, etc. means of *hiñci*, *dāci*, *rahaci*, and so forth. 105. All.
At this time, "once" (*ekadā*) and so forth should be understood. 106.
Regarding *kadā*:
the word *kadā* is seen only when used in conjunction with the word *cana*, as in *kudācana*.

107. “Of cause and effect” (*nimittanimittīnam*) means of the cause and the result. “Common” (*samāne*) means shared. He makes it understood that they are indeed common by means of the phrase beginning with “just as that” (*taṃ yathā*).
Here, however, the beating of the mother is the cause (*nimitta*), and the taking of life is the effect (*nimittī*); “of that” refers to what is not of today. Below.
In the *Tyādi* section, however, the word *karaha* is seen only in conjunction with the word *ci*, as in *karahaci*.

110. Regarding the words expressing numbers (*dhāsa*), it is said—starting with "in the meaning"—that they are included by the term "number-word" (*saṅkhyāsadda*). The particle *paka* also refers to substance, quality, and location.

There is; in that case, if that [base] were also to be included, then since the connection with gender and number applies to the *dhātu* and *pratyaya* ending in *dha*, and since the *Kāśikāvṛtti-pañjikā* states that "that which ends in a *dha*-suffix is without gender and without number," there would be no mention here of its connection with the genders and numbers denoting the letter *pa*;
and such being the case, indeclinability (*avyayatva*) would be intended for it.

It would not [be so]; for if that [suffix] were taken as denoting action (*kiriyā*), then in cases such as *ekadhā bhuñjati* (he eats in one way), *dvidhā bhuñjati* (he eats in two ways), or *dvidhā gacchati* (he goes in two ways), there would be no connection with gender or number at all regarding the actions of eating, going, and so forth, and thus the aforementioned fault would not arise.
Therefore, the author of the Pāṇinian rules, Jayāditya, has taken "manner" (*pakāra*) here specifically as the object of action.
Tampati said: "In substances," and so forth. But why did he say this? He replied: "Substance is ninefold," and so forth.
"Substance is ninefold, quality is manifold"—this is the convention of the Vaiśeṣikas.
In that regard, earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind are the nine substances. Form, taste, smell...
Contact (*phassa*), number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are the qualities (*guṇa*);

by the word "and" (*ca*), heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental formation (*saṅkhāra*), merit (*dhamma*), demerit (*adhamma*), and sound are included—thus, the quality is manifold in twenty-four ways.
Here too, according to the aforementioned *Kāsikāvutti*, it has been analyzed into nine types by Pañcikākāra Jinindabuddhi.

In the phrase "the substance is manifoldly qualified" (*dabbaṃ bahudhā guṇoti*), here too, because it is said that "the action (*kiriyā*) must be brought forth [as the subject], the substance is ninefold, and the quality (*guṇa*) is pointed out, understood, explained, or found," the mode (*pakāra*) presented belongs exclusively to the domain of action.

Since action alone is present everywhere due to the demonstration of application (*payoga*) and the state of exclusion (*byavacchejjabhāva*), the inclusion of a qualifier (*visesana*) is inappropriate; such is the connection.
The commentator states that because the various modes (*pakāra*)— which have as their objects both substance (*dabba*) and quality (*guṇa*)—

are included [in the definition] through the demonstration of application (*payoga*), namely "substance is ninefold" and "quality is manifold," and because there exist modes having substance and quality as their objects that must be excluded,

there is indeed activity (*kiriyā*) in every case regarding the objects of substance and quality according to the method stated by the venerable Buddhaghosa; thus, only the mode that has activity as its object is taken here.
The meaning is that the inclusion of qualifiers by the authors of the *pañjikā* is inappropriate.
"For that very reason" means: because the inclusion of qualifiers is inappropriate, for that very reason he says "in two ways" (*dvīhi*) and so forth; this is the intended sense here.

[In the phrase] "he makes it twofold," even in the application of the action, the manner (*pakāra*) has as its object both substance (*dabba*) and quality (*guṇa*)... [the manner] of the object-substance and the object-quality.

Because it is the state of being split that is being produced, [the object] is not the domain of the action (*kiriyā*); for here, it is not intended to speak of the state of being split as the domain of the act of producing.

Precisely for this reason, in order to indicate that there would be no application of the verbal root with its suffixes (*dhāppaccayantappayoga*) in the case of the inclusion of the "manner" (*pakāra*) in the sense of "lying down" (*sayana*), he says "by two," etc., as in the passage beginning with "here."

Regarding the various ways in which the sense of a substance (*dabbaguṇa*) might be grasped, the following objection raised by others is now refuted with the words beginning "even though" (*sati pi ce*).
The connection is: "by its own nature it is without gender and without number. According to Pāṇini’s rules, suffixes are prescribed when the induction of another number is understood;
thus he says "of a substance," etc. The phrase "even in the induction of another number" refers to what was stated previously.

The number that is established is one thing, and the bringing about of another number different from that is "the bringing about of another number" (*saṅkhyantarāpādana*); the meaning is "even in that case. 113. *Tabba*: That which has such a manner is *tabbā*.

Since the word *ta* refers to the manner (*pakāra*), the meaning stated here is "possessing that manner" (*pakāravatī*). Thus he says, "by the word *ta*" and so forth. "Possessing a manner" means in the sense of possessing a manner. One who has a mild manner is "of a mild nature" (*mudujātiko*).
115. Regarding the question "How many? (*kati*), they say that it expresses number and measure.

This is because the form *kati* is established by applying the suffix *rati* according to the rule *kimhā rati rīvarīvataka rittakā* (Pāṇini 5.2.44), as stated [in the commentary]: "Because it is derived in the domain of number and measure."
And what is *kati*? Because it is both a number (*saṅkhā*) and its object is quantity (*parimāṇa*), it is called *katisaṅkhā*; [the suffix -ī] is used by means of that.

116. Regarding *bahu paccāsatti*: when one related member is shown, because the relation has two aspects, the other related member, being understood through logical connection (*yutti*), is understood as "the other"; thus it is said, "or on account of the relation."
117. "Of the particle *sakiṃ*" means of the particle *sakiṃ*. 118. *So*...
“Khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaṃ” means piece by piece; “khaṇḍaso” means into fragments; “puthu” means variously; “pakāro” means manner; “puthuso” means individually. 119. Regarding the word *abhū*:

surely it is called *abhūta* (unreal) either because of its total non-arising or because of its existence in another state. Likewise, the word *sacca* (truth) also refers to that which has merely arisen.
How is it that the word *abhūta* refers to something other than its own base? He says: “In the case of *abhūtassa*, etc.

If it is asked, “How is the base itself (*vatthāva*) referred to by the word *tad*?”—if the word *abhūta* were a term for what has not yet arisen (*anuppanna*), then the application of the word *tad* would be impossible...

because the word *tad* would only grasp that which is non-existent (*abhūta*), and [the rule] would have been formulated as “in the state of being non-existent” (*abhūtabhāve*) and so forth; therefore, by the power of the application of the word *tad*, [it is understood otherwise].
The word *tas* refers to the state (*avasthā*). And the sound (*sadda*) expects another state (*avatthantara*) that has that as its object;
therefore he says, “because of the expression ‘in the state of that’ (*tabbhāve*),” and so forth. Being (*bhavana*) is *bhāva*; the state in that other state is *tabbhāva*, [meaning] in that.

Therefore he says, “of that which has not come to be,” and so forth. He says “in the object” (*visaye*) because it is either a locative of domain (*visaya-sattamī*) or a locative of association (*saṃsatta-sattamī*).
‘Or when being carried’: by “in the state of a coil” (kuṇḍalattena) is meant “by way of the nature of a coil.
Regarding the statement “is seen” (dissati), since it is said that the meaning understood is “is seen in usage,” he says “the root *dis*,” etc.; this is the sutta.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "there is a *paribhāsā* concerning the *vijjhaṅga*. By the rule 4-1, *ṇovā-pacce*, etc., among the various meanings stated, it is called *paribhāsā* because it speaks (*bhāsati*) around (*pari*) or on all sides (*samantato*).
A *paribhāsā* that has become a constituent part (*aṅga*) of a suffix (*paccaya*) in a rule (*vidhi*) is a *vijjhaṅgaparibhāsā*.
The connection is: "this is the rule (*sutta*) itself, namely 'only the rule' (*vidhiyeva*). [This refers to] the two rules about to be explained: "in another... (*aññasmiṃ*)...
"Regarding the word *sakatthe*," there are two suttas. 125. The word *antarā* has multiple meanings here;

it is understood as denoting "interval" (*antarāla*) and "middle" (*majjha*). It is not used in the sense of "there is no interval between these," for its purpose lies in the mere negation of an interval.
Having established that "there is not," because there is an absence of anything else in between, it is metaphorically designated as "the interval" (*antarāla*). For it is used thus in the world:
"these villages are adjacent," or "these palaces are adjacent"; such a designation is made because of the absence of any other village or palace situated in the interval.
Likewise here too, it is because of the absence of any other phoneme situated in the interval.
They are called "immediate" (*anantara*). Alternatively, the word *antara* signifies "intervention"; because there is an absence of intervention, they are called "immediate.
Or, having applied the suffix *khādi* and then the suffix *ṇi* (according to the manuscript), [the root] *antari* means "to cause an interval," that is, to create an intervention;
then, having applied the suffix *ap* in the sense of the agent, *antara* means "one who intervenes. Since these [factors] do not exist, they are "immediate."

Immediately following. Just as in the expression “trees in the forest,” the trees, being gathered together, receive the designation of a single forest, so too here the consonants, being gathered together, enter into the domain of the designation “conjunction” (*saṃyoga*).
For the term “conjunction” is a description where the aggregate is predominant rather than the individual consonants; therefore, [the text says] “consonants.”
The singular designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is appropriate because it is expressed in the plural. Now, one might object:
"Since phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered, a collection (*samudāya*) cannot exist for those that do not abide simultaneously; therefore, [the term] 'collection' is inappropriate.
This is not incorrect. For the intellect, which grasps each successive [phoneme], conceives of the preceding and following phonemic components as a single collective form.
"He employs collective designation.
Because the word *diti* is not a subject of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) by the rule "when followed by a *ṇ*-anubandha," it falls under the scope of "the first vowel of vowels" (*sarānamādissa*);
whereas because the word *uḷumpa* is a subject of a conjunct consonant, it falls under the scope of "of that [consonant]" (*etassa*). In this regard, there are Rāghava, Venateyya, Menika, and Decca.
"Forms are the end of faults. However, here it is appropriate to say "Koṇḍañña is like one who uses a raft.
For that very reason, what is in the *Pañcika* there should be brought here, and what is here in the *Pañcika* should be brought there.
127. *Kosa* [Abhidharmakośa].
In *kosajja*, there is the elision (*nipātanā*) of its effort (*jatta*); in *ajjava*, [the rule] applies: "Of *uvaṇṇa*, [there is elision] before a vowel" (4-129).
135. In *jovu*, the doubling (*dvitta*) of the letter *y* should be understood.
The analysis [of the compound] is "one who is exceedingly little" (*atisayena appo*) and "one who is exceedingly young" (*atisayena yuvā*).

When "in *sati*" is stated, the word *sati* is understood. However, one might wonder: "Even though there is the word *santa*, how is it that the *santa* which is intended to be expressed as a qualifier is understood?
To address this doubt, [it is explained that] by the rule "after *saṅkhya*, *sacca*, and *tīsā*, etc. (Pāṇini 5.2.49), the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed after words such as *santa*.
Since the suffix *ḍa* is included as a marker (*nimitta*), by the power of that inclusion, only the word *santa* is understood.
To show this, he said: “It moves by taking up a cause,” and so forth. 142.

That which is other than a root (dhātu) is a non-root (adhātu). In the *Pañcikā*, however, since even a base word (*pakati*) is indeed a sound, the mere meaning of the term “non-root” has been stated by means of the phrase beginning with “from a root,” etc.
“Of that” (*tassa*) means of that which does not have the nature of a primary element (*adhātuppakati*); it is said to mean “of the word *adhatu*. “And by that” (*tenaca*) means by the letter *ka*;
“therefore” (*tasmā*) means for that reason. Regarding the mention of “preceding” (*pubba*):

in this very sutta of Pāṇini’s which prescribes the substitution of the vowel *i*, the mention of “preceding” was made for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *i* for what precedes the letter *ka*. Without that mention of “preceding,” [the rule would not apply].

The meaning is as follows: the connection is that [the word] "sace" and so forth expresses [this sense]. Regarding the rule "in a consonant, long and short [vowels]" (1-33), the short vowel was mentioned;
however, in the case of the general designation "assa," the vowel *ā* indeed occurs after the letter *c*. Thus, the form "bahuparibbājakā" arises from the possibility of this [application].
In this context, the *syādi* group [of suffixes] occurs before the letter *k*, whereas the *syādi* group does not occur after the letter *k*.

Now, one might wonder: why is the negative particle (*nañ*) here taken as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation) in the phrase “it would not be so” (*syād ito na*), rather than a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary negation)?

Suspecting this, he begins to state the fault that would arise if it were taken as a *paryudāsa*, starting with the words “In the case of an exclusionary negation” (*pariyudāse*). The word “it would be so” (*syād iti*) [is explained as] from the word *paribbājaka* ending in a *syādi* suffix (a verbal or nominal inflection).
For the word *paribbājaka* ends in a *syādi* suffix within the sentence because it possesses such a suffix; for this very reason, he will say later:

Regarding the phrase “*paribbājakasaddato ettha syādyuppattī*”: having formed *paro* from *asyādi*, the connection is that there is no occurrence of case-endings (*syādi*) from the word *bahuparibbājakasadda*.

Then, with the words “*tato cā*,” meaning “also from the word *bahuparibbājakasadda*,” he says “*avijjamāno syādi*,” etc., demonstrating that even in a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound) containing the negative particle *nañ* used in a prohibitive sense (*pasajjappaṭisedha*), a fault would indeed occur.
Thus ends the commentary on the Fourth Chapter in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*,
a sub-commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*.
The Fifth Chapter.

1. Regarding the phrase "Tija khamāvīmaṃsāsūti," [the author] asks how it is that the specific nature (*pakativisesana*) alone is intended; thus he says, "In the connection" (*sambandhe*), and so forth.

The meaning is that the mutual connection of words depends upon the person (*purisa*). He calls this the "specific nature," meaning it is the qualifier of words. But what, then, is the specific nature?
Regarding the term *phala*, he says: "The inclusion of a specific verbal root (*pakativisesana*)," and so forth. As for the specific verbal root *khama-vīmamsa-sū* mentioned here, he asks:
"In what sense do the *khas* operate? and answers: "Because of the indication of another meaning," and so forth. "Of another meaning" means of another meaning such as sharpening (*nisāna*), etc.
He thus indicates the technical rule (*paribhāsa*): "Between what is explicitly stated and what is inferred, that which is connected to the explicit statement is stronger."

By the phrase “of those [roots] that are directly stated or inferred,” and so forth. “By that very [means]” means by the application (*vidhāna*) of the suffixes *kha* and *mīmsu* to verbal roots (*kiriyārūpa*), specifically the suffix *kha*;

it is implied that this is an application in its own sense (*sakatthe*). By the expression “because it is an act of endurance” (*titikkhakiriyattā*), he shows that the prescription of the technical term “root” (*dhātusaññā*) for those things being chewed, as in the case of others, serves no purpose.
*Titikkhā* means patience or forbearance; *titikkhati* means he is patient or forbears. *Vīmaṃsā* means investigation or examination;
*vīmaṃsati* means he investigates or examines—this is the meaning. Because of the grammatical rule (*niddesa*) stating "tijai," the root belonging to the *bhūvādi* class is understood here.

For when there is such a purpose, although the causative form belonging to the *curādi* class is frequently prescribed, it does not abandon its own inherent nature simply because it is constant. Alternatively, by means of the *curādi* class, which is non-deviating [in this context]...

The term *sāhacariyā* (association) also refers only to the *cur*-class [roots], as in the example: “there is need for a companion for the ox. Here, only the ox (*go*) is understood, not the horse (*asso*), nor the donkey (*gadrabho*).
However, occasionally there may be the inclusion of even the horse as a companion, due to the influence of the context or the speaker’s intention.

But is it not the case that the formulation of grammatical rules with conditions (*sapaccaya-vidhāna*) is untenable in this investigation, because it is vitiated by the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*)?
For instance, when the word *vīmaṃsā* (investigation) is established, the suffix arises; and when that exists, the form *vīmaṃsā* comes into being.
Thus, there is mutual dependence (*itaretaranissaya*), and since functions based on mutual dependence are not applicable here, he said: “of words that are mere restatements,” and so forth.
There is no fault of mutual dependence in the case of the restatement of words that have been established from beginningless time.
The state [of being]. In the absence of the operation of an instigator (*payojaka*), the form is *tejatā*.

2. By the phrase "as before, because of the specific nature of the base (*pakati*) and so forth," [it is shown that] since the relationship depends on the person (*purisa*), [the rule applies] to the cases of "medical treatment" (*tikicchā*) and "doubt" (*saṃsaya*).

Regarding the term *pakativisesana* (qualification of the base), he says: “‘For the sake of treatment,’ etc. He thus extends by analogy (*atidisati*) that all such [expressions] should be stated here as well, according to their respective application.
The meaning of the prefix *vi-* is “confidence” (*vissattha*). Now, one might wonder why there are two examples for a single case-ending (*paccaya*) here;
therefore, he says: “The two examples are given because of a difference in meaning (*atthabheda*). *Niketa* means dwelling (*nivāsa*); *saṅketa* means a characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*).
3. *Nindā* (*nindā* = blame).

From that [root], by the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini] 5.4.38 (*itthiyamaṇattikayakyā ce*), and from that, by the suffix *āp* according to [Pāṇini] 3.2.64 (*itthiyamatvā*), the form [is derived]. That which binds is a *badhaka*.
4. From the suffix *tuṃ*.

He explains the inclusion of the suffix *tuṃ* here by means of the phrase beginning with ‘*tuṃtāya*’. Regarding the words “*tato ce*”: the meaning is “because of that,” namely, because there is the inclusion of the suffix *tuṃ* itself and because there is a designation as a qualifier (*visesanā*).
When there is an inclusion of a suffix, the inclusion of that which begins with it is understood; this is known from the rule:
“In the inclusion of a suffix, since it has been prescribed, there is the inclusion of that which begins with it. This is because it is intended to be expressed as a qualifier.
The inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) [in the rule]... bearing in mind the statement, “In the case of a specific rule, it refers to that which ends with it” (1-13), he says:

‘from which there is a verbal root,’ and so forth. That verbal root is the beginning (*ādi*) of a complex (samudāya); thus it is “that which begins with it” (*tadādi*). That same [root] is at the end of that [complex];
thus it is “that which ends with it” (*tadanta*). The meaning is: there is a mention of a specific complex that both begins with and ends with that [root], and not merely of that which ends with it.
But surely, since [the rule] "vidhibbesanantasse" applies when one wishes to express a qualifier such as *tuṃ* or *smā*, let that inclusion of "ending in that" (*tadanta*) be valid;

however, in the case of taking a suffix (*paccaya*), how can there be an inclusion of "that which begins with it" (*tadādino*) in the absence of an explicit statement? To this he says: "Because of its inseparability from that" (*tadavinābhāvittā*).

Since that which is prescribed does not exist without it by its very nature, it is "inseparable from that" (*tadavinābhāvī*); the state of being so is "inseparability from that" (*tadavinābhāvitta*); therefore [it is understood]. By this...

The meaning is understood through reasoning (*yutti*), as it is stated: "In the case of taking a suffix (*paccaya*), because that [suffix] is prescribed, there is the inclusion of what begins with it.
Let it be so that there is an inclusion of both what begins with that and what ends with that; then he states the fruit of this, beginning with "by that" (*teneva*).
"Together with the *pādi*" means accompanied by the *pādi*. "Due to the absence of the arising of *kha*, *cha*, and *sup*" means due to the non-existence of the occurrence of *kha*, *cha*, and *su*.
The intention is that because the base of the suffix *tuṃ*—of the very kind already described—is what is grasped [by the rule], the application of *kha*, *cha*, and *sānam* does not occur.
From the root *ji* (to conquer) with the prefix *vi-*, in the sense of "desires to conquer" (*vijetum icchati*), the suffix *so* is applied by the rule "after *tuṃ*, etc. (*tuṃsmā*);

there is also the elision of *tuṃ*. When the *e*-vowel caused by that [suffix] is removed, there is doubling (*dvitta*) as *jisa jisa*, and then the elision of the non-initial consonant results in *jihirānaṃ*.
*gī* (5-102). *gī*. Derived from the desiderative (*jigīsappakatito*), [the suffix] *ī* is applied by the rule "in the case of *bhū*, *īūṃ*, etc. (6-4). In that [suffix], another [rule applies]:
"for *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *mhā*, *ssā*, and *ssamhā*, [the following vowel] may optionally be short" (6-33). Thus, by the shortening of *ī*, it becomes *byajigīsi*.

However, if the arising of *s* were to occur after the completion [of the reduplication], then when the doubling is performed in *byajigīsī*, it would apply to the first monophthong of the base ending in the suffix *s*.

Regarding the statement "it becomes a dual form": by the rule *kha cha sānam* (5-69), when *vi* is replaced by *vij*, since the initial *vi* of the whole [form] would be subject to the substitution of *ī* and the status of being a base (*pakati*) would apply to the preceding *sapādi*, there might be the addition of the augment *añ* before the syllable *vi*.
Consequently, one would incur the undesirable result of the form *avivijisī*.

Because *tuṃ* and *sma* are taught as the positions for the primary suffix (*pakatipaccaya*) and the secondary suffix (*paccaya*), the suffixes *kha*, *cha*, and *sa*, along with their endings, are inferred by that gender-sign (*sabhāva-liṅga*);
however, *tuṃ* is not [inferred] here because it is heard [directly]. Thus he says: "Neither its ending, nor *cha* or *chasā*.

In the word *jighacchā*, where there is reduplication (*dvitta*), the *gha* of the preceding syllable becomes [the first letter of the following class] according to the rule: "For the fourth and second [consonants], the third and first [of the following]."
(5-78) *go*. For that [word], by [the rule] “*kavaggahānaṃ cavaggajā*” (5-79), there is *jo*.

Pāṇini also, in this sutta which prescribes the suffix *sap*, employed the word “*vā*” so that a sentence might also occur; [the author] says “‘vākyampi’ etc. in order to refute that as being incorrect.

In the expression *pakatyādi*, the word *ādi* should be understood as referring to specific meanings: *pakativiseso* means a specific base ending in *-tum*, and *icchattho* means a specific meaning of the suffix *-attha*.
"This is the rule" means that "the elision of *tuṃ* [occurs] when *cicchā* follows *te*"—this is the grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*). "Niyogato" means by necessity.
To refute what was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*, namely, "there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) in case of doubt," he says: "In case of doubt," and so forth.
Because a riverbank is insentient, desire is impossible; therefore, the statement "it desires to fall into the riverbank" is itself unestablished as an illustration of desire.
By that unestablished statement, there is the proving of unestablished [terms] such as *kha*, *cha*, and *sāna*; thus, "proving the unestablished by the unestablished" (*asiddhenāsiddhasādhanaṃ*).

"Desire to speak" (*icchāvacanicchā*) means the desire to speak. "Apprehension proceeding from desire" (*icchāyapavattito upaladdhīti*) means apprehension, censure, or full understanding proceeding from desire;
this is the meaning. It is said to be "possessing volition" (*cetanāvati*); therefore, having shown apprehension proceeding from that which possesses volition...

In order to show that this designation applies even to non-sentient things, he says, "And whatever... and so forth. In the case of Devadatta, there is the manual application of a rope, a stake, and so on;
on the bank, there is the scattering of clay and the like. A *rajjū* is a cord. A *khīlo* is a wedge, such as a *saṃkva* and so on.
A *pulo* is a mass of grass and the like. "That dog wishes to kill" (*mimarisati*): here, *mar* means "to give up life," and the suffix *-so* follows the infinitive form (*tumanta*).
Regarding the phrase “*ñi byañjanasse*” (5-170): it is *ñi*. When there is doubling (*dvitta*), there is elision of the preceding *ñ* according to the rule “*kha cha sesvī*” (5-76);
thus, when there is doubling, the *i* of the preceding [syllable] becomes *mi*, as in *marisati*. Likewise, in *pipatisati*, [the root] *path-* means “to go.
She desires to die (*sā mimarisati*); even though she possesses consciousness, the desire for death can arise in a dog whose life is exhausted.
It has been established. The author of the Pāṇinian Vārttika stated, "A prohibition must be formulated for those [roots] whose meaning is 'desire' (*icchā*). To refute that, he says:
"‘bubhukṣituṃ’ and so forth. He states "‘jātipadatthe’ and so forth” to establish the cessation [of the rule] based on the category-meaning (*jātipadārtha*).
The other [term] has the sense of "desiring."

5. That which is performed and connected is *kamma* (action). And that is fivefold, according to its connection with name (*nāma*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kiriyā*), and substance (*davva*).
Among these, *nāmakamma* (action by name) is, for example, "Ḍittho" or "Ḍavittho," due to the connection of the individual body with a name. *Jātikamma* (action by genus) [is as follows:]...

"Go-assa" (of a cow) refers to the connection of the individual substance with its genus, such as "cow-ness" and so forth. Quality-object (*guṇakamma*) refers to the connection of the substance with a quality, such as "white-blue," meaning through qualities like whiteness and so forth.
Action-object (*kiriyākamma*) refers to the connection of the substance with an action, such as "cook" or "drinker," meaning through actions such as cooking and so forth.

Substance-object (*dabbakamma*) refers to the connection of the individual substance with a substance, such as "staff-bearer" or "horned," meaning through substances such as a staff and so forth. Thus, although there is the occurrence of five types of objects for the accusative case, in this context [only the first three are intended].

Since, according to the rule for the genitive case (*īyassa vidhānato*), only an action related to desire (*icchāsambandhi*) is understood here, it is the "action as object" (*kiriyākamma*) alone that is taken;

thus, in order to point out a specific matter, he says "even though" (*yadipi*), and so forth. This collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāyo*) functions in the acceptance of a reason for stating a distinction.

Similarly, the common worldly usage "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) occurs at the commencement of stating a distinction. "Only related to that" (*taṃsambandhiyeva*) means "only related to desire" (*icchāsambandhiyeva*).

In the statement beginning with “one desires one’s own son” (*attanoputtamicchatīti*), Pāṇini prescribes the suffix *cha* (forming *icchā*) by means of another sutta that governs the term *attanō* as being connected to the son and so forth.
However, in the absence of the inclusion of the word *atta* (self), how could it be understood that the son and so forth are connected specifically to oneself?

For, in the absence of a qualifying statement, it would follow that they could also be connected to another. Anticipating this objection, he says: “connected to oneself,” and so forth. This refers to the suffix *īya*.

The term *saṃbandho* (connection) refers even to that which relates to another, as in the case of *pasaṅgo*. Why? He says: "Because of the non-expression of the suffix -īya. This means that when the word *attha* (meaning/object) is not explicitly stated, there is no expression of the suffix -īya.

The third case ending (*tatiyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) or the cause (*hetumhi*), as in *appattiya*. The word *ettha* (here) also applies to the phrase *attano puttamicchati* (he desires his own son). It is not desired.
The *īya*-suffix is not intended [here]. To express the intention of one who says, "It should not be so here," he states: "'Sāpekkhatta yeva' (only the state of being expectant) is the meaning.
If it were to occur even in a state of expectancy when there is a desire to say "he wishes for his own son," then this undesirable consequence would follow;
thus, to demonstrate this, he says: "If, however, here... and so forth.
He states the actual form of the undesirable consequence: “It might be [said] that it is treated as one’s own son.

If it is argued that because the purpose of the self (*attattha*) is already expressed by the suffix *-īya-* itself as it arises, the word *atta* (self) should not be employed, he explains that this too is not consistent, saying:
“And it is not possible,” and so forth. Why is it not possible to say this? He says: “The base,” and so forth. [This refers to] the *apūpa* (cake), etc.
The meaning is: because we observe that even a qualifier which is identical in meaning to its base word is included within the compound word. To show where this is seen, he says:
"Just as... and so forth. [The example is: "His craft, virtue, merchandise, weapon, or purpose is that," according to the rule on the suffix *ṇika* (4.2.78), resulting in *āpūpika*.
He then states the following to establish that this does not apply to words of different meanings, first showing the contrast and then proving it with an example:
“Devadatta’s,” and so forth. He states the reason: “In another compound,” and so forth.

Because the word *devadatta* is employed for the purpose of excluding other compounds—such as in the expression *gurukula*, meaning “the teacher’s family”—the sense is that the referent of *devadatta* is internal (*anta*) to the compound term *gurukula*.
Demonstrating that this is likewise the case here, he says: “So too here,” and so forth. Now, regarding the phrase “one who desires his own son”:
To show why the word *atta* might not be used in a compound within a sentence due to its grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*), he says:

“And yet not,” and so forth. “Of a word” means of a word such as *puttīya*. The connection is: “and yet there is no use of the word *appa*. He states the reason: “Because it ends in -ī,” and so forth. The connection is:
“a word ending in -ī, such as *puttīya*, does not necessarily [end] in -appa. “The use of another word expressing that meaning” refers to the employment of a different synonym.
"Sutaggahaṇan" (the mention of "heard") refers to the mention of what was heard because it had not been heard before.

By this, it is indicated that the status of being a son is established by way of meaning even from the context and so forth; he states that the inclusion of the word "suta" (heard) is for the purpose of indication.

Now, since it is stated in the Sutta that "from the action," one might suspect that [the son] could also arise from a collection of actions; therefore, he says the following to establish the very absence of such a state:

"‘Kamma’ and so forth: that commonality of action (*kamma-sāmāñña*) which is intended to be expressed with a singular number is what is thus stated. He states the inclusion of that which is intended to be expressed with a singular number by saying ‘from the aggregate of actions (*kammasamudāyato*)’.

Why should it not also be [intended] from the perspective of the individual parts (*avayavato*)? Regarding the phrase ‘he desires a great son (*mahantaṃ puttaṃ icchati*)’, having raised the doubt as to why it is not [intended] from the perspective of the individual parts, he says:
‘Because even from the perspective of the individual parts, there is dependence (*sāpekkhattā*) itself. The connection is ‘it is not [the case that] the master (*bhatī*)... And thus, in this way..."

Challenging [the opponent] by saying that even this is not established, he says: “For indeed,” and so forth. To show that when one desires a great son (*mahāputta*)—that is, a son who is both great and a son—this very application is what must be done, he says: “It must necessarily be so,” and so forth. 6.
The Simile.
"It is compared," "it is delimited," or "it is established"—this is the meaning. To the question "Of what kind is the means of comparison (upamāna)?", he says:

"By similarity with what is well-known" (*prasiddhasādhamyāt*), and so forth. "Well-known" (*prasiddha*) refers to [an animal] such as a cow; by its "similarity" (*sādhamya*), that is, by its having an identical form, the establishment of something else that is not well-known, such as a *gavaya*, is the "means of comparison" (*upamāna*).
That which has a common property (*dharma*) is "possessing a common property" (*sadharma*); this refers specifically to the cow and so forth. Its state [is similarity].

Similarity (*sādhamya*). That by which something is established or compared is the means of proof (*sādhana*), namely, the standard of comparison such as a cow. That which is established or compared is the object of proof (*sādhya*), namely, the *gavaya* and so forth.
The means of proving that [object] is "the means of proving the object of proof" (*sādhiyasādhana*).
In the expression "he behaves like a son," the locative sense is understood, just as in "he dwells in a dwelling" (*āvasathaṃ āvasati*).

Just as one performs acts such as giving sweet food and drink toward a young boy as if toward one's own son, so too, by means of the occurrence of this purpose, he says "putte" (toward a son) and so forth, in order to make clear the relationship between the simile and the subject of the simile for both parties.

Since the conduct [of the father] toward the son—who serves as the standard of comparison (upamāna) by virtue of being well-known—is itself well-known, he says "that too is well-known. By that conduct, [he refers to] the conduct directed toward the young boy who is the son.
Alternatively, by taking the term "boy" (*māṇavaka*) in its figurative sense as "son," it is also logical to apply the designation of the object (*visaya*) to the subject (*visayin*) [by metonymy].
As for the meaning of the sentence in this alternative, it is: "He acts like a son—that is, he behaves toward the boy as toward a son; he performs conduct that has the boy as its object.
However, in the commentary (*vutti*), the two aforementioned meanings should be understood by applying them appropriately as the case may be.

Now, one might object: "If the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamāna-upameyyabhāva*) is already expressed by the word *iva* in the compound, then the word *iva* is omitted;

in that case, the relationship of standard and object of comparison exists through the word *putta* alone. Therefore, how is it appropriate to employ the word *māṇavaka*, which expresses the object of comparison whose meaning has already been stated?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the word expressing the standard of comparison," and so forth.

"In conduct distinguished by that" means in conduct distinguished by that simile. Regarding the phrase "because the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison does not cease," this is the intended meaning:

"Since the word for the standard of comparison functions to establish the suffix *-īya* (denoting 'likeness') in regard to conduct distinguished by the standard of comparison, the word for the standard of comparison cannot function without the word for the object of comparison;

thus, the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison does not cease. "Otherwise" means if the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison...

The meaning is that because it shines like two *īyena* birds, there may be the application [of the suffix] to that which is to be compared (*upameyya*). In "it stretches out like a mountain" (*pabbatāyati*), *āya* is the suffix according to [Pāṇini 3.1.137] *kattutāyo*.

Because the object of comparison (*upameyya*) does not cease [to be the subject], the suffix *tip* is applied due to the commonality of the agent (*kattu-sāmañña*) with the object of comparison. 7. The locus (*ādhāra*).

Just as in the immediately preceding sutta the application of the object of comparison (the young brahmin) to the standard of comparison was appropriate, so too here, pointing out that the application of the object of comparison (‘in the palace’ and ‘in the hut’) is likewise, he says: “As in the previous [sutta],” and so forth. The meaning is: because the object of comparison is proximate to the standard of comparison.
But why is this stated, when one who acts like a palace could also be expressed as “one who acts like a palace”?
