Regarding the phrase "it is possible to say," there is no difference in meaning other than a difference in the desire for expression; thus, the suffix *īya* is established here by the same rule as before.
Therefore, fearing that the word *nāttha* might be taken as a separate term, he says "even though" (*yadipi*), and so forth.
8. Kattu.

Here, by the mention of "from the agent" (*kattuto*), the term "object" (*kamma*) is excluded; by the inclusion of "āya," the suffix *ī* is [intended]. But when is the specific nature of the agent understood? To this he says:

"In the case of coreferentiality with words such as *yatthi*, etc. and so forth. The meaning is: when there is coreferentiality with words such as *hatthi* (elephant), as in "pabbatāyi hatthi" (the mountain-like elephant), and so on. 9. In the sense of "burnt" (*jhatthe*).

Regarding this doubt concerning the fourfold scope (*catuṭṭhoccāsaṅkī*), [the author] says: "In the sense of 'becoming what was not previously so' (*abhūtatadbhāve*), when there is a connection with *kar* and so forth, [the suffix *ci* is applied] after a word denoting a modification" (Pāṇini 5.4.50).

Because the suffix *ci* is prescribed when there is a connection with *kar* and so forth in the sense of "becoming what was not previously so," he states: "The state of becoming what was not previously so is qualified by *kar* and so forth.

Since the state of becoming what was not previously so is qualified by *kar* and so forth, the term *bhuvi* ("in the sense of being") must necessarily be included, just as in Pāṇini's system; otherwise, [the rule would fail to apply].
Having raised the doubt that the meaning of the root *karoti* (to do) might also apply here, he states the reason for its exclusion with the words “by that very [reason],” etc.
The meaning is: by that same reason through which the sense of the verbal root *bhū* (to become)—characterized as the transformation from one state to another (*abhūtatadbhāva*)—is expressed.

Having raised the doubt that since the meaning of *bhavati* is obtained by this cause, the meaning of *karoti* would also undesirably be obtained, he says “in the sense of *karoti*,” etc., in order to establish its exclusion. [The example is: *adhavalaṃ dhavalaṃ* (making what was not white, white).
The meaning is that when the suffix *cīp* is to be applied [to the words] *karoti* and *dhavalīkaroti*, the connection of *karoti* is seen precisely through its action (*kamma*).
He states another reason with the words “*iha ce*” and so forth. The word *iti* indicates a cause; since the term *kattū* (agent) is understood here, the meaning is “therefore” (*tato*).

However, because the meaning of *asati* is included within the meaning of *bhavati* itself, its exclusion was not explicitly taught. Regarding the phrase "in that treatise": it refers to the treatise on roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*paccaya*).
The term "reduplication" (*dvibbacana*) refers to the reduplication of the root *paṭ*. From that, by the rule "other suffixes are also seen" (4-120), the suffix *rā* is added.
By the rule "when *rā* is a ligature, the final vowel and following consonant are elided" (4-132), the final vowel and following consonant are dropped.

The prohibition “*acīto*” was not made in the rule for the formation of suffixes (*paccaya-vidhāna-sutta*) in order to signify the absence of a condition (*paccayābhāva*). Therefore, he says: “because of the absence of the prohibition *acīto*.
*Cīti* means “intensely” (*bhuso*); from the nominative singular form *cī*, [the suffix] *ṇa* is added.

Due to the statement regarding *ṇa* and other [suffixes], there is the elision of the case ending according to [Kaccāyana 2.1.19]: “when there is identity of meaning” (*ekatthatāya*). “*Iheceva*” means “in this very sense of *cyattha*. The connection is with the words “and it is not stated” (*na ca vuccate*).

10. Regarding the word *saddā*: Now, it is true that if the term "second case" (*dutiyā*) were not present in the sutta, from where would this distinction—by which the commentary provides the explanation, "from words such as 'sound' ending in the second case"—be obtained?
Nevertheless, even though the rule for suffixes (*paccaya-vidhi*) is stated in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), [the meaning is understood through the context].
In the *Niddesa*, the explanation is given as “sounds, etc. because of the capacity of the accusative case to denote the object (*upādāna*).
“Everywhere” means in all instances such as “he studies that,” “he knows that,” and “Kaṇikā,” etc. (4-14).

Pointing out what is excluded by the restriction [implied] by the term “action” (*kiriyā*), he says: “not time,” and so forth. Even though in cases such as “he studies” (*adhīte*) and so on, [the action occurs] at the present time...

Although the description is given with the instrumental case and the singular number, nevertheless, because those [factors] are not primary, the sense is that the suffix might also occur in other times such as the past (*bhūta*),
etc., and in the plural number for the factors of action (*kamma*) and so forth.
But is it not the case that when the suffix *i* is reached by the rule "the name 'root-meaning' applies" (5-12), this [present rule] is commenced even for the root-meaning itself?
Because of that rule, the suffix *i* should not occur after verbal roots such as *sadda* (sound) and others; yet the application of the suffix *i* is observed.
To demonstrate that this [rule] is not a sublater of the suffix *i*, he says: “he makes smoke,” and so forth. A sentence divided into various parts is a "diverse sentence" (*nānāvākya*);
by virtue of that state of being a diverse sentence, there is a conjunction of this [rule] with the suffix *i*.
Meaning: “*Dhātvatthenāmasmī*” is one sentence, and “*saddādīni karoti*” is another.
These two are distinct sentences—namely, “the suffix *i* occurs after a noun in the sense of a verbal root (*dhātu*),” and “the suffix *āya* occurs in the sense of ‘he performs sounds and so forth.

Their distinctness arises from the completion of each sentence through its respective expectation for a verb; for when the action-word (*kiriyāpada*) is not shared, there is syntactic unity within a single sentence.
There is a separation due to the existence of distinct sentences; and when there are distinct sentences, there is a conjunction.

For it is not only the relationship of general and particular that serves as a cause for sublation, but rather, even syntactical unity [can do so]. An example of this is: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins; let buttermilk be given to Koṇḍañña.
However, when there are distinct sentences, there is a conjunction, as in: "Let the Brahmins be fed; [and] to Māḍhara..."
Just as when [the rule] "let a pair of garments be given" is applied, Māḍhara is fed in his capacity as a brahmin and receives a pair of garments;
yet, by that straightforwardly stated gift of a pair of garments, the meal prescribed for a commoner is not excluded—

so too here, by the straightforward application of this rule, the suffix *ippaccaya* prescribed for a commoner is not excluded due to the requirements of the grammatical characteristic (*lakkhi*) intended by the Teacher.
It is considered that there is no fault of instability regarding the difference or non-difference of the sentence. The connection is with the word *siddham* in those three cases.

The intention is that the suffix *ya* has not been prescribed [there] by Pāṇini and others. In the phrase "having the luster of a water-lily petal" (*jaladala-dittiyaṃ*), the word *māna* [is used] according to rule 5.65;
and by the inclusion of the particle *ca* in rules 3.1.68 (*kattari lo*) and 5.2.70 (*parokkhāyaṃ ce*), the reduplication (*dvitta*) of *dala dala* occurs.
“Of a consonant preceded by *lopa*, etc. (5-75); and because of the doubling [of the letter] *da* according to “after a vowel, two” (1-34), they are *daddallamānā*.
By the phrase “shining forth,” which is a word from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he shows the absence of the *yap*-suffix in the sense of frequent repetition (*kiriyāsamabhihāra*).

And by this, even in cases of intense intensity (*bhusābhikkhañña*) as if in the sense of capability (*sakkate*), there is frequent repetition (*kiriyāsamabhihāra*) and the revolving of the action (*kiriyāparivattana*). And that—
When one person performs an action that ought to be performed by another, and another performs what ought to be performed by the former,

then it should be understood that the suffix *bhavati* occurs. By the characteristic rule stating, “Grammatical operations prescribed as general rules follow their specific application,” the suffix *māna*,
which is prescribed generally after the root *dal* in the sense of “splendor” (*ditti*), will occur in the sense of intensity and repetition, as in *daddalla*.
"Extremely burning" (*mānāti*) means that it burns intensely here; the meaning should also be understood as "burning again and again.

11. "He makes *namo*" means he utters the word *namo*; the meaning "he makes a sound" or "he utters a sound" should not be taken [here], because it is not dependent [on that sense] or because it is not so expressed.
12. *Dhātu*:

"Unproduced" (*aparinipphanna*) means not produced, that is, not existing in a state of accomplishment. "Accomplished by factors of action" (*kārakasādhiya*) means accomplished by the factors of action according to their availability.

"Not being a sentient being" (*asattvabhūta*) means not being a material entity. This word-meaning, which is the form of an action (*kriyārūpa*), is the primary form of the action such as moistening in the case of verbs like *pacati* ("he cooks").

And those things consisting of its parts—such as the placing [of fuel] on the hearth prior to and subsequent to [the cooking], and so forth—and those expressed by words such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) for the sake of that [action] are also included.
Therefore, just as a suffix such as *ti* prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the sense of the root-meaning as defined above expresses that very same thing, there is no distinction;
thus it is expressed with the singular number of non-distinction, and not with the plural. Hence, in this context, it is said: "it is stood upon" (*ṭhīyate*).

[The forms] *devadattena* and *ṭhīyate devadattena* occur. By the statement "not from whatever [source]" and so forth, it is demonstrated that where [a grammatical operation] is not seen from a particular source, it does not occur there.
Since a rule (vidhi) applies to whatever [element] is present, that [element] becomes its correlate (*sambandhī*).

Thus, this meaning of the verbal root—which is distinct from the meanings expressed by nouns and which constitutes the object of the karmapada and other case-terminations—is called the "own-meaning" (*sakattha*).

It should be understood that this *i*-suffix occurs only in the sense of "one's own" (*sakattha*) according to the rule for the *cur*-class and others. Regarding the phrase "and of that" (*tassaca*): it means "and of the vowel *e*.

Now, since the *i*-suffix is prescribed only when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvattha*) is qualified by the prefix *pa-* and so forth—as in examples such as *ati-hatthayati*—the meaning of the verbal root qualified by the prefix *pa-* has already been expressed by that very *i*-suffix prescribed for that purpose. Therefore, what is the purpose [of the present rule]?
In order to explain the purpose of the section on the application of the prefix *padi* for that which has a single cause (*ippaccayanta*), he says: “*Atihatthayati*,” and so forth.
“*Na sāmatthiyaṃ*” means there is no capability; this is the sense. 13.
Truths (*Saccā*).

The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "He explains the meaning (*attha*)," and "He explains the feeling (*veda*). In the case of *sukhāpeti* and so forth, the analysis is by way of "he causes [him] to feel pleasure (*sukha*)" and so on. "By way of an alternative reading" (*vāpāṭhā*) means from a reading by way of an option (*vikappena*).
15. Regarding *curā*:

Since there is no rule (*sutta*) for [the suffix] *sak* in its own sense (*sakatthe*), he asks how it is obtained and says: "'Atthānati desā'—[this refers to] the extension (*atidesa*) of the meaning. Thus, "atthānatidesā" [is the term].

The meaning is: "because no specific meaning whatsoever is stated in the sutta. How is it understood that, by the mere fact that no specific meaning is extended [to other roots], the primary meaning (sakattha) alone is to be expressed by the suffix *ṇi*?

To this he says: "Because the primary meaning is explicitly taught. The meaning is: because the primary meanings such as "theft" (*theyya*) and so forth are explicitly taught in rules such as "cur = theft" (*theyye*).
"By the division of the rule" (*yogavibhāgato*) means by the division of the rule "ṇi. [Thus] *rajjaṃ*.

Regarding the word *kāreti*: here the meaning is that he exercises sovereignty consisting of the seven factors, such as the minister (*sāmañca*) and so forth; the suffix *ṇi* is used in the sense of the activity of the instigator (*payojaka*). [Objection:

But is it not stated in the commentary (*vutti*) that "he causes the agent (*kattāraṃ*) to act"? [Response: True, but the term *payojaka* means one who impels (*codaka*), that is, one who exerts effort (*byāpāraka*). Thus, although the commentary speaks of causing the agent to act, the underlying meaning remains the same.
To explain how there is the status of agent (*kattutta*) for that which is being employed, he says: “being employed,” and so forth.
Showing that the status of agent may exist not only through the actual performance of an action but even by the mere state of being fit [for it], he says: “fit for action,” and so forth.

For in cases such as “he causes a stone to rise up on a balance,” there would be a determination of the status of agent even by way of fitness; however, this is the operation of the instigator (*payojaka*), so he says: “in the instigation,” and so forth.

*Pesana* (sending) is the directing or commissioning of an inferior person, such as a slave, to some purpose. *Ajjesana* (requesting) is the engaging of a superior person, such as a teacher, preceded by an act of honor.
That which has this characteristic—namely, the nature of sending, requesting, and so forth—is described as such (*pesanajjhesanādikalakkhaṇasabhāvo*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), activities that involve acting in accordance [with the wishes of others] are included; thus, for example: "The alms-food causes him to dwell," or "The carpenter caused it to be burned."
It succeeds. For alms-food, when obtained with many condiments, produces a specific satisfaction according to one's desire.

Even a fire, well-kindled in a windless place, removes the calamity of cold—which is opposed to burning—and bestows the capacity conducive to burning; therefore, for those [condiments and the fire] as well, there is a proper status as instigators (*payojaka*).
The term *payojakabyāpāra* may be either a qualification of the condition (*paccaya*) or a qualification of the root (*pakati*).

In that regard, if it were a qualification of the root, then the suffixes *ṇī*, *ṇā*, and *pī* would be prescribed when [the root] is functioning in the sense of the instigator’s activity (*payojakabyāpāra*).

Consequently, in the case of *gami*—which signifies the application (*niyoga*) directed toward the act of going (*gamana*) rather than the act of going itself—the boy would be its instigator; thus, in the expression “he causes the boy to go to the village” (*gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ*), there would be no [expression of] the act of going.
In the case of *payojje*, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) prescribed by [Pāṇini 1.4.52] “*gatibodhāhārārtha...*” does not apply;

therefore, since the position that it qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*) is faulty, he says—“this is a qualifier of the suffix (*pratyayaviśeṣaṇa*), not a qualifier of the base”—in order to show the position that it qualifies the suffix. Regarding the phrase “in the inclusion of the mere instigator (*payojakamātra*)”:
the word *mātra* expresses a general sense, as in the expression “the maiden wards off even a mere person (*kaññā mattaṃ vārayati*)”; [here it refers to] the agent.
The meaning is: "when there is a general inclusion of both that which is employed and that which prompts the employment of instruments and so forth.

The sense is this: "byāpāretveva" means that the expression "byāpāre" alone would have to be used without the mention of the prompter (*payojaka*). The word "taṃ" refers to the mention of the prompter;

it is described as such because its object is distinguished. He states what this distinguished object is: ... [text continues] ... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
"‘Yo loke,’ etc. ‘Itoto’ refers to the reference to the reason that is about to be stated. ‘Taṃ’ refers to the prescription of the suffix *ṇi* after roots such as *cur*.

The word ‘evaṃ’ looks forward to what is about to be stated. The meaning is: ‘That very prescription of *ṇi* after roots such as *cur* would be fruitful in the manner that is about to be explained, and not otherwise. He shows that very manner with the words ‘yadiminā,’ etc."
17. [Objection:

One might understand that the suffix *kyo* occurs even when the agent (*kattar*) is intended, as in the case of *mānantatthādi*, which are external (*parabhūta*). To prevent this, it is stated that "in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*)" is not a qualifier of *kyo*. Thus he says: "of *mānantatthādi*, etc.

For if it were to apply to those prescribed for the agent, then—since both of them would be expressed as primary factors (*padhānattha*) and would therefore be independent of one another—[the rule would fail].
There might be no connection [between the suffix and the meaning], provided that there is no denotation of the agent (*kartṛ*) for those [verbal roots] ending in *-bhū*.

For from the word ‘*ṭhīyate*’ neither the action (*bhāva*) nor the agent is understood; nor from ‘*gamyate*’ is either the object (*karman*) or the agent understood. Rather, only the action and the object are understood.
Therefore he says: “Therefore,” and so forth.
“Of those very same” means of *mānant* and so forth. “By others’ conventional designation” means that for others, such as Kaccāyana, it is designated by the name *parokkhā*.
“Excluding those included therein” means excluding those suffixes that possess the technical designation (*saññā*) of *parokkhā*. Regarding “in non-*parokkha* [suffixes]”:
having here shown the compound with the term *parokkhā* according to the conventional designation of others, he now says “or else,” etc., in order to present it in another way.

"Parokkhā" means "at a time not within the range of the sense-faculties. By this metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), or by way of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-paccaya*), he states the formal derivation of the word as "parokkhā.
These [suffixes] are, however, *a*, *u*, and so forth. "From that" means from the *parokkha* suffix.
Now, in the first alternative, does it not follow that the statement "in those not being *parokkha*" (*aparokkhesu*)—meaning "in those excluding the *parokkha*"—is appropriate?

Regarding the second alternative, however, [the objection is raised]: "If it is said 'in those cases where the parokkhā is excluded,' then how does the explanatory statement 'in those cases where the parokkhā is excluded' apply here?
To this he says: "‘Te pana’ and so forth. "Iha" means "here," that is, in the case of "those not being parokkhā.

But is it not the case that in the sutta beginning with "parokkhe a u" (Pāṇini 3.4.78), the term "parokkhe" is a qualification of the verbal base (pakati), [implying] that the suffixes [are applied] when the action is out of sight?
Having kept in mind how [the action] is enjoined, he says "parokkhe" and so forth. *Bhāva* (being) is the state, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

By the phrase "the state of being currently accomplished," the state of having already been accomplished is excluded. That verbal root-meaning whose characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*)—that is, its inherent nature (*sabhāva*)—is an objective sense consisting of action, which is preceded by another [action] and constitutes a primary component of the principal action, is described as such. [The term] "become a sentient being" (*satvabhūta*)...

The remainder [of the sentence] is "it is understood here" (*patīyati*). There is also the plural form, with the intended meaning being "cooked and uncooked" (*pākāpāke*). "Action" (*kamma*) means that which is performed;

and although there are indeed objects such as nouns and so forth, nevertheless—due to the governing rule concerning verbal roots (*kriyāttha*) and because no other meaning is obtained for roots like *māna* and so on—the connection with "action" (*kiriyā*) alone is understood.
In the case of "well-hearing," it refers to that which is being heard (*sūyamāna*).

In this context, according to the followers of Pāṇini, when an action such as "breaking" seen in the object—e.g., in "he breaks the granary"—is found to reside in the agent simply because it is easy to perform, due to the speaker's desire for a term expressing effortlessness (as in "the granary breaks itself"), then by another sutta, that agent is prescribed as having a status similar to the object: "dependent on the object... (kammanissayaṃ).
"In order that it may become an object (*kāriya*)," he says, relying on that: "When action itself," and so forth. The connection is:
"when action itself is intended to be expressed as having the state of an agent. Having asked "How is it intended to be expressed in that way?

he replies: "Inhering in the self," and so forth. By the word "self" (*atta*), action alone is intended here. "Inhering in the self" (*attasamavetā*) means that which inheres in the self—that is, that which has become a constituent part of the self; of that [action]...
"By means of action" means "by means of the action that is the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

In the phrase "by means of being well-purified, etc.," the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause or an instrument. Regarding the word "atthato" (by way of meaning): the intended meaning is that [the suffix] *kyo* was stated [after the root] precisely because of the sense of "object" (*kamma*), as in the rule "the suffix *kyo* occurs after a root in the sense of object.
For it is said: "By this [statement], 'it is broken' (*bhijjati*), the state of being the object (*kammabhāva*) is understood from the sound [of the word]. Thus, by way of meaning...

This has already been demonstrated by the very statement regarding *kamme* (the locative case). He speaks the following—“*bhijjate* in this word,” and so forth—to clarify what has already been stated.
“*Aññathā*” means if that suffix were not present after *kamma* alone. “*Atoti*” means from the word *bhijjate*. He concludes with “*Tasmā*,” and so forth.
“*Kiṃ vacanena*” means “what is the use of another rule (*sutta*), as in the case of the followers of Pāṇini?”—this is the sense.
Even in the absence of an explicit statement, he says “from the sentence,” etc., in order to explain the method of constructing the words by way of demonstrating the process of word-formation.

“Having extracted from the sentence” means when the words are being formed; the meaning is that they are being produced when the phrase “the granary breaks of its own accord” is separated from the sentence and the word “breaks” is being constructed. “That very same” refers to...
The meaning of the term is simply its commonality [of function]. “In the accomplishment thereof” means in the formation of that word being constructed.
The sense is: “that which lies down (sayati) here for itself (attanā). This is not stated merely to show that “only kamma is the condition”;

rather, he says “by this... and so forth to demonstrate that something else is also required. The particle *ca* is used to conjoin another statement. “By this one is broken” refers to hearing and so forth.
"And this he says" is the meaning. Why does he say "of the agent's object," etc.? It is not a single word that is the example;
rather, the sentence itself regarding the agent's object is the example... [the author] considers that its comprehension occurs through the sentence alone.
Why should a single word not be the example? To this he says: "by words," etc. He says "also the support of the agent," etc., in order to show a second example.
"In this alternative" (*asmiṃ pakkhe*): when this alternative is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kattṛ*). "The state of having that as its object" (*tabbisayattaṃ*):

the state of having the word [ending] of the *karmavācī* (the expression for the object) as its domain. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," he says "in the case of the abstract action and the object," etc., in order to show the application [of the rule] which is obtained by implication (*sāmatthiya-laddha*) when there is the sense of qualifying the specific suffixes of the abstract action and the agent (*kartṛ*).
The connection is: "by this and by that, there is the state of being qualified. What is that?
He says “is qualified” and states “in [the rules] beginning with *mānanta*. To show the purpose, he says “of those beginning with *ty*,” and so forth.

If, by that or that grammatical rule (*dhātu-sutta*), the roots *mān* and others were not applicable in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*kamma*) as well as the agent (*kartr*), how could the suffixes *ky* and others occur after those roots *mān* and others when they are thus qualified?
By this implication (*sāmatthiya*), [it follows that they do apply] in the sense of the abstract state and the object.

Regarding the term *kattari* (in the sense of "agent"): it is understood that suffixes such as *vattamāne*, *anti*, and so forth, occur according to their application among the categories of being (*bhāva*) and the rest, by means of rules beginning with 6.1.
Thus, there is the category of "being. This statement was not undertaken for that purpose;
rather, it was by Pāṇini’s followers that the rule for *māna*, *at*, and so forth was formulated in the sense of agent, object, and being.

The meaning is that [the rule] has not commenced, as if it were another sutta. Now, in order to show that the statement was not commenced for the purpose of prescribing the suffixes *māna* and so forth in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*), nor for the agent (*kartṛ*), but rather that the restriction of roots (*dhātuniyama*) must be stated for the sake of restricting the roots—and that this is obtained by implication alone—he says:
“Even the restriction of the meaning of the action,” and so forth. From a root that is intransitive (*akammaka*), [the suffixes are used] in the sense of the abstract action or the agent.

The connection is as follows: the restriction regarding the meaning of the action—that [the suffixes] denote the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*)—is obtained through the aforementioned capacity (*sāmatthiya*).

Because intransitive verbs (*akammaka*) lack an object, and because even when present, the state (*bhāva*) is not predominant in transitive verbs (*sakammaka*), the intransitives occur in the sense of the agent and the state, but not in the sense of the object;
whereas the transitives, due to the presence of an object, occur in the sense of both the agent and the object.
"Does not bring about this capacity" (*na bhāveti idaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ*).

"It requires an object" (*kammaṃ apekkhati*): when the third person singular ending is applied to roots such as *pac*, in words like *pacati* and so forth, the action of cooking and so on (*pacanādi-kiriyā*) requires an object such as boiled rice (*odanādi*).
"It requires the agent" (*kattuttaṃ apekkhati*): in the case of roots such as *bhū* in words like *bhavati* and so forth...
The action of becoming and so forth requires an agent. 20. Regarding the rule "with the suffixes -ṇa and -ṇā, that which is the purpose":
this refers to the objective purpose for which something is employed.
23. Regarding *jyinanti*: by the rule “in the case of consonants, long [vowels] become short” (1-33), the vowel is shortened.

In all instances, wherever a suffix (*paccaya*) denotes the agent (*kattari*), the verbal derivative (*vikaraṇa*) likewise denotes the agent; wherever they denote the action or the object (*bhāvakammesu*), the verbal derivative likewise denotes the action or the object.

Because it is impossible for a single nature to possess multiple agents [simultaneously] through the diversity of its conditions (*paccaya*), it is therefore prescribed that the suffixes such as *māna* and others, which express these [agents], should not occur together. 27.
*Bhāva* (the abstract state).

"By the distinction of desire for expression" means by the distinction of the desire for expression regarding transitive and intransitive verbs. "In both cases" refers to the states of being (bhāva) and the object (kamma). "It is done" (*karīyati*) means it is to be done (*kattabbo*), or it is a duty (*karaṇīyo*).

"The general rule does not apply where there is an exception"—this is the nature of a general rule (*ussagga-dhamma*). However, due to the authority of the frequentative usage (*bahula-adhikāra*), some general rules also occur even within the domain of exceptions. (55) To demonstrate the intended meaning here by means of the word *bhūta*, he says: “*Bhūtam* means ‘past’,” and so forth. “Otherwise” means if it were not a term denoting what has passed.
"Is it not the case that here the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) is incurred?

For [the suffix] is prescribed when the word *bhūta* exists, and the derivation of the word *bhūta* occurs when that [suffix] exists; thus, the fault of mutual dependence is indeed evident. This is not a fault.

The relationship between word and meaning, established through convention (*saṅketa*), has existed for a long time; there is nothing improper about it. And even when this [relationship] has passed away...

The function [of the suffixes] is to be understood from the very nature of grammatical power (*saddasatti*). Furthermore, it should not be said that even the *ktavantu* suffix and others will occur only in the past tense due to the nature of grammatical power.
This word "past" (*bhūta*) is well-established in the sense of having transcended [time], whereas the *ktavantu* suffix and others are not so established;

therefore, by means of that well-established meaning, the explanation (*anvākhyāna*) of those that are not so established is performed. Moreover, this term "past" is an adjective qualifying the verbal root (*pakati*).

Or it might mean “occurring in the sense of what has not happened,” or it might be a qualification of the meaning of the suffix, namely “in the sense of an agent who has not [yet] acted. To the question, “In that case, whose qualification is this? he says:
“‘Bhūta’ (what has happened) is a qualification of the base (*pakati*). From where does he say this? From the words “If there were a connection,” and so forth.

Now, what fault is there in taking it as a qualification of the meaning of the suffix? He says: “For, in the case of a qualification of the meaning of the suffix,” and so forth. Of the meaning of the suffix...

The meaning is that because the agent (*kattu*) has not yet passed away, the application of the term *ayanti* (they go) is not appropriate. By the word "denoted" (*abhidheyya*), he excludes the purpose (*payojana*) and so forth. 56. Regarding the rule "the suffix *kta* is used for the object":

because it is subordinate when there is an object, the state (*bhāva*) is non-predominant. According to the principle, "when there is a choice between a subordinate and a primary [element], the grammatical operation applies only to the primary," the grammatical condition applies only to the primary object, and not to the state, because the latter is non-predominant in this context.

57. Regarding the statement, "Does he not initiate?"—it is asked, "How is it said 'initiation of action' (kiriyārambhe)? To this he says, "In the case of 'purifying,' etc. That which is the initiation;

the initiation of action itself is "kiriyārambha," and [the term refers] to that. Since it is stated generally as "in the initiation of action" (kiriyārambhe), it is a qualification of the specific meaning of action.
To show that there is no fault whether it be a qualification of the sense of condition (*paccayattha*) or both, he says:
“And this is a qualification of the sense of action,” and so forth. Even in the view that it is a qualification of the sense of condition, he says:

“Of the sense of action as well,” and so forth, to show that by implication (*sāmatthiyā*) the sense of action also occurs at the beginning. He demonstrates this implication with the words: “But the implication is,” and so forth.

The construction is as follows: that which was prescribed by the *Anantara-sutta* also occurs in the sense of the agent (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), even in the case of an undertaking (*ārambha*), because it is stated in a general sense.
"Because it is stated in a general sense" means because it is stated in a general sense [in the rule] "the suffix *kta* [is used] in the sense of the agent and the object" (Pāṇini 3.4.70).

"And it is not stated thus 'in the sense of the agent and the object'" means that the author of the commentary, by saying "according to what is obtained," implies that it was not stated in this manner by the commentator himself.
To the question "Why was it not stated thus?", he says: "'As in the previous [rule],' etc. Since there would be a cognition of indefinite arising, he says "'Because of being restated,' etc.
to negate that. "Māsaṅkī" is in the accusative case; therefore, because of its arising from that very [root], it is in the nominative.

He thinks as follows: "The inclusion of the passive and the object (bhāva-kamma) is drawn along by the word 'ca' (and), and the suffix *kta* is prescribed by this [rule] 'And in the passive and the object'."

Regarding this, it is suspected: "Since [the suffix] *kta* was already established by the previous general rule (*sāmañña*), its mention again is for the purpose of restricting the application of the action;
thus, when 'and as prescribed' (*yathāpattañca*) is stated, the particle *ca* implies that even in cases where the action is prescribed, the suffix *kta* occurs according to what is prescribed.

And so it is understood that, although the commencement [of the rule] pertains to the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), the suffix *kta* occurs as prescribed by the previous statement itself. Thus, indeed...

Since [the action] is established even at the commencement of the bhāva and karma [cases] by the previous [rule], one might ask: why is it stated as "in the agent at the commencement" (*kattari-ārambhe*) alone, and what is the purpose of the particle *ca*?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because the words have the function of restriction," and so forth.

Now, is it not the case that the "commencement" (*ārambha*) is the very moment of the action (*kiriyā-khaṇa*) that has just begun; for [an object] is only considered "completed" (*parisamatta*) when it has been finished through many moments of action?
Regarding the statement “the past time exists,” since the fruit of an action has not yet been fully produced, it is considered as if it were occurring in the present;

thus, to avoid the suspicion that [the past] does not exist, he says “of the fruit of an action,” and so forth. Because even a portion of a mat is a mat, and because that [portion] has been produced, there is the desire for the expression “past.
But is it not the case that, according to the *Ādisutta*, the mat is not yet fully manifested at the moment of the action? For the causes of the mat...
For at that time, there were indeed *bīraṇa* grasses, yet those very [grasses] in that state are not the mat (*kaṭa*).

How then can one say, "the mat is made" (*pakato kaṭo*), seeking grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatta*) between the word *kaṭa* and the word *pakata* in its past tense form? To this he says:

"by that which constitutes the beginning," and so forth. Therein, in that specific sense: *pakattuṃ ārabhi*, *pakattuṃ ārabhīyittha*, *pasottuṃ ārabhi*, or *pasottuṃ ārabhanti*—these are the meanings of the suffix *tto*.

58. Regarding the statement "the word *anārambha* [is used] for the purpose of excluding undertaking (*ārambha*"): because [the prohibition] is already established by the preceding rule when there is an undertaking, the phrase "for the most part" (*yebhuyyena*) was stated even for the case of *apādi*, since it is transitive (*sakammaka*).
Having stated that it has the sense of being transitive, this [transitivity] occurs when these [roots] are joined with *pādi*.
To demonstrate this, he said: “*Pādisahitā*,” and so forth. *Khaṭopikā* means a bed. 59.

Regarding the statement that a verb whose object is not explicitly expressed is here considered intransitive, he said: “*Avijjamāne*,” and so forth. Those who have gone are *yātā*; the act of going is *yānaṃ*.
"Yātaṃ. [The form] *ayoyittha* is *yā*. The suffix *kta* should not be applied here, as it is by the followers of Pāṇini.

"In the completeness of causes" (*kāraṇasāmaggiyaṃ*) means in the excellence of the causal factors such as the rain and so forth. And that excellence itself, by means of the past participle suffix *-tā*, expresses its being in the past tense due to that completeness of causes.

Regarding the phrase *ādhāre ca*: because of the recurrence (*anuvutti*) [of the particle *ca*] here, the remainder of the statement is connected by the word *ca* as "and according to what has been received" (*yathāpattañca*).

Thus, "there would be no removal from anything": when such things as the "support" (*ādhāra*) recur, the meaning is that there would be no removal—that is, no separation—from anything, such as the support.
The intention is that, were that the case, one would have made it a single grammatical connection (*ekayoga*) with the preceding rule.
The construction is: “In the case of *bhāva* (abstract state) and *kamma* (object), [the suffix] is added.

The state (*bhāva*) or the object (*kamma*) of the word *bahula* is precisely the taking of the sense of abundance; thus, the state and the object are the grounds for the application of the word *bahula*, and in that context, the suffix is applied.

The phrase “some say” refers specifically to the followers of Pāṇini. He indicates that even according to that [system], the suffix occurs only when the action is completed, as in the passage beginning with “he too,” etc.

*Nā.* "Bhijjamānaṃ" means being cooked. The construction is: "one who sees by way of another's form. "Keci" refers to those very same [grammarians]. With the words "yathā" and so forth, he demonstrates what is drawn out by the word "ca" in their rule, *matibuddhipūjatthehi ce* (Pāṇini 3.2.188).
Regarding "akkocchi taṃ," he states the analysis (*viggaha*) with respect to the object; "taṃ" is the objective case.

Likewise, above as well, when the suffix *ṇi* of the *cur*-class verbs is elided, the vowel *ā* is dropped according to the principle: "In the absence of the cause, that which depends on the cause also ceases to exist."

The word *kaṭṭha* has many meanings, such as "going" (*gati*) and so forth; therefore, he asks: "What is the meaning here? and replies: "'Here it has the sense of harming' (*hiṃsattha*). Regarding "of the cause":

this refers to fire and so forth, which are the causes of the fruit that is suffering. [An objection: "Let it be so when the word *kaṭṭha* refers to fire and so forth, which are the causes of the fruit; but how is it when it refers to the fruit itself? To this he says: "'When, moreover... and so forth. Here, "anger and so forth" (*kodhādiko*) is intended. 61. *Tuṃ-tā*.

But surely, since this description "in the sense of becoming" (*bhāve*) is made by means of the verb *bhavati* ending in the suffix *-ghaṇ*, the indication of the meaning of the suffix is made as having precisely *bhavati* as its domain;
therefore, the suffix should occur only when that which is the state (*bhāva*) of *bhavati* is to be expressed.
And since that [state] can be denoted only by a suffix arising from *bhavati* itself, the suffix must indeed be applied to *bhavati*. Therefore...
How is it that the suffixes *tum* and so forth occur after roots such as *pac* (to cook) and *cāg* (to give)?

He says: "The meaning of a root (*dhātvaṭṭho*) is being (*bhāvo*), which is the state of becoming (*bhavanaṃ*). For the general sense of action (*kiriyāsāmaññaṃ*) follows all root meanings, and this is the meaning of the verb *bhavati*. Thus, when a definition of the meaning is made by means of that which expresses the general sense of action, it is made with reference to the entire domain of roots; therefore, the intention is that [the suffixes] occur even after *pac* and the like.

But surely, when it is stated here that "the suffixes *tum* and so forth occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*)," it is not understood in what specific kind of state the suffixes *tum* and so forth occur?

And they say: “From which,” and so forth. “Of that” means of the verbal root (*dhātu*). “That which is to be called existence” (*bhāva*) means that which is to be expressed as an abstract state. From what [is it derived]? They say: “From a connection” (*sambandhā*). The meaning is:

there is a connection between the base form (*pakati*) of the suffixes beginning with *-tuṃ* and the very state that is to be expressed. “It should be stood upon” (*ṭhātabbaṃ*) is formed by the suffix *-tabba* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
Now, by the phrase “in the action” (*kriyāyaṃ*), [it refers to] that which has undergone the transformation into the form *da* when expressed by the suffixes beginning with *-tabba*.
To the question, "How is there the apprehension of a state (bhāva)? he says: "Even though," and so forth.

"Designation by means of the action of its own support" means that the designation of a substance-form (dabbarūpa) is by means of the action of its own support; since [words such as] "eye" (cakkhu) and so on are understood through the action of becoming (bhavana), the suffixes *tum* and others occur in the sense of becoming (*bhavanteva*).

Now, one might object: "Since the suffixes beginning with *tum* are prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), the action alone is primary; therefore, the 'object' (*kamma*) as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is not perceived.
How then could there be such an expression as ‘he goes to do a mat’ (*kaṭaṃ kātuṃ gacchati*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Even though" (*yadipi*), etc., in order to establish it.

[The phrase] "made by the meaning of the root" means made by the meaning of the root designated as "action. By the word "exists" (*atthi*), [he refers to cases] such as "the Lord sleeps" (*supyate devadattena*).
This shows that there is no action (*kamma*) to be undertaken there.

According to Kaccāyana’s rule, “*Icchatthesu samānakattukesu tavetuṃ vā*” (4-2-12), the suffixes *tum* and so forth are prescribed separately so that they may occur even when the action is not for the sake of that [desire], provided the agent is the same;
hence he says, “*icchatthesmi’ccādi*. For example: “*bhottuṃ*...”
In such cases as "he cooks," the act of cooking has the act of eating as its purpose; however, in this context, there is no such desire for that purpose.

This is because the act of cooking itself lacks the status of having that [eating] as its purpose—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, with the words beginning "Moreover... (punar ettha), he composes a response to the objection regarding the attainment of the undesirable, stating:
"Even for something not for that purpose," and so forth.

By the phrase "the application of a verbal root having the sense of wishing," it is indicated that in the expression "one who wishes acts" (*icchanto karoti*), the word "wishing" (*icchanto*) has precisely the meaning of the application of a verbal root having the sense of wishing; it does not mean that "wishing" is the instrument for the employment [of the action].

In the case of "he wishes Devadatta while eating," the word "eating" (*bhuñjanto*) does not occur because of the rule stating "when there is a common agent" (*samānakattukesu*). Thus, Devadatta is the agent of the act of eating, whereas he is the object of the act of wishing.
Showing that it should not be said that the sutta has a separate purpose [of its own] in the sense of "it is indeed another," he says:
"Devadatta," and so forth. Regarding "he desires": in the phrase "he desires Devadatta while eating," the word "desires" (icchatī) is used here as a verb.
That which has for its purpose the means of accomplishment—namely, the object designated as "Devadatta while eating"—is what is meant by "he desires" (sādhanattho icchati).
Its state is "tattaṃ" (the state of being so); therefore [it is used]. Since the action stands as the purpose for the desire itself, it is the "state" (bhāva).

Regarding the word "niratthakaṃ" (meaningless): the inclusion of the term "having a common agent" was made for this very purpose; and the intention is that it is "meaningless" because, as previously stated, there is no possibility of such an occurrence.

According to Pāṇini, suffixes such as *tum* and others are prescribed by another rule (*suttantarena*) for verbal roots (*dhātu*) when they are well-supported by meanings such as "one's own" (*sakādi*).

Therefore, he says: “In the employment of roots such as *sakā*,” and so forth. “Siddhā” means that the suffixes beginning with *tum* are established. “Having the action of eating as its meaning” (*bhujikiriyatthā*):

that power whose meaning is the action of eating is understood as having the action of eating as its meaning. He states the reason for this being understood by saying: “For even though it does not exist,” and so forth.
Here, others have described the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapada*) as being non-actional and as something to be restated; he speaks in order to refute that.

"By this [expression] beginning with *teneva* (by that very [reason]), etc.: in the intention of other systems (*parasamaya*), in phrases such as 'he is able to eat,' the sense of capability (*kosalla*) is understood;

in 'he is ill to eat,' it is incapacity (*asatti*); in 'he is fit to eat,' it is suitability (*yogyatā*); in 'he begins to eat,' it is another action consisting of the preliminary effort (*vatthukiriyantara*) toward eating;
in 'he obtains to eat,' it is non-rejection (*appaccakkhāna*); and in cases such as 'there is eating,' it is mere possibility (*sambhavamatta*)."

In expressions such as *vaṭṭati bhottuṃ* (“it is fitting to eat”), the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) is understood. However, in the case of secondary words (*upapada*) such as *sakkoti* (“he is able”), the fact that eating and other actions constitute their meaning is not understood;
therefore, suffixes such as *-tum* occur even when the secondary words have meanings other than those of action.
Even though these other meanings are implied, since the purpose of the infinitive (*tādatthiya*) remains the same, the suffix *-tum* and others prescribed by the preceding rule [still apply].
In order to show that [the suffixes] do not cause an obstruction, he says: "Even though," and so forth.

"The purpose for that very thing exists indeed" means that the capacity for the action of eating exists indeed for [words such as] *sakka* (able), etc.; this is established by the rule beginning with "tuṃ tāye.

Regarding the suffixes *tum* and others prescribed after verbal roots when followed by words expressing completion (*pariyatti*) that are qualified by the sense of "sufficient" (*alam*), others have stated: "when qualified by the sense of 'sufficient,'" and so forth.
Including the word *pahū* within [the category], it is stated as "those capable, etc. (*samatthādi*). The derivation of the term *bhavati* will be explained under the rule *pubbekakattukānaṃ* (5-63).

Regarding the word *abhimata*, according to Kaccāyana’s rule *arahasakkādīsu ce* (4-2-13), because of the particle *ca*, [it means] "this is desired by him," as in examples such as *kālo bhottuṃ* ("it is time to eat"). Just as in *bhottumano* and so forth, [the suffix] applies to others as well.

This explains that this very [sequence] is the order of accomplishment (*nipphattikrama*). "By way of non-deviation" means by way of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); the meaning is that when there is food, there is the state of being; that is, the state of eating the food comes to be.

"The act of going does not have the purpose of eating" means that the action of going is not for the sake of eating. This word *attha* expresses a motive (*payojana*), and it refers to that for the sake of which something proceeds.
That becomes his purpose. And this person will not go for the sake of food; rather, he is merely suspected [of going] on account of some other task.
But when the act of going is undertaken specifically for the sake of food, then it is indeed the case that "he will go to eat."
No *ṇaka* suffix has been prescribed by the followers of Pāṇini in the sense of the infinitive (*tuṃ*), yet they state there: “The agent goes” (*kārako vajati*), and so forth.

He provides the resolution with the words beginning with “previously” (*pubbe*). By the rule beginning with “in the sense of the agent” (*kattari tu*), this *ṇaka* is prescribed generally for all three times;

thus, when a verbal root meaning an action is accompanied by another action as its attendant (*upapada*), the expression of the agent is established. And this [general rule] is not superseded by the specific infinitive suffix *tuṃ*.

"Bādhā" means "distinction," for the suffix *tuṃ* is prescribed in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), whereas *ṇaka* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). Although [the desired meaning] is already established by the preceding *ṇaka* alone, this [suffix *tuṃ*] must indeed be prescribed for the purpose of excluding *ltvā* and the others;
otherwise, one might fear the undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) that *ltvā* and the others would also apply. Anticipating this objection, he says, "If not," and so forth.
He says, "For not," and so forth, in order to clarify precisely the absence of understanding. For (*hi*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmātyatthe*).
"He who goes is the agent; he who goes is distracted"—this is the meaning understood here, but the meaning is not that a *tādatthiya* (possessive) relation is understood through those [suffixes].
The objector, in order to establish a similarity with the *ltvā*-suffixes and others, states "even the *ṇaka*" etc., according to the rule already mentioned, regarding the offense (*āpatti*).
Even if there is no purpose or a purpose already set aside by the *ṇaka*, [the *tādatthiya*]... [is not understood].
Fearing that the suffix *ṇaka* might be applied on the grounds that "it is understood from the treatise (*pakaraṇato gamyate*"), the challenger says: "Now then," and so forth.

The objection raised by the previous passage beginning with "Now then" (*pubbeccādi*)—namely, that "the *ṇaka* is not to be prescribed"—is not yet resolved; for it remains subject to further critique as previously stated. Rather, it should be understood that the resolution being stated here by this passage beginning with "Therefore, not even...
(*tasmā nevi*) is the one intended. Thus, even in the case of forms such as *littvā*, the suffix *ṇaka* is excluded by the rules beginning with *littvādīhi*.
When the understanding of *tādatthiya* (the sense of "for that purpose") has been determined, their occurrence [is established] through the specific nature of *tādatthiya*.

Regarding the statement by the author of the *Vākya*—“The prescription of *ṇaka* when the following word (*upapada*) has the sense of an action is for the purpose of prohibiting *ltvā* and so forth”—the Teacher concludes by saying, “Therefore,” and so on.
Furthermore, let the understanding of *tādatthiya* arise from the very context itself, as well as from the suffix *ca*.

Nevertheless, with the intention that another [word] is subordinate (*vidheyya*), he says: "But even so" (*athāpi*), and so forth. [The term] *gatatta* (the state of having gone) [is explained as follows]:

when a verbal root meaning an action (*kriyāttha*) occurs in the future tense (*bhavissati-kāle*) with another action as its attendant (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇa* and others are prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Regarding that, he says: "He goes for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya vajati*), and so forth.
The intention is that even when not explicitly prescribed, it is established by virtue of being for the sake of that (*tādatthiya*).
62. In compounds such as *paṭisotūnādi*, the analysis is by means of the phrase “having made listening,” and so forth. In *suteneti savanaṃ*, the analysis is [as follows]. 63.
Previously.

It is not overly redundant because [the action] is constant due to its nature as a procedure (*vidhi*). Since the word *eka* has multiple meanings, he specifies: “this word *eka* expresses number. From where does he say this?
From the words beginning with “of sounds” (*saddānam*), etc. He states the meaning that results from the word *eka* expressing number: “delimited by the number one” (*ekasaṅkhyāvacchinno*);
[the phrase] “their meaning” (*tadatthā*) refers to the meaning of the verbal root. Even though it is said that “the operation (*byāpāra*) comes first,”...

It is stated that the operation (*vyāpāra*), which constitutes a single part of the aggregate, is what is being singled out (*niddhāriyamāna*). Nevertheless, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the verbal root denoting the operation is expressed by the word "prior" (*pubba*);
for this very reason, it is stated in the *Vutti*: "Among those [roots], that which is prior is, in its actual sense, a verbal root.

But is it not the case that the capacity (*satti*) is the factor of action (*kāraka*), and that the capacity for the prior-time action is one thing, while the capacity for the subsequent-time action is another?
Therefore, having raised the doubt as to how there can be a single agent, he says "even though" (*yadipi*) and so forth, in order to provide the solution.
"Of the spear-wielder Dabba" means of Dabba, who possesses a spear, such as Devadatta. "The superimposition of that" means the superimposition of oneness.

Since the suffixes *tun* and others are prescribed for the sequential expression of the activities of those who have a single agent, they—having arisen precisely in the sense of the action (*bhāva*)—are able to express the sequence.
The word *bhāveti* is understood here [as the governing verb].
Because the term *ekakattukānaṃ* is plural, the form *bhutvā pitvā vajati* (“having eaten and drunk, he goes”) also occurs.

However, in the case of *bhuttasmiṃ*, because there are multiple agents, the form *bhuñjitvāpi* (“even having eaten”) occurs. Pāṇini, like a carriage, has stated that the application of the rules for *tuṃ* and other suffixes is established even without an explicit separate statement.
‘He sleeps with his mouth open,’ and so forth. Regarding *byādāya*:

from the root *dā* preceded by *vi*, with the suffix *tvā*, the form arises through the substitution of *pya* for *tvā* according to the rule *“pyo vā tvāssa samāse”* (5-064). The meaning is “having made the opening of the mouth. Regarding *byādāna-supanānam antare yo kālo tassa*:
this refers to the time between the opening and the sleeping; it is a “non-indication of distinction,” meaning that no distinction is perceived. Of the distinction... [the text ends].

"By whom and how" is stated because of the existence of certain [factors]. "Even in the case of coexistence" means even when the opening [of the mouth] and the bringing near [of the food] exist simultaneously.
A "heaped-up" mass of rice.
This is favored by the followers of Pāṇini; for [they say] that a mountain distinguished by another river—such as "the mountain not having reached the river"—is expressed [in this way].
When it is said [“the mountain on this side of the river”], the meaning is “a mountain on the near side (*ora*) of the river.

From that, a mountain distinguished by the river situated on the further side (*pāra*) is understood. When it is said “the river beyond the mountain,” the river on the further side is qualified by the mountain on the near side;

thus, when it is said “the river having passed the mountain,” the meaning understood is “the mountain on the near side of the river,” and from that, the river distinguished by the mountain on the near side is cognized.

Since the agent (*bhavatin*) exists in all cases, he shows how its singularity and its status as a prior time (*pubbakālatā*) are understood, with the words "first it does not reach," and so forth. He concludes with "that very [thing]," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "having eaten again and again, he goes," the Pāṇinīyas and others expect a different result; to that he says:
‘Of those having a single agent,’ and so forth. He asks for the reason why [the action] occurs repeatedly with the words ‘If indeed,’ and so forth.

He clarifies what has already been stated with the words ‘By whom,’ and so forth. ‘By whom’ means by the grammarians (*veyyākaraṇehi*). Regarding the phrase ‘having grasped the life-force (*jīvaggāhaṃ*)’ and so forth, since others have understood it otherwise, he says ‘The action,’ and so forth.
‘In its own limb’ means in its own constituent parts, such as the hands and feet. The suffix *ṇam* is the conditional particle (*paccayo*).

The connection is with the word *abhimata*. The connection is with the phrase “this is what is meant by [the question] ‘What by means of the suffix -ṇam?’”. Otherwise, he states the manner of its establishment with the words “*jīvassi*, etc.”.
Having asked “By what distinguished?”, he says “*jīvaggāha*” in order to show that it is distinguished by the seizing of life.
The meaning is: “He made a seizing known as the seizing of life (*jīvaggāha*).”
"Ākhyātaṃ" means "agāhayī" (he grasped); the term *ākhyāta* indicates that it is the object (*kamma*) for the action of grasping in the sense of "that which is to be grasped.
"Tabbisesanampi" means even the qualifier of that action of grasping "that which is to be grasped. "Tathābhūtameva" means precisely that which is to be grasped.
And "tathā" occurs when the suffix *-ṇam* is added to a verb in the accusative case to qualify the action. "*Ṇamantarūpaṃ*" refers to the form ending in *-ṇam*.
The analysis (viggaha) is "rūpaṃ yassa" (that of which the form is...). Here, the connection is with the word "kiñci" (some) in relation to the suffix "ṇaṃ. "Iha" means in this grammar.
"Kiñci payojanaṃ" means some purpose. By the word "ādi" in the phrase "pacāditoti," the suffix "ṇaṃ" not prescribed by those [rules] is included.
64. Nto.
"One who has begun to accomplish but has not reached completion" means one who has begun to produce or bring about something such as a mat, yet has not reached or attained completion or fulfillment.
"That which is occurring and has not ceased" refers to that which, like a mountain and so forth, is constantly occurring and uninterrupted;
the construction is that because it has not reached completion by that very [process], it is called "occurring. This is by way of its own functional activity.
This is stated by way of the activity (*kiriyā*) whose objects are the aforementioned "eating" (*kaṭa*) and so forth; what is meant is this:
"Because the aforementioned eating and so forth are present, the activity directed toward them is also present; thus, by means of that [activity], there is a qualification of the meaning of the verb.
In the case of "Devadatta eats," even though he laughs while eating, chews, speaks, or drinks water, [the action of eating remains the primary referent].
Nevertheless, since there is a commencement of that which is intended to be done while it is still in progress and has not yet reached completion, it is said:

"He has begun to accomplish [it], but has not yet reached its conclusion. Even though no temporal division is discerned in cases such as "the mountains stand," where the mountains and so forth are permanent and thus the past and future are impossible—and consequently the present that excludes them is also impossible—nevertheless, regarding what has been commenced...
It is said, "occurring as it is not yet completed," which is expressed as "proceeding or not yet ceased.
If there were a qualification of the agent (*kattuvisesana*), what fault would there be? Thus he says, "if there were a qualification of the agent," and so forth.

Here too, since the agent is in the present tense, this [suffix] is stated in order to indicate that very present state of the agent. This is because of the many rules such as "not when followed by a word in the same case" (Pāṇini 3.2.124).
The suffix *itappaccaya* is prescribed by the followers of Pāṇini in their Suttas.
However, here, because it is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmañña*), he says: "by way of a general rule," and so forth. The root *as* (in the sense of "being") takes the suffix *itappaccaya*.
By the rules "the *lo* [suffix] is used for the agent" (5-18) and "there is elision of *nta*, *māna*, *anti*, *yi*, *yuṃsu*, etc. (5-130), there is the elision of the letter *a*. Thus, *tapanto*.
‘Tapa’ means to heat. ‘Jappanto’: ‘jappa’ means speech. ‘Paṭhanto’: ‘paṭha’ means uttering. ‘Pacanto’: ‘paca’ means cooking. ‘Dhārayanto’: ‘dhara’ means holding.
The suffix *ṇi* is used for the activity of an instigator; thus, one who employs [the act] to hold is “dhārayanto. ‘Dissanto’: ‘disa’ and ‘dussa’ mean to see;
[the form is derived] by the rule “*divādīhi yaka*” (5-12). ‘Yajanto’: ‘yaja’ means worship of the gods. ‘Arahanto’: ‘araha’ means worthy of worship.

By the phrase "yathā ca" and so forth, he states that in cases such as *apaṭhama-samānādhikaraṇa* (not having the same grammatical base), in words like *saṃvijjamāno*, *virocamāno*, and *jappamāno*, the suffix *-māna* should be regarded as being like the suffix *-anta*. 65.
*Māna* (the suffix -māna).
*Vaya* is a specific state of having passed away (*kālakata*). By the word *mānavo*, he indicates the absence of the suffix *-anta*. In the case of *yujjhamāno*:

from the root *yuj* meaning "to strike with weapons," the suffix *-ya* is applied by the rule "after roots beginning with *div*, [the suffix] *ya* [is added]" (5-12). Then, by the rules "of *tavagga* and *varaṇa*" etc. (1-48), *dh* becomes *jh*; and by the rule "by *vaggalasa*, *t* [becomes *j*]" (1-49), *y* becomes *j*.
Finally, by the rule "for these, when followed by fourth or second [consonants]" etc. (1-35), *jh* becomes *j*. In the case of *naccamāno*: from the root *nacca* meaning "dancing."

67. The suffix *tessa* is used after roots ending in vowels (*savisa*) in the active voice (*kattari*), as well as in the impersonal (*bhāve*) and passive (*kamme*) voices. 68. The suffixes beginning with *ṇu* (*ṇvādi*).
"By the rule *Ṇvādayo*" means by the sutta beginning with *Ṇvādayo*. "By the inclusion of certain roots and so forth" means the sense is:

those which have roots (*dhātu*) as their primary elements (*ādi*)—namely, time (*kāla*) and the rest—are "roots and so forth" (*dhātvādayo*); [the phrase refers to] the inclusion of these. Time (*kāla*) refers to the present tense and so on;

the agent (*kāraka*) refers to the doer (*kartṛ*) and so on. That from which a condition (*paccaya*) is produced according to a specific restriction or rule is the "base" (*pakati*). "Kākriya" refers to *āyukā* and so forth.
*Kāriyavisesaṃ* means a specific grammatical operation (*kāriya*) such as substitution (*ādesa*). *Kāru* refers to a specific craft (*sippijāti*).

Carpenters and others—namely, the five types of craftsmen: carpenters, weavers, dyers, barbers, and potters—are called *kāravo*. When the word *cārudāru* is in use, it will occur elsewhere as well according to the rule of time; the same applies to *kāru* and the others.

69. When it is said, "khacha khachasānaṃ," one asks: "How is there a reference to the end of that? [The author] says: "In the case of the mention of a suffix," and so forth. Is not the meaning already explained?
For in the Sutta, the designation is in the masculine gender as "ekassaro" (a single consonant), and "ādi" (beginning) is its qualifier; this being so, [why is it stated here] in the neuter?

To explain how the commentary is appropriate, he says: “In the word *sadde*,” and so forth. Furthermore, as to why he does not state that there is a dual nature for each individual component—the single-consonant [element] and the word *jāgara*—separately in the case of *jāgareccādo*, etc., he says: “By that very reason,” and so forth.

“By that very reason,” etc., means precisely because of the reason for qualifying the single-consonant [element]. The term “of the single-consonant component” (*avayavekassarassa*) is a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*).

"And that [syllable] is a constituent part, and it consists of a single sound. Now, even though the word *ekassara* (single-sound) is qualified by "beginning with a vowel" (*atha*) and so forth, why does he not state the doubling for a constituent part consisting of a single sound?
He replies: "Because it is the single [vowel] itself that is the beginning.

This means that the constituent part consisting of a single sound is distinct from the first [type of] single sound. Because it is corrupted by a fault, there is no compound here formed with a qualifier (*visesanasa-māsa*).

He states [the objection] regarding the argument for the rule: “*ekassaro*,” and so forth. To the question, “If that were so, what would be the fault? he replies: “*eko ce*,” and so forth. When it is stated that “*sarodī*,” it would follow that only [the vowels] *ī*, *ha*, *gha*, *ṭa*, *na*, and so on, would be [single-syllabled].
But is it not the case that in the word *pacati*, in the very same manner that the word *paca* is single-syllabled, its constituent parts—the syllables *ac* and *pa*—are likewise [single-syllabled]?
And [it applies to] that which consists of a single syllable; consequently, even for its constituent parts, a separate doubling occurs...

because there is a general description (*sāmaññena*) of the initial single-syllable element as the cause of doubling, if doubling were applied separately to the whole and to its single-syllable parts, an undesirable result would follow;
therefore, to exclude this, he says: "by virtue of its occurrence as a single meaningful unit, [the rule applies] to that which possesses parts..."
"Grasping the whole" means: by the single occurrence of the knife, that is, by the occurrence of the sutta for doubling once, through the act of doubling.
"Together with its parts" means: existing together with the aforementioned parts, not without them. He thinks thus: "Of which..."
When a reduplication (dvibbacana) is being performed, there must be the inclusion of all the constituent parts;
it is appropriate that the reduplication applies to that entire aggregate (samudāya) and not to the individual parts.

For if the reduplication were applied to those parts individually, the inclusion of all of them would not be achieved through the production of a single reduplication, nor would it be achieved for the aggregate that possesses those parts. Therefore, the Teacher’s instruction proceeds once again for the sake of reduplicating those [parts].
"It must be so. He states the alternative possibility with the words "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth. In this context, the term *dvibbacana* refers to two things:
a double enunciation (*dvippayoga*) and a double vocalization (*dvibbacana*), which constitute two distinct positions (*pakka*).

Among these, because he perceives a fault in the position of double enunciation (*dvibbacanapakkha*), he demonstrates that he accepts only the position of double vocalization (*dvippayogadvibbacana*). Thus, first of all, he states the fault that would arise in the position of double enunciation:
"Of the first vowel-sound," and so forth. The word *dvi* (two) refers to that which is to be numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*).
And here, that which is to be numbered is either the form of the sound or its utterance (*uccāraṇa*).

In that case, regarding the utterance as the thing to be numbered, reduplication (*dvibbacana*) is not possible, because the utterance is a phenomenon (*dhamma*) that follows the sound. However, when the form of the sound itself is the thing to be numbered, reduplication occurs.
In that regard, there is a fault in the manuscript [reading "tañca"]. Thus it is said: "when two bases (*rūpa*) are being prescribed.

That being the case, since one becomes the locus (*ṭhānī*) for the phenomenon that is to be excluded (*nivutti*), there must be an exclusion of the locus; and because exclusion is a verbal root (*dhātu*), it is called "exclusion" (*nivutti*).
Therefore he says: "due to the absence of a distinction between base and suffix. By this, the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) is prescribed for the base when a suffix follows.
It would not be so; therefore it was said: ‘there would be no repetition of this. [The root] *pipāsati* [is derived from] *pā* = *pāne* (to drink).

In the sense of desire (*icchā*), the suffix *so* is added by the rule “*tuṃsmāccādi*” (5-61) after the infinitive ending *tum*. In the reduplication of ‘*pāsa pāsa*’, there is the elision of the following [consonant] after the preceding one, according to “*rasso pubbassa*” (5-74), and then *kha* is substituted for *cha* by the rule “*sesvassi*”.
However, in the case of a double application (*dvippayoga*) through reduplication, this fault does not enter; thus he says: ‘in the case of repetition (*āvuttiyaṃ*)...’
"Thus, etc. By the phrase "of that which has become twofold," it is indicated that the state of having become twofold belongs to the *dhātu* itself. 70.
In the case of *paro yogavibhāgā*, [the word] *añ-ādi* is understood from the rule *a ña ādīsu*. For if the genitive were intended here as well, then [it would have been stated as] *kha cha...*
He would have made it a single grammatical rule (*yoga*) as follows: "In the case of the *parokkhā* [tenses], *añ* and so forth occur after a single [verbal root] and after two.

Since *añ* and the others prescribed for the *parokkhā* tenses arise from the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself and not from anything else, and because of the proximity of the term *parokkhā*, the word *ca* ("and") includes only those suffixes prescribed after a root; thus he says:

"also in other suffixes prescribed after a root. However, if it is intended to express the sense of intensity (*bhusattha*) or frequency (*ābhikkhaññattha*), [the rule must be formulated differently].
It should be understood that in such cases, forms such as *daddallati* occur with the sense of intensity (*bhusattha*) and so forth.

Since the sense of intensity is applicable in the case of "he walks about with a bewildered mind" (*caṅkamati momūhacittāni*), it can be stated that suffixes such as *-tya* occur in the sense of intensity according to the rule of "frequently" (*bahula*).

The first and the second: these two [rules] concern single vowels (*ekassarā*). In that regard, the doubling of the first single vowel occurs by the rule “*khachasānamekassarodi dve*” (5-69), while the doubling of the second occurs by the rule “*parokkhāyaṃ ce*” (5-70).

Therefore, how could one say that when another [rule] is being stated, it must be a sublater of another? Consequently, even when the doubling of the second has been performed, the doubling of the first [remains].
This rule is indeed an exception to the first dual number; anticipating this, he says: "In the first," and so forth.
Because the context concerns verbal roots (*kriyāttha*), the genitive case in *kriyātthānaṃ* is connected with the singular form *eka-ssa* (of one) by means of the suffix *-rena*.

Thus, since the prescription for the first dual number is established through a connection with another sentence, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding the second [dual]; hence he says: "Of one," and so forth. The word *assa* [refers to] "from a vowel beginning with 'a'."

Regarding this yoga, "prior yoga" (*pubbayoga*) refers to the two preceding suttas. Since, in the rule "vowels [are doubled] after an initial [consonant]" (*ādismā sarā*), doubling of the sound-form is prescribed in a general sense by taking the vowel as the second member, it should be understood that—as in the previous case—the doubling of a consonant associated with a [preceding] consonant is established in that same way;
thus, the doubling of the consonant connected to the first doubling is to be understood as being sublated.
72. "The counter-sign" (*paṭinimitta*): a sign in relation to a sign is a counter-sign; the meaning is "when there is a sign.
73. Just as...
The first dual number is the domain of the first monosyllabic [stem], and the second dual number is the domain of the second monosyllabic [stem];
therefore he says, "according to the domain. Regarding the phrase "the first, second, and third dual numbers":
here, *pū* is the first word-form, *tti* is the second, and *yis* is the third.
76. The remainder [of the rule] is: "The suffix *kha* and so forth are applied.
82. *yuva*.

*Catthaparattā* means "because of being subsequent to a compound" (*cattha-samāsa*). It is connected with *tena paccekā*. The connection is that it is a qualifier (*visesana*) by virtue of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatta*).

Since the teacher has indicated [the term] precisely through the elision of the case-ending (*yovibhattilopa*), he says: "Or the indication is one where the case-ending is dropped (*luttayovibhattiko*).
83. *Lahu* (Light).
It is called *dhūpitā* because it fumigates (*dhūpāyati*). "Of the suffix" means of the *t* suffix.

[Objection: The addition of a *ka*-anubandha might be purposeless; for, since the suffix lacks the *gha*-augment, there would be no grammatical operation (*kāriya*) dependent upon it, and thus by the rule “*na te kānubandhanāgamesu*” (5-85), which prohibits such operations, the *ka*-anubandha would indeed be purposeless.
85. *Nate pucchīyittha*:
having analyzed [the compound] as such, by [Pāṇini 5.1.143] *tasya pṛcchāditas*, the suffix *ṭha* is applied. The remainder is exactly according to the method already stated.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the negation of *e* and *ona*," it is stated because the negation of *e* and *ona* is the primary factor (*pakatta*). In the cases of *cinitabba* and so forth, [the root] *ci* has been used in the sense of the past passive participle (*cīyittha*).
The analysis of *cīyati* is by way of *vāti* and so forth. Regarding *cinituṃ* and the like, [the derivation] is by way of *cinanā* and *yāti*, etc.

Now, since the suffix (*ñi*) is not a *paccaya*, how can *eo* be applied to the *paccaya* by the rule "of *la* and *hu*, when followed by *su*" (5-83)? Anticipating the doubt as to how there could be a prohibition, he says: "of *ñi*, etc.
Now, since there was no occurrence of *yu* or *vaṇṇa* at the beginning, how could there be such an occasion here? To this he says: "of their own *kā* and *pā*, *ku* and *kūṇa*, etc."
“Of *pattokāra*”: this refers to the substitution of *o* for the vowel *u* in the word *dhū*. “Of that which has become *pat* by *yuvaṇṇeccādi*”:
this refers to the substitution of *pat* for the suffixes *tabba*, *tuṃ*, and *ṇin*. Because the rule is optional (*vā*), the suffix *ñi* does not apply.

In the reading *dhunāpetabba*, since *ñi* is not applied, there is no application of the prohibition [stated in] “except elsewhere” (*aññatrāpi*). In the reading *dhunāpeti*, because of the suffix *ti*, [the rule] “sometimes of the verbal suffixes” (*kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ*) applies.

(5-161) And when there is the elision of the suffixal marker (*vikaraṇa*), the vowel *e* [remains]. In the absence of the augment (*āgama*), [the substitution of] *et* would occur by the rule “*yuvaṇṇe*” and so forth;

however, even with that augment, because it ends in *u*, [the substitution does not apply]. With this intention, he says: “Even so,” and so forth. He states another alternative: “When there is the augment,” and so forth. 87. *Añña*.

Regarding *sama*, *dama*, and *upasama*: it pacifies, thus it is a *samaka*; it tames, thus it is a *damaka*. Regarding *jana* (in the sense of producing): it produces, thus it is a *janaka*. Regarding *badha* (in the sense of binding): it binds, thus it is a *bādha* or *bādhaka*. 92. One lies down upon it, thus it is a *nipajjana* (a place for lying down).
It is to be wiped, thus it is *pamajjitabba*. For the purpose of wiping, thus it is *pamajjanāya*. To wipe, thus it is *pamajjituṃ*. It wipes, thus it is *pamajjanaṃ*.
93. In "maṃ vā rundhiti" and so forth, the analysis is "for the purpose of obstructing" (rodhanāya). 94.
In the case of the suffix *kvim*.
Now, one might object: "What is the purpose of including the mention of 'the end' (*anta*), since it has been stated that 'there is elision of the final consonant before *kvim*'?

Should not the elision apply only to the end [of the word], according to the rule *chaṭṭhiyantassa* (1-17)? Keeping this objection in mind, he says "the mention of the end," etc., demonstrating the purpose of its inclusion.
"In the rules for elision" means: in the rules for the elision of *vī* and so forth; [it is understood that] the genitive case is indicated.

The phrase “*vīmantu vantū*” (4-138) indicates the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*). Relying on the operation of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the inclusion of what ends with that) and its subsequent differentiation, [the author] states:
“The operation [applies] to that which ends in the sixth case. By “that which ends,” he means the *ī*-sound and so forth of *vī* and the others.

“Otherwise” means in the absence of the teaching regarding elision (*lopa*) that removes everything [except the suffix]. It might be purposeless [to state this], because the operation of the rule “to that which ends in the sixth case” would still be possible.

Now, wishing to state specifically the intended meaning of those [terms] taught in the sixth [case], he says "tadante" and so forth, in order to show the fault of the occurrence of elision (*lopa*) only within the interior.

101. Regarding the phrase "para atha dvitte," how is it determined that this refers to the absence of sound? He says "para" and so forth. In the immediately preceding sutta, [it was said]: "paripaccasamo..."
Having anticipated the objection—"Since it is stated [as] 'hī' (for), what is determined to follow from that?"—he says "But is it not... and so forth, in order to demonstrate its inappropriateness.
103. "Dhāssa apacurappayogattā" means because of its lack of frequent usage (*abahuppayogattā*).
