104. *Kimhi kto* [is used] in the sense of "he defiles" from the root *dūs*.

Regarding the grammatical maxim (*paribhāsā*) "that which is prescribed when a vowel follows applies to that [vowel] and its beginning," the meaning is: "when a vowel follows, whatever grammatical operation is prescribed occurs with respect to that vowel as the initial element. Thus, *te* refers to when the letter *t* follows.

Having stated "in *vaha*, only when *ta* and *tva* follow," he shows a counter-example (*paccudāharaṇa*) with "it is carried" (*vuyhati*). By means of the case ending (*mulliṅga*), he expresses the meaning of the verbal statement with "they go forth" (*ussā*) and so on.
The analysis is *nidhīyittha*.
When "gamā rāna" is stated, since the root *rā* in the sense of "taking" (*ādāne*) would also be understood, he says "rāna," etc.
110. In the *Vacā-sutta*, it is stated—"vassa"—to show that it refers specifically to the autumn harvest, he says: "‘Vassa,’ indeed," and so forth.
112. *Vaddha*.

Regarding the statement "vatta-vattaneti," since the vowel *u* has not been prescribed here by the suffix *tippaccaya*, he says "vatta-vattaneti" and so forth to show that [the word] was stated with the intention of asking "how?
and so on. Regarding the rule "vuttimatte," it is due to a grammatical substitution (*nipātana*);
for it is said in the rule "sabbādayo vuttimatte" (Pāṇini 1.1.27), "in the sense of vuttimatta," there is a substitution. Regarding "ṭhā = gatinivattiya," here the term used is "gatinivattiya."
Due to the irregularity (*nipātana*), the letter *u* does not occur in this alternative; therefore he says, “*vatti*, etc. The act of turning is *vutti*; [the noun stem] is *vatti*.
Regarding the rule "for all *k* of the root *yaja*," he says, "of *ya* and the vowels."

115. By the phrase "by way of pointing out the distinctness of the letters" (*gāpā byattiniddesena*), he demonstrates that the exposition of the types (*jātiniddesa*) is independent [of the individual letters]. With the words "In *īssecca*, etc.," he clarifies the intended meaning of the text as it was stated.
In the rule *satthaṃ* “*byañjane dīgharassā*” (1-33), [the vowel] is short (*rassa*). 120.
Regarding *ñā*:
the connection is that *nto* is prescribed for the agent (*kattari*) in the present tense (*vattamāne*), according to the rule *nto kattari vattamāne* (5-64).
121. In the case of the *kuppaccaya*, the final letter *k* [of the base] becomes the initial letter *k* of the *kuppaccaya*, with the status of being a constituent part at the end.
"Nāññatra cayādīsu" means that, according to the definitive rule, the suffix *cha* does not occur in meanings other than those beginning with "accumulation" (*caya*).
123. Regarding *jara*:
when the word *jasa* is followed by the suffix *īm*, there is the elision of the letter *a*; however, when followed by *le*, it becomes *jīrāpayati*. This [form] is derived from the root *atiki*.
124. *Disassa* [is the form] of *diṭṭhi*;

*dassanaṃ* means seeing; for the purpose of seeing, *daṭṭhuṃ*. In the case of reduplication (*dvitte*) as in "we two remember" (*saramhā dve*), [the form is] *duddaso*. By the rule "ā ī" etc. (6-33), there is the shortening of the *ī* [in *addakkhi*]. *Dakkhissati* [is formed] by the rule "bhavissati ssati" etc. (6-2); [the suffix] *ssati* [is applied]. 125. *Samā* [is the feminine nominative singular of *sama*].
In the word *vādassare*, by way of alternative analysis (*vikappa*), there is the substitution of *ra* for the letter *da*.
To show that by the power of the grammatical rule, the suffix *dassa* is applied even when *ana* does not follow, he states another position (verse 127).

‘Ādissa,’ etc. In order to show that [the suffix] -la is not applied when there is a fear of confusion with other [words] that do not have the vowel *a*, such that it would be apprehended as being [something else], he says ‘anaghaṇsu,’ etc., to indicate that it is dependent on the sequence [of letters].
‘Āparassa’ means of the letter *da* that follows the vowel *ā*.
In the phrase "vuttiyaṃ etasmiṃ visaye," the meaning of "etasmim" here is "in the domain of a suffix excluding those beginning with *tyādi*.
It is understood that it is made known because it is being cognized. By the words "na ñāpakato," this is shown:

"some things are made known merely by being cognized through following the wording [of the rule], while some are made known by a formal indicator (*ñāpaka*); in this latter case, according to what has been stated, in certain instances..."
“The non-employment of any verbal root (dhātu) is indicated. He states another position with the words “Or, precisely because it is indicative,” and so forth.

He explains this with “For it is capable,” and so on. “Non-employment of the root *as*” means that when any suffix such as *tabba* follows the root *as*, there is no employment of forms such as *bhavitabba*.
“Even without a sutta”: even without a sutta such as “*aty-ādi*” and so forth. He thinks thus:

“That which is accomplished by the substitution of *bhū* for *as*—all that is desired—is established by the verbal root *bhū* alone through the application of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), even without another specific sutta for the substitution of *bhū*.
Furthermore, its status as an indicator (*ñāpaka*) for the non-application of certain [rules] in some instances is also appropriate; what is performed elsewhere may also be meaningful here.”
"Yeti dhātuppayogā yasmiṃ visaye": in whatever object there is an application of verbal roots (*dhātu*), [the term] *pāti* refers to the root *pā* in the sense of "protection" (*rakkhaṇe*);

it does not refer to applications such as *pāyayati* (he causes to drink) or *pāyayitabba* (to be caused to drink). Thus, in the subsequent cases as well, it should be understood according to what is appropriate.

*Brūssa*: of the root *brū* in the sense of "speaking" (*vacane*). *Adissa*: of the root *ad* in the sense of "eating" (*bhakkhaṇe*). *Īādīti*: the suffix *ī* and so forth, occurring after a completed action (*bhūte*). And the connection here is with the phrase "in the case of *ī* and so forth."

In the case of *avabodhe*, it should be connected with *etissa*, with the suffixes beginning with *ṇi*, and with those beginning with *ī*; and in the case of *ajjhene*, it should be connected with *etissa*, with the suffixes of the parokkhā (aorist), with the suffixes beginning with *ṇi*, and with those beginning with *ī*.
Having thus connected [the rule] by stating that there is no application [of the suffix] in all instances, the meaning is to be understood.

The construction is: “It should be known because of its being prescribed extensively. Since it is described by means of the *yak* affix, it is said: “*asa-kkhepanetī massā*”; therefore, he says: “*asassā*,” and so forth.
129. Regarding the statement "Aā Ssāti jātiniddeso," he says: "'Ssaiti,' etc.
Because the form is identical when the initial *sa* is elided, both examples ‘santi’ and ‘santū’ are shown, as the suffix *anti* includes *antu*.

131. The connection is: “And they cause those feet to move. Even though the action is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the suffixes are used for clarity].
The connection [is as follows]. To specify what kind of action [is meant], he says: "whether it be of a general or specific nature.
That distinction is the specific quality by which the action, being distinguished, is expressed by the verbal root itself.

"By way of the difference between the expressive words" means by way of the difference between the roots that express both the general action and the specific action; "by him too" refers to Kaccāyana. *Saṇṭhānaṃ* means configuration (*saṇṭhiti*).
141. One who eats *kiṭṭha* (husks) is called a *kiṭṭhāda*. By metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the term *kiṭṭha* refers to the grain that has arisen in a ploughed field.
142. *Dhasta*.
The absence of stability is "nippaccanta"; here, the prefix *adhi-* is elided.

"He was instructed" means *anusiṭṭha*; the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense (*kamme*). According to the rule *sā sassa sisvā* (5.1.17), it becomes *sāsanāya*, meaning "for the sake of instructing."

147. Now, regarding the phrase *atha bahassā*: why is it that the genitive case is not understood as being connected with the substitution (*ādesa*) of *ḍha*? To this he says: “*Bahassā*,” etc. The term *ḍhayogapajjena* means by way of conjunction (*yoga*) and coalescence (*pajja*), that is, by way of unification together with the letter *ḍha*.

"Because it is stated as *Ḷoca*": he thinks thus—"When this substitution of the conditional suffix (*paccayādesa*) should occur, then these [suffixes] would be indicated by means of a compound (*samāsa*)," and therefore he said, "one should say *haḷ*.
149. Regarding *muhā muddho*:
by the rule "the substitute *dho* occurs after *hetu*" (5-145), its *dho* is applied.
150. *Bhidā imassa* means "of this [root] *pī*. *Tappane* refers to the act of satisfying; *iha* means "in this place. *Pinayī* means "he became fat"—this is the meaning. *Sūyī*:
here the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*); by this, *adīyi*, *aḍīyi*, *alīyi*, and *alūyī* are included. This continues up to the inclusion of the suffix *-ktin*.
“*Lopo vaḍḍhāktissā*” (5-158): this rule extends up to the suffix *ktin*.
151. From the verbal root *dā*, [the form] *dinna* is derived from *adīyittha* (“was taken”), and *dinnavā* is derived from *adadī* (“he gave”).

152. One who has done nothing (*akiri*) or one who thinks "I have done nothing" is *akiṇṇo*; one who has done something is *kiṇṇavā*. One who has filled (*apuri*) or one who thinks "I have filled" is *puṇṇo*; one who has not filled is *apuṇṇavā*. One who has wasted away (*akhiyi*) is *khīṇo* or *khīṇavā*.
153. One who crosses over (*tara*).
*Atarī* and *ajīrī* are compounds formed by means of the suffix *i*. *Ciṇṇo* means "he was piled up" (*cīyittha*); one who piles up (*cināti*) is a "piller" (*ciṇṇavā*). Regarding the root *muc*:
*asakkhi* [is derived from] *satto*, which means "one who possesses being" (*sattavā*). Since the root *saj* means "to cling," for the sake of meter it also becomes *satto* and *sattavā*.
158. Elision (*lopa*) and augmentation (*vaḍḍhana*) constitute increase (*vaḍḍhi*). 159.
The suffix *kvi*.
"He overcomes" (abhibhavati) thus he is "the conqueror" (abhibhū).
162. The connection is that there is the elision of the suffix *māsa*.
163. Having grasped, having made a seizing—that is, having taken hold of—within "grasping and clinging" (*gaha-upādāna*).
"Of one whose connection has been relinquished" (*ossaṭṭhānubandhassa*) means "of one whose connection has been abandoned.

He states the intended meaning of the phrase "for the purpose of excluding the mere *yakāra*," which is "for the purpose of qualification. For indeed, the meaning of a qualification is its separation from the mere *yakāra*;
thus, when there is another word-meaning present, the exclusion of the mere *yakāra* is understood. [The opponent asks: "What fault is there if the mere *yakāra* is taken?"

He said: “Or rather, [the reading] would be *yo vā tvāssa samāsetihī*,” and so forth. Regarding *patvā*: it is either from the root *pata* or *patha*, both meaning “to go,” or from the root *pada*, also meaning “to go.
165. Regarding *tuṃ tayopi*: this is due to the substitution of *tayā* for *tuṃ*.

169. *Disā nāppakketi*: the meaning is that it does not apply when [the condition] has not been reached, but only when it has been reached. *Ñāpakalopo ti*: by the very fact of being an indicator (*ñāpaka*), namely "titālīsā," the letter *v* of the suffix *ktvā* is elided; this is the meaning.
If it is asked, "When 'nassa' is stated, how is it understood that [the rule applies] to the suffixes *na*, *tam*, *māna*, *ti*, and so forth?", he says:

"'Nassa', etc. Because, according to the context, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṇa* by the rule "nantamānatyādīnaṃ" (5-172), it is understood that [the rule applies] to the suffixes *na*, *tam*, *māna*, *ti*, and so forth;
thus he says: "'Or the letter *ka* of the suffixes.'"

173. *Gama* [is derived from] *icchīyateti*, meaning it should be desired. *Esanā* means desire. *Icchīyittha* means desired; *āsana* means that which should be sat upon. For the purpose of sitting on a seat (*āsanāya acchituṃ*). By the rule “In the case of a suffix, long vowels become short” (*byañjane dīgharassā*), [the vowel] becomes short.

In the section on the six suffixes beginning with *amāna*, the substitution of *kuru* was not cited. Regarding the term *karāno*, there is the elision of the *ma* in “*mānassamassa*” (5-16). Why was it not cited as the substitution of *kuru* in the six suffixes beginning with *nta*? To this he says: “*vavatthite*,” etc. (179).
Regarding “of the *ṇo* following a nasal” (*ṇiggahītassa*), this refers to that which has been made a nasal by the rule “*mañcarudhādīnaṃ*” (5-19). *Gahaṇīyaṃ* means that which is to be grasped.
Thus ends the commentary on the Fifth Chapter in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*,
the sub-commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*.
The Sixth Chapter.
1. *Vatta-tadatthasseva*:
"Of that very purpose" means of that purpose which consists of the action (*kriyā*). It belongs to that very self (*attā*) which is designated as the action.

By this, it makes known that this is the locus (*ādhāra*) of the action. With the words "not otherwise," etc., he states the reason for the qualification "of that very purpose. Without the sutta, [the meaning would be] like that of others.
"Without the Sutta. By the phrase "they too will exist only while it is being recited," one understands the remaining statement here: "because it is intended to be spoken thus.

By the particle *eva* (in the phrase "only while it is being recited," i.e., by the word *eva*), [the sense is established]. "The desire for that expression" means the desire for the expression of the present tense.
By the pronoun *taṃ* in the phrase "from its vicinity," the cause for Mahākassapa’s attainment of death—namely, the recollection of Subhadda’s words—is indicated by that pronoun.
A specific type of activity characterized by the experience of suffering is grasped, or rather, those very specific activities currently occurring;
for both of these, death and the manifestation of non-Dhamma (adhamma) are respectively proximate. Therefore he said: "Because of the proximity of the manifestation and death.
He thinks thus: "Even that which is the proximity of the manifestation and death—characterized as such—of that specific activity occurring at that particular time..."
Proximity to that [action] is grasped by the mention of another action currently occurring, just as a region near the Ganges is called "the Ganges," whereby one might say,
"The cows are in the Ganges. The author of the *Vutti* has formulated an alternative position beginning with "Previously" (*pure*),
and he introduces it with the words "By its own nature" (*sabhāvato*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that.
"The time of action" (*kiriyākāla*) means the time when the action is currently occurring. "It remains" (*avasissati*): it remains from the future time indicated by the words *pure* and *purā*.

"At the time of action" (*kiriyā kāle*): this is an explanation [meaning] at the time of the action of dying. "Of that" (*tassa*): of that death which is being explained. Regarding the phrase "because of its being present" (*vattamānattā*):
here, the words "will occur" (*bhavissanti*) are to be supplied as referring to the very present. "By this": by the statement beginning with *pureccādi*. By the words *pure* and *purā*...

When there is an understanding of the future time, [the expressions] "it shines" and "it dies" are employed; here, the time for the actions of shining and dying is primarily applicable at that moment. Thus he says:

"I shall state the primary present tense. Furthermore, the author of the *Vutti* introduces another alternative view with the words "kālecca," and in order to demonstrate that, he turns back to the subject with the words "in the future," and so forth.

In the *Vutti*, "temporal sequence" (*kālabyatti*) refers to the transgression of time; the intention is that by exceeding the present tense, forms such as *atyādi* occur even in the future tense due to the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*).
He demonstrates this very point with the words “*bhavanteva*” and so forth. By the word “*tyādayo*,” there is the inclusion of all verbal roots (*ākhyātika*) by means of the suffix *-ti*.
The connection is with the phrase “the long vowel for *la*. “*Gacchati*” means that it will go to the state of co-occurrence with the suffix *sak* (i.e., it will become *gacchissati*).

3. Regarding the phrase "they will profess" (*paṭijānissantīti*) while [the action] is actually occurring, this is a future tense used for the present; the meaning is "they are professing. Furthermore, regarding the other [forms]:

"he was" (*āsi*) is used for "he has been"; "he will do" (*karissati*) is used for "he did" (*akari*); "you will intend" (*cetessasi*) is used for "you intended" (*cetitā asi*); and "you will eat" (*bhuñjissasi*) is used for "you ate" (*bhuñjitā*).
*Asi* (is). *Anokappanā* is lack of faith (*assaddhā*). *Amarisanaṃ* is intolerance (*akkhamā*). Regarding the phrase *imināva*:

when the words *kodha* (anger) and *saddhā* (faith) are understood from the presence of the word *atthi* as a subordinate term (*upapada*), even though there is another word [present], the meaning is that it is established by this very general term (*sāmaññavacana*).
*Garahāvamā* is a statement of its cause; for by means of "tathāhi" and so forth, it is capable of conveying the sense of censure (*garahā*) itself. *Atthināma*.
“*Īdisanti atthināmā*” means that there exists the eating of yesterday’s porridge; this is the sense.
Even though it exists, not believing it and being indignant, he speaks thus. The intended meaning is “he thinks it does not exist”; therefore he says:
“even though it is before his very eyes,” and so forth (*īdisampi*, etc.). The word *yopi* is connected with the word *sopi* by means of the pronoun *ta*.

It should be understood. Regarding the phrase "it exists" (*atthi*), the meaning of "existing" as stated in the sense of "being present" (*vijjamānattha*) should be seen as applying to all three of the following positions that will be explained.

When only so much is said—"Is it that there is, father?"—the first [position] ends with the words "there is a stump, a rock, etc., having sat down," and the second also ends with the words "there is a stump, a rock, etc., having sat down," while the third begins with "there is something else, etc."
Regarding the term *jigucchaneyya* (to be loathed), he says “*sopanā*,” etc., having kept in mind how a sequence of words reaching the limit of sound can be obtained.
“By this” refers to the statement: “Even when there is no [explicit] meaning, there is still the comprehension of censure. The connection is: “he censures standing and eating.
This was stated according to the tradition of the Sakkas. “*Nissāya nissāya*” means relying upon, that is, depending on each respective place where the Blessed One was seated.

4. Regarding "in the case of a past action-nature" (*bhūte kiriyārūpe*): this refers to that which has the nature of an action. Similarly, "elsewhere as well" (*aññatrāpi*) means in cases other than those formed with *agami*, *agamittha*, and *atīma*—namely, in forms such as *agamum* and so forth, and in forms such as *agamo* and so forth.
In expressions like "slender-waisted" (*anudarā*) and "hairless" (*alomikā*), although a waist or hair actually exists, it is used to indicate the absence of their fullness (*mahattābhāva*).
And because of its multiplicity and for the purpose of expressing the state [of the compound], it is not intended to be stated [as a separate rule].

5. Regarding "Ana Aññapadatthavuttiyā": by the phrase "vakkhamānalakkhaṇo" and so forth, he shows the "meaning of another word" (aññapadattha) that was mentioned. By the author of the *Vuttikāra*, it is stated: "vakkhamānalakkhaṇo."

“Characterized by what will be explained starting with ‘āñāyya’,” etc. By the word “antokatvā” (having included within), he expresses that the prefix *ā-* functions in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
Regarding the phrase “or both day and half-night”: here the word “or” (*vā*) indicates an alternative position.
By the term “half-night” (*aḍḍharatta*), the fourth part of the night is intended to be expressed; thus, the meaning is “the day and its half-night. He states the intended meaning of this as follows:
“*Atīteccādi.* He clarifies the intended meaning in both cases with the words “*Ayaṃ iccādi*.

*Pañcayāmo*: there are five watches (*yāma*) or periods (*pahāra*) for a day, consisting of one watch measuring seven and a half *ghaṭikās*—namely, the three *ghaṭikās* plus forty-five *vināḍikas* of the latter part of the past night, and the three *ghaṭikās* plus forty-five *vināḍikas* of the former part of the future night. Thus, it is called *pañcayāmo* because it possesses five watches.
The last watch has passed, or its latter half;
the blow occurred before dawn, or likewise during half of that time.
That period between the stated limits is considered the present time.
By the negation of that, whatever else [is meant], that is considered "not belonging to today" (*anajjatana*).

In cases such as *agamattha* ("you have gone"), because there is an absence of a consonant related to the suffixes *-aī*, *-issa*, etc., the suffix *-iña* does not apply. Regarding the phrase "even in a mixture," this means even when the past tense is mixed with "today. To demonstrate how it applies in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) where there is a mixture, he says: "'In the sense of exclusion' (*pariyudāse tāve*), etc.

"Dependent on 'today'" (*ajjatananissaya*) means dependent on that which pertains to the portion of "today" within the mixture. However, in the case of the question "What is the meaning? (*atthuti pañhe*), it is "dependent on what is other than that" (*tadaññanissaya*).
"By way of a mixture (byāmissa) from that point on"—this means, other than a support [for a precept] from today onwards as opposed to one from a previous day, that is, excluding the mixed [cases].

"In the past" (bhūtakāle) means at a time other than the mixed [cases]. "The inclusion" (pasaṅga) refers to the inclusion of [suffixes] such as *ā* and *ñu*. "Only from today" (*ajjahiyyova*) is stated for the purpose of showing the exclusion of the mixed [cases]. 6.
The Subsequent (Para).

"Compound" (*samāsa*) refers here to either a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) or a kāraka compound (*kārakasamāsa*). And its status as a "convention" (*nipātanatā*) is due to its being a specific term (*visesato*).
"And this" (*etañca*) means "and this [term] *parokkha*. A qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) of the meaning of the verb root (*kriyattha*) is a "verb-root-attribute" (*kriyatthopādhi*).

It is a qualification (*visesana*) of that verb-root-attribute by way of the instrument (*sādhana*) of the past tense (*bhūtānajjatana*), but not directly; such is the meaning. Why is it not a direct qualification?
Thus he says, "Because there is no exclusion. To clarify that very point, he says, "For instance," and so forth.
By the word "being established" (*sādhiyamānā*), he indicates that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) has not yet reached its final completion. They exist as faculties (*indriyānaṃ*).

Because those faculties have existing (*santo*) objects (*visaya*), that is their nature (*sambhāva*); therefore [the term is used]. "No" (*na*) is in the sense of negation, by way of the means of establishment (*sādhanadvārena*).
The meaning is that because there exists something to be excluded when there is a qualifying attribute (*visesana*), the aforementioned fault does not arise.

To demonstrate the very existence of this fault, he says: “*Yass’iccādi*” (“Of which...,” etc.). “*Yassa*” refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvattha*). “*Tattha*” means in that non-evident meaning of the verbal root. With the words beginning with “*Nanu ceccādi*,” he raises an objection:
since the capacity (*satti*) is the inherent nature (*sabhāva*) of the factors of action (*kāraka*), would that [capacity] also not be non-evident? “*Asatto*” means incapable.

Keeping in mind that it is improper to apply the first person (*asmākāraka*) to a verb whose object is *attan* (self) because it is directly perceived by oneself (*attano paccakkha*), the author of the *Vutti* stated what he did;

to illustrate that, [the commentator] says: “But is it not so,” and so forth. For even an action that makes itself known becomes "remote" (*parokkhā*) when it is not clearly perceived due to distraction of mind; therefore, this applies even in the case of the highest person (*uttama-visaya*).

Let its state of being indirect (parokkha) indeed be so. To show that even when one is awake, if there is non-apprehension due to mental affliction or intoxication, it [the state of being indirect] still occurs, the word "distracted" (byāsatta) was stated.
At the time of production (*abhinibbattikāla*) means at the time of the arising of the action; "I was asleep, what did I prattle?
I was intoxicated, what did I prattle?"—this is the illustration here. The mention of "asleep" (*sutta*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the object of the mind's distraction.
7. "Eyyā" etc.
was stated in order to make it known that the sense of the optative (eyyādi-attha) is included by "eyyādotīminā.

Although one might have said "tanti" (the rule) with reference to the word *nimitta* (cause), "soti" (that) was stated with reference to the word *visaya* (object). "Tesam" refers to the optative and the rest. It shows the object.
Regarding the phrase “*hetuphalesviccādiko*”: by the word “etc. (*ādi*), the *pañhapatthanā* and other such [grammatical rules] are included. Now, one might ask:
since there is no mention of the term “hypothetical” (*kriyātipatti*) here, how can it be understood? To this he says: “‘*Kriyāti pattiyan*’ etc.
The connection is that the explanation (*vivaraṇa*) has been made as “in the case of hypothetical [mood]” (*kriyātipatti*).
"By way of the denotable meaning" means by way of the sense of the term *kriyā-saṅkhāta* (action-concept).

It is "because it qualifies the meaning of the action already performed," that is, because it qualifies the verbal root (*dhātu*) which has been added [to the prefix] under the heading of the meaning of action. This is what is meant:

"In *atipatti*, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the action already undertaken; and being a qualifier, it ought not to be straight [in its application], for what then? By way of the denotable meaning. For instance, *atipatana*..."
"It is called *kriyātipatti* because it does not apply to the action itself, since it is not applicable to the meaning of the action;

therefore, while the term *kriyātipatti* mentioned as 'the non-occurrence of the action' (*atipatti*) serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the action, it is explained as *kriyātipatti* by way of its referent.
The phrase "due to the occurrence of incompatible conditions" (*vidhurappaccayopanipātato*) means "due to the convergence of contrary conditions" (*viruddhappaccayasamavāyato*).

"Due to the deficiency of causes" means due to the absence of that cause which belongs to an effect possessing a cause. Regarding the phrase "in this case," the meaning is: "in the domain of the present.
"In the case of the lapse of action" refers to the lapse of action such as the past and so forth. "By a sign" means by a characteristic.
At the time when one understands the lapse through a sign that makes it known, the present time does not remain; it passes away.
He says: "By the transgression of the present state. He clarifies that very point with the words "simultaneous" (*samakāla*) and so forth.

"Simultaneous" means at one and the same moment. Since a past tense suffix (*kriyātipatti*) cannot occur for something that is presently existing, it follows that the status of [the action] as "eating" and so on belongs only to what remains—namely, the past and the future;
otherwise, it would be untenable. Thus it is stated in the *Vutti*: "By implication," and so forth.

Regarding the term *liṅgena* (by a sign): here, when there was previously a journey by the right side, the observation of the non-appearance of carts on the road is the sign (*liṅga*) for the fact that the journey by the right side has the non-appearance of carts as its cause. For the inference of the journey by the right side, going by another way and so forth is the sign.
For the inference of the occurrence of the action of [not seeing] carts, the placing of heavy loads upon the carts and so forth is the sign. In the first stage of life...

Having recognized through signs that others had attained the state of Arahantship and the renunciation that serves as its cause during their first stage of life— by means of the sign of attaining Arahantship after having gone forth—

one understands the non-occurrence of renunciation by the sign of being occupied with household duties and so forth, and the non-occurrence of Arahantship by the sign of the absence of the cause for renunciation and the lack of its presence;
thus, the non-occurrence of an action that actually took place is to be understood by means of such a sign.
If one who has attained such direct knowledge (abhiññā) applies [the practice], it should be understood that they apply it having known everything through direct knowledge itself.
However, the phrase "as determined by the characteristic" is stated because it occurs in the majority of cases. 8.
Cause (hetu).

By the phrase "due to the constant cultivation" (*niccabhāvanā-hetu*), etc., it is demonstrated that here there is only the relationship of cause and fruit, and not [the acquisition of] attainment (*patti*).
"By way of examples of all grammatical suffixes" (*sabbapaccayodāharaṇavasena*) means by way of examples of all suffixes such as the optative (*eyya*), etc.

Because it was stated "due to the existence of both cause and fruit," he shows the causes and fruits with the words "killing," etc. Thus, because of the existence of cause and fruit, and because they are prescribed at all times—

In this context, even when [the term] "occurring" (*vattamāna*) is present, the sense is that one "reaches" (*pappoti*). And that [sense] is both the state of being a cause and the state of possessing a cause.

Regarding the phrase "the latter and latter word" and so forth in the question: "question" (*pañha*) refers to the preceding word, while "inquiry" (*sampucchana*) refers to the subsequent word, and so on.
It should be understood as follows. *Sampucchanā* (consultation) is mutual questioning; it has the sense of requesting, such as by saying "give" and so forth.

*Iṭṭhāsiṃsanā* (desiring what is wished for) is the longing for the attainment of that which is desired but not yet attained. The meaning should be understood by connecting *pīti* (joy), which is differentiated according to the occasion and the distinction of its objects.
The phrase "of that which has become a sign," and so forth, shows the appropriate time. "Of that which has become a sign" means...

[It refers to] that which has become the cause for the successful accomplishment of various duties. "Injunction" (*vidhi*) means invitations, entreaties, requests, and commissions pertaining to matters of this life and the life to come.
And here, the fifth case-ending is prescribed by others in the instances of permission and attainment; however, in the five cases beginning with those of this life, the seventh case-ending is used.
But here, since both of those are indeed specific types of injunctions, they are included within "injunction," and thus it is said [in the rule] "for the purpose of enjoining *eyya* and so forth."
The author of the commentary (*vuttikāra*), wishing now to explain this, says: “Even at the time when permission has been obtained,” and so forth.

He makes the sequence of the injunction (*vidhi*) clear through such expressions as “you should act thus. Although [the teacher] is merely granting permission or explaining, he indeed instigates activity toward the actions;
therefore, the meaning should be understood by connecting it with the phrase “because he instigates (*byāpāreti*) [one] toward the undertaking.”

Now, in order to state what was said by certain grammarians (*byākaraṇaññū*) who follow the rule of the seventh case (*sattamī*) for the sense of "instructing" (*pesana*), as well as for the senses of "prescription" (*vidhi*), "desire" (*icchita*), and "excessive occurrence" (*ativuttika*), he says:
"Even in instructing," and so forth. "With its root" (*samūlataṃ*) means with the root of the formulation of the seventh case rule according to certain grammarians (*saddikā*).
This refers to the Kaccāyana-sutta: "The seventh case is used in the senses of permission (*anumati*) and possibility (*parikappa*)" (3.1.11). For one who desires to act...
*Anumati* is the granting of permission to another; *parikappa* is imagining, observing, examining, as well as cause, fruit, action, and possibility.
The meaning is that the seventh case ending occurs in the sense of permission (*anumati*) and in the sense of imagining (*parikappa*).

By the inclusion of the word "sense" (*attha*), it also applies in the cases of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantana*), entreaty (*āmantaṇā*), persuasion (*ajjhesana*), aspiration (*patthanā*), and the attainment of what is possible (*pattakāla*).
10. *Tu* is stated as being used in expressions such as *gacchatu* (let him go) and *gacchantu* (let them go). *Dadātu* is used in the sense of requesting.
11. *Satya*.

And this very application [of the term] applies to the state of an Arahant; therefore, it should be understood by connecting it thus: "May your lordship indeed exercise sovereignty, for your lordship is an Arahant.
12. *Sambhā*:
Readiness and determination are the meaning of this word; "conviction in power" means conviction in capability.
This is the meaning. The connection (*sambandha*) illustrates the following of usage. Regarding "even when it is understood" (*gammamāne*):

this refers to cases where [the sense] is understood even though not explicitly stated by verbal roots such as *bhū* (to become) and so forth, as exemplified by the statement, “One might even split a mountain with one’s head.

Although there is a possibility (*sambhāvanā*) regarding the object of the capacity (*alam-attha*), expressed by the word *alaṃ* due to great strength in the act of killing an elephant, words such as *na bhavanti* and so forth do not occur because the word *alaṃ* has the sense of *trālaṃ* (enough).

"He will kill. Regarding the term *dhātu*: here, by the mention of *dhātu*, the verbal roots beginning with *bhū* are understood, either because the word *dhātu* is conventionally established (*ruḷha*) in that sense or by the technical designation of the ancient masters (*pubbācariya*).
"Has been uttered" means [the root] such as *bhavaṃ* (you may eat), and so forth.
13. *Māyo*.
In "sūti-māsūti," the word *su* [is used]. Here means in this example. The remainder is that the word *mā* causes the cessation [of the suffix].

By the word "commenced" (*āraddha*), he shows the present time of going to the forest. From a verbal root in which the meaning of the *ṇi*-suffix is included within itself, even in the absence of the *ṇi*-suffix.

The relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*); therefore he says: "In the connection of the meaning of the verbal root, characterized by the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
In all cases, the meaning expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*) is the qualified, while that expressed by a word ending in a nominal suffix (*syādyanta*) is the qualifier.
"Desired" (*iṭṭha*) means desired by others. Because the sense of "knowing" possesses the sense of "going," [it is included] under the rule: "Roots with the sense of going take an object" (5-59).
In the Sutta, by the word *gamana* (going), the sense of "knowing" (*jānana*) is also included on the principle that "those things whose meaning is going have the meaning of understanding.
Thus, the meaning is "the state of having the sense of going" by virtue of this inclusion of the sense of knowing. [The term] *abhimata* refers to what is accepted by the Pāṇinīyas.

Likewise, he states the meaning of the word: "'Anantareṇa gatatta' means 'by that which has been stated immediately prior, acting as the instrument' (*karaṇa*). *Abhimata* refers specifically to the Pāṇinīyas themselves.
He says "the aggregate" (*samuccaya*), etc., in order to state the aggregate intended here.

Now, one might wonder how there can be an accumulation (*cīyamānatā*) of many actions when there is only a single action of entering and a single action of reciting; therefore, he says "due to the difference in the means" (*sādhanabhede*), etc.

The meaning is that even for the action of wandering, there is a differentiation due to the difference in the means such as monasteries (*maṭha*) and so forth. "Of that which has that action as its primary [object]" (*takkiriyāppadhānassa*)—that is to say...
The act of washing is the primary function of this agent. Even when it performs an action as if directing others, it is not engaged in another action as its primary function;
rather, it is engaged only in that specific action as its primary function.
14. Pubba...

Because this treatise has the form of a "Great Saying" (mahāvākya), it constitutes a portion of that [Great Saying] in relation to it—just as "the present tense is *tiṅ*," "the future," and so forth, are portions of a sentence.
Therefore, he says, "by means of portions of sentences. For this very reason, he stated: "Now, the exclusion of the members of the sentence is being performed.

Having thus shown its character as an injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*), he now says, "Or else, for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), [it concerns] *iti* and so forth," in order to show its character as a restrictive statement (*niyamavākya*).

He clarifies the very nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama-sutta*) with the words beginning "by those" (*tehi*). "By those various suttas" means by those various suttas such as "when [the suffix] *vartamāna* occurs, [the endings] *anti* and so forth.
"By this" refers to this sutta beginning with "prior and subsequent" (*pubbapara*).

Now, if only "in the substitutes for *tumha* and *amha*" were stated, would it not follow that the distinction—namely, "in the agents expressed by the words *tumha* and *amha*, and in those expressed by other words"—would not be established?
From what is this understood? He says: “*Kattukamme*,” etc. Furthermore, he will state the application [of these suffixes] to the agent (*kattā*) and so forth.

By the phrase “only for the agent and the object” (*kattukammānameva*), he excludes the abstract state (*bhāva*). And thus he will say: “because of the absence of being expressible by the words *tumha* and *amha*.

The passage beginning with “asatvabhūtāya” provides the reason for the possibility of the singular number; however, the passage beginning with “*tumhāmhe*” provides the reason for the possibility of the first person.
How are the middle, superior, and first persons understood in relation to abstract states (*bhāva*) and the like?

Furthermore, how is it that there is no application of the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ*, which denote the agent (*kāraka*) expressed by the verb, since these words are distinguished by their respective case-endings (*saññā-vibhatti*)?

To resolve this doubt, the author now explains what was stated in the *Vutti*: "If the suffixes *māna* and so forth were not prescribed for abstract states and the like, then [the following would apply] regarding *māna* and the others..."

By the force of the statement, "The application of [suffixes such as] *kyal* and so forth is simply not possible for others (*paresu*) such as those expressing the sense of existence (*bhāva*) and so on," it is understood that when the agents are expressed by words like *tumhe* (you),

the middle endings (*majjhima*) and so forth apply. To show that the word-forms *tumhe* and so on are not employed there because the meaning of the agent (*kāraka*) denoted by *tumhe* and so on has already been signaled (*saññāpita*) by the verb (*ākhyāta*) prescribed for that context, the passage beginning with "In the case of *tumhe* and so on" (*tumhādisu*) is commenced.
If that were so, the very use of the word *tumhādisa* (you and others) would not occur; thus he says, “If it were so, *micca*, etc. He states the resolution: “By the word *sasaddena* (with sound).

By the word *tumhādisa*, the plurality already expressed by the term *brāhmaṇā* is restated by the word *bahavo* (many). He asks, “In the absence of the [restating] word, how is there coreferentiality?
and answers with “*Anujjamānassa*, etc.”—that is, of that which is to be restated (*anuvaditabbassa*).

Regarding the agent indicated by [the verb] *gacchati* and so forth, the phrase "by way of restatement" (*anuvādena*) means by way of restating [the pronouns] *tumha* and so on. This refers to the statement of Kaccāyana: "Even when a noun is employed, the nominative case is used if it is in grammatical apposition" (3-1-5).
Therefore, he says: "By that also," and so forth. For in cases such as *tayā paccate*, there is no grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇattā*).

It does not occur. For instance, *iccetaṃ* [in the example] expresses the agent (*kartṛvācī*), while *paccateccetaṃ* expresses the object (*karmavācī*), because verbal suffixes (*ākhyātappaccaya*) are prescribed for the object.
The sequence for establishing the system of Pāṇini’s school is: “*Ehi maññe rathena gamissasi*” (Come, I think you will go by chariot), according to the rule beginning with “*parihāse*” (in jest).
“In the employment of *maññati*” means in the employment of the root *man* by way of its accompanying word (*upapada*). “From the root” means from *gami* and so forth. [The term] *uttama*.
In the masculine singular, *patta* means "having reached [the thought], 'I will go'. In the middle [person], *abhimata* means "intended," as in "you will go" (*gamissasi*).
In the middle [person], *patta* means "you think," as in "you think [you will go]. In the third person singular, *miṭṭha* means "it is intended," as in "he thinks. This is what is meant:
when one should say "you think you will go by chariot" (*maññase tvaṃ rathena gamissāmīti*), it becomes "I think you will go by chariot" (*maññe tvaṃ rathena gamissasīti*).
(Thus it was said). Nothing such as "Come, consider me," etc., has been stated in the *Vutti*.

In order to demonstrate the connection in such a way that the medium and superior [levels of discourse] are established according to their respective objects, he says: "In this manner, the connection here is as follows," and so forth.

While establishing the connection favored by others, he says: "But not thus," and so forth. Then, with the words "Now it is said," etc., he states the intention of the opponent: "That which," and so forth.
"When there is such a connection" means when the connection is made thus: "You think, 'I am going by chariot.
"And that [usage] follows accordingly" means that very usage follows accordingly, namely: "I think, 'You are going by chariot.
"By way of conceiving another mode" means by way of conceiving another mode, namely: "You think, 'I am going by chariot.'"
15. Regarding "Āī tenacāti samāsitattena ca": if there were a grasping of [the vowels] beginning with *ss* and *ty*, then one would not have stated them by means of a compound as "āīssādīsūti.
17. Regarding "Bhūssa":

In order to show that the rule concerning what has been done and what has not been done is constant and powerful, and thus occurs first, he says: “Because of the connection with what has been done and what has not been done,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “in the case of *a* and so on” (*aādyapekkhe*), it is understood as “in the case of *a* and others” (*aādīsūti*) due to the recurrence of the word “and so on.”

23. Regarding the objection: "But why was it said, 'one shall hear [the suffix] *s*'? Should it not have been stated that 'there is elision of *kara* by the rule *kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ micceva* (5-161), and thus one should say *karassa ku*"?
Keeping this challenge in mind, he says: "In some cases, there is elision of the *vikaraṇas*, etc. This is because one must follow other actual applications [of the rules].
The connection is that it is not possible to understand the elision (*olopa*) without following the application (*payoga*).

25. One who possesses a grammatical operation (*kāriya*) known as *āhaṅsa* is called a "possessor of an operation" (*kāriyī*); by means of that, another possessor of an operation is struck, meaning he is harmed.
“*Sahossehīti*” means “together with the *okāra* of *karassa* and with the *ssena* [of *hāssa*], together with the *ssena* of *hāssa*. Now, one might wonder:
“How is it understood that the region (*deso*) is stated as being together with *ossehi*? To this he says: “By the power of the expression *saha*. The meaning is:
by the power of the statement that the word *saha* [is used] with the sense of “together” (*sahattha*) and with the [suffix] *ssena*. He clarifies the intended meaning: “In this way...”
By the words *maññate* and so forth. It appears as if the reading should be *evaṃ maññate ossānaṃ manādesitte* and so on;
for by that very reading, the capacity for simultaneous expression (*sahavacanasāmatthiya*) is clearly established.

However, the statement *evaṃ maññate ossānaṃ mantādesatte hāssacā* would be meaningless, since one simply says *hā to ce* when *ossānaṃ* undergoes the substitution of *man*. Thus it is said, and so forth.
By means of the recitation... because there is no possibility of the substitution of *ossāna* for *anta*. Here, there is no genitive of relation between the substitute and the original;
rather, it is specified by a genitive of qualification (*visesana-chaṭṭhī*) in the word *sso*, and by an instrumental of accompaniment (*sahattha-tatiyā*) in the word *ssenā*.
"In both cases" refers to the instances of *ssatyādi* and *ssādī*.

28. Regarding "Āī pubbasaralopo": in the two instances where there is the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix and the substitution of the vowel *ā*, there is the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*).

In the word *agāti*, there is the elision of the letter *l* (*lalopa*), and in the substitution of the vowel *ā*, there is the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*).

[the forms] *agañchā* and *agacchī* are formed by the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).

[The vowel] is long according to the rule "In consonants, long and short [vowels are interchangeable]" (1-33).

The meaning is "grasping by way of conventional usage. Because it has been grasped, the suffixes beginning with *tvā* are grasped as its related [elements]; this is the connection.
"Providing a basis" occurs only by way of specific distinction (*byatti*), not by way of generality; thus he says, "By this," and so forth.
The elision of the penultimate vowel and so forth is governed by the rule: “When ‘r’ is the suffix, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel and so forth” (4-132). 42.
Regarding “of the substitutes beginning with ā,” this refers to the substitutes beginning with *ā*.

Thus ends the commentary on the Sixth Chapter in the *Sāratthavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Moggallānapañcikā*.
And thus the commentary *Sāratthavilāsinī* is completed in every respect.
[It was composed] by one who always bestows what is excellent, upon that which is served by infinite beings.
By the virtuous one dwelling there, who was presided over by the Lord of the Beautiful—
a leader endowed with the qualities of generosity, prowess, wisdom, compassion, and so forth— who was praised,
possessed of the perception of what is beneficial, renowned, and celebrated as beautiful.
In a dwelling suited for seclusion, with excellent surroundings,
agreeable to the mind of yogis, and most beautiful for its spaciousness—
this was composed this evening by the Elder, who desires to illuminate the Dispensation.
May this [work], which constantly delights the minds of the learned and wise who have plunged into the ultimate truth,
endure for a long time, having been composed by one who serves the pollen upon the lotus feet of the Guru. 5.
Those whose wisdom has not been accumulated, nor refined through the company of many beings, are utterly struck down by delusion and do not understand anything at all.
What need is there for them to listen to the words of others, who have no teachers here in this world?
Those who are sprinkled with the dust of his feet are indeed virtuous and secluded.
By that merit produced from composing this work on the Teacher,
which serves as a cause for the arising of the noble dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One;
Unstained even by the impurities of worldly pleasures,
may I practice the arising of the sublime teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By churning the ocean of infinite and boundless jewels...
Having obtained the essence through the supreme wisdom that churns and stirs,
they are themselves blissful and bring happiness to others;
thus do these teachers, preeminent in their virtues, truly triumph.
He who, devoted to adorning his neck with commentaries on the Vinaya and other texts,
rendered the stainless doctrine of the Conqueror free from confusion for the wise; he who is worthy of praise by all,
whose mind is most pleasing to the minds of the virtuous, and who is great— [to him I pay homage].
My master, the preeminent teacher, the son of Sārī, reigns victorious on this earth.
King Vikramabāhu, who has subdued his enemies with his own arms, is his brother and lord of the world;
and he who is the Lord of the Three Siṃhala Lands, the slayer of Sammita, is one of great prowess.
Fearless, valiant, with arms that grant victory and the like, he was the victorious Lord of Laṅkā;
by depending on him, this fruit has borne its result for a long time, continuously and eternally for the virtuous.
May there be success!
By way of the lineage of Aggamahāpaṇḍita Abhayārāma,
this *Sāratthavilāsinī*, which is a commentary on the *Pañcikā*, was composed.
Having transcribed it in Burmese characters and having purified it to the best of one's ability;
By means of the Sakya convention, on the day of Thursday, the tenth lunar day,
in the year [marked] by the yutta [era], the great kingdom of the island of Laṅkā was once again seized by [the enemies] with the Bhāsa,
Padīpa, Kātanta, Kāsika, Pañcika, and other [treatises].
Having compared them, investigated them, and recited them again and again,
having removed defects such as omissions or additions in their respective places,
and having established the pure octads and years, they were brought to their natural state.
Displaying what is pure as if it were impure, let her purify herself through textual purity.
